chunks.traduccion: Therefore, in this matter Pythius seems to have erred because he did not observe that the individual arts are composed of two things, from work and its reasoning. Of these, however, one is proper to those who are trained in each thing, that is, the effect of the work, the other is common to all learned men, that is, reasoning, as is the case with physicians and musicians concerning the rhythm of the veins and the movement of the foot. But if it is necessary to heal a wound or rescue a patient from danger, the musician will not come, but that will be the proper work of the physician. Likewise, the organ will be played not by the physician but by the musician, so that the ears may receive pleasure from the songs.

chunks.texto: Similiter cum astrologis et musicis est disputatio communis de sympathia stellarum et symphoniarum in quadratis et trigonis diatessaron et diapente, a geometris [divisus] qui graece λόγος ὀπτικός appellatur, ceterisque omnibus doctrinis multae res vel omnes communes sunt dumtaxat ad disputandum. Operum vero ingressus, qui manu aut tractationibus ad elegantiam perducuntur, ipsorum sunt qui proprie una arte ad faciendum sunt instituti. Ergo satis abunde videtur fecisse qui ex singulis doctrinis partes et rationes earum mediocriter habet notas eas quae necessariae sunt ad architecturam, uti si quid de his rebus et artibus iudicare et probare opus fuerit ne deficiatur.
chunks.traduccion: Similarly, astronomers and musicians share discussion of the correspondence between the stars and musical consonances, in squares and trines, and in the intervals of a fourth and a fifth; they share with geometers the theory of sight, which the Greeks call logos optikos. Many matters, or indeed all, are common to the disciplines at the level of theoretical discussion. The practical execution of works, however, brought to refinement by hand and skilled manipulation, belongs to those trained to practise a particular art. It is therefore amply sufficient for the architect to have a moderate knowledge of the parts and principles of each discipline that are necessary for architecture, so that he is not found wanting when required to judge and approve matters concerning them.

chunks.texto: Quibus vero natura tantum tribuit sollertiae, acuminis, memoriae, ut possint geometriam, astrologiam, musicen ceterasque disciplinas penitus habere notas, praetereunt officia architectorum et efficiuntur mathematici. Itaque faciliter contra eas disciplinas disputare possunt, quod pluribus telis disciplinarum sunt armati. Hi autem inveniuntur raro, ut aliquando fuerunt Aristarchus Samius, Philolaus et Archytas Tarentini, Apollonius Pergaeus, Eratosthenes Cyrenaeus, Archimedes et Scopinas ab Syracusis, qui multas res ⟨mechanicas,⟩ organicas, gnomonicas numero naturalibusque rationibus inventas atque explicatas posteris reliquerunt.
chunks.traduccion: Those whom nature has endowed with such skill, intellectual acuity and memory that they thoroughly master geometry, astronomy, music and the other disciplines go beyond the duties of architects and become mathematicians. They can readily discuss these disciplines, armed as they are with many intellectual weapons. Such people are rare: among them were Aristarchus of Samos, Philolaus and Archytas of Tarentum, Apollonius of Perga, Eratosthenes of Cyrene, and Archimedes and Scopinas of Syracuse. They left to posterity many mechanical and gnomonic inventions discovered and explained through calculation and the principles of nature.

chunks.texto: Cum ergo talia ingenia ab naturali sollertia non passim cunctis gentibus sed paucis viris habere concedatur, officium vero architecti omnibus eruditionibus debeat esse exercitatum, et ratio propter amplitudinem rei permittat non iuxta necessitatem summas sed etiam mediocres scientias habere disciplinarum, peto, Caesar, et a te et ab îs, qui ea volumina sunt lecturi, ut, si quid parum ad regulam artis grammaticae fuerit explicatum, ignoscatur. Namque non uti summus philosophus nec rhetor disertus nec grammaticus summis rationibus artis exercitatus, sed ut architectus his litteris imbutus haec nisus sum scribere. De artis vero potestate quaeque insunt in ea ratiocinationes polliceor, uti spero, his voluminibus non modo aedificantibus sed etiam omnibus sapientibus cum maxima auctoritate me sine dubio praestaturum.
chunks.traduccion: Since such gifts of natural ingenuity are granted only to a few people rather than to all peoples everywhere, and since an architect’s duties require training in all these branches of knowledge, the breadth of the subject reasonably permits a moderate rather than a supreme command of the disciplines needed for the work. I therefore ask you, Caesar, and those who will read these volumes to forgive anything expressed without strict observance of grammatical rules. I have attempted to write as an architect instructed in these studies, rather than as a great philosopher, an eloquent rhetorician or a grammarian thoroughly trained in the principles of the art. As for the powers of the art itself and the reasoning it involves, I undertake, as I hope, to establish my authority in these volumes beyond doubt, for the benefit of builders and of all learned readers.

chunks.texto: Architectura autem constat ex ordinatione, quae graece τάξις dicitur, et ex dispositione, hanc autem Graeci διάθεσιν vocitant, et eurythmia et symmetria et decore et distributione, quae graece οἰκονομία dicitur.
chunks.traduccion: Architecture rests upon Order (ordinatio), which the Greeks call τάξις; Arrangement (dispositio), which they term διάθεσιν; and further upon Eurythmy, Symmetry, Propriety (decor), and Economy (distributio), which in Greek is called οἰκονομία.

chunks.texto: Ordinatio est modica membrorum operis commoditas separatim universeque proportionis ad symmetriam comparatio. Haec componitur ex quantitate, quae graece ποσότης dicitur. Quantitas autem est modulorum ex ipsius operis e singulisque membrorum partibus sumptio universi operis conveniens effectui. Dispositio autem est rerum apta conlocatio elegansque compositionibus effectus operis cum qualitate. Species dispositionis, quae graece dicuntur ἰδέαι, sunt hae: ichnographia, orthographia, scaenographia. Ichnographia est circini regulaeque modice continens usus, e qua capiuntur formarum in solis arearum descriptiones. Orthographia autem est erecta frontis imago modiceque picta rationibus operis futuri figura. Item scaenographia est frontis et laterum abscedentium adumbratio ad circinique centrum omnium linearum responsus. Hae nascuntur ex cogitatione et inventione. Cogitatio est cura, studii plena et industriae vigilantiaeque, effectus propositi cum voluptate. Inventio autem est quaestionum obscurarum explicatio ratioque novae rei vigore mobili reperta. Hae sunt terminationes dispositionum.
chunks.traduccion: Order is the balanced adjustment of the individual members of the work taken separately, and, for the work as a whole, the comparison of the proportion with a view to a symmetrical result. It is composed of quantity, which in Greek is called ποσότης. Quantity, in turn, consists in taking the modules from the members of the work itself and, from the several parts of those members, producing the harmonious and fitting effect of the work as a whole. Arrangement, for its part, is the apt placement of the elements and the elegant effect of the work that results from their combinations according to its character. The kinds of arrangement, which in Greek are called ἰδέαι, are these: the ground plan (ichnographia), the elevation (orthographia), and the perspective (scaenographia). The ground plan is the measured use of compass and rule, by which the outlines of forms are set out upon the surfaces of the sites. The elevation is the upright image of the facade, drawn to scale as a figure of the work to come. Likewise, the perspective is the sketch of the facade together with its receding sides, with all the lines converging upon the center of a circle. These arise from reflection and invention. Reflection is the studious, industrious, and vigilant care devoted to the pleasurable accomplishment of a design. Invention, for its part, is the unravelling of obscure problems and the reasoned discovery of a new principle through a lively agility of mind. Such are the determinations of arrangement.

chunks.texto: Eurythmia est venusta species commodusque in compositionibus membrorum aspectus. Haec efficitur cum membra operis convenientis sunt altitudinis ad latitudinem, latitudinis ad longitudinem, et ad summam omnia respondent suae symmetriae.
chunks.traduccion: Eurythmy is a beautiful appearance and a graceful, becoming aspect in the composition of the members. This is achieved when the members of the work are of a height suited to their width, a width suited to their length, and, in sum, all correspond to their symmetry.

chunks.texto: Item symmetria est ex ipsius operis membris conveniens consensus ex partibusque separatis ad universae figurae speciem ratae partis responsus. Uti in hominis corpore e cubito, pede, palmo, digito ceterisque particulis symmetros est eurythmiae qualitas, sic est in operum perfectionibus. Et primum in aedibus sacris aut e columnarum crassitudinibus aut triglypho aut etiam embatere, ballista e foramine ⟨capituli⟩, quod Graeci περίτρητον vocitant, navibus interscalmio, quae διάπηγμα dicitur, item ceterorum operum e membris invenitur symmetriarum ratiocinatio.
chunks.traduccion: Symmetria is the fitting correspondence among the members of a work and the relationship of its separate parts, measured by a determined unit, to the appearance of the whole. Just as the human body has commensurable relations among forearm, foot, palm, finger and other members, so do completed buildings. In sacred temples the measure is taken from the diameter of a column, a triglyph or an embater; in a ballista, from the opening of its capital, which the Greeks call peritreton; in ships, from the spacing between thole-pins, called dipegma. In other works too, the system of commensurability is derived from their members.

chunks.texto: Decor autem est emendatus operis aspectus probatis rebus compositi cum auctoritate. Is perficitur statione, quod graece θεματισμῷ dicitur, seu consuetudine aut natura. Statione, cum Iovi Fulguri et Caelo et Soli et Lunae aedificia sub divo hypaethraque constituentur; horum enim deorum et species et effectus in aperto mundo atque lucenti praesentes videmus. Minervae et Marti et Herculi aedes doricae fient; his enim diis propter virtutem sine deliciis aedificia constitui decet. Veneri, Florae, Proserpinae, fontium nymphis corinthio genere constitutae aptas videbuntur habere proprietates, quod his diis propter teneritatem graciliora et florida foliisque et volutis ornata opera facta augere videbuntur iustum decorem. Iunoni, Dianae, Libero Patri ceterisque diis qui eadem sunt similitudine si aedes ionicae construentur, habita erit ratio mediocritatis, quod et ab severo more doricorum et ab teneritate corinthiorum temperabitur earum institutio proprietatis.
chunks.traduccion: Decorum, in turn, is the faultless appearance of a work composed, with authority, of approved elements. It is achieved by prescription—which in Greek is called θεματισμός, by usage, or by nature. By prescription, when temples to Jupiter the Lightning-bringer, to the Heaven, the Sun, and the Moon are erected in the open air and unroofed (hypaethral); for of these gods we behold the semblance and the active power present before us in the open and resplendent sky. The temples of Minerva, Mars, and Hercules will be made Doric, since to these gods, on account of their valour, it befits that buildings be raised without refinements. For Venus, Flora, Proserpina, the Spring (Fons), and the Water-Nymphs (Lymphae), temples built in the Corinthian manner will be seen to possess fitting qualities, since to these deities, on account of their gentleness, works that are more slender and florid—adorned with leaves and volutes—will seem to enhance their due grace. If temples are made Ionic for Juno, Diana, Father Liber, and the other gods of like nature, a due moderation will be observed, for the establishment of their character will temper both the severe manner of the Doric and the delicacy of the Corinthian.

chunks.texto: Ad consuetudinem autem decor sic exprimitur, cum aedificiis interioribus magnificis item vestibula convenientia et elegantia erunt facta. Si enim interiora prospectus habuerint elegantes, aditus autem humiles et inhonestos, non erunt cum decore. Item si doricis epistyliis in coronis denticuli sculpentur aut in pulvinatis columnis ex ionicis epistyliis [capitulis] exprimentur triglyphi, translatis ex alia ratione proprietatibus in aliud genus operis offendetur aspectus, aliis ante ordinis consuetudinibus institutus.
chunks.traduccion: Propriety according to custom is achieved when magnificent interiors are accompanied by fitting and elegant vestibules. If the interiors offer elegant views but the entrances are low and undistinguished, the building will lack propriety. Likewise, if dentils are carved in the cornices of Doric entablatures, or triglyphs are introduced into Ionic entablatures with cushion-capital columns, the transfer of features from one system to another kind of work will offend the eye, because the established conventions of the orders are different.

chunks.texto: Naturalis autem decor sic erit, si primum omnibus templis saluberrimae regiones aquarumque fontes in îs locis idonei eligentur in quibus fana constituantur, deinde maxime Aesculapio, Saluti, ut eorum deorum quorum plurimi medicinis aegri curari videntur. Cum enim ex pestilenti in salubrem locum corpora aegra translata fuerint et e fontibus salubribus aquarum usus subministrabuntur, celerius convalescent. Ita efficietur uti ex natura loci maiores auctasque cum dignitate divinitas excipiat opiniones. Item naturae decor erit, si cubiculis et bybliothecis ab oriente lumina capiuntur, balneis et hibernaculis ab occidente hiberno, pinacothecis et quibus certis luminibus opus est partibus a septentrione, quod ea caeli regio neque exclaratur neque obscuratur solis cursu sed est certa inmutabilis die perpetuo.
chunks.traduccion: Propriety according to nature is achieved, first, by choosing the healthiest regions and suitable springs of water for the places where sanctuaries are established, especially those of Aesculapius and Salus, through whose healing arts many sick people appear to recover. When the sick are transferred from an unhealthy place to a healthy one and supplied with water from wholesome springs, they recover more quickly. The nature of the place thus enhances the deity’s reputation and dignity. Natural propriety also requires bedrooms and libraries to receive light from the east, baths and winter rooms from the winter sunset, and picture galleries and rooms needing steady light from the north, since that quarter is neither brightened nor darkened by the sun’s course but remains constant throughout the day.

chunks.texto: Distributio autem est copiarum locique commoda dispensatio parcaque in operibus sumptus ratione temperatio. Haec ita observabitur, si primum architectus ea non quaeret, quae non poterunt inveniri aut parari nisi magno. Namque non omnibus locis harenae fossiciae nec caementorum nec abietis nec sappinorum nec marmoris copia est, sed aliud alio loco nascitur, quorum comportationes difficiles sunt et sumptuosae. Utendum autem est, ubi non est harena fossicia, fluviatica aut marina lota; inopiae quoque abietis aut sappinorum vitabuntur utendo cupresso, populo, ulmo, pinu; reliquaque his similiter erunt explicanda.
chunks.traduccion: Distributio is the suitable allocation of materials and ground and the prudent, economical control of expenditure. It is observed when the architect does not seek materials that can be obtained only with great difficulty. Pit sand, rubble stone, fir, sappinus timber and marble are not abundant everywhere: different materials occur in different places, and their transport can be difficult and costly. Where pit sand is unavailable, river sand or washed sea sand should be used. A shortage of fir or sappinus can be met by using cypress, poplar, elm, pine and other similar timbers.

chunks.texto: Alter gradus erit distributionis, cum ad usum patrum familiarum et ad pecuniae copiam aut ad eloquentiae dignitatem aedificia apte disponentur. Namque aliter urbanas domos oportere constitui videtur, aliter quibus ex possessionibus rusticis influunt fructus, non item feneratoribus, aliter beatis et delicatis, potentibus vero, quorum cogitationibus respublica gubernatur, ad usum conlocabuntur; et omnino faciendae sunt aptae omnibus personis aedificiorum distributiones.
chunks.traduccion: A second aspect of distributio concerns arranging buildings to suit the needs of householders, their financial resources and the standing associated with eloquence. Town houses call for one arrangement, the houses of those who receive produce from rural estates for another; moneylenders require another, the wealthy and refined another, and those whose deliberations govern the commonwealth another. The arrangement of buildings must, in every case, suit the people for whom they are intended.

chunks.texto: Partes ipsius architecturae sunt tres: aedificatio, gnomonice, machinatio. Aedificatio autem divisa est bipertito, e quibus una est moenium et communium operum in publicis locis conlocatio, altera est privatorum aedificiorum explicatio. Publicorum autem distributiones sunt tres, e quibus est una defensionis, altera religionis, tertia opportunitatis. Defensionis est murorum turriumque et portarum ratio ad hostium impetus perpetuo repellendos excogitata; religionis deorum inmortalium fanorum aediumque sacrarum conlocatio; opportunitatis communium locorum ad usum publicum dispositio, uti portus, fora, porticus, balinea, theatra, ambulationes ceteraque quae isdem rationibus in publicis locis designantur.
chunks.traduccion: The parts of architecture proper are three: construction, the making of sundials, and mechanics. Construction, in turn, is divided into two branches: the first is the laying-out of city walls and of works for common use in public places, the second the raising of private buildings. Public works admit of three classes: the first concerns defense, the second religion, and the third convenience. To defense belongs the design of walls, towers, and gates, devised to repel the assaults of enemies in perpetuity; to religion, the placing of shrines and sacred temples to the immortal gods; to convenience, the provision of common spaces for public use—such as harbors, fora, colonnades, baths, theaters, promenades, and the other works laid out on the same principles in public places.

chunks.texto: Haec autem ita fieri debent, ut habeatur ratio firmitatis, utilitatis, venustatis. Firmitatis erit habita ratio, cum fuerit fundamentorum ad solidum depressio, quaque e materia, copiarum sine avaritia diligens electio; utilitatis autem, ⟨cum fuerit⟩ emendata et sine inpeditione usus locorum dispositio et ad regiones sui cuiusque generis apta et commoda distributio; venustatis vero, cum fuerit operis species grata et elegans membrorumque commensus iustas habeat symmetriarum ratiocinationes.
chunks.traduccion: These constructions must be achieved in such a way that solidity (firmitas), utility (utilitas), and beauty (venustas) are taken into account. Solidity will have been considered when the excavation of the foundations is deepened to firm ground (solidum) and when a diligent selection of materials is made from among those available, without sparing any expense (sine avaritia); utility, when the arrangement of the spaces is impeccable and presents no impediments to their use, and when the distribution of each type of building is suitable, comfortable, and properly oriented to its region; and beauty, when the appearance of the work is pleasing and elegant, and when the proportion of the members maintains a just calculation of symmetries (symmetriarum ratiocinationes).

chunks.texto: In ipsis vero moenibus ea erunt principia. Primum electio loci saluberrimi. Is autem erit excelsus et non nebulosus, non pruinosus regionesque caeli spectans neque aestuosas neque frigidas sed temperatas, deinde si vitabitur palustris vicinitas. Cum enim aurae matutinae cum sole oriente ad oppidum pervenient et his ortae nebulae adiungentur spiritusque bestiarum palustrium venenatos cum nebula mixtos in habitatorum corpora flatu spargent, efficient locum pestilentem. Item si secundum mare erunt moenia spectabuntque ad meridiem aut occidentem non erunt salubria, quod per aestatem caelum meridianum sole exoriente calescit, meridie ardet, item quod spectat ad occidentem, sole exorto tepescit, meridie calet, vespere fervet.
chunks.traduccion: But for the city walls themselves the governing principles will be these. First comes the choice of a thoroughly healthy site: one that is elevated, free from mist and frost, facing quarters of the sky that are neither sweltering nor cold but temperate, and, further, removed from the neighborhood of marshes. For when the morning breezes reach the town at sunrise, bringing with them the mists that have gathered and, mingled with those mists, the poisonous exhalations of the marsh creatures, and scatter them by their breath into the bodies of the inhabitants, they render the place pestilential. Likewise, walls set along the coast and facing south or west will be unhealthy; for in summer the southern sky grows warm at sunrise and burns at midday, while a westward aspect grows warm at sunrise, is hot at midday, and blazes in the evening.

chunks.texto: Igitur mutationibus caloris et refrigerationis corpora quae in his locis sunt vitiantur. Hoc autem licet animadvertere etiam ex îs quae non sunt animalia. In cellis enim vinariis tectis lumina nemo capit a meridie nec ab occidente sed a septentrione, quod ea regio nullo tempore mutationes recipit sed est firma perpetuo et inmutabilis. Ideo etiam ea granaria quae ad solis cursum spectant bonitatem cito mutant, obsoniaque et poma quae non in ea parte caeli ponuntur quae est aversa a solis cursu, non diu servantur.
chunks.traduccion: Therefore, the bodies that are in these places are spoiled by changes in heat and cooling. This may be observed even from those that are not animals. For in roofed wine cellars no one receives light from the south or from the west, but from the north, because that region at no time receives changes, but is permanently fixed and unchangeable. Therefore also those granaries that look towards the course of the sun quickly change their quality, and food and fruits that are not placed in that part of the sky that is turned away from the course of the sun are not preserved for long.

chunks.texto: Nam semper calor cum excoquit e rebus firmitatem et vaporibus fervidis eripit exsugendo naturales virtutes, dissolvit eas et fervore mollescentes efficit inbecillas. Ut etiam in ferro animadvertimus, quod quamvis natura sit durum, in fornacibus ab ignis vapore percalefactum ita mollescit uti in omne genus formae faciliter fabricetur, et idem cum molle et candens refrigeretur, tinctum frigida redurescit et restituitur in antiquam proprietatem.
chunks.traduccion: For heat bakes the moisture out of all things and, snatching it away in rising vapors, deprives them of their natural strength; it dissolves them and, melting them by its warmth, renders them weak and soft. As we also observe in iron, that although it is hard by nature, when heated in furnaces by the vapors of fire it softens so much that it can be easily fashioned into every kind of form, and the same thing, when cooled while soft and red-hot, hardens when cold and is restored to its former properties.

chunks.texto: Licet etiam considerare haec ita esse ex eo quod aestate non solum in pestilentibus locis sed etiam in salubribus omnia corpora calore fiant inbecilla, et per hiemem etiam quae pestilentissimae sint regiones efficiantur salubres. Ideo quod a refrigerationibus solidantur. non minus etiam quae ab frigidis regionibus corpora traducuntur in calidas, non possunt durare sed dissolvuntur, quae autem ex calidis locis sub septentrionum regiones frigidas, non modo non laborant inmutatione loci valetudinibus sed etiam confirmantur.
chunks.traduccion: It is also possible to consider that this is so from the fact that in summer, not only in pestilent places but also in healthy ones, all bodies become weak from the heat, and during winter even the most pestilent regions become healthy. For this reason, when bodies are transferred from cold to warm ones, they cannot last but are dissolved, but those which come from warm places to cold regions of the north, not only do not suffer from the change of place, but are even strengthened.

chunks.texto: Quare cavendum esse videtur in moenibus conlocandis ab îs regionibus quae caloribus flatus ad corpora hominum possunt spargere. Namque e principiis, quae Graeci στοιχεῖα appellant, ut omnia corpora sunt composita, id est e calore et umore, terreno et aere, et ita mixtionibus naturali temperatura figurantur omnium animalium in mundo generatim qualitates.
chunks.traduccion: Therefore, it seems that one must be careful in placing walls away from those regions that can spread hot winds to human bodies. For just as all bodies are composed of the principles that the Greeks call stoicheia, that is, of heat and moisture, of earth and air, so the qualities of all animals in the world are generally formed by natural mixtures of temperature.

chunks.texto: ergo in quibus ⟨vis⟩ corporibus cum exsuperat e principiis calor, tunc interficit dissolvitque cetera fervore. haec autem vitia efficit fervidum ab certis partibus caelum, cum insidit in apertas venas plus quam patitur e mixtionibus naturali temperatura corpus. item si umor occupavit corporum venas inparesque eas fecit, cetera principia liquido corrupta diluuntur et dissolvuntur compositionibus virtutes. item haec e refrigerationibus umoris ventorum et aurarum infunduntur vitia corporibus. non minus aeris etiamque terreni in corpore naturalis compositio augendo aut minuendo infirmat cetera principia, terrena cibi plenitate, aer gravitate caeli.
chunks.traduccion: In any body where heat predominates over the other principles, its excessive warmth destroys and dissolves them. An overheated climate produces these defects when it enters the open veins beyond what the body’s natural balance can bear. If moisture fills the veins in excess, the other principles are weakened as though diluted, and the strength of their composition is dissolved. Cold moisture in winds and breezes likewise introduces these disorders. An increase or decrease in the natural proportions of air and earth also weakens the other principles: the earthy element through excessive food, and the airy element through the oppressive condition of the atmosphere.

chunks.texto: Sed si qui voluerit diligentius haec sensu percipere, animadvertat attendatque naturas avium et piscium et terrestrium animalium, et ita considerabit discrimina temperaturae. Aliam enim mixtionem habet genus avium, aliam piscium, longe aliter terrestrium natura. Volucres minus habent terreni, minus umoris, caloris temperate, aeris multum. Igitur levioribus principiis compositae facilius in aeris impetum nituntur. Aquatiles autem piscium naturae quod temperatae sunt a calido plurimumque ex aeris et terreni ⟨principiis⟩ sunt compositae sed umoris habent oppido quam paulum, quo minus habent e principiis umoris in corpore, facilius in umore perdurant, itaque cum ad terram perducuntur, animam cum aqua relinquunt. Item terrestria quod e principiis ab aere caloreque sunt temperata minusque habent terreni plurimumque umoris, quod abundant umidae partes, non diu possunt in aqua vitam tueri.
chunks.traduccion: But if anyone wishes to perceive these things more carefully with his senses, let him observe and pay attention to the natures of birds and fish and terrestrial animals, and thus he will consider the differences in elemental composition. For the genus of birds has one mixture, that of fish another, and the nature of terrestrial animals is very different. Birds have less of the earth, less of the moisture, and temperate heat, and much of the air. Therefore, being composed of lighter principles, they more easily rely on the force of the air. But the aquatic natures of fish, because they are temperate from the heat and are composed of both air and earth, but have little moisture, because they have less of the moisture principles in their bodies, they more easily persist in moisture, and therefore when they are brought to land, they yield up their vital breath with the water. Likewise, terrestrial animals, because they are temperate from the principles of air and heat, have less of the earth and much of the moisture, because their moist parts abound, cannot long maintain life in water.

chunks.texto: Ergo si haec ita videntur quemadmodum proposuimus, et e principiis animalium corpora composita sensu percipimus et e superationibus aut defectionibus ea laborare dissolvique iudicamus, non dubitamus quin diligentius quaeri oporteat uti temperatissimas caeli regiones eligamus, cum quaerenda fuerit in moenium conlocationibus salubritas.
chunks.traduccion: Therefore, if these things appear as we have proposed, and we judge that they suffer and are dissolved from excesses or defects, we do not doubt that it is necessary to seek more carefully how to choose the most temperate regions of the sky, since healthiness must be sought in the placement of walls.

chunks.texto: Itaque etiam atque etiam veterem revocandam censeo rationem. Maiores enim pecoribus immolatis, quae pascebantur in îs locis, quibus aut oppida aut castra stativa constituebantur, inspiciebant iocinera, et si erant livida et vitiosa primo, alia immolabant dubitantes, utrum morbo an pabuli vitio laesa essent. Cum pluribus experti erant et probaverant integram et solidam naturam iocinerum ex aqua et pabulo, ibi constituebant munitiones; si autem vitiosa inveniebant, iudicio transferebant item humanis corporibus pestilentem futuram nascentem in his locis aquae cibique copiam, et ita transmigrabant et mutabant regiones quaerentes omnibus rebus salubritatem.
chunks.traduccion: Again and again I think the old reason should be recalled. For the ancients examined the livers of the sacrificed cattle which were grazing in those places where towns or permanent camps were established, and if they were livid and defective at first, they sacrificed others, doubting whether they were damaged by disease or by the defect of the fodder. When they had tried many and had proved the intact and solid nature of the livers from water and fodder, they established fortifications there; but if they found them defective, they transferred the judgment to human bodies, and the future abundance of water and food growing in these places would be pestilent, and so they migrated and changed regions, seeking health in all things.

chunks.texto: Hoc autem fieri, uti pabulo ciboque salubres proprietates terrae videantur, licet animadvertere et cognoscere ex agris Cretensium, qui sunt circa Pothereum flumen, quod est Cretae inter duas civitates Gnoson et Gortynam. Dextra enim et sinistra eius fluminis pascuntur pecora; sed ex his quae pascuntur proxime Gnoson si * * * quae autem ex altera parte proxime Gortynam, non habent apparentem splenem. Unde etiam medici quaerentes de ea re invenerunt in his locis herbam, quam pecora rodendo inminuerunt lienes. Ita eam herbam colligendo curant lienosos hoc medicamento, quod etiam Cretenses ἄσπληνον vocitant. Ex eo licet scire cibo atque aqua proprietates locorum naturaliter pestilentes aut salubres esse.
chunks.traduccion: The properties of the land as revealed through fodder and food may be observed in the Cretan fields around the river Pothereus, between Knossos and Gortyna. Cattle graze on both banks. Those near Knossos […] whereas those on the other side near Gortyna have no visible spleen. Investigating this, physicians found a local plant whose consumption by the cattle reduced their spleens. They therefore collected it to treat patients with diseases of the spleen; the Cretans call the remedy asplenon (ἄσπληνον). Food and water thus reveal whether a place’s natural properties are healthy or unhealthy.

chunks.texto: Item si in paludibus moenia constituta erunt, quae paludes secundum mare fuerint, spectabuntque ad septentrionem aut inter septentrionem et orientem, eaeque paludes excelsiores fuerint quam litus marinum, ratione videbuntur esse constituta. Fossis enim ductis fit aquae exitus ad litus, et mare tempestatibus actum in paludes redundantia motionibus concitata marisque mixtionibus non patitur bestiarum palustrium genera ibi nasci, quaeque de superioribus locis natando proxime litus perveniunt, inconsueta salsitudine necantur. Exemplar autem huius rei Gallicae paludes possunt esse quae circum ⟨cingunt⟩ Altinum, Ravennam, Aquileiam aliaque quae in eiusmodi locis municipia sunt proxima paludibus, quod his rationibus habent incredibilem salubritatem.
chunks.traduccion: Likewise, if walls are built in marshes, which marshes are next to the sea, and face north or between north and east, and those marshes are higher than the seashore, they will seem to have been built for a reason. For by digging ditches, the water is brought to the shore, and the sea, increased by storms, overflowing into the marshes, agitated by the movements and mixtures of the sea, does not allow the kinds of marsh animals to be born there, and those that swim from higher places to reach the shore are killed by the unusual salinity. An example of this can be the marshes of Gaul which are around Altinus, Ravenna, Aquileia and others which are in such places towns close to the marshes, because for these reasons they have an incredible salubrious effect.

chunks.texto: Quibus autem insidentes sunt paludes et non habent exitus profluentes neque per flumina neque per fossas, uti Pomptinae, stando putescunt et umores graves et pestilentes in îs locis emittunt. Item in Apulia oppidum Salpia vetus, quod Diomedes ab Troia rediens constituit sive quemadmodum nonnulli scripserunt Elpias Rhodius, in eiusmodi locis fuerat conlocatum, ex quo incolae quotannis aegrotando laborantes aliquando pervenerunt ad M. Hostilium ab eoque publice petentes impetraverunt ut is idoneum locum ad moenia transferenda conquireret eligeretque. Tunc is moratus non est, sed statim rationibus doctissime quaesitis secundum mare mercatus est possessionem loco salubri ab senatuque populoque Romano petît ut liceret transferre oppidum, constituitque moenia et areas divisit nummoque sestertio singulis municipibus mancipio dedit. His confectis lacum aperuit in mare et portum e lacu municipio perfecit. Itaque nunc Salpini quattuor milia passus progressi ab oppido veteri habitant in salubri loco.
chunks.traduccion: Marshes that remain stagnant and have no outlet through rivers or ditches, such as the Pontine Marshes, become putrid and emit heavy, unhealthy vapors. Old Salpia in Apulia, founded by Diomedes on his return from Troy or, according to other writers, by Elpias of Rhodes, stood in such a place. Its inhabitants, afflicted by illness every year, eventually appealed to Marcus Hostilius and obtained his agreement to seek a suitable site for moving the town. He acted without delay: after careful investigation he purchased land in a healthy place by the sea, obtained permission from the Roman Senate and people, built the walls, divided the building plots and conveyed each plot to a citizen for one sestertius. He then opened the lake to the sea and made it a harbour for the town. The people of Salpia now live in a healthy place, four Roman miles from the old town.

chunks.texto: Cum ergo his rationibus erit salubritatis moenium conlocandorum explicatio regiones[que] electae fuerint fructibus ad alendam civitatem copiosae et viarum munitiones aut opportunitates fluminum seu per portus marinae subvectionis habuerit ad moenia comportationes expeditas, tunc turrium murorumque fundamenta sic sunt facienda uti fodiantur, si queat inveniri, ad solidum et in solido, quantum ex amplitudine operis pro ratione videatur, crassitudine ampliore quam parietum qui supra terram sunt futuri, et ea impleantur quam solidissima structura.
chunks.traduccion: When, therefore, the healthiness of the site for the walls has been secured on these principles, and a region has been chosen abounding in produce to feed the city, and the road network—or the advantage of a river, or the access of a sea-port—has provided ready means of transport to the walls, then the foundations of the towers and walls are to be laid in the following manner. Let them be dug down, if firm ground can be reached, to solid bottom and set within the solid, to a depth proportionate to the scale of the work, and made of a greater thickness than the walls that are to rise above the ground; and let the trenches be filled with the most solid masonry that can be laid.

chunks.texto: Item turres sunt proiciendae in exteriorem partem, uti cum ad murum hostis impetu velit adpropinquare, a turribus dextra ac sinistra lateribus apertis telis vulnerentur. Curandumque maxime videtur ut non facilis aditus sit ad oppugnandum murum, sed ita circumdandum ad loca praecipitia et excogitandum uti portarum itinera non sint directa sed scaeva. Namque cum ita factum fuerit, tum dextrum latus accedentibus quod scuto non erit tectum proximum erit muro. Conlocanda autem oppida sunt non quadrata nec procurrentibus angulis sed circinationibus, uti hostis ex pluribus locis conspiciatur. In quibus enim anguli procurrunt, difficiliter defenditur, quod angulus magis hostem tuetur quam civem.
chunks.traduccion: Likewise, the towers must be projected beyond the outer face of the wall, so that when an enemy seeks to press an assault against it, he may be wounded by missiles from the towers on his right and left, his flanks lying exposed. Above all, care must be taken that there be no easy approach for storming the wall; rather, the ground about the towers should be so disposed that the way to the gates runs not straight but obliquely, bearing to the left. For when this is done, the right side of those advancing—the side not covered by the shield—will lie nearest the wall. Towns ought to be laid out not as a square, nor with projecting angles, but in a rounded circuit, so that the enemy may be observed from several points; for where angles project, defense is difficult, since the angle shields the enemy rather than the townsman.

chunks.texto: Crassitudinem autem muri ita faciendam censeo uti armati homines supra obviam venientes alius alium sine inpeditione praeterire possint. dum in crassitudine perpetuae taleae oleagineae ustilatae quam creberrime instruantur, uti utraeque muri frontes inter se, quemadmodum fibulis, his taleis conligatae aeternam habeant firmitatem. Namque ei materiae nec caries nec tempestates nec vetustas potest nocere, sed ea et in terra obruta et in aqua conlocata permanet sine vitiis utilis sempiterno. Itaque non solum in muro sed etiam in substructionibus quique parietes murali crassitudine erunt faciundi hac ratione religati non cito vitiabuntur.
chunks.traduccion: I hold that the thickness of the wall should be such that armed men meeting upon it can pass one another without hindrance; and within that thickness let continuous tie-beams of charred olive-wood be set as closely as possible, so that the two faces of the wall, bound together by these beams as if by clamps, may possess lasting strength. For no decay, no tempest, and no lapse of time can harm that material; rather, whether buried in the earth or set in water, it endures sound and serviceable for ever. And so, not only in the walls but also in the substructures, and in any partitions built to the thickness of a wall, whatever is bound together in this manner will not soon fall into decay.

chunks.texto: Intervalla autem turrium ita sunt facienda ut ne longius sit alia ab alia sagittae missionis, uti si qua oppugnetur, tum a turribus quae erunt dextra sinistra scorpionibus reliquisque telorum missionibus hostes reiciantur. Etiamque contra interiores ⟨partes⟩ turrium dividendus est murus intervallis tam magnis quam erunt turres, ut itinera sint interioribus partibus turrium contignata, neque ea ferro fixa. Hostis enim si quam partem muri occupaverit, qui repugnabunt rescindent et si celeriter administraverint, non patientur reliquas partes turrium murique hostem penetrare, nisi se voluerit praecipitare.
chunks.traduccion: The intervals between the towers should be so arranged that no one tower stands further from the next than a bowshot, so that if any point is besieged, the enemy may be driven off by scorpions and other missiles from the towers to right and left. Opposite the lower part of the towers the wall should likewise be interrupted by gaps as wide as the towers themselves, and the passages across these gaps, within the towers, should be floored with timber that is not fastened with iron. For should the enemy seize any part of the wall, the defenders will cut away these timbers; and if they act quickly, they will not suffer the enemy to penetrate the remaining towers and stretches of wall—unless he is willing to fling himself headlong.

chunks.texto: Turres itaque rotundae aut polygonoe sunt faciendae. Quadratas enim machinae celerius dissipant, quod angulos arietes tundendo frangunt; in rotundationibus autem, uti cuneos ad centrum adigendo, laedere non possunt. Item munitiones muri turriumque aggeribus coniunctae maxime sunt tutiores, quod neque arietes neque suffossiones neque machinae ceterae eis valent nocere.
chunks.traduccion: The towers, therefore, should be built round or polygonal; for siege-engines dismantle square towers the more readily, since the rams shatter the corners by their battering, whereas in rounded forms, driving the stones towards the center as if with wedges, they can do no harm. Likewise, fortifications of wall and towers joined with earthworks are by far the safest, since neither rams nor mining nor the other engines have power to injure them.

chunks.texto: Sed non in omnibus locis est aggeris ratio facienda, nisi quibus extra murum ex alto loco plano pede accessus fuerit ad moenia oppugnanda. Itaque in eiusmodi locis primum fossae sunt faciendae latitudinibus et altitudinibus quam amplissimis, deinde fundamentum muri deprimendum est infra alveum fossae et id extruendum est ea crassitudine ut opus terrenum facile sustineatur.
chunks.traduccion: A rampart, however, need not be raised in every place, but only where, outside the wall, there is level approach from higher ground for an assault upon it. In such places, first let ditches be dug as broad and deep as possible; then let the foundation of the wall be sunk within the bed of the ditch and built of such a thickness that it may readily bear the weight of the earthwork.

chunks.texto: Item interiore parte substructionis fundamentum distans ab exteriore introrsus amplo spatio, ita uti cohortes possint quemadmodum in acie instructae ad defendendum supra latitudinem aggeris consistere. Cum autem fundamenta ita distantia inter se fuerint constituta, tunc inter ea alia transversa, coniuncta exteriori et interiori fundamento, pectinatim disposita, quemadmodum serrae dentes solent esse, conlocentur. Cum enim sic erit factum, tunc ita oneris terreni magnitudo distributa in parvas partes neque universa pondere premens ⟨non⟩ poterit ulla ratione extrudere muri substructiones.
chunks.traduccion: On the inner side of the substructure, likewise, let a further foundation be laid at a generous distance from the outer, so that cohorts may take their stand upon the breadth of the rampart, drawn up as if in line of battle to defend it. And when the two foundations have been set thus apart, let other foundations be laid between them, joining the outer to the inner and arranged comb-wise, after the manner of the teeth of a saw. For when this is done, the great mass of earth, distributed into small portions and no longer bearing down with its whole weight, will by no means be able to thrust out the substructures of the wall.

chunks.texto: De ipso autem muro e qua materia struatur aut perficiatur, ideo non est praefiniendum, quod in omnibus locis quas optamus copias, eas non possumus habere. Sed ubi sunt saxa quadrata sive silex seu caementum aut coctus later sive crudus, his erit utendum. Non enim uti Babylone abundantes liquido bitumine pro calce et harena ex cocto latere factum habent murum, sic item possunt omnes regiones seu locorum proprietates habere tantas eiusdem generis utilitates, uti ex his comparationibus ad aeternitatem perfectus habeatur sine vitio murus.
chunks.traduccion: As to the material of which the wall is to be built or finished, no fixed rule can be laid down, since we cannot everywhere command the resources we should wish. But wherever there are squared stones, or flint, or rubble, or fired or unfired brick, these are to be used. For not every region or locality can possess advantages of the same kind in such measure as Babylon, which, abounding in liquid bitumen in place of lime and sand, has its wall built of fired brick; yet from such resources as each affords, a wall may be made faultless and enduring for all time.

chunks.texto: Moenibus circumdatis sequuntur intra murum arearum divisiones platearumque et angiportûm ad caeli regionem directiones. Dirigentur haec autem recte, si exclusi erunt ex angiportis venti prudenter. Qui si frigidi sunt, laedunt; si calidi, vitiant; si umidi, nocent. Quare vitandum videtur hoc vitium et avertendum ne fiat quod in multis civitatibus usu solet venire. Quemadmodum in insula Lesbo oppidum Mytilenae magnificenter est aedificatum et eleganter, sed positum non prudenter. In qua civitate Auster cum flat, homines aegrotant; cum Corus, tussiunt; cum Septentrio, restituuntur in salubritatem, sed in angiportis et plateis non possunt consistere propter vehementiam frigoris.
chunks.traduccion: Once the walls have been built, there follow, within them, the apportionment of the building plots and the laying-out of the streets and lanes according to the quarters of the sky. These will be rightly directed if the winds are prudently excluded from the lanes; for if they are cold they are hurtful, if hot they enervate, if damp they are noxious. This fault, then, must be avoided, and care taken lest there befall what commonly happens in many cities. At Mytilene, for instance, in the island of Lesbos, the town is built with magnificence and elegance, but sited without prudence: in that city, when the south wind blows the people fall ill; when the north-west wind blows they cough; and when the north wind blows they are restored to health, yet cannot linger in the lanes and streets because of the sharpness of the cold.

chunks.texto: Ventus autem est aeris fluens unda cum certa motus redundantia. Nascitur, cum fervor offendit umorem et impetus spiritus factionis exprimit vim flatus. Id autem verum esse ex aeolis aereis licet aspicere et de latentibus caeli rationibus artificiosis rerum inventionibus divinitatis exprimere veritatem. Fiunt enim aeoli pilae aereae cavae, — hae habent punctum angustissimum—quae aqua infunduntur conlocanturque ad ignem; et antequam calescant, non habent ullum spiritum, simul autem ut fervere coeperint, efficiunt ad ignem vehementem flatum. Ita scire et iudicare licet e parvo brevissimoque spectaculo de magnis et inmanibus caeli ventorumque naturae rationibus.
chunks.traduccion: Wind is a flowing wave of air with a certain excess of motion. It arises when heat meets moisture and the impulse generated in producing breath forces out the power of the blast. This can be observed in bronze aeolipiles, through ingenious devices that reveal the truth of the hidden workings of the heavens. Hollow bronze spheres are made with a very narrow opening, filled with water and set beside a fire. Before they grow hot they give off no breath; as soon as they begin to boil, they produce a violent blast towards the fire. From a small and very brief demonstration, one may thus learn and judge the great and immense principles governing the heavens and the nature of the winds.

chunks.texto: ⟨Venti autem si ex habitationibus⟩ exclusi fuerint, non solum efficient corporibus valentibus locum salubrem, sed etiam si qui morbi ex aliis vitiis forte nascentur, qui in ceteris ⟨minus⟩ salubribus locis habent curationes medicinae contrariae, in his propter exclusiones ventorum temperatura expeditius curabuntur. Vitia autem sunt, quae difficulter curantur in regionibus, quae sunt supra scriptae, haec: gravitudo arteriace, tussis, pleuritis, pthisis, sanguinis eiectio et cetera, quae non detractionibus sed adiectionibus curantur. Haec ideo difficulter medicantur, primum quod ex frigoribus concipiuntur, deinde quod defatigatis morbo viribus eorum aer agitatus est ⟨molestus; namque ubi⟩ ventorum agitationibus extenuatur, a vitiosis corporibus detrahit sucum et efficit ea exiliora. Contra vero lenis et crassus aer, qui perflatus non habet neque crebras redundantias, propter inmotam stabilitatem adiciendo ad membra eorum alit eos et reficit, qui in his sunt inpliciti morbis.
chunks.traduccion: If the winds are excluded from dwellings, they will not only make the place healthy for sound bodies; should diseases happen to arise from other causes, which in other, less healthy places require contrary medical treatment, they will be cured more readily here through the temperate conditions produced by excluding the winds. The ailments difficult to cure in the regions described above are heaviness of the windpipe, cough, pleurisy, consumption, the spitting of blood, and the others treated by additions rather than subtractions. They are difficult to treat first because they arise from cold, and then because moving air troubles those whose strength has been exhausted by disease: where the air is thinned by the agitation of the winds, it draws moisture from diseased bodies and makes them more wasted. Mild, dense air, by contrast, free from draughts and frequent surges, by its unmoving stability nourishes and restores the limbs of those afflicted by these diseases.

chunks.texto: Nonnullis placuit esse ventos quattuor: ab oriente aequinoctiali Solanum, a meridie Austrum, ab occidente aequinoctiali Favonium, ab septentrionali Septentrionem. Sed qui diligentius perquisierunt tradiderunt eos esse octo, maxime quidem Andronicus Cyrrestes, qui etiam exemplum conlocavit Athenis turrem marmoream octagonon et in singulis lateribus octagoni singulorum ventorum imagines excalptas contra suos cuiusque flatus designavit, supraque eam turrim metam marmoream perfecit et insuper Tritonem aereum conlocavit dextra manu virgam porrigentem, et ita est machinatus uti vento circumageretur et semper contra flatum consisteret supraque imaginem flantis venti indicem virgam teneret.
chunks.traduccion: Archaeological note — Bk. 1.6 (the winds and the Tower of the Winds). The layout of the city, Vitruvius says, must orient the streets by the winds: along the lines dividing the eight winds —Solanus (E), Auster (S), Favonius (W), Septentrio (N) and, at the corners, Eurus (SE), Africus (SW), Caurus or Corus (NW), and Aquilo (NE)— so that no street channels the wind against the houses. Against those who counted only four winds, Vitruvius praises those who recognized eight, and cites as a living witness Andronicus of Cyrrhus, who raised at Athens an octagonal marble tower with a figure of each wind on its face and, at the apex, a bronze Triton turning to point to the quarter from which the wind blew. This is the Tower of the Winds (Horologion) in the Roman Agora of Athens (c. 50 BCE), of Pentelic marble, with nine sundials and a water-clock within: one of the very few buildings of classical antiquity to survive almost intact —and one that links this chapter to the gnomonics of Book IX.

chunks.texto: Itaque sunt conlocati inter Solanum et Austrum ab oriente hiberno Eurus, inter Austrum et Favonium ab occidente hiberno Africus, inter Favonium et Septentrionem Caurus, quem plures vocant Corum, inter Septentrionem et Solanum Aquilo. Hoc modo videtur esse expressum uti pateat numerus et nomina et partes unde flatus certi ventorum spirent. Quod cum ita exploratum habeatur, ut inveniantur regiones et ortus eorum sic erit ratiocinandum.
chunks.traduccion: Thus Eurus lies between Solanus and Auster, blowing from the winter sunrise; Africus lies between Auster and Favonius, from the winter sunset; Caurus, which many call Corus, lies between Favonius and Septentrio; and Aquilo lies between Septentrio and Solanus. This defines the number and names of the winds and the quarters from which they blow. With that established, the following method will determine their directions and points of origin.

chunks.texto: Conlocetur ad libellam marmoreum amusium mediis moenibus, aut locus ita expoliatur ad regulam et libellam ut amusium non desideretur, supraque eius loci centrum medium conlocetur aeneus gnomon indagator umbrae, qui graece σκιαθήρας dicitur. Huius antemeridiana circiter hora quinta sumenda est extrema gnomonis umbra et puncto signanda, deinde circino diducto ad punctum quod est gnomonis umbrae longitudinis signum, ex eoque a centro circumagenda linea rotundationis. Itemque observanda postmeridiana istius gnomonis crescens umbra, et cum tetigerit circinationis lineam et fecerit parem antemeridianae umbrae postmeridianam, signanda puncto.
chunks.traduccion: Let a marble plane be set level in the center of the city, or let the ground be smoothed with a straightedge and level so that a marble plane is unnecessary. Place a bronze gnomon, a shadow-tracer, at its center. At about the fifth hour of the morning mark the tip of the gnomon’s shadow. With the compasses opened from the center to that mark, describe a circle. Then observe the growing shadow in the afternoon; when it touches the circle and equals the length of the morning shadow, mark that point as well.

chunks.texto: Ex his duobus signis circino decusatim describendum, et per decusationem et medium centrum linea perducenda ad extremum, ut habeatur meridiana et septentrionalis regio. Tum postea sumenda est sexta decima pars circinationis lineae totius rotundationis, centrumque conlocandum in meridiana linea qua tangit circinationem, et signandum dextra ac sinistra in circinatione et meridiana et septentrionali parte. Tunc ex signis his quattuor per centrum medium decusatim lineae ab extremis ad extremas circinationes perducendae. Ita Austri et Septentrionis habebitur octavae partis designatio. Reliquae partes dextra ac sinistra tres et tres aequales his distribuendae sunt in tota rotundatione, ut aequales divisiones octo ventorum designatae sint in descriptione. Tum per angulos inter duas ventorum regiones et platearum et angiportorum videntur deberi dirigi descriptiones.
chunks.traduccion: From the two shadow-marks draw intersecting arcs with the compasses. Through their intersection and the center draw a line to the circumference, establishing south and north. Take one-sixteenth of the entire circumference and, with the compasses centered where the meridian meets it, mark that distance on either side at both the southern and northern ends. From the four marks draw intersecting lines through the center from one side of the circle to the other. This defines one-eighth of the circle for Auster and one-eighth for Septentrio. Divide the remaining regions into three equal sectors on either side, completing the eight wind divisions. The lines of streets and lanes should run along the angles between two wind regions.

chunks.texto: His enim rationibus et ea divisione exclusa erit ex habitationibus et vicis ventorum vis molesta. Cum enim plateae contra directos ventos erunt conformatae, ex aperto caeli spatio impetus ac flatus frequens conclusus in faucibus angiportorum vehementioribus viribus pervagabitur. Quas ob res convertendae sunt ab regionibus ventorum directiones vicorum, uti advenientes ad angulos insularum frangantur repulsique dissipentur.
chunks.traduccion: These principles and this division keep the troublesome force of the winds out of dwellings and streets. When streets face directly into the winds, the gusts from the open sky are confined in the narrow mouths of the lanes and pass through with greater force. The directions of the streets must therefore be turned away from the wind regions, so that incoming currents strike the corners of the blocks and are broken, repelled and dispersed.

chunks.texto: Fortasse mirabuntur î, qui multa ventorum nomina noverunt, quod a nobis expositi sunt tantum octo esse venti. Si autem animadverterint orbis terrae circumitionem per solis cursum et umbras gnomonis aequinoctialis ex inclinatione caeli ab Eratosthene Cyrenaeo rationibus mathematicis et geometricis methodis esse inventam ducentorum quinquaginta duûm milium stadiûm, quae fiunt passus trecenties et decies quinquies centena milia, huius autem octava pars, quam ventus tenere videtur, est triciens nongenta triginta septem milia et passus quingenti, non debebunt mirari, si in tam magno spatio unus ventus vagando inclinationibus et recessionibus varietates mutatione flatus faciat.
chunks.traduccion: Perhaps those acquainted with many names of winds will be surprised that we have set down only eight. But if they observe that the circuit of the earth's globe, by the course of the sun, the shadows of the equinoctial gnomon, and the inclination of the heavens, was found by Eratosthenes of Cyrene through mathematical reckoning and geometrical method to be two hundred and fifty-two thousand stadia, which make thirty-one million five hundred thousand paces, and that the eighth part of this, which a single wind appears to occupy, is three million, nine hundred and thirty-seven thousand five hundred paces. They will not be surprised that, in so vast a space of the earth, a single wind, ranging with its inclinations and retreats, gives rise to varieties and shifts of breezes.

chunks.texto: itaque dextra et sinistra austrum leuconotus et altanus flare solet, ⟨circa⟩ africum libonotus et subvesperus, circa favonium argestes et certis temporibus etesiae, ad latera cauri circius et corus, circa septentrionem thracias et gallicus, dextra ac sinistra aquilonem supernas et caecias, circa solanum carbas et certo tempore ornithiae, euri vero medias partes tenentis in extremis euricircias et volturnus. sunt autem et alia plura nomina flatusque ventorum e locis aut fluminibus aut montium procellis tracta,
chunks.traduccion: On either side of Auster usually blow Leuconotus and Altanus; on either side of Africus, Libonotus and Subvesperus; around Favonius, Argestes and, at certain seasons, the Etesiae; beside Caurus, Circias and Corus; around Septentrio, Thracias and Gallicus; beside Aquilo, Supernas and Caecias; around Solanus, Carbas and, at a particular season, the Ornithiae; and on the outer sides of Eurus, Eurocircias and Volturnus. Many other names and winds also derive from places, rivers or mountain storms.

chunks.texto: Praeterea aurae matutinae, qua sol cum emergit de subterranea parte versando pulsat aeris umorem et impetu scandendo praeurens exprimit aurarum antelucano impetu flatus. Qui cum exorto sole permanserunt, Euri venti tenent partes, et ea re quod ex auris procreatur, ab Graecis εὖρος videtur esse appellatus, crastinusque dies propter auras matutinas αὔριον fertur esse vocitatus. Sunt autem nonnulli qui negant Eratosthenem potuisse veram mensuram orbis terrae colligere. Quae sive est certa sive non vera, non potest nostra scriptura non veras habere terminationes regionum unde spiritus ventorum oriuntur.
chunks.traduccion: Moreover, there are the morning breezes; for the sun, as it emerges from beneath the earth, strikes the moisture of the air in its turning and, rising with force, draws out the breath of the dawning breezes. Those that linger on after the sun has risen belong to the quarter of Eurus; and because this wind is begotten of the breezes (aurae), it seems to have taken from the Greeks the name Euros, and the morrow likewise is called aurion from these same morning breezes. Now there are some who deny that Eratosthenes could have arrived at a true measure of the earth's circumference. Yet whether his reckoning be exact or not, our treatise cannot fail to set down the true bounds of the regions from which the winds arise.

chunks.texto: Ergo si ita est, tantum erit uti non certam mensurae rationem, sed aut maiores impetus aut minores habeant singuli venti. Quoniam haec a nobis sunt breviter exposita, ut facilius intellegatur, visum est mihi in extremo volumine formas, sive uti Graeci dicunt, σχήματα duo explicare: unum ita deformatum ut appareat unde certi ventorum spiritus oriantur, alterum quemadmodum ab impetu eorum aversis directionibus vicorum et platearum evitentur nocentes flatus. Erit autem in exaequata planitie centrum ubi est littera A, gnomonis autem antemeridiana umbra ubi est B; et a centro ubi est A, diducto circino ad id signum umbrae ubi est B, circumagatur linea rotundationis. Reposito autem gnomone ubi antea fuerat, expectanda est dum decrescat faciatque iterum crescendo parem antemeridianae umbrae postmeridianam tangatque lineam rotundationis ubi erit littera C. Tunc a signo ubi est B et a signo ubi est C, circino decusatim describatur ubi erit D; deinde per decusationem et centrum ubi est A perducatur linea ad extremum, in qua linea erunt litterae E et F. Haec linea erit index meridianae et septentrionalis regionis.
chunks.traduccion: If, then, this is so, the only difference will be that each several wind has a force now greater, now less, while the method of measurement itself remains fixed. Since these matters have been briefly set forth by us, I have thought it well, that they may be the more easily understood, to append at the end of this book two figures—or, as the Greeks call them, schemata: the one drawn so as to show plainly from which quarters the several winds arise; the other, how their harmful blasts may be turned aside by setting the lines of the streets and quarters away from their force. The procedure is as follows. On a leveled surface let the center be marked with the letter A, and the tip of the gnomon's morning shadow with the letter B; then, opening the compasses from the center A to the shadow-mark B, describe the line of the circumference. Setting the gnomon back in its former place, one must wait until the shadow shortens and then lengthens again, until the afternoon shadow equals the morning shadow and touches the circumference at the point that shall be the letter C. Then from the marks B and C, with the compasses, strike two arcs crossing at the point that shall be D; and through the intersection D and the center let a line be carried to the circumference, upon which line shall be the letters E and F. This line will be the indicator of the southern and northern quarters.

chunks.texto: Tunc circino totius rotundationis sumenda est pars XVI, circinique centrum ponendum est in meridiana linea, qua tangit rotundationem, ubi est littera E, et signandum dextra sinistra, ubi erunt litterae G H. Item in septentrionali parte centrum circini ponendum in rotundationis et septentrionali linea, ubi est littera F, et signandum dextra ac sinistra, ubi sunt litterae I et K, et ab G ad K et ab H ad I per centrum lineae perducendae. Ita quod erit spatium ab G ad H, erit spatium venti austri et partis meridianae; item quod erit spatium ab I ad K, erit septentrionis. Reliquae partes dextra ter ac sinistra ter dividendae sunt aequaliter, quae sunt ad orientem, in quibus litterae L M, et ab occidente, in quibus sunt litterae N et O. Ab M ad O et ab L ad N perducendae sunt lineae decusatim. Et ita erunt aequaliter ventorum octo spatia in circumitione. Quae cum ita descripta erunt, in singulis angulis octagoni, cum a meridie incipiemus, inter eurum et austrum in angulo erit littera G, inter austrum et africum H, inter africum et favonium N, inter favonium et caurum O, inter caurum et septentrionem K, inter septentrionem et aquilonem I, inter aquilonem et solanum L, inter solanum et eurum M. Ita his confectis inter angulos octagoni gnomon ponatur, et ita dirigantur angiportorum divisiones.
chunks.traduccion: Next, a sixteenth part of the whole circumference is to be taken with the compasses. Setting the compass-point on the meridian line where it meets the circle at the southern end, marked with the letter E, make two marks to right and left, where the letters G and H shall be placed; likewise, at the northern end, marked with the letter F, set the compass-point and make marks to right and left, where the letters I and K shall fall; then draw lines through the center, from G to K and from H to I. Thus the space from G to H will be the sector of the South wind (Auster) and the meridian quarter, and the space from I to K that of the North wind (Septentrio). The remaining parts—three on the right and three on the left—are to be divided equally: to the east, where the letters L and M stand; and to the west, where the letters N and O stand. From M to O and from L to N let lines be drawn through the center. Thus there will be eight equal spaces for the winds around the circumference. When the diagram is so drawn, the angles of the octagon, beginning from the south, will be these: the letter G at the angle between Eurus and Auster; H between Auster and Africus; N between Africus and Favonius; O between Favonius and Caurus; K between Caurus and Septentrio; I between Septentrio and Aquilo; L between Aquilo and Solanus; and M between Solanus and Eurus. When these are completed, a chord is set between the angles of the octagon, and so the divisions of the lanes and streets are directed.

chunks.texto: Divisis angiportis et plateis constitutis arearum electio ad opportunitatem et usum communem civitatis est explicanda aedibus sacris, foro reliquisque locis communibus. Et si erunt moenia secundum mare, area ubi forum constituatur eligenda proxime portum, sin autem mediterraneo, in oppido medio. Aedibus vero sacris, quorum deorum maxime in tutela civitas videtur esse, et Iovi et Iunoni et Minervae in excelsissimo loco unde moenium maxima pars conspiciatur areae distribuantur. Mercurio autem in foro, aut etiam ut Isidi et Serapi in emporio, Apollini Patrique Libero secundum theatrum, Herculi in quibus civitatibus non sunt gymnasia neque amphitheatra ad circum, Marti extra urbem sed ad campum, itemque Veneri ad portum. Id autem etiam Etruscis haruspicibus disciplinarum scripturis ita est dedicatum: extra murum Veneris, Volcani, Martis fana ideo conlocari uti non insuescat in urbe adulescentibus seu matribus familiarum veneria libido, Volcanique vi e moenibus religionibus et sacrificiis evocata ab timore incendiorum aedificia videantur liberari. Martis vero divinitas cum sit extra moenia dedicata, non erit inter cives armigera dissensio, sed ab hostibus ea defensa belli periculo conservabit.
chunks.traduccion: Once the lanes and streets have been laid out, sites must be chosen for sacred temples, the forum and other public places, with regard to the city’s convenience and common use. In a coastal town the forum should be near the harbour; in an inland town, at its center. Temples of the gods under whose special protection the city stands, such as Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, should occupy the highest place, from which most of the walls can be seen. Mercury’s temple belongs in the forum or trading center, as do those of Isis and Serapis; Apollo’s and Father Liber’s near the theater; Hercules’s near the circus in towns without gymnasia or amphitheatres; Mars’s outside the city beside the exercise ground; and Venus’s likewise near the harbour. Etruscan haruspical writings prescribe that the shrines of Venus, Vulcan and Mars stand outside the walls, so that erotic passion does not become habitual among the young and the matrons, and so that Vulcan’s power, summoned beyond the walls through rites and sacrifices, appears to free buildings from fear of fire. Mars’s divinity, consecrated outside the walls, is to prevent armed discord among the citizens and defend the city from its enemies.

chunks.texto: Item Cereri extra urbem loco, quo ⟨non quolibet⟩ nomine semper homines nisi per sacrificium necesse habeant adire; cum religione, caste sanctisque moribus is locus debet tueri. Ceterisque diis ad sacrificiorum rationes aptae templis areae sunt distribuendae. De ipsis autem aedibus sacris faciundis et de earum symmetriis in tertio et quarto volumine reddam rationes, quia in secundo visum est mihi primum de materiae copiis, quae in aedificiis sunt parandae, quibus sint virtutibus et quem habeant usum, exponere, ⟨deinde⟩ commensus aedificiorum et ordines et genera singula symmetriarum peragere et in singulis voluminibus explicare.
chunks.traduccion: Likewise, Ceres is to have a site outside the city, in a place to which people need not go for any ordinary reason, but only for sacrifice. That place must be maintained with religion, chastity and holy customs. Suitable sites for the temples of the other gods are to be assigned according to the requirements of their sacrifices. I shall explain the construction of the sacred temples themselves and their systems of symmetria in the third and fourth volumes. In the second, I have thought it appropriate first to set out the supplies of materials to be prepared for building, their qualities and their uses; afterwards I shall examine the commensurations of buildings, the orders and each type of symmetria, explaining them in their respective volumes.

chunks.texto: Dinocrates architectus cogitationibus et sollertia fretus, cum Alexander rerum potiretur, profectus est e Macedonia ad exercitum regiae cupidus commendationis. Is e patria a propinquis et amicis tulit ad primos ordines et purpuratos litteras ut aditus haberet faciliores, ab eisque exceptus humane petît uti quamprimum ad Alexandrum perduceretur. Cum polliciti essent, tardiores fuerunt idoneum tempus expectantes. Itaque Dinocrates ab his se existimans ludi ab se petît praesidium. Fuerat enim amplissima statura, facie grata, forma dignitateque summa. His igitur naturae muneribus confisus vestimenta posuit in hospitio et oleo corpus perunxit caputque coronavit populea fronde, laevum umerum pelle leonina texit, dextraque clavam tenens incessit contra tribunal regis ius dicentis.
chunks.traduccion: Dinocrates the architect, trusting in his ideas and ingenuity, left Macedonia for the army while Alexander was in power, eager to win the king’s favor. He brought letters from relatives and friends at home to the leading officers and courtiers, hoping to gain easier access. They received him kindly, and he asked to be brought before Alexander as soon as possible. Although they promised to do so, they delayed while waiting for a suitable occasion. Thinking that they were making a fool of him, Dinocrates sought a resource within himself. He was very tall, with a pleasing face and an impressive, dignified physique. Trusting in these natural gifts, he left his clothes at the inn, anointed his body with oil, crowned his head with poplar leaves, draped a lion’s skin over his left shoulder and, holding a club in his right hand, advanced towards the tribunal where the king was administering justice.

chunks.texto: Novitas populum cum avertisset, conspexit eum Alexander. Admirans ei iussit locum dari ut accederet, interrogavitque quis esset. At ille: «Dinocrates», inquit, «architectus Macedo, qui ad te cogitationes et formas adfero dignas tuae claritati. Namque Athon montem formavi in statuae virilis figuram, cuius manu laeva designavi civitatis amplissimae moenia, dextera pateram quae exciperet omnium fluminum quae sunt in eo monte aquam, ut inde in mare profunderetur».
chunks.traduccion: The unusual sight drew the crowd’s attention, and Alexander saw him. Astonished, he ordered room to be made for him to approach and asked who he was. “Dinocrates,” he replied, “a Macedonian architect, bringing you ideas and designs worthy of your glory. I have designed Mount Athos in the form of a male statue: in its left hand I have represented the walls of a very large city, and in its right a patera, a ritual bowl, to receive the water of all the mountain’s rivers and pour it into the sea.

chunks.texto: Delectatus Alexander ratione formae statim quaesiit, si essent agri circa qui possent frumentaria ratione eam civitatem tueri. Cum invenisset non posse nisi transmarinis subvectionibus, «Dinocrates», inquit, «attendo egregiam formae compositionem et ea delector, sed animadverto si qui deduxerit eo loci coloniam fore ut iudicium eius vituperetur. Ut enim natus infans sine nutricis lacte non potest ali neque ad vitae crescentis gradus perduci, sic civitas sine agris et eorum fructibus in moenibus affluentibus non potest crescere nec sine abundantia cibi frequentiam habere populumque sine copia tueri. Itaque quemadmodum formationem puto probandam, sic iudico locum inprobandum, teque volo esse mecum, quod tua opera sum usurus».
chunks.traduccion: Delighted by the account of the design, Alexander immediately asked whether there was farmland nearby capable of supplying the city with grain. Learning that it could be sustained only by supplies brought from overseas, he said: “Dinocrates, I appreciate the excellence of your design and take pleasure in it, but anyone who founded a colony there would, I see, be criticized for his judgment. Just as a newborn child cannot be nourished without its nurse’s milk or develop through the stages of growing life, so a city cannot grow without farmland and its produce flowing into its walls, maintain a numerous population without abundant food, or sustain its people without supplies. I therefore approve the design but reject the site. Nevertheless, I want you to remain with me, for I shall make use of your services.

chunks.texto: Ex eo Dinocrates ab rege non discessit et in Aegyptum est eum persecutus. Ibi Alexander cum animadvertisset portum naturaliter tutum, emporium egregium, campos circa totam Aegyptum frumentarios, inmanis fluminis Nili magnas utilitates, iussit eum suo nomine civitatem Alexandriam constituere. Ita Dinocrates a facie dignitateque corporis commendatus ad eam nobilitatem pervenit. Mihi autem, imperator, staturam non tribuit natura, faciem deformavit aetas, valetudo detraxit vires. Itaque quoniam ab his praesidiis sum desertus, per auxilia scientiae scriptaque ut spero perveniam ad commendationem.
chunks.traduccion: From then on Dinocrates did not leave the king and followed him to Egypt. There, when Alexander had observed a naturally safe harbor, an excellent emporium, corn fields around the whole of Egypt, and the great benefits of the immense river Nile, he ordered him to found the city of Alexandria in his own name. Thus Dinocrates, commended by his face and dignity of body, attained that nobility. But to me, emperor, nature has not given stature, age has disfigured my face, and illness has sapped my strength. Therefore, since I am deserted by these protections, I hope to attain commendation through the aids of science and writings.

chunks.texto: Cum autem ⟨quae⟩ primo volumine de officio architecturae terminationibusque artis perscripsi, item de moenibus et intra moenia arearum divisionibus, insequatur ordo de aedibus sacris et publicis aedificiis itemque privatis quibus proportionibus et symmetriis debeant esse uti explicentur, non putavi ante ponendum nisi prius de materiae copiis, e quibus conlatis aedificia structuris et materiationibus perficiuntur, quas habeant in usu virtutes exposuissem quibusque rerum natura e principiis essent temperatae dixissem. Sed antequam naturales res incipiam explicare, de aedificiorum rationibus unde initia ceperint et uti creverint eorum inventiones ante ponam, et insequar ingressus eorum, qui antiquitates rerum naturae et initia humanitatis et inventiones perquisitas scriptorum praeceptis dedicaverunt. Itaque quemadmodum ab his sum institutus exponam.
chunks.traduccion: In the first book I described the architect’s duties and the boundaries of the art, as well as city walls and the division of building plots within them. The next subject in order would be the proportions and commensurabilities required for sacred, public and private buildings. Before that, however, I thought it necessary to explain the properties in use of the materials assembled to complete buildings in masonry and timber, and the natural principles of which those materials are composed. Before discussing their nature, I shall first describe the beginnings of building and the development of its inventions. I shall follow those writers who investigated the early history of nature, the beginnings of human society and its inventions, and committed their precepts to writing. I shall explain these matters as I have learned them from those authors.

chunks.texto: Homines vetere more ut ferae in silvis et speluncis et nemoribus nascebantur ciboque agresti vescendo vitam exigebant. Interea quodam in loco ab tempestatibus et ventis densae crebritatibus arbores agitatae et inter se terentes ramos ignem excitaverunt, et eius flamma vehementi perterriti qui circa eum locum fuerunt sunt fugati. postea re quieta propius accedentes cum animadvertissent commoditatem esse magnam corporibus ignis teporem, ligna adicientes et îs conservantes alios adducebant et nutu monstrantes ostendebant quas haberent ex eo utilitates. In eo hominum congressu cum profundebantur aliter ⟨atque aliter⟩ e spiritu voces, cotidiana consuetudine vocabula ut obtigerant constituerunt, deinde significando res saepius in usu ex eventu fari fortuito coeperunt et ita sermones inter se procreaverunt.
chunks.traduccion: In the earliest ages of the world, men were born like the wild beasts in forests, caves, and groves, and passed their lives feeding upon wild fare. Meanwhile, in a certain place, trees densely crowded and tossed by storms and winds, and rubbing their branches one against another, kindled fire; and those who were about that place, terrified by the fierce flame, were put to flight. Afterwards, when it had grown quiet, drawing nearer they perceived that the warmth of the fire was of great comfort to their bodies; and, adding wood and so keeping it alive, they brought others to it, and by signs made plain what advantages they had from it. In that gathering of men, as their voices were uttered in differing ways with the breath, they established by daily use words as chance had brought them; then, signifying the things in more frequent use, they came by chance to speak, and thus speech was born among them.

chunks.texto: Ergo cum propter ignis inventionem conventus initio apud homines et concilium et convictus esset natus, et in unum locum plures convenirent habentes ab natura praemium praeter reliqua animalia ut non proni sed erecti ambularent mundique et astrorum magnificentiam aspicerent, item manibus et articulis quam vellent rem faciliter tractarent, coeperunt in eo coetu alii de fronde facere tecta, alii speluncas fodere sub montibus, nonnulli hirundinum nidos et aedificationes earum imitantes de luto et virgulis facere loca quae subirent. Tunc observantes aliena tecta et adicientes suis cogitationibus res novas, efficiebant in dies meliora genera casarum.
