chunks.traduccion: The discovery of fire thus first gave rise to gatherings, deliberation and communal life, and brought more people together in one place. Nature had given them an advantage over the other animals: they walked upright rather than bent towards the ground, could contemplate the magnificence of the world and stars, and could handle whatever they wished with their hands and fingers. In that gathering some began to make shelters from foliage, others to dig caves beneath hills, and others, imitating swallows and their nests, to build places of mud and twigs in which to shelter. By observing one another’s dwellings and adding new ideas of their own, they made better kinds of huts each day.

chunks.texto: Cum essent autem homines imitabili docilique natura, cotidie inventionibus gloriantes alius alii ostendebant aedificiorum effectus, et ita exercentes ingenia certationibus in dies melioribus iudiciis efficiebantur. Primumque furcis erectis et virgulis interpositis luto parietes texerunt. Alii luteas glaebas arefacientes struebant parietes, materia eos iugumentantes, vitandoque imbres et aestus tegebant harundinibus et fronde. Posteaquam per hibernas tempestates tecta non potuerunt imbres sustinere, fastigia facientes, luto inducto proclinatis tectis stillicidia deducebant.
chunks.traduccion: But since they were of an imitative and teachable nature, daily glorying in their inventions, they pointed out to one another the results of their building; and thus, sharpening their wits in rivalry, they grew day by day of sounder judgment. At first, with forked stakes set up and twigs laid between, they wove their walls with mud. Others built walls of lumps of dried clay, binding them together with timber, and, to keep off the rains and the heat, they covered them with reeds and leaves. Afterwards, when the roofs could not withstand the rains through the winter storms, they made gables, and, overlaying them with mud, carried off the drippings by the sloping roofs.

chunks.texto: Haec autem ex îs, quae supra scriptae sunt, originibus instituta esse possumus sic animadvertere, quod ad hunc diem nationibus exteris ex his rebus aedificia constituuntur, uti Gallia, Hispania, Lusitania, Aquitania, scandulis robusteis aut stramentis. Apud nationem Colchorum in Ponto, propter silvarum abundantiam, arboribus perpetuis planis dextra ac sinistra in terra positis, spatio inter eas relicto quanto arborum longitudines patiuntur, conlocantur in extremis partibus earum supra alterae transversae, quae circumcludunt medium spatium habitationis. Tum insuper alternis trabibus ex quattuor partibus angulos iugumentantes et ita parietes arboribus statuentes ad perpendiculum imarum educunt ad altitudinem turres, intervallaque, quae relinquuntur propter crassitudinem materiae, schidiis et luto obstruunt. Item tecta, recidentes ad extremos ⟨angulos⟩ transtra, traiciunt gradatim contrahentes, et ita ex quattuor partibus ad altitudinem educunt medio metas, quas fronde et luto tegentes efficiunt barbarico more testudinata turrium tecta.
chunks.traduccion: From what has been said above we may see that these things were originally established as has been described, since to this day the buildings of foreign nations are made of such materials: in Gaul, Spain, Lusitania, and Aquitaine, roofed with oak shingles or with thatch. Among the Colchians in Pontus, where forests abound, whole trees are laid flat upon the ground to right and to left, a space being left between them as wide as the length of the trees allows; and upon the outer ends of these, others are laid across, so enclosing the dwelling-space within. Then, binding together the four corners with beams laid alternately, and raising the walls of tree-trunks set plumb above the lower ones, they carry up towers to a height; and the gaps that are left, by reason of the thickness of the timber, they stop with chips and mud. The roofs, drawing in by degrees from the extreme angles, they raise pyramid-fashion; and these they cover with foliage and mud, thus fashioning, after the barbarian manner, the testudinate (covered) roofs of their towers.

chunks.texto: Phryges vero, qui campestribus locis sunt habitantes, propter inopiam silvarum egentes materiae, eligunt tumulos naturales eosque medios fossura detegentes et itinera perfodientes dilatant spatia, quantum natura loci patitur. Insuper autem stipites inter se religantes metas efficiunt, quas harundinibus et sarmentis tegentes exaggerant supra habitationes e terra maximos grumos. Ita hiemes calidissimas, aestates frigidissimas efficiunt tectorum rationes. Nonnulli ex ulva palustri componunt tuguria tecta. Apud ceteras quoque gentes ex cannula pari similique ratione casarum perficiuntur constitutiones. Non minus etiam Massiliae animadvertere possumus sine tegulis, subacta cum paleis terra, tecta. Athenis Areopagi antiquitatis exemplar ad hoc tempus luto tectum; item in Capitolio commonefacere potest et significare mores vetustatis Romuli casa et in arce sacrorum stramentis tecta.
chunks.traduccion: The Phrygians, who dwell in the plains and, for want of timber through the scarcity of forests, choose natural hillocks; these they cleave down the middle with trenches, hollow out passages, and enlarge the space within as far as the nature of the site allows. Over them they set a framework of logs tied together, which they cover with reeds and brushwood, and heap great mounds of earth above their dwellings. Thus they make their houses very warm in winter and very cool in summer. Some build their huts of marsh sedge. Among other peoples too, and in certain places, dwellings are raised upon the same and like principles. No less may one observe at Massilia roofs without tiles, made of earth kneaded with straw. At Athens, the Areopagus, a relic of antiquity, is to this day roofed with mud; and on the Capitol, the hut of Romulus and the thatched roofs of the shrines upon the citadel can still signify and recall the customs of antiquity.

chunks.texto: Ita his signis de antiquis inventionibus aedificiorum sic ea fuisse ratiocinantes possumus iudicare. Cum autem cotidie faciendo tritiores manus ad aedificandum perfecissent et sollertia ingenia exercendo per consuetudinem ad artes pervenissent, tum etiam industria in animis eorum adiecta perfecit ut qui fuerunt in his studiosiores fabros esse se profiterentur. Cum ergo haec ita fuerint primo constituta et natura non solum sensibus ornavisset gentes quemadmodum reliqua animalia, sed etiam cogitationibus et consiliis armavisset mentes et subiecisset cetera animalia sub potestate, tunc vero ex fabricationibus aedificiorum gradatim progressi ad ceteras artes et disciplinas, e fera agrestique vita ad mansuetam perduxerunt humanitatem.
chunks.traduccion: From these tokens, then, we may judge that the building-inventions of the ancients were of this kind, and so reason concerning them. And as, by daily practice, men’s hands grew more skilled in building, and as by exercising their wits they attained through habit to the arts, then industry, added to their minds, brought it about that those who were the more diligent in such things should claim to be craftsmen. Since, therefore, these things were thus first established, and since nature had not only endowed mankind with the senses, as it had the other animals, but had also armed their minds with thought and judgment, and had set the other animals beneath their dominion, they advanced by degrees from the building of houses to the other arts and disciplines, and led humanity from a wild and rustic life to a gentler civilization.

chunks.texto: Tum autem struentes animose et aevo prospicientes maioribus cogitationibus ex varietate artium natis, non casas sed etiam domos fundatas et latericiis parietibus aut e lapide structas materiaque et tegula tectas perficere coeperunt; deinde observationibus studiorum e vagantibus iudiciis et incertis ad certas symmetriarum perduxerunt rationes. Posteaquam animadverterunt profusos esse partus naturae et abundantem materiae copiam ad aedificationes ab ea comparatam, tractando nutrierunt et auctam per artes ornaverunt voluptatibus elegantiam vitae. Igitur de his rebus, quae sunt in aedificiis ad usum idoneae, quibusque sunt qualitatibus et quas habeant virtutes, ut potuero, dicam.
chunks.traduccion: Then, schooling their minds and looking forward to greater conceptions born of the variety of the arts, they began to build, not huts, but houses with foundations, with walls of brick or stone, and roofed with timber and tiles; and next, by careful observation, they were led from wavering and uncertain notions to fixed rules of symmetry. When they perceived that nature had brought forth her materials in abundance, and had furnished a plentiful store for building, they tended these with care, and, enlarging them through the arts, adorned the elegance of life with its pleasures. I shall therefore speak, as best I can, of those things which are fit for use in building, with what properties they are endowed, and how they possess their excellences.

chunks.texto: Sed si qui de ordine huius libri disputare voluerit, quod putaverit eum primum institui oportuisse, ne putet me erravisse, sic reddam rationem. Cum corpus architecturae scriberem, primo volumine putavi quibus eruditionibus et disciplinis esset ornata ⟨oportere⟩ exponere, finireque terminationibus eius species et e quibus rebus esset nata dicere. ergo in primo de artis officio itemque quid oporteat esse in architecto, ibi pronuntiavi., in hoc de naturalibus materiae rebus, quem habeant usum, disputabo. Namque hic liber non profitetur unde architectura nascatur, sed unde origines aedificiorum sunt institutae et quibus rationibus enutritae et progressae sint gradatim ad hanc finitionem.
chunks.traduccion: But should anyone wish to dispute the order of this book, thinking that it ought to have been placed first, lest he suppose that I have erred, I will render my reason thus. When I was writing the body of architecture, I thought in the first volume to set forth with what branches of learning and disciplines it is adorned, to define its departments, and to say from what things it has sprung; and there I declared what an architect ought to be. In the first, therefore, I treat of the duty of the art; in this, of the natural properties of materials, and what use they have. For this book does not profess to show whence architecture is born, but whence the origins of building were established, and by what means they were fostered and advanced by degrees to their present condition.

chunks.texto: Ergo ita suo ordine et loco huius erit voluminis constitutio. Nunc revertar ad propositum et de copiis, quae aptae sunt aedificiorum perfectionibus, quemadmodum videantur esse ab natura rerum procreatae quibusque mixtionibus principiorum congressus temperentur, ne obscura sed perspicua legentibus sint, ratiocinabor. Namque nulla materiarum genera neque corpora neque res sine principiorum coetu nasci neque subici intellectui possunt, neque aliter natura rerum praeceptis physicorum veras patitur habere explicationes, nisi causae, quae insunt in his rebus, quemadmodum et quid ita sint, subtilibus rationibus habeant demonstrationes.
chunks.traduccion: This volume, then, will have its constitution in its own order and place. Now I shall return to my purpose and reason concerning the materials suitable for the perfecting of buildings: how they appear to have been brought forth by the nature of things, and by what minglings of their first principles their combinations are tempered; and I shall make this not obscure but clear to my readers. For no kinds of matter, no bodies, no things can come into being without a concurrence of first principles, nor be brought within the understanding; nor, otherwise, can the precepts of the physicists touching the nature of things have true explanations, unless the causes inherent in these things—how and why they are as they are—be demonstrated by subtle reasoning.

chunks.texto: Thales primum aquam putavit omnium rerum esse principium. Heraclitus Ephesius, qui propter obscuritatem scriptorum a Graecis σκοτεινὸς est appellatus, ignem. Democritus, quique est eum secutus, Epicurus, atomos, quas nostri insecabilia corpora, nonnulli individua vocitaverunt. Pythagoreorum vero disciplina adiecit ad aquam et ignem aera et terrenum. Ergo Democritus, etsi non proprie res nominavit sed tantum individua corpora proposuit, ideo ea ipsa dixisse videtur, quod ea cum sint disiuncta nec laeduntur nec interitionem recipiunt nec sectionibus dividuntur, sed sempiterno aevo perpetuo infinitam retinent in se soliditatem.
chunks.traduccion: Thales first held water to be the principle of all things. Heraclitus of Ephesus, whom the Greeks called skoteinos (σκοτεινός) because of the obscurity of his writings, held fire to be that principle. Democritus and his follower Epicurus proposed atoms, which some Latin writers call indivisible bodies and others individual particles. The Pythagorean school added air and earth to water and fire. Democritus, although he did not name the substances individually but proposed indivisible bodies, seems to have held that these bodies, being separate, cannot be damaged, destroyed or divided by cutting, but retain an inexhaustible solidity throughout eternity.

chunks.texto: Ex his ergo congruentibus, cum res omnes coire nascique videantur, et hae in infinitis generibus rerum naturae sint disparatae, putavi oportere de varietatibus et discriminibus usus earum, quasque haberent in aedificiis qualitates, exponere; uti, cum fuerint notae, non habeant qui aedificare cogitant errorem, sed aptas ad usum copias aedificiis comparent.
chunks.traduccion: Since all things appear to arise from combinations of these principles, yet occur in infinitely different forms in nature, I thought it necessary to explain the varieties of materials, the differences in their uses and their qualities in buildings. With that knowledge, those planning to build can avoid error and obtain materials suited to the work.

chunks.texto: Itaque primum de lateribus, qua de terra duci eos oporteat, dicam. Non enim de harenoso neque calculoso luto neque sabulone soluto sunt ducendi, quod ex his generibus cum sint ducti primum fiunt graves, deinde cum ab imbribus in parietibus sparguntur, dilabuntur et dissolvuntur, paleaeque in his non cohaerescunt propter asperitatem. Faciendi autem sunt ex terra albida cretosa sive de rubrica aut etiam masculo sabulone. Haec enim genera propter levitatem habent firmitatem et non sunt in opere ponderosa et faciliter aggerantur.
chunks.traduccion: I shall first discuss bricks and the earth from which they should be molded. They should not be made from sandy or gravelly clay or loose sand: bricks of these materials are heavy, break up and dissolve when rain strikes the walls, and do not bind well with straw because of their roughness. They should instead be made from whitish clayey earth, red earth or coarse, firm sand. These materials combine lightness with strength, add little weight to the work and are readily laid up.

chunks.texto: Ducendi autem sunt per vernum tempus et autumnale, ut uno tenore siccescant. Qui enim per solstitium parantur, ideo vitiosi fiunt, quod summum corium sol acriter cum praecoquit, efficit ut videatur aridum, interior autem sit non siccus. Et cum postea siccescendo se contrahit, perrumpit ea quae erant arida. Ita rimosi facti efficiuntur inbecilli. Maxime autem utiliores erunt, si ante biennium fuerint ducti; namque non ante possunt penitus siccescere. Itaque cum recentes et non aridi sunt structi, tectorio inducto rigidoque obsolidate, permanente ipsi sidentes non possunt eandem altitudinem, qua est tectorium, tenere, contractioneque moti non haerent cum eo, sed ab coniunctione eius disparantur. Igitur tectoria ab structura seiuncta, propter tenuitatem per se stare non possunt, sed franguntur, ipsique parietes fortuito sidentes vitiantur. Ideo etiam Uticenses laterem, si sit aridus et ante quinquennium ductus, cum arbitrio magistratus fuerit ita probatus, tunc utuntur in parietum structuris.
chunks.traduccion: Bricks should be molded in spring or autumn so that they dry evenly. Those made at midsummer are defective because the sun rapidly bakes their outer skin, making it appear dry while the interior remains moist. As the interior later contracts in drying, it breaks through the dry surface, leaving the bricks cracked and weak. Bricks are most useful if molded two years before use, since they cannot dry thoroughly sooner. If fresh, undried bricks are built into a wall and coated with plaster that then sets hard, the bricks continue to settle and cannot retain the plaster’s height. Their shrinkage separates them from it; the plaster, detached from the masonry and too thin to support itself, breaks, while the settling walls are also damaged. For this reason the people of Utica use bricks in walls only after they have dried for five years and have been approved by a magistrate’s inspection.

chunks.texto: fiunt autem laterum genera tria. unum quod graece Lydium appellatur, id est quo nostri utuntur, longum sesquipede, latum pede. ceteris duobus Graecorum aedificia struuntur. ex his unum πεντάδωρον, alterum τετράδωρον dicitur. δῶρον autem Graeci appellant palmum, quod munerum datio graece δῶρον appellatur, id autem semper geritur per manus palmum. ita quod est quoquoversus quinque palmorum pentadoron, quod quattuor tetradoron dicitur, et quae sunt publica opera πεντάδωρον, quae privata τετράδωρον struuntur.
chunks.traduccion: Now there are three kinds of bricks. One which is called Lydian in Greek, that is, which our people use, is a foot and a half long and a foot wide. With the other two Greek buildings are built. Of these one is called pentadoron, the other tetradoron. But the Greeks call doron a palm, because the giving of gifts is called doron in Greek, and this is always done with the palm of the hand. So that which is five palms in each direction is called pentadoron, that which is four is called tetradoron, and which are public works are built pentadoron, and which are private tetradoron.

chunks.texto: fiunt autem cum his lateribus semilateria, quae cum struuntur, una parte lateribus ordines, altera semilateres ponuntur. ergo ex utraque parte ad lineam cum struuntur, alternis coriis parietes alligantur et medii lateres supra coagmenta conlocati et firmitatem et speciem faciunt utraque parte non invenustam. Est autem in Hispania ulteriore civitas Maxilua, et Callet, et in Asia Pitane, ubi lateres cum sunt ducti et arefacti, proiecti natant in aqua. natare autem eos posse ideo videtur quod terra est de qua ducuntur pumicosa. ita cum est levis, aere solidata non recipit in se nec combibit liquorem. igitur levi raraque cum sit proprietate, quocumque pondere fuerit cogitur ab rerum natura quemadmodum pumex uti ab aqua sustineatur. sic autem magnas habent utilitates, quod neque in aedificationibus sunt onerosi, et cum non patiantur penetrare in corpus umidam potestatem, a tempestatibus non dissolvuntur.
chunks.traduccion: Half-bricks are made along with these bricks. In laying them, courses of full bricks are placed on one face and half-bricks on the other. With both faces built to the line and the courses alternating, the walls are bonded: the middle of a brick lies over the joint below, giving both strength and an attractive appearance on each face. At Maxilua and Callet in Further Spain, and at Pitane in Asia, bricks, once molded and dried, float when thrown into water. This appears to be because the earth from which they are made is pumice-like: light and consolidated with air, it neither admits nor absorbs water. Being naturally light and porous, yet resistant to moisture entering their substance, such bricks are supported by water like pumice, whatever their total weight. They have great advantages: they do not burden buildings, and storms do not dissolve them.

chunks.texto: In caementiciis autem structuris primum est de harena quaerendum, ut ea sit idonea ad materiem miscendam neque habeat terram commixtam. Genera autem harenae fossiciae sunt haec: nigra, cana, rubra, carbunculus. Ex his quae in manu confricata fecerit stridorem, erit optima; quae autem terrosa fuerit, non habebit asperitatem. Item si in vestimentum candidum ea coniecta fuerit, postea excussa vel icta id non inquinarit neque ibi terra subsiderit, erit idonea.
chunks.traduccion: For rubble masonry, the first requirement is sand suitable for mixing mortar and free from earth. The kinds of pit sand are black, gray, red and carbunculus. The best sand makes a gritty sound when rubbed in the hand; sand mixed with earth lacks that roughness. If sand is thrown onto a white cloth and shaken off, leaving neither a stain nor a deposit of earth, it is suitable.

chunks.texto: Sin autem non erunt harenaria, unde fodiatur, tum de fluminibus aut e glarea erit excernenda, non minus etiam de litore marino. Sed ea in structuris haec habet vitia: difficulter siccescit, neque onerari se continenter paries patitur, nisi intermissionibus requiescat, neque concamerationes recipit. Marina autem hoc amplius, quod etiam parietes, cum in îs tectoria facta fuerint, remittente se salsugine eorum dissolvuntur.
chunks.traduccion: But if there are no sand pits from which it can be dug, sand must be sifted from rivers or gravel, and likewise from the seashore. In masonry it has these defects: it dries with difficulty, the wall cannot tolerate continuous loading unless it rests at intervals, and it cannot support vaults. Sea sand has the further disadvantage that walls, after they have been plastered, break down as their salinity is released.

chunks.texto: fossiciae vero celeriter in structuris siccescunt, et tectoria permanent, et concamerationes patiuntur, sed eae quae sunt de harenariis recentes. si enim exemptae diutius iacent, ab sole et luna et pruina concoctae resolvuntur et fiunt terrosae. ita cum in structuram coiciuntur, non possunt continere caementa, sed ea ruunt et labuntur oneraque parietes non possunt sustinere. recentes autem fossiciae cum in structuris tantas habeant virtutes, eae in tectoriis ideo non sunt utiles quod pinguitudini eius calx commixta propter vehementiam non potest sine rimis inarescere. fluviatica vero, propter macritatem uti signinum, liaculorum subactionibus in tectorio recipit soliditatem.
chunks.traduccion: Pit sand, by contrast, dries quickly in masonry, allows plaster to remain sound and supports vaulting, provided it is fresh from the pit. If left exposed too long, sun, moon and frost break it down and make it earthy. Used in masonry in that condition, it cannot bind the rubble: the stones fall and slip, and the walls cannot carry their loads. Although fresh pit sand has these advantages in masonry, it is unsuitable for plaster because its rich texture, mixed with lime, dries too vigorously to avoid cracking. River sand, by contrast, because of its leaner texture, acquires a firm surface in plaster under the action of polishing tools, as does signinum.

chunks.texto: De harenae copiis cum habeatur explicatum, tum etiam de calce diligentia est adhibenda, uti de albo saxo aut silice coquatur; et quae erit ex spisso et duriore, erit utilis in structura, quae autem ex fistuloso, in tectoriis. Cum ea erit extincta, tunc materia ita misceatur, ut, si erit fossicia, tres harenae et una calcis infundatur; si autem fluviatica aut marina, duo harenae, una calcis coiciatur. Ita enim erit iusta ratio mixtionis temperaturae. Etiam in fluviatica aut marina si qui testam tunsam et succretam ex tertia parte adiecerit, efficiet materiae temperaturam ad usum meliorem.
chunks.traduccion: Having explained the supplies of sand, I must also discuss lime, which should be burned from white stone or silex. Lime from dense, harder stone is useful in masonry; lime from porous stone is useful in plaster. Once the lime has been slaked, mix the mortar in these proportions: three parts sand to one part lime when pit sand is used, or two parts sand to one part lime when river or sea sand is used. These give the correct balance of the mixture. Adding one-third of crushed and sifted potsherd to river- or sea-sand mortar improves its composition for use.

chunks.texto: Quare autem cum recipit aquam et harenam calx, tunc confirmat structuram, haec esse causa videtur, quod e principiis, uti cetera corpora, ita et saxa sunt temperata. Et quae plus habent aeris, sunt tenera; quae aquae, lenta sunt ab umore; quae terrae, dura; quae ignis, fragiliora. Itaque ex his saxa si, antequam coquantur, contusa minute mixta harenae in structuram coiciantur, non solidescunt nec eam poterunt continere. Cum vero coniecta in fornacem ignis vehementi fervore correpta amiserint pristinae soliditatis virtutem, tunc exustis atque exhaustis eorum viribus relinquuntur patentibus foraminibus et inanibus.
chunks.traduccion: The reason why lime, on receiving water and sand, strengthens masonry appears to be that stones, like other bodies, are compounded from the elements. Those containing more air are soft; those containing more water are pliant through moisture; those containing more earth are hard; those containing more fire are more brittle. If such stones, before firing, are finely crushed, mixed with sand and put into masonry, they do not set and cannot hold it together. When placed in a kiln and seized by the violent heat of the fire, however, they lose the strength of their original solidity: their powers are burned out and exhausted, leaving open pores and voids.

chunks.texto: (Ideo autem, quo pondere saxa coiciuntur in fornacem, cum eximuntur, non possunt ad id respondere, sed cum expenduntur, permanente ea magnitudine, excocto liquore circiter tertia parte ponderis inminuta esse inveniuntur.) Ergo liquor, qui est in eius lapidis corpore, et aer cum exustus et ereptus fuerit, habueritque in se residuum calorem latentem, prius quem ex ignis vi recepit, intinctus in aqua, umore penetrante in foraminum raritates, confervescit et ita refrigeratus reicit ex calcis corpore fervorem. Igitur cum patent foramina eorum et raritates, harenae mixtionem in se corripiunt et ita cohaerescunt siccescendoque cum caementis coeunt et efficiunt structurarum soliditatem.
chunks.traduccion: (Thus stones cannot weigh the same when removed from the kiln as when put into it: weighed after firing, they are found to have lost approximately one-third of their weight, while retaining the same volume, because their liquid has been driven off.) Once the liquid and air in the stone have been burned out and removed, the latent heat remaining in it, previously received from the force of the fire, causes it to seethe when immersed in water, as moisture penetrates the open pores. On cooling in this way, it expels the heat from the substance of the lime. Its pores and voids, now open, take up the sand mixture and cohere; as they dry, they bind with the rubble and produce the solidity of the masonry.

chunks.texto: Est etiam genus pulveris quod efficit naturaliter res admirandas. nascitur in regionibus Baianis in agris municipiorum quae sunt circa Vesuvium montem. quod commixtum cum calce et caemento non modo ceteris aedificiis praestat firmitates, sed etiam moles cum struuntur in mari, sub aqua solidescunt. hoc autem fieri hac ratione videtur quod sub his montibus et terrae ferventes sunt et fontes crebri, qui non essent, si non in imo haberent aut e sulphure aut alumine aut bitumine ardentes maximos ignes. igitur penitus ignis et flammae vapor per intervenia permanans et ardens efficit levem eam terram, et ibi quod nascitur tofus exsurgens est sine liquore. ergo cum tres res consimili ratione ignis vehementia foratae in unam pervenerint mixtionem, repente recepto liquore una cohaerescunt et celeriter umore duratae solidantur, neque eas fluctus neque vis aquae potest dissolvere.
chunks.traduccion: There is also a kind of powder that naturally produces remarkable effects. It occurs in the region of Baiae and around the towns near Mount Vesuvius. Mixed with lime and rubble, it strengthens ordinary buildings and even causes harbour works built in the sea to harden under water. This appears to happen because beneath those mountains lie hot earth and numerous springs, which could not exist without great subterranean fires burning in sulphur, alum or bitumen. The fire and heat of the flame pass through the interstices, burning and lightening the earth; the tuff formed there is likewise free from liquid. When three substances similarly altered by intense fire are brought into one mixture and suddenly receive water, they cohere and harden rapidly through moisture, so that neither waves nor the force of water can break them down.

chunks.texto: ardores autem esse in his locis etiam haec res potest indicare quod in montibus Cumanorum Baianis sunt loca sudationibus excavata, in quibus vapor fervidus ab imo nascens ignis vehementia perforat eam terram per eamque manando in his locis oritur et ita sudationum egregias efficit utilitates. non minus etiam memorantur antiquitus crevisse ardores et abundavisse sub Vesuvio monte et inde evomuisse circa agros flammam. ideoque tunc quae spongia sive pumex Pompeianus vocatur excocto ex alio genere lapidis in hanc redacta esse videtur generis qualitatem.
chunks.traduccion: The existence of heat in these places is also shown by the chambers excavated for sweat baths in the hills of Cumae and Baiae. Hot vapor rising from below penetrates the earth through the force of fire, flows through it and emerges in the chambers, making them very effective for sweating. It is also recorded that in ancient times heat increased beneath Vesuvius and that flames spread from it over the surrounding countryside. What is called sponge-stone or Pompeian pumice therefore appears to have been transformed by burning from another kind of stone into its present character.

chunks.texto: id autem genus spongiae quod inde eximitur non in omnibus locis nascitur, nisi circum Aetnam et collibus Mysiae quae a Graecis κατακεκαυμένη nominatur et si quae eiusdem modi sunt locorum proprietates. si ergo in his locis aquarum ferventes inveniuntur fontes et montibus excavatis calidi vapores, ipsaque loca ab antiquis memorantur pervagantes in agris habuisse ardores, videtur esse certum ab ignis vehementia ex tofo terraque, quemadmodum in fornacibus ex calce, ita ex his ereptum esse liquorem.
chunks.traduccion: But that kind of sponge which is taken from there does not grow in all places, except around Etna and the hills of Mysia which the Greeks call κατακεκαυμένη and if there are any properties of the same kind in the places. Therefore if in these places boiling springs of water are found and hot vapors are found in excavated mountains, and if in the same places ancient people are mentioned as having had burnings pervading the fields, it seems certain that the liquid was extracted from the tuff and earth by the force of the fire, just as in kilns from lime, so from these.

chunks.texto: igitur dissimilibus et disparibus rebus correptis et in udam potestatem conlatis, calida umoris ieiunitas aqua repente satiata latenti calore confervescit et vehementer efficit ea coire celeriterque communibus corporibus unam soliditatis percipere virtutem. Relinquetur desideratio, quoniam item sunt in Etruria ex aqua calida crebri fontes, quid ita non etiam ibi nascitur pulvis, e quo eadem ratione sub aqua structura solidescat. itaque visum est antequam desideraretur de his rebus quemadmodum esse videantur exponere.
chunks.traduccion: When these unlike substances are brought together, their hot, moisture-starved material is suddenly supplied with water. Their latent heat causes the mixture to seethe, binds the components strongly together and quickly gives them a single, solid character. A question remains: since Etruria also has many hot springs, why does it not produce a powder that enables masonry to harden under water in the same way? I have therefore thought it appropriate to explain the matter before the question is asked.

chunks.texto: omnibus locis et regionibus non eadem genera terrae nec lapides nascuntur, sed nonnulla sunt terrena, alia sabulosa itemque glareosa, aliis locis harenosa non minus materia, et omnino dissimili disparique genere in regionum varietatibus qualitates insunt in terra. maxime autem id sic licet considerare quod qua mons Appenninus regiones Italiae Etruriaeque circa cingit, prope in omnibus locis non desunt fossicia harenaria, trans Appenninum vero quae pars est ad Adriaticum mare, nulla inveniuntur, item Achaia Asia omnino trans mare nec nominantur quidem. igitur non in omnibus locis quibus effervent aquae calidae crebri fontes, eaedem opportunitates possunt similiter concurrere, sed omnia uti natura rerum constituit, non ad voluptatem hominum sed ut fortuito disparata procreantur.
chunks.traduccion: The same kinds of soil and stone do not occur in every region. Some soils are earthy, others sandy or gravelly; elsewhere there are sand and soft tuff. Across different regions the earth has unlike and diverse qualities. This is especially evident where the Apennines enclose the regions of Italy and Etruria: sand pits are found almost everywhere on that side, while on the Adriatic side none are found; nor are they mentioned in Achaia, Asia and the lands across the sea. The same favorable conditions therefore do not necessarily coincide wherever hot springs abound. Nature produces things in diverse ways, as circumstance determines, rather than to suit human wishes.

chunks.texto: ergo quibus locis non sunt terrosi montes sed genere materiae, est autem materiae potestas mollior quam tofus, solidior quam terra ignis vis per eius venas egrediens adurit eam. quod est molle et tenerum exurit, quod autem asperum relinquit. quo penitus ab imo vehementia vaporis adusto, nonnullis locis procreatur id genus harenae, quod dicitur carbunculus itaque uti Campania exusta terra cinis, sic in Etruria excocta materia efficitur carbunculus. utraque autem sunt egregia in structuris, sed alia in terrenis aedificiis alia etiam in maritimis molibus habent virtutem..
chunks.traduccion: Where there are no earthy mountains but soft tuff, fire issuing through its veins burns away the softer parts and leaves the harder residue. Thus, just as burned earth in Campania becomes volcanic ash, burned tuff in Etruria becomes carbunculus sand. Both are excellent in masonry, but one works in buildings on land while the other also serves in structures built in the sea. The material involved is softer than tuff but more solid than earth; when thoroughly burned by subterranean heat, it produces in some places the kind of sand called carbunculus.

chunks.texto: De calce et harena quibus varietatibus sint et quas habeant virtutes dixi. sequitur ordo de lapidicinis explicare, de quibus et quadrata saxa et caementorum ad aedificia eximuntur copiae et comparantur. haec autem inveniuntur esse disparibus et dissimilibus virtutibus. sunt enim aliae molles, uti sunt circa urbem Rubrae Pallenses Fidenates Albanae, aliae temperatae, uti Tiburtinae Amiterninae Soractinae et quae sunt his generibus, nonnullae durae, uti siliceae. sunt etiam alia genera plura, uti in Campania rubrûm et nigrûm tofûm, in Umbria et Piceno et in Venetia albus, quod etiam serra dentata uti lignum secatur.
chunks.traduccion: I have discussed the varieties of lime and sand and their properties. Next come the stone quarries from which ashlar and rubble for buildings are cut and prepared. Their properties differ. Some stones are soft, such as the red stones near Rome and those of Pallene, Fidenae and the Alban district; others are intermediate, such as those of Tibur, Amiternum and Soracte; others, such as hard silex, are very hard. There are many further kinds, including red and black tuffs in Campania, and stones in Umbria, Picenum and Venetia, some of which can be cut with a toothed saw like timber.

chunks.texto: sed haec omnia quae mollia sunt hanc habent utilitatem quod ex his saxa cum sunt exempta in opere faciliter tractantur. et si sunt in locis tectis, sustineant laborem, si autem in apertis et patentibus, gelicidiis et pruina congesta friantur et dissolvuntur. item secundum oram maritimam ab salsugine exesa diffluunt neque perferunt aestus. Tiburtina vero et quae eodem genere sunt omnia sufferunt et ab oneribus et a tempestatibus iniurias, sed ab igni non possunt esse tuta simulque sunt ab eo tacta dissiliunt et dissipantur, ideo quod temperatura naturali parvo sunt umore itemque non multum habent terreni sed aeris plurimum et ignis. igitur cum et umor et terrenum in his minus inest, tum etiam ignis, tactu et vi vaporis ex his aere fugato, penitus insequens interveniorum vacuitates occupans fervescit et efficit a suis ardentia corporibus ⟨carbonibus⟩ similia.
chunks.traduccion: Soft stones are easily worked when freshly quarried. Under cover they serve well, but in exposed places frost and hoarfrost cause them to crumble and dissolve. Near the sea, salt also eats into them, and they do not withstand intense heat. Travertine and stones of the same kind withstand both loads and weather, but are unsafe in fire: once heated they crack and disintegrate. Their natural composition contains little moisture or earth and much air and fire. With moisture and earth scarce, heat expels the air, fills the intervening voids, and makes the stone itself burn like the bodies already on fire.

chunks.texto: sunt vero item lapidicinae complures in finibus Tarquiniensium, quae dicuntur Anicianae, colore quemadmodum Albanae, quarum officinae maxime sunt circa lacum Vulsiniensem, item praefectura Statonensi. haec autem habent infinitas virtutes. neque enim his gelicidiorum tempestas neque ignis tactus potest nocere, sed est firma et ad vetustatem ideo permanens quod parum habet e naturae mixtione aeris et ignis, umoris autem temperate plurimumque terreni. ita spissis comparationibus solidata neque ab tempestatibus neque ab ignis vehementia nocetur.
chunks.traduccion: There are also many stones in the territory of the Tarquinians, which are called Anician, in color like the Alban, whose quarries are principally around Lake Volsini, as well as in the prefecture of Staton. These have infinite virtues. For neither the storm of frost nor the touch of fire can harm them, but they are strong and durable because they have little of the natural mixture of air and fire, but a moderate and very earthy moisture. Thus, solidified by thick layers, they are not harmed by the violence of storms or fire.

chunks.texto: id autem maxime iudicare licet e monumentis quae sunt circa municipium Ferenti ex his facta lapidicinis. namque habent et statuas amplas factas egregie et minora sigilla floresque et acanthos eleganter scalptos. quae cum sint vetusta, sic apparent recentia uti si sint modo facta. non minus etiam fabri aerarii de his lapidicinis in aeris flatura formis comparatis habent ex his ad aes fundendum maximas utilitates. quae si prope urbem essent, dignum esset ut ex his officinis omnia opera perficerentur.
chunks.traduccion: This may be judged especially from monuments made of these stones around Ferentium. They include large statues excellently executed, smaller figures, flowers and acanthus leaves skilfully carved. Although old, they appear as fresh as if made recently. Bronze-workers also find the stones very useful when prepared as molds for casting bronze. If these quarries were near Rome, it would be appropriate to use their stone for all building works.

chunks.texto: cum ergo propter propinquitatem necessitas cogat ex Rubris lapidicinis et Pallensibus et quae sunt urbi proximae copiis uti, si qui voluerit sine vitiis perficere, ita erit praeparandum. cum aedificandum fuerit, ante biennium ea saxa non hieme sed aestate eximantur, et iacentia permaneant in locis patentibus. quae autem eo biennio a tempestatibus tacta laesa fuerint, ea in fundamenta coiciantur. cetera quae non erunt vitiata, ab natura rerum probata durare poterunt supra terram aedificata. nec solum ea in quadratis lapidibus sunt observanda sed etiam in caementiciis structuris.
chunks.traduccion: Since, therefore, necessity compels us to use the resources of Rubri and Pallensi, and those which are near the city, if anyone wishes to complete it without defects, this is how it should be prepared. When it is to be built, let those stones be taken out two years before, not in winter but in summer, and let them remain lying in open places. But those which have been damaged by storms during those two years, let them be cast into the foundations. The rest, which will not be defective, will be able to last built above ground, as proven by the nature of things. And not only should these be observed in square stones, but also in rubble masonry.

chunks.texto: Structurarum genera sunt haec, reticulatum quo nunc omnes utuntur, et antiquum quod incertum dicitur. ex his venustius est reticulatum, sed ad rimas faciendas ideo paratum quod in omnes partes dissoluta habet cubilia et coagmenta. incerta vero caementa alia super alia sedentia inter seque imbricata non speciosam sed firmiorem quam reticulata praestant structuram.
chunks.traduccion: Archaeological note — II.8, masonry bonds. Vitruvius contrasts two arrangements of wall facing: reticulatum, customary in his time, and the older incertum. He considers the former more elegant (venustius), though more prone to cracking because of the arrangement of beds and joints; the latter he judges less handsome but stronger. Vitruvian terminology has decisively influenced modern archaeological nomenclature, although that classification should not be projected without qualification on to every phase of Roman construction. Opus incertum uses irregular pieces visible in the facing; opus reticulatum arranges cubilia with their faces forming a diagonal network. Later or combined techniques, such as brick facings and so-called opus mixtum, belong to developments beyond the passage’s immediate description. Vitruvius subsequently compares these fabrics with Greek procedures, including emplekton and the use of transverse elements (διάτονοι).

chunks.texto: utraque autem ex minutissimis sunt instruenda, uti materia ex calce et harena crebriter parietes satiati diutius contineantur. molli enim et rara potestate cum sint, exsiccant sugendo e materia sucum. cum autem superarit et abundarit copia calcis et harenae, paries plus habens umoris non cito fiet evanidus, sed ab his continetur. simul autem umida potestas e materia per caementorum raritatem fuerit exsucta calxque ab harena discedat et dissolvatur, item caementa non possunt cum his cohaerere, sed in vetustatem parietes efficiunt ruinosos.
chunks.traduccion: Both kinds should be built with very small stones, so that abundant mortar of lime and sand saturates the walls and holds them together longer. Soft, porous stones dry out by drawing moisture from the mortar. If lime and sand are plentiful, the wall retains more moisture and does not quickly weaken. But once the pores of the stones have absorbed the mortar’s moisture, the lime separates from the sand and disintegrates; the rubble can no longer adhere, and the walls become ruinous with age.

chunks.texto: id autem licet animadvertere etiam de nonnullis monumentis, quae circa urbem facta sunt e marmore seu lapidibus quadratis intrinsecusque medio calcata structuris, vetustate evanida facta materia caementorumque exsucta raritate, proruunt et coagmentorum ab ruina dissolutis iuncturis dissipantur.
chunks.traduccion: This can be observed in monuments near Rome whose outer faces were made of marble or ashlar, with a rubble core packed between them. As the mortar weakens with age and the porous rubble dries it out, the monuments collapse; the joints of their facing stones loosen and the work breaks apart.

chunks.texto: quodsi qui noluerit in id vitium incidere, medio cavo servato secundum orthostatas, intrinsecus ex rubro saxo quadrato aut ex testa aut ex silicibus ordinariis struat bipedales parietes, et cum his ansis ferreis et plumbo frontes vinctae sint. ita enim non acervatim sed ordine structum opus poterit esse sine vitio sempiternum, quod cubilia et coagmenta eorum inter se sedentia et iuncturis alligata non protrudent opus neque orthostatas inter se religatos labi patiuntur.
chunks.traduccion: To avoid this defect, leave the space behind the facing stones and build inner walls two feet thick of squared red stone, fired brick or ordinary hard stone. Tie the inner work to the outer faces with iron clamps secured with lead. Built in regular courses rather than loose heaps, the work can remain sound: the beds and bonded joints keep the masonry from thrusting out, while the connected facing stones prevent it from slipping.

chunks.texto: Itaque non est contemnenda Graecorum structura. non enim utuntur e molli caemento structura polita, sed cum discesserunt a quadrato, ponunt de silice seu lapide duro ordinaria, et ita uti latericia struentes alligant eorum alternis coriis coagmenta, et sic maxime ad aeternitatem firmas perficiunt virtutes. haec autem duobus generibus struuntur. ex his unum isodomum, alterum pseudisodomum appellatur.
chunks.traduccion: Greek masonry should therefore not be disparaged. The Greeks do not make a carefully finished facing of soft rubble: when not using ashlar, they build with ordinary hard stone, laying it like brick and bonding the joints in alternating courses. They thus achieve lasting strength. They build this masonry in two forms, one called isodomon and the other pseudisodomon.

chunks.texto: isodomum dicitur cum omnia coria aequa crassitudine fuerint structa, pseudisodomum cum inpares et inaequales ordines coriorum diriguntur. ea utraque sunt ideo firma, primum quod ipsa caementa sunt spissa et solida proprietate neque de materia possunt exsugere liquorem sed conservant eam in suo umore ad summam vetustatem, ipsaque eorum cubilia primum plana et librata posita non patiuntur ruere materiam, sed perpetua parietum crassitudine religata continent ad summam vetustatem.
chunks.traduccion: Masonry is called isodomon when every course has the same height, and pseudisodomon when the courses differ in height. Both are strong because their dense, solid stones do not draw liquid from the mortar but preserve its moisture. Their beds, laid flat and level, prevent the mortar from slipping, while the continuous thickness and bonding of the walls hold the work securely together.

chunks.texto: altera est quam ἔμπλεκτον appellant, qua etiam nostri rustici utuntur. quorum frontes poliuntur, reliqua ita uti sunt nata cum materia conlocata alternis alligant coagmentis. sed nostri celeritati studentes, erecta conlocantes frontibus serviunt et in medio farciunt fractis separatim cum materia caementis. ita tres suscitantur in ea structura crustae, duae frontium et una media farturae. Graeci vero non ita, sed plana conlocantes et longitudines eorum alternis in crassitudinem instruentes, non media farciunt sed e suis frontatis perpetuam et unam crassitudinem parietum consolidant. praeterea interponunt singulos crassitudine perpetua utraque parte frontatos, quos διάτονοι appellant, qui maxime religando confirmant parietum soliditatem.
chunks.traduccion: Another kind, called emplekton, is also used by our country builders. Its faces are dressed, while the stones within are left in their natural state and bonded with mortar in alternating courses. Our builders, pursuing speed, set the facings upright and fill the middle separately with rubble and mortar, producing three distinct layers: two outer faces and an inner filling. The Greeks instead lay their stones flat and alternate their lengths through the thickness. They do not merely fill the middle but make one continuous thickness from face to face. They also insert stones that run through the full thickness and project at both faces, called diatonoi; these ties greatly strengthen the walls.

chunks.texto: itaque si qui voluerit ex his commentariis animadvertere et eligere genus structurae, perpetuitatis poterit rationem habere. non enim quae sunt e molli caemento subtili facie venustatis, non eae possunt esse in vetustate non ruinosae. itaque cum arbitri communium parietum sumuntur, non aestimant eos quanti facti fuerint, sed cum ex tabulis inveniunt eorum locationes, pretia praeteritorum annorum singulorum deducunt octogesimas et ita ex reliqua summa ⟨pro rata⟩ parte reddi pro his parietibus sententiam pronuntiant eos non posse plus quam annos LXXX durare.
chunks.traduccion: Anyone wishing to examine these observations and select a kind of masonry can therefore take account of its durability. Walls built from soft rubble, however finely finished, cannot remain free from decay as they age. Accordingly, when valuers assess party walls, they do not simply allow their original cost: after establishing the date of the contract from the records, they deduct one-eightieth of the price for each year that has elapsed and award the appropriate proportion of the remainder. Their assessment assumes that such walls cannot endure for more than eighty years.

chunks.texto: De latericiis vero dummodo ad perpendiculum sint stantes nihil deducitur, sed quanti fuerint olim facti, tanti esse semper aestimantur. itaque nonnullis civitatibus et publica opera et privatas domos etiam regias e latere structas licet videre, et primum Athenis murum qui spectat ad Hymettum montem et Pentelensem, item Patris in aede Iovis et Herculis latericias cellas, cum circa lapidea in aede epistylia sint et columnae, in Italia Arretio vetustum egregie factum murum, Trallibus domus regibus Attalicis facta quae ad habitandum semper datur ei qui civitatis gerit sacerdotium. item Lacedaemone e quibusdam parietibus etiam picturae excisae intersectis lateribus inclusae sunt in ligneis formis et in comitium ad ornatum aedilitatis Varronis et Murenae fuerunt adlatae.
chunks.traduccion: In brick walls, provided they remain plumb, no deduction is made: they are always valued at their original cost. In some cities public works, private houses and royal palaces can therefore be seen built of brick. Examples include the Athenian wall facing Hymettus and Pentelicus; the brick cellae in the temples of Jupiter and Hercules at Patras, with stone columns and architraves around them; the ancient, excellently built wall at Arretium in Italy; and the house at Tralles built for the Attalid kings, assigned as a residence to whoever holds the city’s priesthood. At Sparta, paintings were cut out of brick walls, enclosed in wooden frames and brought to the Comitium to adorn the aedileship of Varro and Murena.

chunks.texto: Croesi domus, quam Sardiani civibus ad requiescendum aetatis otio, seniorum collegio gerusiam dedicaverunt. item Halicarnasso potentissimi regis Mausoli domus cum Proconnensio marmore omnia haberet ornata, parietes habet latere structos, qui ad hoc tempus egregiam praestant firmitatem ita tectoriis operibus expoliti uti vitri perluciditatem videantur habere. neque is rex ab inopia id fecit. infinitis enim vectigalibus erat fartus, quod imperabat Cariae toti.
chunks.traduccion: The house of Croesus, which the people of Sardis assigned to the citizens of their city to rest in the leisure of their age, to the college of elders. Likewise, the house of the most powerful king Mausolus at Halicarnassus, although it was adorned with Proconnesian marble, has walls built of brick, which for this time show excellent strength, so polished by the works of painting that they seem to have the translucency of glass. Nor did that king do this from want. For he was enriched by immense revenues, since he ruled all Caria.

chunks.texto: acumen autem eius et sollertiam ad aedificia paranda sic licet considerare. cum esset enim natus Mylasis et animadvertisset Halicarnasso locum naturaliter esse munitum idoneum portum emporiumque utile, ibi sibi domum constituit. is autem locus est theatri curvaturae similis. itaque in imo secundum portum forum est constitutum. per mediam autem altitudinis curvaturam praecinctionemque platea ampla latitudine facta, in qua media Mausoleum ita egregiis operibus est factum ut in septem spectaculis nominetur. in summa arce media Martis fanum habens statuam colossicam acrolithon nobili manu Leocharis factam. hanc autem statuam alii Leocharis alii Timothei putant esse. in cornu autem summo dextro Veneris et Mercurii fanum ad ipsum Salmacidis fontem.
chunks.traduccion: His judgment and skill in planning buildings may be understood as follows. Born at Mylasa, he observed that Halicarnassus offered natural defenses, a suitable trading center and a useful harbour, and established his residence there. The site curves like a theater. At its lowest part, beside the harbour, he laid out the forum; halfway up the curving slope he made a broad street, with the Mausoleum at its center, a work of such distinction that it was numbered among the Seven Wonders. At the center of the summit stood the temple of Mars with a colossal acrolithic statue, attributed by some to Leochares and by others to Timotheus. On the right-hand height stood the temple of Venus and Mercury, near the spring of Salmacis.

chunks.texto: is autem falsa opinione putatur venerio morbo inplicare eos qui ex eo biberint. sed haec opinio quare per orbem terrae falso rumore sit pervagata non pigebit exponere. non enim quod dicitur molles et inpudicos ex ea aqua fieri, id potest esse, sed est eius fontis potestas perlucida saporque egregius. cum autem Melas et Areuanias ab Argis et Troezene coloniam communem eo loci deduxerunt, barbaros Caras et Lelegas eiecerunt. Hi autem ad montes fugati inter se congregantes discurrebant et ibi latrocinia facientes crudeliter eos vastabant. postea de colonis unus ad eum fontem propter bonitatem aquae quaestus causa tabernam omnibus copiis instruxit eamque exercendo eos barbaros allectabat. ita singillatim decurrentes et ad coetus convenientes e duro feroque more commutati in Graecorum consuetudinem et suavitatem sua voluntate reducebantur. ergo ea aqua non inpudico morbi vitio sed humanitatis dulcedine mollitis animis barbarorum eam famam est adepta.
chunks.traduccion: It is falsely believed that this spring causes an effeminate condition in those who drink from it. I shall explain how that mistaken report spread. Its water cannot produce the softness and immodesty alleged: it is clear and excellent to taste. When Melas and Arevanias brought a joint colony from Argos and Troezen, they expelled the local Carians and Leleges. Driven into the mountains, these people gathered in bands, raided the settlers and devastated the district. One colonist later built a tavern beside the spring, attracted by the water’s quality, and by conducting his business drew the local people to it. Coming first singly and then in groups, they gradually exchanged their harsh customs for the gentler ways of the Greeks. The water acquired its reputation not by causing a bodily disease but by softening their dispositions through the civilising appeal of human society.

chunks.texto: Relinquitur nunc quoniam ad explicationem moenium eorum sum invectus, ut tota uti sunt definiam. quemadmodum enim in dextra parte fanum est Veneris et fons supra scriptus, ita in sinistro cornu regia domus, quam rex Mausolus ad suam rationem conlocavit. conspicitur enim ex ea ad dextram partem forum et portus moeniumque tota finitio, sub sinistram secretus sub moenibus latens portus ita ut nemo possit quid in eo geratur aspicere nec scire,
chunks.traduccion: Since I have been led to describe the city, it remains to set out its overall arrangement. Just as the temple of Venus and the spring described above stand on the right, the royal palace stands on the left. Mausolus placed it to serve his own purposes: to the right it commands a view of the forum, the harbour and the whole circuit of the walls; to the left lies a harbour concealed beneath the walls, where no one else could see or know what was being done.

chunks.texto: at rex ipse de sua domo remigibus et militibus sine ullo sciente quae opus essent imperaret. itaque post mortem Mausoli Artemisia uxore eius regnante Rhodii indignantes mulierem imperare civitatibus Cariae totius, armata classe profecti sunt uti id regnum occuparent. tum Artemisiae cum esset id renuntiatum, in eo portu abstrusam classem celatis remigibus et epibatis comparatis, reliquos autem cives in muro esse iussit. cum autem Rhodii ornata classe in portum maiorem exposuissent, plausum iussit ab muro his dare pollicerique se oppidum tradituros. qui cum penetravissent intra murum relictis navibus inanibus, Artemisia repente fossa facta in pelagum eduxit classem ex portu minore et ita invecta est in maiorem. expositis autem militibus classem Rhodiorum inanem abduxit in altum. ita Rhodii non habentes quo se reciperent, in medio conclusi in ipso foro sunt trucidati.
chunks.traduccion: From his own house the king could direct the rowers and soldiers without anyone else knowing what was required. After Mausolus’s death, when his wife Artemisia ruled, the Rhodians, indignant that a woman should govern all the cities of Caria, sailed with an armed fleet to seize the kingdom. Informed of their approach, Artemisia ordered her own fleet concealed in the smaller harbour, with rowers and marines ready, while the other citizens occupied the walls. When the Rhodians entered the larger harbour, she had the citizens salute them from the walls and promise to surrender the town. The Rhodians left their ships empty and entered within the walls. Artemisia then brought her fleet out of the smaller harbour through the opening to the sea and round into the larger harbour. Landing her soldiers, she seized the empty Rhodian ships and took them out to sea. With no route of retreat, the Rhodians were surrounded and killed in the forum.

chunks.texto: ita Artemisia in navibus Rhodiorum suis militibus et remigibus inpositis Rhodum est profecta. Rhodii autem cum prospexissent suas naves laureatas venire, opinantes cives victores reverti hostes receperunt. tum Artemisia Rhodo capta principibus occisis tropaeum in urbe Rhodo suae victoriae constituit aeneasque duas statuas fecit unam Rhodiorum civitatis alteram suae imaginis. eam ita figuravit Rhodiorum civitati stigmata inponentem. id autem postea ⟨tollere⟩ Rhodii religione inpediti quod nefas est tropaea dedicata removeri, circa eum locum aedificium struxerunt et id electa Graia statione texerunt ne qui posset aspicere, et id ἄβατον vocitari iusserunt.
chunks.traduccion: Artemisia then sailed to Rhodes in the Rhodians’ ships with her own soldiers and rowers aboard. Seeing their ships arrive crowned with laurel, the Rhodians thought their victorious citizens were returning and admitted the enemy. After taking Rhodes and killing its leaders, Artemisia erected a trophy of her victory and two bronze statues: one representing the city of Rhodes and the other herself. She represented herself branding the Rhodian city. The Rhodians later refrained from removing the monument for religious reasons, since a dedicated trophy could not lawfully be taken away. They built an enclosure around the place and screened it so that no one could look upon it, ordering it to be called the abaton (ἄβατον), the inaccessible precinct.

chunks.texto: Cum ergo tam magna potentia reges non contempserint latericiorum parietum structuras, quibus ex vectigalibus et praeda saepius licitum fuerat non modo caementicio aut quadrato saxo sed etiam marmoreo habere, non puto oportere inprobare quae sunt e latericia structura facta aedificia, dummodo recte sint tecta. sed id genus quid ita populo Romano in urbe fieri non oporteat exponam, quaeque sunt eius rei causae et rationes non praetermittam.
chunks.traduccion: Since powerful kings did not disdain brick walls, although their revenues and spoils allowed them to use rubble, ashlar or even marble, I do not think brick buildings should be rejected, provided they are properly roofed. I shall explain why the Roman people do not use such walls in the city, and shall set out the causes and reasons.

chunks.texto: leges publicae non patiuntur maiores crassitudines quam sesquipedales constitui loco communi. ceteri autem parietes, ne spatia angustiora fierent, eadem crassitudine conlocantur. latericii vero nisi diplinthii aut triplinthii fuerint, sesquipedali crassitudine non possunt plus quam unam sustinere contignationem. in ea autem maiestate urbis et civium infinita frequentia innumerabiles habitationes opus est explicare. ergo cum recipere non possint areae planatae tantam multitudinem ad habitandum in urbe, ad auxilium altitudinis aedificiorum res ipsa coegit devenire. itaque pilis lapideis structuris testaceis parietibus caementiciis altitudines extructae contignationibus crebris coaxatae cenaculorum ad summas utilitates perficiunt despectationes. ergo moenibus e contignationibus areis alto spatio multiplicatis populus Romanus egregias habet sine inpeditione habitationes.
chunks.traduccion: Public regulations do not allow party walls thicker than a foot and a half, and other walls are built to the same thickness to avoid narrowing the available space. Yet brick walls of that thickness cannot support more than one story unless they are two or three bricks thick. The greatness of Rome and the immense number of its citizens require countless dwellings. Since the ground area cannot accommodate so many people, necessity has forced recourse to building upwards. Stone piers, fired-brick masonry and rubble walls, raised high and joined by frequent timber floors, provide useful upper-story dwellings. By multiplying floor space vertically, the Roman people obtain ample housing without obstructing the ground.

chunks.texto: Quoniam ergo explicata ratio est quid ita in urbe propter necessitatem angustiarum non patiuntur esse latericios parietes, cum extra urbem opus erit his uti, ⟨ut sint⟩ sine vitiis ad vetustatem sic erit faciendum. summis parietibus structura testacea sub tegula subiciatur altitudine circiter sesquipedali, habeatque proiecturas coronarum. ita vitari poterunt quae solent in his fieri vitia. cum enim in tecto tegulae fuerint fractae aut a ventis deiectae, qua possint ex imbribus aquae perpluere, non patietur lorica testacea laedi laterem, sed proiectura coronarum reiciet extra perpendiculum stillas et ea ratione servaverit integras parietum latericiorum structuras.
chunks.traduccion: Having explained why restricted sites prevent the use of brick walls in Rome, I shall describe how to make them durable where they are used outside the city. At the tops of the walls, beneath the roof tiles, build a fired-brick course about a foot and a half high, with projecting cornices. This prevents the usual damage: if roof tiles break or are displaced by wind and rainwater enters, the fired-brick protection prevents it from harming the unfired bricks. The projecting cornice throws the drops beyond the face of the wall and preserves the brick masonry intact.

chunks.texto: De ipsa autem testa, si sit optima seu vitiosa ad structuram, statim nemo potest iudicare, quod in tempestatibus et aestate in tecto cum est conlocata, tunc, si est firma, probatur; namque quae non fuerit ex creta bona aut parum erit cocta, ibi se ostendet esse vitiosam gelicidiis et pruina tacta. Ergo quae non in tectis poterit pati laborem, ea non potest in structura oneri ferendo esse firma. Quare maxime ex veteribus tegulis tecta ⟨et ex vetere testa⟩ structi parietes firmitatem poterunt habere.
chunks.traduccion: No one can immediately judge whether a fired brick is good or bad for masonry. Its strength is tested by exposure to weather and age when used on a roof. If it is made from unsuitable clay or insufficiently fired, frost reveals its weakness. A material that cannot endure service on a roof cannot be strong enough to bear a load in masonry. Walls made of old, tested roof tiles will therefore be especially strong.

chunks.texto: craticii vero velim quidem ne inventi essent. quantum enim celeritate et loci laxamento prosunt, tanto maiori et communi sunt calamitati, quod ad incendia uti faces sunt parati. itaque satius esse videtur inpensa testaceorum in sumptu quam compendio craticiorum esse in periculo. etiamque in tectoriis operibus rimas hi faciunt arrectariorum et transversariorum dispositione. cum enim linuntur, recipientes umorem turgescunt, deinde siccescendo contrahuntur et ita extenuati disrumpunt tectoriorum soliditatem. sed quoniam nonnullos celeritas aut inopia aut in pendenti loco dissaeptio cogit, sic erit faciundum. solum substruatur [aliae], ut sit intactum ab rudere et pavimento. obruta enim in his cum sunt, vetustate marcida fiunt, deinde subsidentia proclinantur et disrumpunt speciem tectoriorum. De parietibus et apparitione generatim materiae eorum, quibus sint virtutibus et vitiis quemadmodum potui exposui, de contignationibus autem et copiis earum, quibus comparentur ut ad vetustatem non sint infirmae, uti natura rerum monstrat explicabo.
chunks.traduccion: I wish timber-framed partition walls had never been invented. Their speed of construction and saving of space are outweighed by the greater and more general danger they create, for they are ready-made torches for a fire. It is better to incur the expense of fired-brick walls than to save money through timber framing and live in danger. Such framing also cracks the plaster along the upright and cross-members: when plastered, the timbers absorb moisture and swell, then shrink as they dry and break the plaster’s cohesion. Where speed, lack of resources or the need for a partition on an upper floor makes timber framing necessary, its base should be built up so that the timbers do not touch the rubble bedding or floor pavement. If buried in those layers, they decay with age, settle, lean and break the plaster surface. I have explained wall construction, its materials and their strengths and weaknesses as well as I can. I shall now discuss timber floors and the supplies used for them, explaining the natural properties needed for durability.

chunks.texto: Materies caedenda est a primo autumno ad id tempus quod erit antequam flare incipiat favonius. vere enim omnes arbores fiunt praegnantes et omnes suae proprietatis virtutem efferunt in frondem anniversariosque fructus. cum ergo inanes et tumidae temporum necessitate eorum fuerint, vanae fiunt et raritatibus inbecillae, uti etiam corpora muliebria cum conceperint, fetus a partu non iudicantur integra, neque in venalibus ea cum sunt praegnantia praestantur sana, ideo quod in corpore praeseminatio crescens ex omnibus cibi potestatibus detrahit alimentum in se, et quo firmior efficitur ad maturitatem partus, eo minus patitur esse solidum id ipsum ex quo procreatur. itaque edito fetu quod prius in aliud genus incrementi detrahebatur cum disparatione procreationis est liberatum, inanibus et patentibus venis in se recipiens lambendo sucum etiam solidescit et redit in pristinam naturae firmitatem.
chunks.traduccion: Timber should be felled from the beginning of autumn until before Favonius starts to blow. In spring, all trees become, as it were, pregnant and direct their natural strength into foliage and annual fruit. Drained and swollen by the demands of the season, they become porous and weak. The same comparison is made with women’s bodies: after conception they are not considered unimpaired until delivery, nor are they warranted as healthy in sales while pregnant, because the growing foetus drew nourishment from the body and weakened the source from which it developed. After delivery, nourishment was no longer diverted into another growing body; the open veins again took up sustenance, restoring solidity and the former natural strength.

chunks.texto: eadem ratione autumnali tempore maturitate fructuum flaccescente fronde, ex terra recipientes caudices arborum in se sucum recuperantur et restituuntur in antiquam soliditatem. at vero aeris hiberni vis comprimit et consolidat eas per id ut supra scriptum est tempus. ergo si ea ratione et eo tempore quod est supra scriptum caeditur materies, erit tempestiva.
chunks.traduccion: For the same reason, in the autumn season, when the leaves of the fruit ripen and fall, the trees, receiving sap from the earth through their roots, are recovered and restored to their former solidity. But the force of the winter air compresses and consolidates them for the time mentioned above. Therefore, if the material is cut down for that reason and at the time mentioned above, it will be in season.

chunks.texto: caedi autem ita oportet uti incidatur arboris crassitudo ad mediam medullam, et relinquatur, uti per eam exsiccescat stillando sucus. ita qui inest in his inutilis liquor effluens per torulum non patietur emori in eo saniem nec corrumpi materiae aequalitatem. tum autem cum sicca et sine stillis erit arbor, deiciatur et ita erit optima in usu.
chunks.traduccion: The tree should first be cut through to the middle of its pith and left standing so that the sap can drain through the cut. The useless liquid within can then flow out rather than decay and damage the timber. When the tree is dry and no longer dripping, it should be felled; it will then be in the best condition for use.

chunks.texto: hoc autem ita esse licet animum advertere etiam de arbustis. ea enim cum suo quoque tempore ad imum perforata castrantur, profundunt e medullis quem habent in se superantem et vitiosum per foramina liquorem, et ita siccescendo recipiunt in se diuturnitatem. qui autem non habent ex arboribus exitus umores intra concrescentes putrescunt et efficiunt inanes eas et vitiosas. ergo si stantes et vivae siccescendo non senescunt, sine dubio cum eae ad materiam deiciuntur, cum ea ratione curatae fuerint, habere poterunt magnas in aedificiis ad vetustatem utilitates.
chunks.traduccion: The same can be observed in trees: when pierced at the base in the proper season, they discharge through the openings the excessive, harmful sap in their pith, and drying in this way increases their longevity. Liquids that have no outlet, by contrast, putrefy within the tree and leave it hollow and defective. If trees left standing and alive resist decay when drained in this manner, then timber felled for use, once so treated, can undoubtedly provide great durability in buildings.

chunks.texto: Hae autem inter se discrepantes et dissimiles habent virtutes, uti robur ulmus populus cupressus abies ceteraque quae maxime in aedificiis sunt idonea. namque non potest id robur quod abies, nec cupressus quod ulmus, nec cetera easdem habent inter se natura rerum similitates, sed singula genera principiorum proprietatibus comparata alios alii generis praestant in operibus effectus.
chunks.traduccion: But they have virtues that are different and dissimilar from each other, such as the oak, the elm, the poplar, the cypress, the fir, and the others that are most suitable for buildings. For the oak cannot be the same as the fir, nor the cypress as the elm, nor the others have the same natural similarities between themselves, but each kind of principle has properties comparable to those of another kind in works.

chunks.texto: et primum abies aeris habens plurimum et ignis minimumque umoris et terreni levioribus rerum natura e potestatibus comparata non est ponderosa. itaque rigore naturali contenta non cito flectitur ab onere, sed directa permanet in contignatione. sed ea quod habet in se plus caloris, procreat et alit cariem ab eaque vitiatur, etiamque ideo celeriter accenditur quod quae inest in eo corpore aeris raritas, ut est patens accipit ignem et ita vehementem ex se mittit flammam.
chunks.traduccion: Fir contains much air and fire but little moisture and earth, so its lighter constituent principles make it relatively light. Its natural rigidity prevents it from bending readily under a load, and it remains straight in floor framing. Because it contains more heat, however, it breeds and nourishes decay and is damaged by it. It also catches fire quickly: its porous, air-filled substance readily admits fire and gives out an intense flame.

chunks.texto: ex ea autem antequam est excisa quae pars est proxima terrae per radices recipiens ex proximitate umorem enodis et liquida efficitur. quae vero est superior, vehementia caloris eductis in aera per nodos ramis, praecisa alte circiter pedes XX et perdolata propter nodationis duritiem dicitur esse fusterna. ima autem cum excisa quadrifluviis disparatur eiecto torulo ex eadem arbore ad intestina opera comparatur et ⟨ab⟩ infima fusterna sappinea vocatur.
chunks.traduccion: In the uncut tree, the part nearest the ground receives moisture through the roots and is relatively free from knots and full of sap. In the upper part, heat draws branches out through knots into the air; cut at about twenty feet and hewn, this knotty timber is called fusterna. The lower part, when cut and split into four, has the central round core removed and is prepared for interior joinery; this is called sappinea, in distinction from the lower part of the fusterna.

chunks.texto: contra vero quercus terrenis principiorum satietatibus abundans parumque habens umoris et aeris et ignis, cum in terrenis operibus obruitur, infinitam habet aeternitatem. ex eo cum tangitur umore non habens foraminum raritates propter spissitatem non potest in corpus recipere liquorem, sed fugiens ab umore resistit et torquetur et efficit in quibus est operibus ea rimosa.
chunks.traduccion: Oak, by contrast, contains much earth and little moisture, air or fire, and lasts indefinitely when buried in earthworks. When exposed to moisture, its dense texture and lack of open pores prevent it from absorbing liquid. Resisting moisture, it twists and causes cracks in the work in which it is used.

chunks.texto: aesculus vero quod est omnibus principiis temperata, habet in aedificiis magnas utilitates, sed ea, cum in umore conlocatur, recipiens penitus per foramina liquorem eiecto aere et igni operatione umidae potestatis vitiatur. cerrus [quercus] fagus quod pariter habent mixtionem umoris et ignis et terreni, aeris plurimum, per huius raritates umores penitus recipiendo celeriter marcescunt. populus alba et nigra, item salix tilia cum non sint dura terreni mixtione, propter raritatem sunt candida et in sculpturis commodam praestant tractabilitatem vitex ignis et aeris habendo satietatem, umoris temperate, parum autem terreni, habens leviore temperatura comparata egregiam habere videtur in usu rigiditatem..
chunks.traduccion: Aesculus, with a balanced mixture of the elements, is very useful in buildings. In damp conditions, however, its pores admit water as air and fire are expelled, and moisture causes it to decay. Cerrus, a kind of oak, and beech, containing balanced amounts of moisture, fire and earth but much air, are porous and quickly decay when thoroughly wetted. White and black poplar, willow, lime and vitex contain much fire and air, moderate moisture and little earth; their light composition gives them useful rigidity. Because they are not hardened by much earth, they remain soft and readily workable for carving.

chunks.texto: alnus autem, quae proxima fluminum ripis procreatur et minime materies utilis videtur, habet in se egregias rationes. etenim est aere et igni plurimo temperata, non multum terreno, umore paulo. itaque in palustribus locis infra fundamenta aedificiorum palationibus crebre fixa, recipiens in se quod minus habet in corpore liquoris, permanet inmortalis ad aeternitatem et sustinet inmania pondera structurae et sine vitiis conservat. ita quae non potest extra terram paulum tempus durare, ea in umore obruta permanet ad diuturnitatem.
chunks.traduccion: Alder, which grows beside rivers and appears of little use as timber, has remarkable properties. It contains much air and fire, little earth and little moisture. Driven densely as piles beneath foundations in marshy places, it takes up the liquid lacking in its substance and remains durable, carrying enormous masonry loads without damage. Timber that lasts only a short time out of the ground can thus endure for a long time when buried in moisture.

chunks.texto: est autem maxime id considerare Ravennae, quod ibi omnia opera et publica et privata sub fundamentis eius generis habeant palos. ulmus vero et fraxinus maximos habent umores minimumque aeris et ignis, terreni temperate ⟨ea e⟩ mixtione comparatae. sunt in operibus cum fabricantur lentae et ab pondere umoris non habent rigorem et celeriter pandant. simul autem vetustate sunt aridae factae aut in agro perfecto qui est eis liquor stantes emoriuntur, fiunt duriores et in commissuris et coagmentationibus ab lentitudine firmas recipiunt catenationes.
chunks.traduccion: This is particularly evident at Ravenna, where all public and private buildings have alder piles beneath their foundations. Elm and ash contain much moisture, little air and fire, and a moderate amount of earth. When used green they are flexible, and their moisture makes them lack rigidity and bend readily under load. Once dried by age, or drained of their sap while standing, they become harder; their pliancy makes them effective in joints and connections.

chunks.texto: item carpinus quod est minima ignis et terreni mixtione, aeris autem et umoris summa continetur temperatura, non est fragilis sed habet utilissimam tractabilitatem. itaque Graeci quod ex ea materia iuga iumentis comparant, quod apud eos iuga ζυγά
chunks.traduccion: vocitantur, item ζυγίην eam appellant. non minus est admirandum de cupresso et pinu, quod eae habentes umoris abundantiam aequamque ceterorum mixtionem, propter umoris satietatem in operibus solent esse pandae, sed in vetustatem sine vitiis conservantur, quod is liquor qui inest penitus in corporibus earum habet amarum saporem, qui propter acritudinem non patitur penetrare cariem neque eas bestiolas quae sunt nocentes. ideoque quae ex his generibus opera constituuntur permanent ad aeternam diuturnitatem.

chunks.texto: item cedrus et iuniperus easdem habent virtutes et utilitates, sed quemadmodum ex cupressu et pinu resina, ex cedro oleum quod cedrium dicitur nascitur, quo reliquae res cum sunt unctae, uti etiam libri, a tineis et carie non laeduntur. arboris autem eius sunt similes cupresseae foliaturae, materies vena directa. Ephesi in aede simulacrum Dianae, ex ea lacunaria et ibi et in ceteris nobilibus fanis propter aeternitatem sunt facta. nascuntur autem eae arbores maxime Cretae et Africae et nonnullis Syriae regionibus.
chunks.traduccion: Cedar and juniper have similar properties and uses. Just as cypress and pine yield resin, cedar produces an oil called cedrium; objects such as books, when anointed with it, are protected from moths and decay. The tree’s foliage resembles cypress, and its timber is straight-grained. At Ephesus the temple’s statue of Diana was made from it, as were the coffered ceilings there and in other celebrated sanctuaries, because of its durability. These trees grow principally in Crete, Africa and parts of Syria.
