chunks.texto: vox autem est spiritus fluens aeris, e tactu sensibilis auditu. ea movetur circulorum rotundationibus infinitis, uti si in stantem aquam lapide inmisso nascantur innumerabiles undarum circuli crescentes, a centro quam latissime possint et vagantes, nisi angustia loci interpellaverit aut aliqua offensio quae non patitur designationes earum undarum ad exitus pervenire. itaque cum interpellentur offensionibus, primae redundantes insequentium disturbant designationes.
chunks.traduccion: But the voice is like a flowing breath of air, and it is truly perceptible to the ear. It moves through the endless roar of the circles, as if a stone were thrown into stagnant water; countless circles of waves are born, growing from the center as wide as they can, and wandering, unless the narrowness of the place interrupts them or some offense prevents the designs of these waves from reaching their outlet. And so, when they are interrupted by offenses, the first overflow of the following ones disturbs their designs.

chunks.texto: eadem ratione vox item ad circinum efficit motiones, sed in aqua circuli planitiae in latitudine moventur, vox et in latitudine progreditur et altitudinem gradatim scandit. igitur ut in aqua undarum designationibus, item in voce cum offensio nulla primam undam interpellaverit, non disturbat secundam nec insequentes, sed omnes sine resonantia perveniunt ad imorum et ad summorum aures.
chunks.traduccion: In the same way, the voice makes its movements as if traced by a compass (ad circinum). But whereas in water the circles move in breadth over the flat surface, the voice advances at once in breadth and ascends gradually in height. Therefore, as with the waves on the surface of water, so with the voice: when the first wave meets no obstacle, it does not impede the second or the third, but all reach, without resonance, the ears of those below and those above.

chunks.texto: ergo veteres architecti naturae vestigia persecuti indagationibus vocis scandentis theatrorum perfecerunt gradationes, et quaesierunt per canonicam mathematicorum et musicam rationem ut quaecumque vox esset in scaena, clarior et suavior ad spectatorum perveniret aures. uti enim organa aeneis lamminis aut corneis ἠχεῖα ad chordarum sonitûm claritatem perficiuntur, sic theatrorum per harmonicen ad augendam vocem ratiocinationes ab antiquis sunt constitutae.
chunks.traduccion: Therefore, the ancient architects, following the steps of nature, investigating the rising sound of theaters, completed the gradations, and sought, through the canonical method of mathematics and music, that whatever voice was on the stage, it should reach the ears of the spectators in a clear and sweet manner. For just as organs are made of brass plates or ox horns for the clarity of the heart's sound, so the ancients established the reasoning of theaters to augment the voice through harmonics.

chunks.texto: Harmonice autem est musica litteratura obscura et difficilis, maxime quidem quibus graecae litterae non sunt notae. quam si volumus explicare, necesse est etiam graecis verbis uti, quod nonnulla eorum latinas non habent appellationes. itaque ut potuero quam apertissime ex Aristoxeni scripturis interpretabor et eius diagramma subscribam finitionesque sonituum designabo, uti qui diligentius attenderit facilius percipere possit.
chunks.traduccion: Harmonic theory is a difficult and obscure branch of learning, especially for those unfamiliar with Greek. To explain it, we must use Greek terms, since some have no Latin equivalents. I shall therefore interpret the writings of Aristoxenus as clearly as I can and set out his diagram and the limits of the notes, so that attentive readers may understand them more readily.

chunks.texto: vox enim mutationibus cum flectitur alias fit acuta alias gravis, duobusque modis movetur, e quibus unus effectus habet continuatos, alter distantes. continuata vox neque in finitionibus consistit neque in loco ullo, efficitque terminationes non apparentes, intervalla autem media apparentia, uti sermone cum dicamus sol lux flos vox. nunc enim nec unde incipit nec ubi desinit intellegitur, sed quod ex acuta facta est gravis et ex gravi acuta, apparet auribus. per distantiam autem e contrario. namque cum flectitur inmutatione vox statuit se in alicuius sonitus finitione, deinde in alterius, et id ultro citro crebre faciendo ⟨non⟩ constans apparet sensibus, uti in cantionibus cum flectentes vocem varietatem facimus modulationis. itaque intervallis ea cum versatur, et unde initium fecit et ubi desiit apparet in sonorum patentibus finitionibus, medianis autem patentia intervallis obscurantur.
chunks.traduccion: As the voice changes inflection, it becomes high or low and moves in two ways: continuously or by distinct intervals. Continuous movement settles at no fixed pitch; its boundaries are imperceptible, although the intervening movement is audible, as when we say sol, lux, flos, vox in ordinary speech. We do not identify its precise starting and stopping points, but the ear hears the change from high to low and from low to high. Movement by intervals is different. The voice settles at one definite pitch, then another, and repeatedly passes between them, as in singing when changes of pitch produce melodic variety. The beginnings and endings are then perceptible at the clearly defined notes, while the intervening passage is obscured by the intervals.

chunks.texto: Genera vero sunt modulationum tria, primum quod Graeci nominant ἁρμονίην, secundum χρῶμα, tertium διάτονον. est autem harmoniae modulatio ab arte concepta, et ea re cantio eius maxime gravem et egregiam habet auctoritatem. chroma subtili sollertia ac crebritate modulorum suaviorem habet delectationem. diatoni vero quod naturalis est, facilior est intervallorum distantia. in his tribus generibus dissimiles sunt tetrachordorum dispositiones, quod harmonia [tetrachordorum] et tonos et dihesis habet binas. dihesis autem est toni pars quarta, ita in hemitonio duae diheses sunt conlocatae. chromati duo hemitonia in ordine sunt composita, tertium trium hemitoniorum est intervallum; dia⟨tono⟩ toni duo sunt continuati, tertium hemitonium finit tetrachordi magnitudinem. ita in tribus generibus tetrachorda ex duobus tonis et hemitonio sunt peraequata, sed ipsa cum separatim uniuscuiusque generis finibus considerantur, dissimilem habent intervallorum designationem.
chunks.traduccion: There are three genera of melody: the first, called harmonia by the Greeks, is the enharmonic; the second is chroma, the chromatic; and the third is the diatonic. The enharmonic is an artistic construction whose melody has a particularly grave and distinguished character. The chromatic offers a gentler pleasure through the subtle skill and closeness of its steps. The diatonic is natural and its intervals are easier to grasp. The tetrachords are divided differently in the three genera. The enharmonic contains two whole tones and two dieses; a diesis is one-quarter of a tone, so two dieses make a semitone. The chromatic has two successive semitones and a third interval of three semitones. The diatonic has two successive whole tones, with a final semitone completing the tetrachord. Each genus therefore spans two tones and a semitone, although the division of that span differs.

chunks.texto: igitur intervalla tonorum et hemitoniorum et ⟨diheseon⟩ tetrachordorum in voce divisit natura finîtque terminationes eorum mensuris intervallorum quantitate, modisque certis distantibus constituit qualitates, quibus etiam artifices qui organa fabricant ex natura constitutis utendo comparant ad concentus convenientes eorum perfectiones.
chunks.traduccion: Nature has divided the voice into the intervals of tones, semitones and dieses within the tetrachords, fixing their limits by the size of the intervals and establishing distinct qualities at definite distances. Instrument makers use these natural divisions to bring their finished instruments into consonance.

chunks.texto: Sonitus, qui graece φθόγγοι dicuntur, in unoquoque genere sunt X et VIII, e quibus VIII sunt in tribus generibus perpetui et stantes, reliqui X cum communiter modulantur sunt vagantes. stantes autem sunt qui inter mobiles [sunt] interpositi, continent tetrachordi coniunctionem et e generum discriminibus suis finibus sunt permanentes, appellantur autem sic, proslambanomenos, hypate hypaton, hypate meson, mese, nete synhemmenon, paramese, nete diezeugmenon, nete hyperbolaeon. mobiles autem sunt qui in tetrachordo inter inmotos dispositi in generibus ex locis loca mutant, vocabula autem habent haec, parhypate hypaton, lichanos hypaton, parhypate meson, lichanos meson, trite synhemmenon, <paranete synhemmenon,> trite diezeugmenon, paranete diezeugmenon, trite hyperbolaeon, paranete hyperbolaeon.
chunks.traduccion: The notes, called phthongoi (φθόγγοι) in Greek, number eighteen in each genus. Eight remain fixed in all three genera; the other ten are movable when the genera are considered together. The fixed notes, interposed among the movable ones, maintain the connection of the tetrachords and retain their positions as the genera change. Their names are proslambanomenos, hypate hypaton, hypate meson, mese, nete synhemmenon, paramese, nete diezeugmenon and nete hyperbolaeon. The movable notes occupy positions between the fixed notes within a tetrachord and change their places with the genus. They are parhypate hypaton, lichanos hypaton, parhypate meson, lichanos meson, trite synhemmenon, ⟨paranete synhemmenon⟩, trite diezeugmenon, paranete diezeugmenon, trite hyperbolaeon and paranete hyperbolaeon.

chunks.texto: ei autem qua moventur, recipiunt virtutes alias, intervalla enim et distantias habent crescentes. itaque parhypate, quae in harmonia distat ab hypate <dimidium> hemitonium, in chroma transmutata habet hemitonium. quae lichanos in harmonia dicitur, ab hypate distat hemitonium, in chroma translata progreditur duo hemitonia, in diatono distat ab hypate tria hemitonia. ita X sonitus propter translationes in generibus efficiunt triplicem modulationum varietatem.
chunks.traduccion: The movable notes acquire different properties as their intervals and distances increase. Thus parhypate, which in the enharmonic lies half a semitone above hypate, lies a semitone above it in the chromatic. Lichanos is a semitone above hypate in the enharmonic, two semitones above it in the chromatic, and three in the diatonic. Through their changes of position in the genera, these ten notes produce three different arrangements of melody.

chunks.texto: Tetrachorda autem sunt quinque: primum gravissimum, quod graece dicitur ὕπατον, secundum medianum, quod appellatur μέσον, tertium coniunctum, quod συνημμένον dicitur, quartum disiunctum, quod διεζευγμένον nominatur, quintum, quod est acutissimum, graece ὑπερβόλαιον dicitur. Concentus, quos natura hominis modulari potest, graece quae συμφωνίαι dicuntur, sunt sex: diatessaron, diapente, diapason, et disdiatessaron, et disdiapente, et disdiapason.
chunks.traduccion: There are five tetrachords: the lowest, called hypaton (ὕπατον); the middle, meson (μέσον); the conjunct, synhemmenon (συνημμένον); the disjunct, diezeugmenon (διεζευγμένον); and the highest, hyperbolaion (ὑπερβόλαιον). The consonances that the human voice can produce, called symphonies (συμφωνίαι) in Greek, are six: diatessaron, diapente, diapason, disdiatessaron, disdiapente and disdiapason.

chunks.texto: ideoque et a numero nomina ceperunt, quod cum vox constiterit in una sonorum finitione ab eaque se flectens mutaverit et pervenerit in quartam terminationem, appellatur diatessaron, in quintam diapente [in sextam diapason, in octavam et dimidiam diapason et diatessaron, in nonam et dimidiam diapason diapente, in XII disdiapason].
chunks.traduccion: These consonances take their names from number. When the voice starts at a definite note and moves to the fourth position, the interval is called diatessaron; when it reaches the fifth, diapente. [The following numerical sequence is excluded from the constituted Latin text: at the sixth, diapason; at the eighth and a half, diapason and diatessaron; at the ninth and a half, diapason and diapente; at the twelfth, disdiapason.]

chunks.texto: non enim inter duo intervalla, cum chordarum sonitus aut vocis cantus factus fuerit, nec inter tria aut sex aut septem possunt consonantiae fieri, sed uti supra scriptum est, diatessaron et diapente et ex ordine ad disdiapason convenientiae ex natura vocis congruentis habent finitiones, et ei concentus procreantur ex coniunctione sonituum [qui graece φθόγγοι dicuntur].
chunks.traduccion: Consonance does not arise at the second or third interval, or at the sixth or seventh, whether produced by strings or by the singing voice. Rather, as explained above, the fourth and fifth and the sequence extending to the double octave have limits determined by the natural agreement of the voice. These consonances arise from the combination of notes [called phthongoi in Greek].

chunks.texto: Ita ex his indagationibus mathematicis rationibus fiant vasa aerea pro ratione magnitudinis theatri eaque ita fabricentur ut cum tangantur, sonitum facere possint inter se diatessaron diapente et ex ordine ad disdiapason. postea inter sedes theatri constitutis cellis, ratione musica ibi conlocentur ita uti nullum parietem tangant circaque habeant locum vacuum et ab summo capite spatium, ponanturque inversa et habeant in parte quae spectat ad scaenam suppositos cuneos ne minus altos semipede, contraque eas cellas relinquantur aperturae inferiorum graduum cubilibus longae pedes duo, altae semipede.
chunks.traduccion: On these principles, bronze vessels should be made by mathematical calculation in proportion to the size of the theater. They must be fashioned so that, when struck, they sound in relation to one another at a fourth, a fifth and successively up to the double octave. Vaulted chambers should then be built among the seats and the vessels placed in them according to musical principles. Each vessel must touch none of the surrounding walls and must have free space around it and above. Set the vessels upside down, supported on wedges at least half a foot high on the side facing the stage. Opposite the chambers, leave openings in the beds of the lower seating steps, two feet long and half a foot high.

chunks.texto: designationes autem eorum, quibus in locis constituantur, sic explicentur. si non erit ampla magnitudine theatrum, media altitudinis transversa regio designetur et in ea tredecim cellae duodecim aequalibus intervallis distantes confornicentur, uti ea echea quae supra scripta sunt ad neten hyperbolaeon sonantia in cellis, quae sunt in cornibus extremis, utraque parte prima conlocentur, secunda ab extremis diatessaron ad neten diezeugmenon, tertia diatessaron ad paramesen, quarta ad neten synhemmenon, quinta diatessaron ad mesen, sexta diatessaron ad hypaten meson, in medio unum diatessaron ad hypaten hypaton.
chunks.traduccion: Their positions should be laid out as follows. In a theater of modest size, mark a transverse line halfway up the seating and construct thirteen vaulted chambers along it, separated by twelve equal intervals. On each side, place first in the outermost chamber a vessel sounding nete hyperbolaeon. In the next chamber inward, place one a fourth away, sounding nete diezeugmenon; in the third, one a fourth away at paramese; in the fourth, one at nete synhemmenon; in the fifth, one a fourth away at mese; and in the sixth, one a fourth away at hypate meson. In the central chamber, place a single vessel a fourth away at hypate hypaton.

chunks.texto: ita hac ratiocinatione vox a scaena uti ab centro profusa se circumagens tactuque feriens singulorum vasorum cava excitaverit auctam claritatem et concentu convenientem sibi consonantiam. sin autem amplior erit magnitudo theatri, tunc altitudo dividatur in partes IIII, uti tres efficiantur regiones cellarum transverse designatae, una harmoniae, altera chromatos, tertia diatoni. et ab imo quae erit prima, ea ex harmonia conlocetur ita uti in minore theatro supra scriptum est.
chunks.traduccion: With this arrangement, the voice spreading from the stage as from a center strikes the hollow of each vessel and acquires greater clarity, producing through resonance a consonance in harmony with itself. In a larger theater, divide the height of the seating into four parts and arrange three transverse rows of chambers: one for the enharmonic genus, another for the chromatic and the third for the diatonic.

chunks.texto: in mediana autem prima in extremis cornibus ad chromaticen hyperbolaeon habentia sonitum ponantur, in secundis ab his diatessaron ad chromaticen diezeugmenon, in tertiis ad chromaticen synhemmenon, quartis diatessaron ad chromaticen meson, quintis diatessaron ad chromaticen hypaton, sextis ad paramesen, quod et ad chromaticen hyperbolaeon diapente et ad chromaticen synhemmenon diatessaron habet consonantiae communitatem.
chunks.traduccion: In the middle row, place at each outer end a vessel sounding chromatic hyperbolaeon. Place in the second chamber a vessel a fourth away at chromatic diezeugmenon; in the third, one at chromatic synhemmenon; in the fourth, one a fourth away at chromatic meson; in the fifth, one a fourth away at chromatic hypaton; and in the sixth, one at paramese. This last note has a fifth in common with chromatic hyperbolaeon and a fourth with chromatic synhemmenon.

chunks.texto: in medio nihil est conlocandum, ideo quod sonitûm nulla alia qualitas in chromatico genere symphoniae consonantiam potest habere. in summa vero divisione et regione cellarum in cornibus primis ad diatonon hyperbolaeon fabricata vasa sonitu ponantur, in secundis diatessaron ad diatonon <diezeugmenon>, tertiis ad diatonon synhemmenon, quartis diatessaron ad diatonon meson, quintis diatessaron ad diatonon hypaton, sextis diatessaron ad proslambanomenon, in medio ad mesen, quod ea et ad proslambanomenon diapason et ad diatonon hypaton diapente habet symphoniarum communitates.
chunks.traduccion: Nothing should be placed in the central chamber, since no other pitch in the chromatic genus can form the required consonance. In the upper row, place at the outer ends vessels sounding diatonic hyperbolaeon; in the second chambers, a fourth away at diatonic ⟨diezeugmenon⟩; in the third, at diatonic synhemmenon; in the fourth, a fourth away at diatonic meson; in the fifth, a fourth away at diatonic hypaton; and in the sixth, a fourth away at proslambanomenos. In the middle, place a vessel at mese, which forms an octave with proslambanomenos and a fifth with diatonic hypaton.

chunks.texto: haec autem si qui voluerit ad perfectum facile perducere, animadvertat in extremo libro diagramma musica ratione designatum, quod Aristoxenus magno vigore et industria generatim divisis modulationibus constitutum reliquit. de quo si qui ratiocinationibus his attenderit, ad [naturas vocis et] audientium delectationes facilius valuerit theatrorum efficere perfectiones.
chunks.traduccion: Anyone wishing to carry this arrangement through accurately should consult the musical diagram at the end of this book, which Aristoxenus established with great care and effort by distinguishing the melodic genera. Attention to that diagram and these calculations will make it easier to complete theaters that give pleasure to their listeners.

chunks.texto: Dicet aliquis forte multa theatra quotannis Romae facta esse neque ullam rationem harum rerum in his fuisse, sed errabit in eo, quod omnia publica lignea theatra tabulationes habent complures, quas necesse est sonare. hoc vero licet animadvertere etiam ab citharoedis, qui superiore tono cum volunt canere, avertunt se ad scaenae valvas et ita recipiunt ab earum auxilio consonantiam vocis. cum autem ex solidis rebus theatra constituuntur, id est ex structura caementorum, lapide, marmore, quae sonare non possunt, tunc echeis hae rationes sunt explicandae.
chunks.traduccion: Someone may object that many theaters are built in Rome each year without any provision of this kind. The objection overlooks the many boarded surfaces in public wooden theaters, which necessarily resonate. The same effect can be observed in cithara players: when they wish to sing in a higher register, they turn toward the stage doors and obtain support for the resonance of their voices. When theaters are built of solid materials—rubble masonry, stone or marble—which do not resonate in this way, the system of sounding vessels must be employed.

chunks.texto: sin autem quaeritur in quo theatro ea sint facta, Romae non possumus ostendere sed in Italiae regionibus et in pluribus Graecorum civitatibus, etiamque auctorem habemus Lucium Mummium, qui diruto theatro Corinthiorum ea aenea Romam deportavit et de manubiis ad aedem Lunae dedicavit. multi etiam sollertes architecti, qui in oppidis non magnis theatra constituerunt, propter inopiam fictilibus doliis ita sonantibus electis hac ratiocinatione compositis perfecerunt utilissimos effectus.
chunks.traduccion: If one asks in which theaters this arrangement has been used, we cannot point to an example at Rome, but there are examples in the regions of Italy and in many Greek cities. We also have the testimony of Lucius Mummius, who, after the destruction of the theater at Corinth, brought its bronze vessels to Rome and dedicated them from the spoils at the temple of Luna. Many resourceful architects working in small towns, unable to afford bronze, have selected earthenware jars with the appropriate tones and arranged them on these principles, obtaining highly useful results.

chunks.texto: Ipsius autem theatri conformatio sic est facienda uti quam magna futura est perimetros imi, centro medio conlocato circumagatur linea rotundationis, in eaque quattuor scribantur trigona paribus lateribus ⟨quae paribus⟩ intervallis, extremam lineam circinationis tangant, quibus etiam in duodecim signorum caelestium <⟨astrologia⟩> astrologi ex musica convenientia astrorum ratiocinantur. ex his trigonis cuius latus fuerit proximum scaenae, ea regione qua praecidit curvaturam circinationis, ibi finiatur scaenae frons, et ab eo loco per centrum parallelos linea ducatur, quae disiungat proscaenii pulpitum et orchestrae regionem.
chunks.traduccion: The configuration of the theater itself is to be made in such a way that, however large the perimeter will be, a line of the rounding (rotundatio) is described about the center placed in the middle, and four triangles are inscribed in it with equal sides and intervals, which touch the outermost line of the circumference, by which astrologers also reason from the concordance of the stars in the twelve celestial signs. From these triangles, the side of which is closest to the stage, in the region where it intersects the curvature of the circumference, the front of the stage is to end there, and from that place a parallel line is drawn through the center, which separates the stage platform of the proscenium and the region of the orchestra.

chunks.texto: ita latius factum fuerit pulpitum quam Graecorum, quod omnes artifices in scaena dant operam, in orchestra autem senatorum sunt sedibus loca designata. et eius pulpiti altitudo sit ne plus pedum quinque, uti qui in orchestra sederint, spectare possint omnium agentium gestus. cunei spectaculorum in theatro ita dividantur uti anguli trigonorum, qui currunt circum curvaturam circinationis, dirigant ascensus scalasque inter cuneos ad primam praecinctionem, supra autem alternis itineribus superiores cunei medii dirigantur.
chunks.traduccion: The stage-platform (pulpitum) should be made wider than that of the Greeks, because all the artists work on the stage. Places are designated for the seats of the senators in the orchestra. And the height of the stage platform should not exceed five feet, so that whoever sits in the orchestra can watch the movements of all the actors. The wedges of the spectacles in the theater should be divided in such a way that the corners of the triangles, which run around the curvature of the circumference, direct the ascents and stairs between the wedges to the first enclosure, and above all, the upper wedges in the middle should be directed by alternate routes.

chunks.texto: Hi autem qui sunt in imo et dirigunt scalaria, erunt numero VII, reliqui quinque scaenae designabunt compositionem, et unus medius contra se valvas regias habere debet, et qui erunt dextra sinistra hospitaliorum designabunt compositionem, extremi duo spectabunt itinera versurarum. gradus spectaculorum ubi subsellia componantur ne minus alti sint palmopede, <ne plus pedem> et digitos sex, latitudines eorum ne plus pedes duo semis, ne minus pedes duo constituantur.
chunks.traduccion: But those who are at the bottom and direct the stairs will be seven in number, the remaining five stages will designate the composition, and the one in the middle should have the royal doors opposite it, and those who will be on the right and left of the hospitals will designate the composition, the two outermost will watch the routes of the turns. The steps of the spectacles where the seats are arranged should be no less than a palm's breadth high, <no more than a foot> and six fingers, their widths should be no more than two and a half feet, no less than two feet.

chunks.texto: tectum porticus quod futurum est in summa gradatione, cum scaenae altitudine libratum perficiatur, ideo quod vox crescens aequaliter ad summas gradationes et tectum perveniet. namque si non erit aequale, quo minus fuerit altum, vox praeripietur ad eam altitudinem quam perveniet primo.
chunks.traduccion: The roof of the portico at the top of the seating should be level with the top of the stage building, so that the rising voice reaches the upper rows and the roof together. If these heights are unequal, the voice will be intercepted at the lower level it first encounters.

chunks.texto: orchestra inter grados imos quod diametron habuerit, eius sexta pars sumatur, et in cornibus utrimque ad eius mensurae perpendiculum inferiores sedes praecidantur, et qua praecisio fuerit, ibi constituantur itinerum supercilia. ita enim satis altitudinem habebunt eorum confornicationes.
chunks.traduccion: Take one-sixth of the diameter of the orchestra measured between the lowest seating tiers. At the two ends of the orchestra, cut back the lower seats vertically to this height and place the lintels of the passages at the resulting level. Their vaults will then have sufficient height.

chunks.texto: scaenae longitudo ad orchestrae diametron duplex fieri debet. podii altitudo ab libramento pulpiti cum corona et lysi duodecumam orchestrae diametri. supra podium columnae cum capitulis et spiris altae quarta parte eiusdem diametri, epistylia et ornamenta earum columnarum altitudinis quinta parte. pluteum insuper cum unda et corona inferioris plutei dimidia parte. supra id pluteum columnae quarta parte minore altitudine sint quam inferiores, epistylium et ornamenta earum columnarum quinta parte. item si tertia episcenos futura erit, mediani plutei summum sit dimidia parte, columnae summae medianarum minus altae sint quarta parte, epistylia cum coronis earum columnarum item habeant altitudinis quintam partem.
chunks.traduccion: The length of the stage building should be twice the diameter of the orchestra. The podium, including its crowning moldings, should rise one-twelfth of that diameter above the stage platform. The columns above it, including capitals and bases, should be one-quarter of the same diameter in height; their architraves and entablatures, one-fifth of the column height. The parapet above, including its cymatium and cornice, should be half the height of the lower parapet. The columns above this parapet should be one-quarter shorter than those below, with their entablatures one-fifth of their own height. If there is a third stage elevation, its upper parapet should be half the height of the middle parapet; the uppermost columns should be one-quarter shorter than the middle columns, and their architraves and cornices should likewise be one-fifth of the column height.

chunks.texto: Nec tamen in omnibus theatris symmetriae ad omnes rationes et effectus possunt respondere, sed oportet architectum animadvertere quibus proportionibus necesse sit sequi symmetriam et quibus ad loci naturam aut magnitudinem operis temperari. sunt enim res quas et in pusillo et in magno theatro necesse est eadem magnitudine fieri propter usum, uti gradus diazomata pluteos itinera ascensus pulpita tribunalia et si qua alia intercurrunt ex quibus necessitas cogit discedere ab symmetria ne inpediatur usus. non minus si qua exiguitate copiarum, id est marmoris, materiae reliquarumque rerum quae parantur, in opere defuerint, paulum demere aut adicere, dum id ne nimium inprobe fiat sed cum sensu, non erit alienum. hoc autem erit si architectus erit usu peritus, praeterea ingenio mobili sollertiaque non fuerit viduatus.
chunks.traduccion: Yet in all theaters symmetries cannot correspond to all reasons and effects, but the architect must observe with what proportions it is necessary to follow symmetry and with which to temper it to the nature of the place or the size of the work. For there are things which in both a small and a large theater it is necessary to make the same size for the sake of use, such as steps, diazomata, shelves, itinerant ascents, pulpits, tribunals, and if there are such things which intersect from which necessity compels a departure from symmetry lest use be hindered. Not less, if there is any scarcity of supplies, that is, of marble, materials, and other things which are prepared, in the work, a little should be taken away or added, provided that this is not done too improperly but with sense, it will not be out of place. This will be the case if the architect is skilled in use, and moreover is not deprived of mobile talent and skill.

chunks.texto: Ipsae autem scaenae suas habent rationes explicitas ita uti mediae valvae ornatus habeant aulae regiae, dextra ac sinistra hospitalia, secundum autem spatia ad ornatus comparata, quae loca Graeci περιάκτοι dicunt ab eo quod machinae sunt in his locis versatiles trigonoe habentes singulares species ornationis, quae cum aut fabularum mutationes sunt futurae seu deorum adventus cum tonitribus repentinis, [ea] versentur mutentque speciem ornationis in frontes. secundum ea loca versurae sunt procurrentes, quae efficiunt una a foro, altera a peregre aditus in scaenam.
chunks.traduccion: The scenes themselves have their own elaborate arrangements, such that the middle doors have decorations for the royal courts, the right doors for the hospitals, and the spaces for the decorations, which the Greeks call periaktos, from the fact that in these places there are machines, each with three kinds of decorations, which, when changes in the plays are to come or the arrival of the gods with sudden thunder, are turned and change the kind of decorations in front. According to these places, there are turnings that run forward, one forming the forum, the other the entrance to the stage.

chunks.texto: genera autem sunt scaenarum tria, unum quod dicitur tragicum, alterum comicum, tertium satyricum. horum autem ornatus sunt inter se dissimili disparique ratione, quod tragicae deformantur columnis et fastigiis et signis reliquisque regalibus rebus, comicae autem aedificiorum privatorum et maenianorum habent speciem prospectusque fenestris dispositos imitatione, communium aedificiorum rationibus, satyricae vero ornantur arboribus speluncis montibus reliquisque agrestibus rebus in topeodis speciem deformati.
chunks.traduccion: There are three kinds of scenes, one which is called tragic, the other comic, the third satirical. But the decorations of these are different from each other and in different ways, because the tragic ones are deformed with columns and pinnacles and standards and other royal things, while the comic ones have the appearance of private and walled buildings and have windows arranged in imitation of public buildings, while the satirical ones are decorated with trees, caves, mountains and other rural things deformed into the appearance of a landscape.

chunks.texto: In Graecorum theatris non omnia isdem rationibus sunt facienda, quod primum in ima circinatione ut in latino trigonorum IIII, in eo quadratorum trium anguli circinationis lineam tangunt, et cuius quadrati latus est proximum scaenae praeciditque curvaturam circinationis, ea regione designatur finitio proscaenii. et ab ea regione ad extremam circinationem curvaturae parallelos linea designatur, in qua constituitur frons scaenae, per centrumque orchestrae proscaenii regioni parallelos linea describitur et qua secat circinationis lineas dextra ac sinistra in cornibus hemicycli centra signantur, et circino conlocato in dextra ab intervallo sinistro circumagitur circinatio ad proscaenii sinistram partem, item centro conlocato in sinistro cornu ab intervallo dextro circumagitur ad proscaenii dextram partem.
chunks.traduccion: In Greek theaters, not everything should be done according to the same principles, because first, in the lower circle, as in the Latin trigon IV, the squares of the three corners touch the line of the circle, and the side of the plaza that is next to the stage and cuts the curvature of the circle, in that region, the end of the proscenium is designated. And from that region to the end of the circle, a line parallel to the curvature is drawn, in which the front of the stage is formed, and through the center of the orchestra, a line parallel to the proscenium region is described, and because it cuts the lines of the circle, the right and left lines are marked in the centers of the horns of the hemicycle. And having been placed on the right, from the left interval, the circle moves towards the left side of the proscenium; likewise, placed in the center of the left wing, it moves from the right interval towards the right side of the proscenium.

chunks.texto: ita tribus centris hac descriptione ampliorem habent orchestram Graeci et scaenam recessiorem minoreque latitudine pulpitum, quod λογεῖον appellant, ideo quod ⟨apud⟩ eos tragici et comici actores in scaena peragunt, reliqui autem artifices suas per orchestram praestant actiones, itaque ex eo scaenici et thymelici graece separatim nominantur. eius logei altitudo non minus debet esse pedum X, non plus duodecim. gradationes scalarum inter cuneos et sedes contra quadratorum angulos dirigantur ad primam praecinctionem, a praecinctione inter eas iterum mediae dirigantur, et ad summam quotiens praecinguntur, altero tanto semper amplificantur.
chunks.traduccion: Nomenclature note — Bk. 5.7.2 (the Greek stage). Technical terms retained with the Graecism and transliteration at first occurrence: orchestra (ὀρχήστρα), the circular space of the chorus; proscaenium / λογεῖον (logeîon), the raised platform of the actors; σκηνή (skené), the stage-building; παρασκήνια (paraskénia), its side-wings.

chunks.texto: Cum haec omnia summa cura sollertiaque explicata sunt, tunc etiam diligentius est animadvertendum uti sit electus locus, in quo leniter adplicet se vox neque repulsa resiliens incertas auribus referat significationes. sunt enim nonnulli loci naturaliter inpedientes vocis motus, uti desonantes, qui graece dicuntur κατηχοῦντες, circumsonantes qui apud eos nominantur περιηχοῦντες, item resonantes qui dicuntur ἀντηχοῦντες, consonantesque quos appellant συνηχοῦντας. desonantes sunt in quibus vox prima cum est elata in altitudinem, offensa superioribus solidis corporibus repulsaque residens in imo opprimit insequentis vocis elationem,
chunks.traduccion: When all this has been set out with the utmost care and skill, then still greater vigilance is needed to ensure that a site is chosen on which the voice settles gently and is not thrown back in such a way as to carry uncertain meanings to the ears. There are, indeed, places that by their nature hinder the movement of the voice: the dissonant, called in Greek κατηχοῦντες (katechountes); the circumsonant, which they name περιηχοῦντες (periechountes); the resonant, called ἀντηχοῦντες (antechountes); and the consonant, which they call συνηχοῦντες (synechountes). The dissonant are those in which the first voice, rising aloft, strikes solid bodies above and, driven back, settles below and smothers the rise of the voice that follows.

chunks.texto: circumsonantes autem in quibus circumvagando coacta exsolvens in medio, sine extremis casibus sonans ibi extinguatur incerta verborum significatione, resonantes vero in quibus cum in solido tactu percussa resiliat, imagines exprimendo novissimos casus duplices faciat auditu. item consonantes sunt in quibus ab imis auxiliata cum incremento scandens egrediatur ad aures diserta verborum claritate. ita si in locorum electione fuerit diligens animadversio, emendatus erit prudentia ad utilitatem in theatris vocis effectus. formarum autem descriptiones inter se discriminibus his erunt notatae uti quae Graecorum habent usus ex quadratis designentur,, latina e paribus lateribus trigonorum. ita his praescriptionibus qui voluerit uti, emendatas efficiet theatrorum perfectiones.
chunks.traduccion: The circumsonant are those in which the voice, forced to wander round, dissolves in the middle and, sounding there without its final syllables, dies away in an uncertain meaning of the words. The resonant are those in which, striking against a solid body, it rebounds and, forming echoes, doubles the last syllables to the ear. The consonant are those in which the voice, supported from below, rises with increasing strength and reaches the ears with distinct clarity of words. Thus, if due attention is given to the choice of site, prudence will secure, to good effect, the sound of the voice in theaters. The layouts of the plans will be marked by this difference between them: those designed from squares serve Greek usage; the Latin, from triangles of equal sides. Whoever chooses to follow these prescriptions will achieve theaters of finished perfection.

chunks.texto: Post scaenam porticus sunt constituendae, uti cum imbres repentini ludos interpellaverint, habeat populus quo se recipiat ex theatro choragiaque laxamentum habeant ad comparandum. uti sunt porticus Pompeianae itemque Athenis porticus Eumenicae Patrisque Liberi fanum, et exeuntibus e theatro sinistra parte odeum, quod Themistocles columnis lapideis dispositis, navium malis et antemnis e spoliis Persicis pertexit, ideo autem etiam incensum Mithridatico bello rex Ariobarzanes restituit, Smyrnae Stratoniceum, Trallibus porticus ex utraque parte est scaenae supra stadium, ceterisque civitatibus quae diligentiores habuerunt architectos circa theatra sunt porticus et ambulationes.
chunks.traduccion: Behind the stage, porticos are to be built, so that when sudden showers interrupt the games, the people may have a place to retreat from the theater and a place to rest while preparing for the festivities. Such are the porticos of Pompeii, and also in Athens the porticos of the Eumenes and the Parumontes and the temples of Liber, and on the left side of those leaving the theater, the ode, which Themistocles covered with stone columns, the masts of ships, and the antlers from the spoils of the Persians, and the same incense burner was restored by King Ariobarzanes during the Mithridatic war, the Stratoniceum at Smyrna, the porticos at Trallis on both sides of the stage above the stadium, and in other cities that have had more diligent architects, there are porticos and walks around the theaters.

chunks.texto: quae videntur ita oportere conlocari uti duplices sint habeantque exteriores columnas doricas cum epistyliis et ornamentis ex ratione modulationis perfectas. latitudines autem earum ita oportere fieri videntur uti quanta altitudo columnae fuerit exterioris, tantam latitudinem habeant ab inferiore parte columnarum extremarum ad medias et a medianis ad parietes qui circumcludunt porticus ambulationes. medianae autem columnae quinta parte altiores sint quam exteriores, sed aut ionico aut corinthio genere deformentur.
chunks.traduccion: which seem to be so placed that they are double and have exterior Doric columns with epistyles and ornaments perfect in proportion to the modulation. Their widths seem to be made so that the height of the exterior columns is such that they have as much width from the lower part of the outer columns to the middle ones and from the middle ones to the walls that enclose the portico walks. The middle columns, however, are to be a fifth higher than the exterior ones, but are to be shaped either in the Ionic or Corinthian style.

chunks.texto: columnarum autem proportiones et symmetriae non erunt isdem rationibus quibus in aedibus sacris scripsi. aliam enim in deorum templis debent habere gravitatem, aliam in porticibus et ceteris operibus subtilitatem. itaque si dorici generis erunt columnae, dimetiantur earum altitudines cum capitulis in partes XV. ex eis partibus una constituatur et fiat modulus, ad cuius moduli rationem omnis operis erit explicatio. et in imo columnae crassitudo fiat duorum modulorum, intercolumnium quinque et moduli dimidia parte, altitudo columnae praeter capitulum XIIII modulorum, capituli altitudo moduli unius, latitudo modulorum duorum et moduli sextae partis. ceteri operis modulationes uti in aedibus sacris in libro IIII scriptum est ita perficiantur.
chunks.traduccion: The proportions and commensurability of these columns do not follow the same rules as those prescribed for sacred buildings: temples require one degree of dignity, porticoes and other works another degree of slenderness. For Doric columns, divide their height, including the capitals, into fifteen parts. One part becomes the module governing the whole work. Make the lower diameter two modules and the intercolumniation five and a half. The shaft, excluding the capital, is fourteen modules high; the capital is one module high and two and one-sixth modules wide. Complete the remaining members according to the temple rules given in Book IV.

chunks.texto: sin autem ionicae columnae fient, scapus praeter spiram et capitulum in octo et dimidiam partem dividatur et ex his una crassitudini columnae detur, <spira> cum plintho dimidia crassitudine constituatur, capituli ratio ita fiat uti in libro tertio est demonstratum. si corinthia erit, scapus et spira uti in ionica, capitulûm autem quemadmodum in quarto libro est scriptum, ita habeant rationem. stylobatisque adiectio quae fit per scamillos inpares, ex descriptione quae supra scripta est in libro tertio sumatur. epistylia coronae ceteraque omnia ad columnarum rationem ex scriptis voluminum superiorum explicentur.
chunks.traduccion: If the columns are Ionic, divide the shaft, excluding the base and capital, into eight and a half parts, and assign one part to the column’s diameter. The base, including its plinth, should be half a diameter high; the capital should follow the proportions described in Book III. For Corinthian columns, the shaft and base should follow the Ionic proportions, and the capital those given in Book IV. The addition to the stylobate made by means of the scamilli inpares should follow the description in Book III. The architraves, cornices, and remaining members should be proportioned to the columns as explained in the preceding books.

chunks.texto: Media vero spatia quae erunt subdiu inter porticus, adornanda viridibus videntur, quod hypaethroe ambulationes habent, magnam salubritatem, et primum oculorum quod ex viridibus subtilis et extenuatus aer propter motionem corporis influens perlimat speciem et ita auferens ex oculis umorem crassum, aciem tenuem et acutam speciem relinquit. praeterea cum corpus motionibus in ambulatione calescat, umores ex membris aer exsugendo inminuit plenitates extenuatque dissipando quod plus inest quam corpus potest sustinere.
chunks.traduccion: The middle spaces, which will lie open to the sky between the porticoes, seem fit to be planted with greenery, because the walks of the hypaethroe have great health benefits, and first of all for the eyes, because the subtle and thin air flowing in from the greenery due to the movement of the body refines the appearance and, taking away the thick moisture from the eyes, leaves a thin and sharp appearance. Moreover, when the body is heated by the movements of walking, the air, by sucking the moisture from the limbs, diminishes the fullness and thins it by dissipating what is more in it than the body can bear.

chunks.texto: hoc autem ita esse ex eo licet animadvertere, quod sub tectis cum sint aquarum fontes aut etiam sub terra palustris abundantia, ex his nullus surgit umor nebulosus, sed in apertis hypaethrisque locis cum sol oriens vapore tangat mundum, ex umidis et abundantibus excitat umores et eos conglobatos in altitudinem tollit. ergo si ita videtur uti in hypaethris locis ab aere umores ex corporibus exsugantur molestiores, quemadmodum ex terra per nebulas videntur, non puto dubium esse quin amplissimas et ornatissimas subdiu hypaethrusque conlocari oporteat in civitatibus ambulationes.
chunks.traduccion: But this is so from the fact that, when there are springs of water under roofs or even an abundance of marshes under the ground, no misty moisture rises from these, but in open and humid places, when the rising sun touches the world with vapor, it stirs up the moisture from the moist and abundant places and carries the accumulated moisture to a height. Therefore, if it seems that in humid places the more troublesome moistures are sucked out of the bodies from the air, just as they are seen from the ground through mists, I do not think there is any doubt that the most spacious and most ornate promenades should be placed in cities under humid and humid conditions.

chunks.texto: eae autem uti sint semper siccae et non lutosae, sic erit faciendum. fodiantur et exinaniantur quam altissime. dextra atque sinistra structiles cloacae fiant inque earum parietibus qui ad ambulationem spectaverint, tubuli instruantur inclinati fastigio cloacis. his perfectis compleantur ea loca carbonibus, deinde insuper sabulone eae ambulationes sternantur et exaequentur. ita propter carbonum raritatem naturalem et tubulorum in cloacas instructionem excipientur aquarum abundantiae, et ita siccae et sine umore perfectae fuerint ambulationes.
chunks.traduccion: But that they may always be dry and not muddy, this is what must be done. They shall be dug and emptied as deep as possible. On the right and left, constructed sewers shall be made, and in their walls, which face the passage, pipes shall be laid out, inclined with a peak into the sewers. When these are completed, those places shall be filled with coal, then on top of that, those passages shall be spread out and leveled with sand. Thus, because of the natural scarcity of coal and the direction of the pipes into the sewers, abundance of water shall be taken care of, and thus the passages shall be dry and free from moisture.

chunks.texto: Praeterea in his operibus thensauri sunt civitatibus in necessariis rebus a maioribus constituti. in conclusionibus enim reliqui omnes faciliores sunt apparatus quam lignorum. sal enim facile ante inportatur, frumenta publice privatimque expeditius congeruntur et si defit, holeribus carne seu leguminibus defenditur, aquae fossuris puteorum et de caelo repentinis tempestatibus ex tegulis excipiuntur. de lignatione quae maxime necessaria est ad cibum coquendum, difficilis et molesta est apparatio, quod et tarde comportatur et plus consumitur.
chunks.traduccion: Furthermore, in these works, the cities have treasuries for the necessary things, established by their forebears against times of need; for in a siege all other supplies are more easily obtained than firewood. The rest are easier to prepare than for wood. For salt is easily brought in beforehand, grain is more expediently stored both publicly and privately, and if it is lacking, it is protected with vegetables, meat or legumes, water is collected from the roof tiles by digging wells and from sudden storms of the sky. The preparation of wood, which is most necessary for cooking food, is difficult and troublesome, because it is both slow to be brought in and consumed more.

chunks.texto: in eiusmodi temporibus tunc eae ambulationes aperiuntur et mensurae tributim singulis capitibus designantur. ita duas res egregias hypaethroe ambulationes praestant, unam in pace salubritatis, alteram in bello salutis. ergo his rationibus ambulationum explicationes non solum post scaenam theatri sed etiam omnium deorum templis effectae magnas civitatibus praestare poterunt utilitates. Quoniam haec nobis satis videntur esse exposita, nunc insequentur balinearum dispositionum demonstrationes.
chunks.traduccion: At such times, then, those walks are thrown open and measured spaces are allotted tribe by tribe. Thus, the walks of the hypaethro perform two excellent functions, one in peace of health, the other in war of safety. Therefore, with these reasons, the explanations of the walks, carried out not only behind the scenes in theaters but also in the temples of all the gods, will be able to perform great benefits for the cities. Since these seem to us to have been sufficiently explained, now there will follow demonstrations of the arrangements of the baths.

chunks.texto: primum eligendus locus est quam calidissimus, id est aversus ab septentrione et aquilone. ipsa autem caldaria tepidariaque lumen habeant ab occidente hiberno, si autem natura loci inpedierit, utique a meridie, quod maxime tempus lavandi a meridiano ad vesperum est constitutum. et item est animadvertendum uti caldaria muliebria et virilia coniuncta et in isdem regionibus sint conlocata. sic enim efficietur ut vasaria et hypocausis communis sit eorum utrisque. aenea supra hypocausim tria sunt componenda, unum caldarium, alterum tepidarium, tertium frigidarium, et ita conlocanda uti ex tepidario in caldarium quantum aquae caldae exierit, influat
chunks.traduccion: First, a place should be chosen that is as warm as possible, that is, facing away from the north and the north-east. The caldariums and tepidariums themselves should have light from the winter west, but if the nature of the place prevents this, then from the south, since the best time for bathing is from midday to evening. It should also be noted that the caldariums for women and men should be connected and placed in the same areas. For in this way it will be ensured that there is something common to both of them in the vases and hypocauses. Three bronze vessels should be arranged above the hypocauses, one caldarium, the other tepidarium, and the third frigidarium, and they should be placed in such a way that as much hot water as comes out of the tepidarium into the caldarium, it flows

chunks.texto: suspensurae caldariorum ita sunt faciendae ut primum sesquipedalibus tegulis solum sternatur inclinatum ad hypocausim, uti pila cum mittatur non possit intro resistere sed rursus redeat ad praefurnium ipsa per se. ita flamma facilius pervagabitur sub suspensione. supraque laterculis besalibus pilae struantur ita dispositae uti bipedales tegulae possint supra esse conlocatae. altitudinem autem pilae habeant pedes duo eaeque struantur argilla cum capillo subacta, supraque conlocentur tegulae bipedales quae sustineant pavimentum.
chunks.traduccion: The suspensions of the boilers are to be made in such a way that first the floor is laid with half-foot tiles inclined towards the hypocausis, so that when the ball is thrown in it cannot resist but returns to the pre-furnace by itself. In this way the flame will spread more easily under the suspension. Above this, the pillars (pilae) are raised with small bessal bricks, arranged so that two-foot tiles can be placed above. The height of the balls, however, should be two feet, and they should be laid with clay with hair pressed down, and above them are placed two-foot tiles that support the floor.

chunks.texto: concamarationes vero si ex structura factae fuerint, erunt utiliores, sin autem contignationes fuerint, figlinum opus subiciatur, sed hoc ita erit faciendum. regulae ferreae aut arcus fiant eaeque uncinis ferreis ad contignationem suspendantur quam creberrimis, eaeque regulae sive arcus ita disponantur uti tegulae sine marginibus sedere in duabus invehique possint, et ita totae concamarationes in ferro nitentes sint perfectae. earumque camararum superiora coagmenta ex argilla cum capillo subacta liniantur, inferior autem pars, quae ad pavimentum spectat, primum testa cum calce trullizetur, deinde opere albario sive tectorio poliatur. eaeque camarae in caldariis si duplices factae fuerint, meliorem habebunt usum. non enim a vapore umor corrumpere poterit materiem contignationis, sed inter duas camaras vagabitur.
chunks.traduccion: If the chambers are made of a structure, they will be more useful, but if they are floors, then pottery work should be placed under them, but this should be done in this way. Iron rules or arches should be made and they should be hung on iron hooks as thick as possible to the floor, and these rules or arches should be arranged so that the tiles can sit without edges on two and can be driven in, and thus the entire chambers should be perfect, shining in iron. And the upper joints of their chambers should be lined with clay with hair, but the lower part, which looks to the floor, should first be troweled with clay and lime, then polished with whitewash or plaster. And if these chambers in the boilers are made double, they will have a better use. For the moisture from the steam will not be able to corrupt the material of the floor, but will wander between the two chambers.

chunks.texto: magnitudines autem balneorum videntur fieri pro copia hominum, <dummodo> sint ita compositae. quanta longitudo fuerit, tertia dempta, latitudo sit praeter scholam labri et alvei. labrum utique sub lumine faciundum videtur, ne stantes circum suis umbris obscurent lucem. scholas autem labrorum ita fieri oportet spatiosas uti cum priores occupaverint loca, circum expectantes reliqui recte stare possint. alvei autem latitudo inter parietem et pluteum ne minus sit pedes senos, ut gradus inferior inde auferat et pulvinus duos pedes.
chunks.traduccion: The sizes of the baths seem to be made according to the number of people, <provided> they are arranged in such a way. Whatever the length is, subtract a third, the width is to be in addition to the width of the basin and the basin. The basin certainly seems to be made under the light, so that those standing around it do not obscure the light with their shadows. The basins, however, must be made so spacious that when the first have taken their places, the rest, looking around, can stand upright. The width of the basin between the wall and the shelf should not be less than six feet, so that the lower step takes away from it and the cushion two feet.

chunks.texto: laconicum sudationesque sunt coniungendae tepidario, eaeque quam latae fuerint, tantam altitudinem habeant ad imam curvaturam hemisphaerii. mediumque lumen in hemisphaerio relinquatur ex eoque clipeum aeneum catenis pendeat, per cuius reductiones et demissiones perficietur sudationis temperatura. ipsumque ad circinum fieri oportere videtur, ut aequaliter a medio flammae vaporisque vis per curvaturae rotundationes pervagetur.
chunks.traduccion: The laconic and the tepidariums are to be connected, and however wide they are, they should have as much height to the lowest curvature of the hemisphere. And a central lumen should be left in the hemisphere and from it a brass cup should hang with chains, by the reductions and lowerings of which the temperature of the sweating will be perfected. And it seems necessary to make it like a compass, so that the force of the flame and vapors from the middle should spread evenly through the roundings of the curvature.

chunks.texto: Nunc mihi videtur, tametsi non sint italicae consuetudinis palaestrarum aedificationes, traditae tamen explicare et quemadmodum apud Graecos constituantur monstrare. in palaestris peristylia quadrata sive oblonga ita sunt facienda uti duorum stadiorum habeant ambulationis circumitionem, quod Graeci vocant δίαυλον, ex quibus tres porticus simplices disponantur, quarta quae ad meridianas regiones est conversa, duplex, uti cum tempestates ventosae sint, non possit aspergo in interiorem partem pervenire.
chunks.traduccion: Now it seems to me that, even if they are not the buildings of the Italian custom of the gymnasiums, they should nevertheless explain the traditional ones and show how they are constructed among the Greeks. In the gymnasiums, square or oblong peristyles should be made so that they have a circumference of two stadia for walking, which the Greeks call δίαυλον, from which three simple porticos should be arranged, the fourth, which faces the southern regions, should be double, so that when there are windy storms, the spray cannot reach the inner part.

chunks.texto: constituantur autem in tribus porticibus exhedrae spatiosae, habentes sedes in quibus philosophi rhetores reliquique qui studiis delectantur sedentes disputare possint. in duplici autem porticu conlocentur haec membra. ephebeum in medio, hoc autem est exhedra amplissima cum sedibus, tertia parte longior sit quam lata. sub dextro coryceum, deinde proxime conisterium, a conisterio in versura porticus frigida lavatio, quam Graeci λουτρόν vocitant. ad sinistram ephebei elaeothesium, proxime autem elaeothesium <frigidarium>, ab eoque iter in propnigeum in versura porticus. proxima autem introrsus e regione frigidarii conlocetur concamerata sudatio longitudine duplex quam latitudo, quae habeat in versuris ex una parte laconicum ad eundem modum uti quam supra scriptum est, compositum, ex adverso laconici caldam lavationem. in palaestra peristylia, quemadmodum supra scriptum est, ita debent esse [perfecta] distributa.
chunks.traduccion: In the three porticos, spacious rooms should be set up, with seats in which philosophers, rhetoricians, and others who delight in studies can sit and debate. In the double portico, these members should be placed. The ephebeum in the middle, which is the largest exedra with seats, which is one-third longer than it is wide. On the right, the coryceum, then next to it, the conisterium, from the conisterium, in the turn of the portico, a cold bath, which the Greeks call λουτρόν. On the left, the ephebeum, the elaeothesium, and next to it, the elaeothesium, and from there a path to the propnigeum, in the turn of the portico. But next to it, inward, opposite the frigidarium, a conchamarata sweating room should be placed, twice as long as it is wide, which should have a laconic bath on one side in the turns in the same way as written above, and a hot bath on the opposite side of the laconic bath. In the palaestra, the peristyle, as written above, should be distributed in this way.

chunks.texto: extra autem disponantur porticus tres, una ex peristylo exeuntibus, duae dextra atque sinistra stadiatae, ex quibus una quae spectaverit ad septentrionem, perficiatur duplex amplissima latitudine, altera simplex ita factae uti in partibus quae fuerint circa parietes et quae erit ad columnas, margines habeant uti semitas non minus pedum denûm mediumque excavatum uti gradus sint in descensu marginibus sesquipedem ad planitiem, quae planities sit non minus pedes XII. ita qui vestiti ambulaverint circum in marginibus, non inpedientur ab unctis se exercentibus.
chunks.traduccion: Outside, three porticos are to be arranged, one leading from the peristyle, and two on the right and left, of which one, which faces north, is to be completed as a double, with a very ample width, the other single, so made that in the parts which will be around the walls and which will be at the columns, the edges should be like paths of not less than ten feet and the middle should be excavated so that there are steps in the descent from the edges, one half-foot to the plain, which plain should be no less than twelve feet. Thus, those who walk around the edges dressed will not be hindered by the anointed exercising themselves.

chunks.texto: haec autem porticus ξυστός apud Graecos vocitatur, quod athletae per hiberna tempora in tectis stadiis exercentur. proxime autem xystum et duplicem porticum designentur hypaethroe ambulationes, quas Graeci παραδρομίδες, nostri xysta appellant, in quas per hiemem ex xysto sereno caelo athletae prodeuntes exercentur. faciunda autem xysta sic videntur ut sint inter duas porticus silvae aut platanones et in his perficiantur inter arbores ambulationes ibique ex opere signino stationes. post xystum autem stadium ita figuratum ut possint hominum copiae cum laxamento athletas certantes spectare. Quae in moenibus necessaria videbantur esse ut apte disponantur, perscripsi.
chunks.traduccion: This portico is called the ξυστός among the Greeks, because athletes exercise in covered stadia during the winter months. Next to the xystum and the double portico are designated the hypaethroe walks, which the Greeks call παραδρομίδας, ours xysta, in which athletes, coming out of the xystum in clear weather, exercise during the winter. The xystum is made in such a way that there are forests or plane trees between the two porticos and in these walks are made between the trees and there are stations according to the work I design. After the xystum is the stadium, so shaped that crowds of people can watch the athletes competing with ease. I have written down what seemed to be necessary in the walls to be arranged appropriately.

chunks.texto: de opportunitate autem portuum non est praetermittendum, sed quibus rationibus tueantur naves in his ab tempestatibus explicandum. hi autem naturaliter si sint bene positi habeantque acroteria sive promunturia procurrentia, ex quibus introrsus curvaturae sive versurae ex loci natura fuerint conformatae, maximas utilitates videntur habere. circum enim porticus sive navalia sunt facienda sive ex porticibus aditus ad emporia, turresque ex utraque parte conlocandae, ex quibus catenae traduci per machinas possint.
chunks.traduccion: The suitability of harbors must also be considered, together with the means of protecting ships from storms. Natural sites offer great advantages when projecting headlands form inward-curving bays or sheltered angles. Build porticoes or shipyards around them, with access from the porticoes to the trading facilities. Place towers on both sides of the entrance, from which chains can be drawn across by machinery.

chunks.texto: Sin autem non naturalem locum neque idoneum ad tuendas ab tempestatibus naves habuerimus, ita videtur esse faciendum uti si nullum flumen in his locis inpedierit sed erit ex una parte statio, tunc ex altera parte structuris sive aggeribus expediantur progressus. et ita conformandae portuum conclusiones. eae autem structurae quae in aqua sunt futurae, videntur sic esse faciendae uti portetur pulvis a regionibus quae sunt a Cumis continuatae ad promunturium Minervae, isque misceatur uti in mortario duo ad unum respondeant.
chunks.traduccion: If there is no natural site suitable for sheltering ships from storms, proceed as follows. Where no river obstructs the site and there is an anchorage on one side, extend masonry works or embankments from the other to form the harbor enclosure. For structures to be built in water, bring volcanic powder from the region extending from Cumae to the promontory of Minerva and mix it into mortar in a ratio of two parts powder to one part lime.

chunks.texto: deinde tunc in eo loco qui definitus erit, arcae stipitibus robusteis et catenis inclusae in aquam demittendae destinandaeque firmiter, deinde inter ea extrastilis inferior pars sub aqua exaequanda et purganda, et caementis ex mortario, materia mixta quemadmodum supra scriptum est, ibi congerendum, doneque compleatur structurae spatium quod fuerit inter arcas. hoc autem munus naturale habent ea loca quae supra scripta sunt. Sin autem propter fluctus aut impetus aperti pelagi destinae arcas non potuerint continere, tunc ab ipsa terra sive crepidine pulvinus quam firmissime struatur, isque pulvinus exaequata struatur planitia minus quam dimidiae partis, reliquum quod est proxime litus, proclinatum latus habeat.
chunks.traduccion: Then, in the place that will be determined, the caissons (arcae), framed with stout posts and chains, are to be lowered into the water and firmly placed, then the lower part inside the water is to be leveled and cleaned with the help of the ladles, and rubble and mortar, the material mixed as described above, are to be piled there, until the structure is completed, filling the space between the arks. Now, the places described above have this natural function. But if, due to waves or the force of the open sea, the arks cannot be contained, then a cushion is to be built as firmly as possible from the land itself or from the shore, and this cushion, when leveled, is to be built so that less than half of the surface is level, the remainder, which is closest to the shore, has a sloping side.

chunks.texto: deinde ad ipsam aquam et latera pulvino circiter sesquipedales margines struantur aequilibres ex planitia quae est supra scripta, tunc proclinatio ea impleatur harena et exaequetur cum margine et planitia pulvini. deinde insuper eam exaequationem pila quam magna constituta fuerit ibi struatur, eaque cum erit extructa, relinquatur ne minus duos menses ut siccescat. tunc autem succidatur margo quae sustinet harenam. ita harena fluctibus subruta efficiet in mare pilae praecipitationem. hac ratione quotienscumque opus fuerit, in aquam poterit esse progressus.
chunks.traduccion: Then, to the water itself and the sides of the cushion, margins of about one and a half feet are built, equal to the level described above. Then, that slope is filled with sand and made equal to the edge and level of the cushion. Then, on top of that leveling, a large pile is built there, and when it is built, it is left for at least two months to dry. Then, however, the edge that supports the sand is cut away. Thus, the sand, crushed by the waves, will cause the pile to precipitate into the sea. In this way, whenever necessary, it will be possible to advance into the water.

chunks.texto: In quibus autem locis pulvis non nascitur, his rationibus erit faciendum uti arcae duplices relatis tabulis et catenis conligatae in eo loco qui finitus erit constituantur, et inter destinas creta in aeronibus ex ulva palustri factis calcetur. cum ita bene calcatum et quam densissime fuerit, tunc cocleis rotis tympanis conlocatis locus qui ea saeptione finitus fuerit exinaniatur sicceturque, et ibi inter saeptiones fundamenta fodiantur. si terrena erunt, usque ad solidum crassiora quam qui murus supra futurus erit, et tunc structura ex caementis calce et harena compleantur.
chunks.traduccion: In places where pozzolana (pulvis) is not found, it will be necessary to do this by placing double caissons, tied together with burnt sticks and chains, in the place that will be finished, and between the designated places, chalk will be trampled in aerofoils made of marsh bulrush. When it has been trampled well and as densely as possible, then with augers and drum wheels placed, the place that will be finished with that partition will be emptied and dried, and there between the partitions the foundations will be dug. If they will be earthen, they will be emptied and dried until solid, thicker than the wall that will be above, and then the structure will be completed with rubble, lime, and sand.

chunks.texto: sin autem mollis locus erit, palis ustilatis alneis aut oleagineis configantur et carbonibus compleantur, quemadmodum in theatrorum et muri fundationibus est scriptum. deinde tunc quadrato saxo murus ducatur iuncturis quam longissimis, uti maxime medii lapides coagmentis contineantur. tunc qui locus erit inter murum ruderatione sive structura compleatur. ita erit uti possit turris insuper aedificari.
chunks.traduccion: But if the place is soft, it is to be driven with piles of charred alder or olive-wood and packed with charcoal, as is written in the foundations of theaters and walls. Then the wall is to be built with squared stone with the joints as long as possible, so that the middle stones are held together with mortar. Then whatever space there is between the wall is to be filled with rubble or masonry. It will be so that a tower can be built on top.

chunks.texto: His perfectis navaliorum ea erit ratio ut constituantur spectantia maxime ad septentrionem. nam meridianae regiones propter aestus cariem tineam teredines reliquaque bestiarum nocentium genera procreant alendoque conservant, eaque aedificia minime sunt materianda propter incendia. de magnitudinibus autem finitio nulla debet esse, sed faciunda ad maximum navium modum, uti etsi maiores naves subductae fuerint, habeant cum laxamento ibi conlocationem. Quae necessaria ad utilitatem in civitatibus publicorum locorum succurrere mihi potuerunt, quemadmodum constituantur et perficiantur in hoc volumine scripsi, privatorum autem aedificiorum utilitates et eorum symmetrias insequenti volumine ratiocinabor
chunks.traduccion: When these are completed, the plan for the shipyards will be to build those facing mainly to the north. For the southern regions, because of the heat, breed and nourish moths, beetles, and other kinds of harmful animals, and those buildings should be least materialized because of fires. There should be no limitation on the sizes, but the maximum size of the ships should be made, so that even if larger ships are removed, they can still be accommodated there with ease. I have written in this volume how these necessary utilities in the cities of public places can be of assistance to me, but I will discuss the utilities and their symmetries of private buildings in the following volume.

chunks.texto: Aristippus philosophus Socraticus naufragio cum eiectus ad Rhodiensium litus animadvertisset geometrica schemata descripta, exclamavisse ad comites ita dicitur bene speremus, hominum enim vestigia video statimque in oppidum Rhodum contendit et recta gymnasium devenit, ibique de philosophia disputans muneribus est donatus, ut non tantum se ornaret sed etiam eis qui una fuerunt et vestitum et cetera quae opus essent ad victum praestaret. cum autem eius comites in patriam reverti voluissent interrogarentque eum quidnam vellet domum renuntiari, tunc ita mandavit dicere, eiusmodi possessiones et viatica liberis oportere parari quae etiam e naufragio una possent enatare.
chunks.traduccion: Aristippus, the Socratic philosopher, shipwrecked and cast ashore on the coast of Rhodes, noticed geometrical figures drawn in the sand and is said to have cried out to his companions: “Let us be of good hope, for I see the traces of men.” He made at once for the city of Rhodes and went straight to the gymnasium, where, discoursing on philosophy, he was rewarded with gifts so generous that he could provide not only for himself but also for those who were with him, with clothing and everything else needed for life. When his companions wished to return home and asked what message he would have them carry back, he bade them say this: that children ought to be furnished with such possessions and such provisions for the journey as could swim ashore with them even from a shipwreck.

chunks.texto: namque ea vera praesidia sunt vitae quibus neque fortunae tempestas iniqua neque publicarum rerum mutatio neque belli vastatio potest nocere. non minus eam sententiam augendo Theophrastus, hortando doctos potius esse quam pecuniae confidentes ita ponit, doctum ex omnibus solum neque in alienis locis peregrinum neque amissis familiaribus et necessariis inopem amicorum sed in omni civitate esse civem difficilesque fortunae sine timore posse despicere casus, at qui non doctrinarum sed felicitatis praesidiis putaret se esse vallatum, labidis itineribus vadentem non stabili sed infirma conflictari vita.
chunks.traduccion: For these are the true safeguards of life: neither the adverse storms of fortune, nor upheavals in public affairs, nor the devastation of war can harm them. Theophrastus develops the same idea, urging people to become learned rather than to put their trust in wealth. The educated person alone is not a stranger in foreign lands or left without friends when family and companions are lost; in every city such a person is a citizen and can face the hazards of fortune without fear. By contrast, one who trusts in good luck rather than learning walks on slippery paths and struggles through a fragile, uncertain life.

chunks.texto: Epicurus vero non dissimiliter ait pauca sapientibus fortunam tribuere, quae autem maxima et necessaria sunt, animi mentisque cogitationibus gubernari. haec ita etiam plures philosophi dixerunt. non minus poetae qui antiquas comoedias graece scripserunt, easdem sententias versibus in scaena pronuntiaverunt, ut Crates Chionides Aristophanes, maxime etiam cum his Alexis, qui Athenienses ait oportere ideo laudari quod omnium Graecorum leges cogunt parentes <ali> a liberis, Atheniensium non omnes nisi eos qui liberos artibus erudissent. omnia enim munera fortunae cum dantur ab ea faciliter adimuntur, disciplinae vero coniunctae cum animis nullo tempore deficiunt, sed permanent stabiliter ad summum exitum vitae.
chunks.traduccion: Epicurus likewise says that fortune grants the wise relatively little, whereas the greatest and most necessary matters are governed by thought and judgment. Many other philosophers held the same view. The authors of ancient Greek comedy — Crates, Chionides, Aristophanes and, above all, Alexis — expressed similar ideas on stage. Alexis praises the Athenians because, whereas Greek laws generally require children to support their parents, the Athenians impose that duty only in respect of parents who have taught their children an art. Fortune may take away everything it has given; learning, once joined to the mind, remains steadfast to the end of life.

chunks.texto: itaque ego maximas infinitasque parentibus ago atque habeo gratias, quod Atheniensium legem probantes me arte erudiendum curaverunt, et ea quae non potest esse probata sine litteratura encyclioque doctrinarum omnium disciplina. cum ergo et parentium cura et praeceptorum doctrinis auctas haberem copias disciplinarum, philologis et philotechnis rebus commentariorumque scripturis me delectans eas possessiones animo paravi, e quibus haec est fructuum summa, nullas plus habendi esse necessitates eamque esse proprietatem divitiarum maxime, nihil desiderare. sed forte nonnulli haec levia iudicantes putant eos esse sapientes qui pecunia sunt copiosi. itaque plerique ad id propositum contendentes audacia adhibita cum divitiis etiam notitiam sunt consecuti.
chunks.traduccion: I therefore give and owe the greatest, indeed boundless, thanks to my parents, who, approving the law of the Athenians, took care that I should be trained in an art, and in one that cannot be mastered without letters and the encyclopedic education that embraces all the disciplines. Having thus enlarged my store of learning through my parents’ care and my teachers’ instruction, and delighting in literary and technical studies and in the writing of treatises, I acquired for my mind possessions whose chief fruit is this: that one has no need to possess more, and that the truest property of wealth is to desire nothing. Some, perhaps, think these things of little account and hold that the wise are those who abound in money. Many, therefore, pursuing that aim with boldness, have won notoriety together with riches.

chunks.texto: ego autem, Caesar, non ad pecuniam parandam ex arte dedi studium, sed potius tenuitatem cum bona fama quam abundantiam cum infamia sequendam probavi. ideo notities parum est adsecuta. sed tamen his voluminibus editis, ut spero, etiam posteris ero notus. neque est mirandum quid ita pluribus sim ignotus. ceteri architecti rogant et ambiunt ut architectent, mihi autem a praeceptoribus est traditum rogatum non rogantem oportere suscipere curam, quod ingenuus color movetur pudore petendo rem suspiciosam. nam beneficium dantes non accipientes ambiuntur. quid enim putemus suspicari qui rogetur de patrimonio sumptus faciendos committere gratiae petentis, nisi praedae compendiique eius causa iudicet faciundum?.
chunks.traduccion: I, however, Caesar, have not applied myself to making money by my art; I have preferred slender means with a good name to abundance with disrepute. For this reason I have gained little renown. Yet, now that these volumes are published, I hope to be known even to posterity. Nor should it surprise anyone that I am unknown to so many. Other architects solicit and canvass for commissions; but I was taught by my masters that one should undertake a charge when asked, not by asking, because a freeborn man’s complexion is changed by shame when he petitions for something that arouses suspicion. For it is those who confer a favor who are courted, not those who receive it. What, then, are we to suppose a man suspects when he is asked to entrust the spending of his patrimony to the goodwill of a petitioner, if not that the petitioner judges the work worth doing for his own plunder and profit?

chunks.texto: itaque maiores primum a genere probatis operam tradebant architectis, deinde quaerebant si honeste essent educati, ingenuo pudori non audaciae protervitatis permittendum iudicantes. ipsi autem artifices non erudiebant nisi suos liberos aut cognatos et eos viros bonos instituebant, quibus tantarum rerum fidei pecuniae sine dubitatione permitterentur. Cum autem animadverto ab indoctis et inperitis tantae disciplinae magnitudinem iactari et ab îs qui non modo <> architecturae sed omnino ne fabricae quidem notitiam habent, non possum non laudare patres familiarum eos qui litteraturae fiducia confirmati per se aedificantes ita iudicant, si inperitis sit committendum, ipsos potius digniores esse ad suam voluntatem quam ad alienam pecuniae consumere summam.
chunks.traduccion: Our predecessors therefore entrusted building works first to architects whose family standing had been tested, and then enquired whether they had received an honorable education. They judged that responsibility should rest with the restraint of a freeborn man, rather than the audacity of the shameless. Craftsmen themselves trained only their sons or relatives, forming them as upright men to whose integrity funds for important works could safely be entrusted. Yet when I see so great a discipline handled at the whim of the uneducated and inexperienced, including men who know neither architecture nor even the craft of building, I cannot but commend those householders who, trusting in their literary education, build for themselves. If the work must be entrusted to the inexperienced, they judge themselves more entitled to spend their money according to their own judgment than according to someone else’s.

chunks.texto: itaque nemo artem ullam aliam conatur domi facere, uti sutrinam fullonicam aut ex ceteris quae sunt faciliores, nisi architecturam, ideo quod qui profitentur non arte vera sed falso nominantur architecti. quas ob res corpus architecturae rationesque eius putavi diligentissime conscribendas, opinans munus omnibus gentibus non ingratum futurum. igitur quoniam in quinto de opportunitate communium operum perscripsi, in hoc volumine privatorum aedificiorum ratiocinationes et commensus symmetriarum explicabo.
