chunks.traduccion: Thus no one attempts to practise any other art at home — shoemaking, fulling or any of the other easier crafts — except architecture, because those who profess it are called architects not by virtue of true art but falsely. For these reasons I judged that the body of architecture and its principles should be set down with the utmost care, believing that this would be a service not unwelcome to all peoples. Accordingly, since in the fifth book I have written of the fitness of public works, in this volume I shall set out the principles of private buildings and the commensurability of their proportions.

chunks.texto: Haec autem ita erunt recte disposita, si primo animadversum fuerit quibus regionibus aut quibus inclinationibus mundi constituantur. namque aliter Aegypto, aliter Hispania, non eodem modo Ponto, dissimiliter Romae, item ceteris terrarum et regionum proprietatibus oportere videntur constitui genera aedificiorum, quod alia parte solis cursu premitur tellus, alia longe ab eo distat, alia per medium temperatur. igitur uti constitutio mundi ad terrae spatium inclinatione signiferi circuli et solis cursu disparibus qualitatibus naturaliter est conlocata, ad eundem modum etiam ad regionum rationes caelique varietates videntur aedificiorum debere dirigi conlocationes.
chunks.traduccion: These buildings will be rightly disposed if attention is first paid to the regions and latitudes of the world in which they are set. For it seems that the kinds of building ought to be constituted in one way in Egypt, in another in Spain, not in the same way in Pontus, differently at Rome, and so on according to the properties of other lands and regions; for in one part the earth is oppressed by the course of the sun, in another it lies far from it, and in another it is tempered by an intermediate position. Therefore, just as the constitution of the heavens in relation to the extent of the earth is naturally disposed with unequal qualities by the inclination of the zodiac and the course of the sun, so the disposition of buildings ought likewise to be governed by the character of each region and the variety of its climate.

chunks.texto: sub septentrione aedificia testudinata et maxime conclusa et non patentia sed conversa ad calidas partes oportere fieri videntur. contra autem sub impetu solis meridianis regionibus, quod premuntur a calore, patentiora conversaque ad septentrionem et aquilonem sunt faciunda. ita quod ultra natura laedit, arte erit emendandum. item reliquis regionibus ad eundem modum <debet> temperari, quemadmodum caelum est ad inclinationem mundi conlocatum.
chunks.traduccion: In the north, it seems, buildings should be vaulted, closed in as much as possible rather than open, and turned towards the warm quarters. In southern regions, on the contrary, which lie under the full force of the sun and are oppressed by its heat, they should be built more open and turned towards the north and north-east. Thus what nature harms by excess must be corrected by art. In the other regions, too, buildings must be tempered in the same way, according to how the climate is disposed in relation to the inclination of the world.

chunks.texto: Haec autem ex natura rerum sunt animadvertenda et consideranda atque etiam ex membris corporibusque gentium observanda. namque sol quibus locis mediocriter profundit vapores, in his conservat corpora temperata, quaeque proxime currendo deflagrat, eripit exurendo temperaturam umoris. contra vero refrigeratis regionibus, quod absunt a meridie longe, non exhauritur a caloribus umor, sed ex caelo roscidus aer in corpora fundens umorem efficit ampliores corporaturas vocisque sonitus graviores. ex eo quoque quae sub septentrionibus nutriuntur gentes inmanibus corporibus, candidis coloribus, directo capillo et rufo, oculis caesis, sanguine multo ab umoris plenitate caelique refrigerationibus sunt conformati.
chunks.traduccion: These matters are to be observed and considered from the nature of things, and also studied in the limbs and bodies of peoples. For where the sun pours out its heat in moderation, it keeps bodies temperate; where it runs close and scorches, it burns away their due proportion of moisture; in cold regions, on the other hand, which lie far from the south, moisture is not drawn off by heat, but the dewy air, pouring moisture from the sky into bodies, produces larger frames and deeper voices. Hence, too, the peoples reared under the north are formed with huge bodies, fair complexions, straight red hair, gray-blue eyes and abundant blood, because of the fullness of moisture and the coldness of the climate;

chunks.texto: qui autem sunt proximi ad axem meridianum subiectique solis cursui, brevioribus corporibus, colore fusco, crispo capillo, oculis nigris, cruribus validis, sanguine exiguo solis impetu perficiuntur. itaque etiam propter sanguinis exiguitatem timidiores sunt ferro resistere, sed ardores ac febres sufferunt sine timore, quod nutrita sunt eorum membra cum fervore. itemque corpora quae nascuntur sub septentrione a febri sunt timidiora et inbecilla, sanguinis autem abundantia ferro resistunt sine timore.
chunks.traduccion: those, on the other hand, who live nearest to the southern pole and beneath the course of the sun are formed by its force with shorter bodies, dark complexions, curly hair, black eyes, strong legs and little blood. Hence, because of the scarcity of their blood, they are more afraid of resisting the sword, but they endure heat and fevers without fear, since their limbs have been nourished in heat; whereas bodies born under the north are more fearful of fever and weaker against it, but, owing to the abundance of their blood, they resist the sword without fear.

chunks.texto: Non minus sonus vocis in generibus gentium dispares et varias habet qualitates, ideo quod terminatio orientis et occidentis circa terrae librationem, qua dividitur pars superior et inferior mundi, habere videtur libratam naturali modo circumitionem, quam etiam mathematici ὁρίζοντα dicunt. igitur cum id habemus certum ab imo sustinens, ab labro quod est in regione septentrionali, linea traiecta ad id quod est supra meridianum axem ab eoque altera obliqua in altitudinem ad summum cardinem qui est post stellas septentrionum, sine dubitatione animadvertemus ex eo esse schema trigonii mundo, uti organi quam σαμβύκη graeci dicunt.
chunks.traduccion: No less does the sound of the voice have unequal and varied qualities among the different kinds of peoples, because the boundary of east and west around the level of the earth, by which the upper and lower parts of the world are divided, appears to have a circuit naturally leveled, which the mathematicians also call ὁρίζων, the horizon. Taking this as certain, if a line is drawn from the edge in the northern region to the edge above the southern axis, and from there another line obliquely upwards to the highest pole, behind the stars of the Bear, we shall perceive without doubt that the world thereby has the figure of a triangle, like that of the instrument the Greeks call σαμβύκη, the sambuca.

chunks.texto: itaque quod est spatium proximum imo cardini ab axis linea in meridianis finibus, sub eo loco quae sunt nationes propter brevitatem altitudinis ad mundum sonitum vocis faciunt tenuem et acutissimum, uti in organo chorda quae est proxima angulo. secundum eam autem reliquae ad mediam Graeciam remissiones efficiunt in nationibus sonorum scansione, item a medio in ordinem crescendo ad extremos septentriones sub altitudines caeli nationum spiritus sonitibus gravioribus a natura rerum exprimuntur. ita videtur mundi conceptio tota propter inclinationem consonantissime per solis temperaturam ad harmoniam esse composita.
chunks.traduccion: Accordingly, the peoples who dwell in the space nearest the lower pole, in the southern regions measured from the line of the axis, produce a thin and very high-pitched sound of voice because of their small elevation in relation to the world, like the string nearest the angle of the instrument. Next to them, the other peoples, as far as central Greece, produce successive descents in the scale of sounds. Likewise, increasing in due order from the middle to the farthest north, beneath the heights of the sky, the breath of the peoples is uttered by nature in deeper tones. Thus the whole conception of the world, because of its inclination, appears to be composed in perfect consonance, through the tempering of the sun, according to harmony.

chunks.texto: igitur quae nationes sunt inter axis meridiani cardinem ac septentrionalis medio positae, uti in diagrammate musico medianae vocis habent sonitum in sermone, quaeque progredientibus ad septentrionem sunt nationes, quod altiores habent distantias mundi, spiritus vocis habentes umore repulsos ad hypatas et proslambanomenon, a natura rerum sonitu graviore coguntur uti. eadem ratione e medio progredientibus ad meridiem gentes paranetarum <netarum> que acutissimam sonitus vocis perficiunt tenuitatem.
chunks.traduccion: Therefore the peoples situated midway between the pole of the southern axis and that of the northern have in their speech the sound of the middle voice, as in the musical diagram; the peoples one meets advancing towards the north, because they lie at greater distances in relation to the world, have the breath of their voices driven back by moisture towards the hypatae and the proslambanomenos, and are compelled by nature to use a deeper sound; and by the same reasoning the peoples one meets advancing from the middle towards the south produce the extreme, high-pitched thinness of voice of the paranetae and the netae.

chunks.texto: hoc autem verum esse, ex umidis naturae locis graviora fieri et ex fervidis acutiora, licet ita experiendo animadvertere. calices duo in una fornace aeque cocti aequoque pondere ad crepitumque uno sonitu sumantur. ex his unus in aquam demittatur, postea ex aqua eximatur, tunc utrique tangantur. cum enim ita factum fuerit, largiter inter eos sonitus discrepabit aequoque pondere non poterunt esse. ita et hominum corpora uno genere figurationis et una mundi coniunctione concepta alia propter regionis ardorem acutum spiritum aeris exprimunt acutum, alia propter umoris abundantiam gravissimas effundunt sonorum qualitates.
chunks.traduccion: That this is true — that moist places by nature produce deeper sounds and hot places higher ones — may be observed by the following experiment. Take two cups fired equally in the same kiln, of equal weight and giving the same note when struck. Plunge one of them into water and then take it out; then strike both. When this has been done, the sound will differ widely between them, and they can no longer be of equal weight. In the same way the bodies of men, though conceived with one kind of form and under one conjunction of the heavens, emit in some cases a sharp breath because of the heat of the region, and in others, because of the abundance of moisture, pour out sounds of the deepest quality.

chunks.texto: Item propter tenuitatem caeli meridianae nationes ex acuta fervore mente expeditius celeriusque moventur ad consiliorum cogitationes. septentrionales autem gentes infusae crassitudine caeli, propter obstantiam aeris umore refrigeratae stupentes habent mentes. hoc autem ita esse a serpentibus licet aspicere, quae per calorem cum exhaustam habent umoris refrigerationem, tunc acerrime moventur, per brumalia autem et hiberna tempora ab mutatione caeli refrigeratae, inmotae sunt stupore. ita non est mirandum, si acutiores efficit calidus aer hominum mentes, refrigeratus autem contra tardiores.
chunks.traduccion: Moreover, owing to the thinness of the air, the southern peoples, their minds made keen by heat, are quicker and readier in devising counsel; whereas the northern peoples, steeped in a dense and humid air and their wits chilled by its resistance, are slow and dull. The like may be seen in serpents, which move most nimbly in the heat, when their moisture is drawn off, but in the cold of winter, numbed by the change of climate, lie torpid. It is no wonder, then, that warm air makes the mind keener, and cold air the duller.

chunks.texto: cum sint autem meridiane nationes animis acutissimis infinitaque sollertia consiliorum, simul ut ad fortitudinem ingrediuntur ibi succumbunt, quod habent exsuctas ab sole animorum virtutes. qui vero refrigeratis nascuntur regionibus, ad armorum vehementiam paratiores sunt magnis virtutibus sine timore, sed tarditate animi sine considerantia inruentes sine sollertia suis consiliis refragantur. cum ergo haec ita sint ab natura rerum in mundo conlocata et omnes nationes inmoderatis mixtionibus disparatae, veros inter spatium totius orbis terrarum regionesque medio mundi populus Romanus possidet fines.
chunks.traduccion: But although the southern nations have the keenest minds and boundless ingenuity in counsel, the moment they enter upon deeds of courage they fail, for the sun has drained the vigor from their spirits; whereas those born in colder regions are readier for the clash of arms and charge without fear in their great courage, yet, being slow of mind, they rush in without judgment and so thwart their own designs. Since nature has so ordered these things throughout the world, and all the nations differ in their unequal blendings, it is in the true mean, midway between the regions of the whole earth, that the Roman people hold their dominion.

chunks.texto: namque temperatissimae ad utramque partem et corporum membris animorumque vigoribus pro fortitudine sunt in Italia gentes. quemadmodum enim Iovis stella inter Martis ferventissimam et Saturni frigidissimam media currens temperatur, eadem ratione Italia inter septentrionalem meridianamque ab utraque parte mixtionibus temperatas et invictas habet laudes. itaque consiliis refringit barbarorum virtutes, forti manu meridianorum cogitationes. ita divina mens civitatem populi Romani egregia temperataque regione conlocavit, uti orbis terrarum imperii potiretur.
chunks.traduccion: For the races of Italy are the most temperate on either hand, alike in bodily frame and in strength of mind for valour. Just as the planet Jupiter, coursing between the burning heat of Mars and the icy cold of Saturn, is thereby tempered, so Italy, lying between north and south, is blended of both and holds praises unsurpassed: by counsel she breaks the courage of the barbarians, and by strength of hand the designs of the southern peoples. Thus the divine mind set the city of the Roman people in a region excellent and temperate, that it might win the empire of the whole earth.

chunks.texto: quodsi ita est uti dissimiles regiones ab inclinationibus caeli variis generibus sint comparatae, ut etiam naturae gentium disparibus animis et corporum figuris qualitatibusque nascerentur, non dubitemus aedificiorum quoque rationes ad nationum gentiumque proprietates apte distribuere, cum habeamus ab ipsa rerum natura sollertem et expeditam monstrationem. Quoad potui summa ratione proprietates locorum ab natura rerum dispositas animadvertere exposui et quemadmodum ad solis cursum et inclinationes caeli oporteat ad gentium figuras constituere aedificiorum qualitates dixi. itaque nunc singulorum generum in aedificiis commensus symmetriarum et universos et separatos breviter explicabo.
chunks.traduccion: But if it is so that dissimilar regions are arranged in various kinds by the inclinations of the sky, so that the natures of nations are born with dissimilar minds and shapes and qualities of bodies, let us not doubt that the proportions of buildings also are aptly distributed according to the properties of the nations, since we have a skilful and ready demonstration from the nature of things themselves. I have explained as far as I could observe the properties of places arranged by the nature of things with the greatest reason, and I have said how the qualities of buildings should be arranged according to the shapes of nations according to the course of the sun and the inclinations of the sky. Therefore I will now briefly explain the commensurate symmetries of each kind in buildings, both universal and separate.

chunks.texto: Nulla architecto maior cura esse debet nisi uti proportionibus ratae partis habeant aedificia rationum exactiones. cum ergo constituta symmetriarum ratio fuerit et commensus ratiocinationibus explicati, tum etiam acuminis est proprium providere ad naturam loci aut usum aut speciem < detractionibus aut> adiectionibus temperaturas ⟨et⟩ efficere, cum de symmetria sit detractum aut adiectum, uti id videatur recte esse formatum in aspectuque nihil desideretur.
chunks.traduccion: No architect should have greater care than that the buildings should have the exactitudes of the proportions of the approved part. Therefore, when the system of symmetries has been established and has been measured by explained reasoning, then it is also characteristic of acumen to provide for the nature of the place or the use or the appearance <and to effect tempers by deductions or> additions, when symmetry has been subtracted or added, so that it appears to be correctly formed and nothing is wanting in appearance.

chunks.texto: alia enim ad manum species esse videtur, alia in excelso, non eadem in concluso, dissimilis in aperto, in quibus magni iudicii est opera quid tandem sit faciundum. non enim veros videtur habere visus effectus, sed fallitur saepius iudicio ab eo mens. quemadmodum etiam in scaenis pictis videntur columnarum proiecturae, mutulorum ecphorae, signorum figurae prominentes, cum sit tabula sine dubio ad regulam plana. similiter in navibus remi cum sint sub aqua directi, tamen oculis infracti videntur, et quatenus eorum partes tangunt summam planitiem liquoris, apparent uti sunt directi, cum vero sub aqua sunt demissi, per naturae perlucidam raritatem remittunt enatantes ab suis corporibus fluentes imagines ad summam aquae planitiem atque eae ibi commotae efficere videntur infractum remorum oculis aspectum.
chunks.traduccion: For there seems to be one kind of appearance at hand, another in a lofty place, not the same in a confined place, unlike in an open place, in which it is a matter of great judgment what is to be done. For the sight does not seem to have true effects, but the mind is often deceived by its judgment. Just as in painted scenes the projections of columns, the eaves of the masts, the figures of signs are seen to be prominent, when the table is undoubtedly level to the rule. Similarly, in ships, when the oars are straight under water, they nevertheless appear to be broken to the eye, and insofar as their parts touch the highest level of the liquid, they appear to be straight, but when they are lowered under water, by the transparent rarity of nature, they send back floating images flowing from their bodies to the highest level of the water, and these, being moved there, seem to produce a broken appearance of the oars to the eye.

chunks.texto: hoc autem sive simulacrorum inpulsu seu radiorum ex oculis effusionibus uti physicis placet videmus, utraque ratione videtur ita esse uti falsa iudicia oculorum habeat aspectus.
chunks.traduccion: Now, whether we see this through the impact of images or through the effusions of rays from the eyes, as is pleasing to the physical, for both reasons it seems to be the case that the eyes have false judgments of appearance.

chunks.texto: cum ergo quae sunt vera falsa videantur et nonnulla aliter quam sunt oculis probentur, non puto oportere esse dubium quin ad locorum naturas aut necessitates detractiones aut adiectiones fieri debeant sed ita uti nihil in his operibus desideretur. haec autem etiam ingeniorum acuminibus non solum doctrinis efficiuntur.
chunks.traduccion: Therefore, since what is true is seen as false and is proved to the eye in some way than it is, I do not think there should be any doubt that deductions or additions should be made according to the nature or necessities of the place, so that nothing is wanting in these works. But these things are also accomplished by the acumen of genius, not only by doctrine.

chunks.texto: igitur statuenda est primum ratio symmetriarum, a qua sumatur sine dubitatione commutatio. deinde explicetur operis futuri locorum imum spatium longitudinis <et latitudinis>, cuius cum semel constituta fuerit magnitudo, sequatur eam proportionis ad decorem apparatio, uti non sit considerantibus aspectus eurythmiae dubius. de qua quibus rationibus efficiatur est mihi pronuntiandum, primumque de cavis aedium uti fieri debeant dicam.
chunks.traduccion: First establish the system of proportions [from which any modification can confidently be derived]. Then set out the fundamental length and width of the intended building. Once its dimensions have been fixed, arrange its proportions in accordance with decor, so that its eurythmy is clear to the observer. I must explain how this is achieved, beginning with the arrangement of the courts of houses.

chunks.texto: Cava aedium quinque generibus sunt distincta, quorum ita figurae nominantur, tuscanicum, corinthium, tetrastylon, displuviatum, testudinatum. tuscanica sunt in quibus trabes in atrii latitudine traiectae habeant interpensiva et collicias ab angulis parietum ad angulos tignorum intercurrentes, item asseribus stillicidiorum in medium compluvium deiectus. in corinthiis isdem rationibus trabes et compluvia conlocantur, sed a parietibus trabes recedentes in circumitionis circa columnas componuntur. tetrastyla sunt quae subiectis sub trabibus angularibus columnis et utilitatem trabibus et firmitatem praestant, quod neque ipsae magnum impetum coguntur habere neque ab interpensivis onerantur.
chunks.traduccion: The central courts of houses, or cava aedium, are divided into five types: Tuscan, Corinthian, tetrastyle, displuviate and testudinate. In the Tuscan type, beams spanning the width of the atrium carry the cross-members and valleys that run from the corners of the walls to the corners of the beams; the rafters direct the rain toward the central compluvium. In the Corinthian type, the beams and compluvium are arranged on the same principles, but the beams are set back from the walls and supported on columns around the opening. The tetrastyle type has columns beneath the beams at the corners, giving practical support and stability: the beams need neither span so great a distance nor bear the load of the intervening members unsupported.

chunks.texto: displuviata autem sunt in quibus deliquiae arcam sustinentes stillicidia reiciunt. haec hibernaculis maxime praestant utilitates, quod compluvia eorum erecta non obstant luminibus tricliniorum. sed ea habent in refectionibus molestiam magnam, quod circa parietes stillicidia defluentia cum tument fistulae, quae non celeriter recipiunt ex canalibus aquam defluentem, itaque redundantes restagnant et intestinum et parietes in eis generibus aedificiorum corrumpunt. testudinata vero ibi fiunt, ubi non sunt impetus magni et in contignationibus supra spatiosae redduntur habitationes.
chunks.traduccion: There are rain-pits in which the drops, supporting the ark, are rejected. These are of the greatest use to winter quarters, because their rain-pits, when erected, do not obstruct the lights of the dining rooms. But they are a great nuisance in the kitchens, because around the walls the dripping water is contained by pipes which do not quickly receive the water flowing from the channels, and therefore overflowing, it stagnates and corrupts the interior and walls of those types of buildings. But the vaulted ones are made where there are no great draughts and the dwellings are made spacious on the upper floors.

chunks.texto: Atriorum vero latitudines ac longitudines tribus generibus formantur. et primum genus distribuitur uti longitudo cum in quinque partes divisa fuerit, tres partes latitudini dentur, alterum cum in tres partes dividatur, duae partes latitudini tribuantur, tertium uti latitudo in quadrato paribus lateribus describatur inque eo quadrato diagonios linea ducatur, et quantum spatium habuerit ea linea diagonii, tanta longitudo atrio detur.
chunks.traduccion: The breadth and length of atria are determined by three types. The first is laid out so that, the length being divided into five parts, three are given to the breadth; the second, the length being divided into three parts, assigns two to the breadth; the third is set out by describing upon the breadth a square with equal sides, drawing a diagonal across that square, and giving the atrium a length equal to that diagonal.

chunks.texto: Altitudo eorum, quanta longitudo fuerit quarta dempta, sub trabes extollatur; reliquum lacunariorum et arcae supra trabes spatio tribuatur. Alis dextra ac sinistra latitudinis ⟨spatium⟩, cum sit atrii longitudo ab XXX pedibus ad pedes XL, ex tertia parte eius constituatur. ab XL ad pedes L longitudo dividatur in partes tres ⟨semis⟩, ex his una pars alis detur. cum autem erit longitudo ab quinquaginta pedibus ad sexaginta, quarta pars longitudinis alis tribuatur. a pedibus LX ad LXXX longitudo dividatur in partes quattuor et dimidiam, ex his una pars fiat alarum latitudo. a pedibus octoginta ad pedes centum in quinque partes divisa longitudo iustam constituerit latitudinem alarum. trabes earum liminares ita altae ponantur, ut altitudines latitudinibus sint aequales. imagines cum suis ornamentis ad latitudinem alarum sint constitutae.
chunks.traduccion: Raise the atrium to the underside of the beams to a height equal to its length less one-quarter; allow the remaining space for the coffering and structure above the beams. The widths of the alae on either side should be proportioned to the atrium’s length. For a length of thirty to forty feet, give them one-third; for forty to fifty feet, divide the length into three and a half parts and give them one; for fifty to sixty feet, give them one-quarter; for sixty to eighty feet, divide it into four and a half parts and give them one; for eighty to one hundred feet, divide it into five parts to establish their width. Set their lintel beams at a height equal to the width of the alae. Arrange the ancestral images and their ornaments in proportion to that width.

chunks.texto: Tablinum, si latitudo atrii erit pedum viginti, dempta tertia eius spatio, reliquum tribuatur. si erit ab pedibus XXX ad XL, ex atrii latitudine tablino dimidium tribuatur. cum autem ab XL ad LX, latitudo dividatur in partes quinque, ex his duae tablino constituantur. non enim atria minora maioribus easdem possunt habere symmetriarum rationes. si enim maiorum symmetriis utemur in minoribus, neque tablina neque alae utilitatem poterunt habere, sin autem minorum in maioribus utemur, vasta et inmania in his ea erunt membra. itaque generatim magnitudinum rationes exquisitas et utilitati et aspectui conscribendas putavi.
chunks.traduccion: For the tablinum, if the breadth of the atrium is twenty feet, a third part being deducted, the remainder is assigned to it; if from thirty to forty feet, half the breadth is given to the tablinum; and from forty to sixty, the breadth is divided into five parts, of which two are assigned to it. For the smaller atria cannot have the same proportions as the larger.

chunks.texto: altitudo tablini ad trabem adiecta latitudinis octava constituatur. lacunaria eius tertia latitudinis ad altitudinem adiecta extollantur. fauces minoribus atriis e tablini latitudine dempta tertia, maioribus dimidia constituantur.. Latitudines ostiorum ad altitudinem si dorica erunt uti dorica, si ionica erunt uti ionica perficiantur, quemadmodum de thyromatis in quarto libro rationes symmetriarum sunt expositae. compluvii lumen latum latitudinis atrii ne minus quarta, ne plus tertia parte relinquatur, longitudo uti atrii pro rata parte fiat.
chunks.traduccion: The height of the tabulin added to the beam is to be one-eighth of the width. Its ceilings are to be raised by one-third of the width added to the height. The openings for the smaller atriums are to be one-third deducted from the width of the tabulin, and for the larger ones, half. The images are also to be set high with their ornaments to the width of the wings. The widths of the forum to the height, if they are Doric, are to be completed as Doric, if they are Ionic, as Ionic, as the reasons for symmetry are explained in the fourth book of the Thyromata. The width of the floodlight is to be left no less than a quarter, no more than a third, the length is to be made as the proportion of the atrium.

chunks.texto: Peristyla autem in transverso tertia parte longiora sint quam introrsus, columnae tam altae quam porticus latae fuerint. peristyliorum intercolumnia ne minus trium, ne plus quattuor columnarum crassitudine inter se distent. sin autem dorico more in peristylo columnae erunt faciundae, uti in quarto libro de doricis scripsi ita moduli sumantur et ad eos modulos triglyphorumque rationes disponantur.
chunks.traduccion: Peristyles should be a third longer across than from front to back, and the columns as high as the porticoes are broad. The intercolumniations should be spaced not less than three nor more than four column-diameters apart. But if the columns of the peristyle are to be Doric, the modules are to be taken as I set down for the Doric order.

chunks.texto: Tricliniorum quanta latitudo fuerit, bis tanta longitudo fieri debebit. altitudines omnium conclaviorum, quae oblonga fuerint, sic habere debent rationem uti longitudinis et latitudinis mensura componatur et ex ea summa dimidium sumatur et quantum fuerit tantum altitudini detur. sin autem exhedrae aut oeci quadrati fuerint, latitudinis dimidia addita altitudines educantur. pinacothecae uti exhedrae amplis magnitudinibus sunt constituendae. oeci corinthii tetrastylique quique Aegyptii vocantur latitudinis et longitudinis uti supra tricliniorum symmetriae scriptae sunt, ita habeant rationem, sed propter columnarum interpositiones spatiosiores constituantur.
chunks.traduccion: Dining rooms should be twice as long as they are wide. For an oblong room, add its length and width and assign half that sum to its height. Square exedras or oeci should rise to one and a half times their width. Picture galleries, like exedras, should be generously dimensioned. Corinthian, tetrastyle and so-called Egyptian halls should follow the same length-to-width proportions as dining rooms, but their overall dimensions must be greater to allow for the intervening columns.

chunks.texto: inter corinthios autem et aegyptios hoc erit discrimen. corinthii simplices habent columnas aut in podio positas aut in imo, supraque habent epistylia et coronas aut ex intestino opere aut albario, praeterea supra coronas curva lacunaria ad circinum delumbata. in aegyptiis autem supra columnas epistylia et ab epistyliis ad parietes qui sunt circa inponenda est contignatio, supra coaxationem, pavimentum, subdiu ut sit circumitus. deinde supra epistylium ad perpendiculum inferiorum columnarum inponendae sunt minores quarta parte columnae. supra earum epistylia et ornamenta lacunariis ornantur et inter columnas superiores fenestrae conlocantur. ita basilicarum ea similitudo, non corinthiorum tricliniorum, videtur esse.
chunks.traduccion: Between the Corinthian and the Egyptian halls (oeci) there will be this difference. The Corinthian have a single tier of columns, set either upon a podium or upon the ground, and above them architraves and cornices, whether of joinery or of plaster, and over the cornices a vault rounded on the compass. In the Egyptian, above the lower columns an architrave is laid, and from it to the surrounding walls a floor is set, to make an open walk in the air; then, plumb above the lower columns and set back, a second tier, a fourth smaller, is raised; above their architraves and ornaments the ceiling is coffered, and windows are set between the upper columns. Thus they have the air not so much of Corinthian dining-rooms as of basilicas.

chunks.texto: fiunt autem etiam non italicae consuetudinis oeci, quos Graeci cyzicenos appellant. hi conlocantur spectantes ad septentrionem et maxime viridia prospicientes, valvasque habent in medio ipsi autem sunt ita longi et lati uti duo triclinia cum circumitionibus inter se spectantia possint esse conlocata, habentque dextra ac sinistra lumina fenestrarum valvata, uti de lectis per spatia fenestrarum viridia prospiciantur. altitudines eorum dimidia latitudinis addita constituuntur.
chunks.traduccion: There are also made halls (oeci) not in the Italian manner, which the Greeks call Cyzicene. These are set facing north and looking out, for choice, upon the gardens, with folding doors in the middle. They are so long and broad that two sets of dining-couches, facing one another, can be placed with room to pass around them; and they have windows opening on either hand upon the gardens, so that from the couches one may look out over the greenery.

chunks.texto: In his aedificiorum generibus omnes sunt faciendae earum symmetriarum rationes quae sine inpeditione loci fieri poterunt, luminaque parietum altitudinibus si non obscurabuntur, faciliter erunt explicata, sin autem inpedientur ab angustiis aut aliis necessitatibus, tunc erit ut ingenio et acumine de symmetriis detractiones aut adiectiones fiant, uti non dissimiles veris symmetriis perficiantur venustates.
chunks.traduccion: In all these kinds of building the schemes of symmetry are to be carried out so far as the site allows without hindrance; and the openings for light are easily contrived, provided they are not darkened by party-walls.

chunks.texto: Nunc explicabimus quibus proprietatibus genera aedificiorum ad usum et caeli regiones aptas debeant spectare. hiberna triclinia et balnearia ad occidentem hibernum spectent, ideo quod vespertino lumine opus est uti, praeterea quod etiam sol occidens adversus habens splendorem, calorem remittens efficit vespertino tempore regionem tepidiorem. cubicula et bybliothecae ad orientem spectare debent, usus enim matutinum postulat lumen, item in bybliothecis libri non putrescent. nam quaecumque ad meridiem et occidentem spectant, ab tineis et umore libri vitiantur, quod venti umidi advenientes procreant eas et alunt infundentesque umidos spiritus pallore volumina corrumpunt.
chunks.traduccion: We shall now explain with what properties the several kinds of building should be suited to their use and to the quarters of the sky they face. Winter dining-rooms and baths should look towards the winter sunset, because the evening light is needed, and because the setting sun, casting its glow full upon them, gives off a warmth that makes the quarter milder towards evening. Bedrooms and libraries should face the east, for their use demands the morning light, and in libraries the books will not rot; whereas in those rooms that face south and west the books are spoiled by worms and damp, since the moist winds that rise from those quarters breed and nourish the worms and, spreading their damp breath, corrupt the rolls with mold.

chunks.texto: triclinia verna et autumnalia ad orientem. tum enim praetenta luminibus adversus solis impetus progrediens ad occidentem efficit ea temperata ad id tempus quo his solitum est uti. aestiva ad septentrionem, quod ea regio non ut reliquae per solstitium propter calorem efficiuntur aestuosae, eo quod est aversa a solis cursu semper refrigerata et salubritatem et voluptatem in usu praestat. non minus pinacothecae et plumariorum textrina pictorumque officinae, uti colores eorum in opere propter constantiam luminis inmutata permaneant qualitate.
chunks.traduccion: Spring and autumn dining rooms east. For with the lights shining against the sun's attacks, advancing towards the west, it creates a temperature at the time when it is customary to use them. Summer north, because that region does not become sultry like the rest during the solstice due to heat, because it is turned away from the sun's course, it is always cooled and provides health and pleasure in use. No less are the galleries and the textile workshops of the painters, so that their colors in their work remain unchanged in quality due to the constancy of the light.

chunks.texto: Cum ad regiones caeli ita ea fuerint disposita, tunc etiam animadvertendum est quibus rationibus privatis aedificiis propria loca patribus familiarum et quemadmodum communia cum extraneis aedificari debeant. namque ex his quae propria sunt, in ea non est potestas omnibus intro eundi nisi invitatis, quemadmodum sunt cubicula triclinia balneae ceteraque quae easdem habent usus rationes. communia autem sunt quibus etiam invocati suo iure de populo possunt venire, id est vestibula cava aedium, peristylia quaeque eundem habere possunt usum. igitur îs qui communi sunt fortuna, non necessaria magnifica vestibula nec tabulina neque atria, quod aliis officia praestant ambiundo neque ab aliis ambiuntur.
chunks.traduccion: Since they have been so arranged for the regions of heaven, then it is also necessary to observe by what reasons private buildings should be built, the proper places for the fathers of families, and how common ones with strangers should be built. For of those things which are proper, there is no power for all to enter therein except those who are invited, as there are chambers, dining rooms, baths, and other things which have the same uses. But there are also common ones into which even those who are invited by their own right from the people can come, that is, vestibules, caves, peristyles, which can have the same use. Therefore, those who are in common fortune, do not need magnificent vestibules, nor small tables, nor courts, because they perform services to others by surrounding them rather than being surrounded by others.

chunks.texto: qui autem fructibus rusticis serviunt, in eorum vestibulis stabula tabernae, in aedibus cryptae horrea apothecae ceteraque quae ad fructus servandos magis quam ad elegantiae decorem possunt esse, ita sunt facienda. item feneratoribus et publicanis commodiora et speciosiora et ab insidiis tuta, forensibus autem et disertis elegantiora et spatiosiora ad conventus excipiundos, nobilibus vero qui honores magistratusque gerundo praestare debent officia civibus, faciunda sunt vestibula regalia alta, atria et peristylia amplissima, silvae ambulationesque laxiores ad decorem maiestatis perfectae, praeterea bybliothecas, pinacothecas, basilicas non dissimili modo quam publicorum operum magnificentia ⟨habeant⟩ comparatas, quod in domibus eorum saepius et publica consilia et privata iudicia arbitriaque conficiuntur.
chunks.traduccion: But those who live by the produce of the countryside should have, in their vestibules, stables and shops, and in the house itself cellars, granaries, storerooms and the like, contrived rather for keeping the produce than for elegance. For moneylenders and tax-farmers, houses more comfortable and handsome, and secure against intrigue; for advocates and men of eloquence, houses more elegant and roomy, to receive their callers; but for nobles, who in holding office and magistracies must render services to the citizens, there must be made lofty royal vestibules, the most ample atria and peristyles, with groves and broad walks finished in keeping with their dignity, and besides these, libraries and basilicas appointed with a magnificence not unlike that of public buildings — since in the houses of such men both public counsels and private suits and arbitrations are very often conducted.

chunks.texto: ergo si his rationibus ad singulorum generum personas, uti in libro primo de decore est scriptum, ita disposita erunt aedificia, non erit quod reprehendatur. habebunt enim ad omnes res commodas et emendatas explicationes. earum autem rerum non solum erunt in urbe aedificiorum rationes, sed etiam ruri, praeterquam quod in urbe atria proxima ianuis solent esse, ruri ab pseudourbanis statim peristylia, deinde tunc atria habentia circum porticus pavimentatas spectantes ad palaestras et ambulationes. Quoad potui urbanas rationes aedificiorum summatim perscribere, proposui, nunc rusticorum expeditionum ⟨apparationes⟩ ut sint ad usum commodae quibusque rationibus conlocare oporteat eas dicam.
chunks.traduccion: Therefore, if buildings are arranged in this way for each class of persons, as is written in the first book of the Decorum, there will be nothing to be criticized for. For they will have convenient and improved explanations for all things. Now there will be the rules for buildings not only in the city, but also in the country, besides the fact that in the city the atriums are usually close to the doors, but in the country the peristyle immediately after the pseudo-urban ones, then the atriums having paved porches around the porticoes facing the palaestras and the walks. As far as I could write down the urban rules for buildings in summary, I proposed, now I will tell you the expeditions of the countrymen so that they are convenient for use and in what ways it is necessary to place them.

chunks.texto: primum de salubritatibus, uti in primo volumine de moenibus conlocandis scriptum est, regiones aspiciantur et ita villae conlocentur. magnitudines earum ad modum agri copiasque fructuum comparentur. chortes magnitudinesque earum ad pecorum numerum atque quot iuga boum opus fuerit ibi versari, ita finiantur. in chorte culina quam calidissimo loco designetur, coniuncta autem habeat bubilia, quorum praesepia ad focum et orientis caeli regionem spectent, ideo quod boves lumen et ignem spectando horridi non fiunt. item agricolae religione inpediti non putant oportere aliam regionem caeli boves spectare nisi ortum solis.
chunks.traduccion: First of all, concerning health, as is written in the first volume on the placing of walls, let the regions be considered and the villages placed accordingly. Their sizes should be compared to the size of the field and the abundance of fruits. The cohorts and their sizes should be determined according to the number of cattle and how many yokes of oxen it will be necessary to turn there. In the cohort, the kitchen should be designated in the warmest place, and the cattle should be connected, the stalls of which should look at the hearth and the eastern sky, so that the oxen do not become horrified by looking at light and fire. Likewise, farmers who are inexperienced in the regions do not think that it is necessary for the oxen to look at any other sky region than the rising of the sun.

chunks.texto: bubilium autem debent esse latitudines nec minores pedum denûm nec maiores quindenûm, longitudo uti singula iuga ne minus pedes occupent septenos. balnearia item coniuncta sint culinae, ita enim lavationi rusticae ministratio non erit longe. torcular item proximum sit culinae, ita enim ad molarios fructus commoda erit ministratio, habeatque coniunctam vinariam cellam habentem ab septentrione lumina fenestrarum. cum enim alia parte habuerit qua sol calfacere possit, vinum quod erit in ea cella confusum ab calore efficietur inbecillum.
chunks.traduccion: The widths of the cattle pens should be neither less than ten feet nor more than fifteen, and the length should be such that each row does not occupy less than seven feet. The baths should also be connected to the kitchen, for thus the service of the country will not be far. The winepress should also be close to the kitchen, for thus the service of the olive trees will be convenient, and it should have a wine cellar connected to it, having windows facing north. For since it has another side from which the sun can warm it, the wine that will be in that cellar will be confused by the heat and become weak.

chunks.texto: olearia autem ita est conlocanda ut habeat a meridie calidisque regionibus lumen. non enim debet oleum congelari sed tepore caloris extenuari. magnitudines autem earum ad fructuum rationem et numerum doliorum sunt faciundae, quae cum sint cullearia, per medium occupare debent pedes quaternos. ipsum autem torcular si non cocleis•torquetur sed vectibus et prelo premitur, ne minus longum pedes XL constituatur, ita enim erit vectiario spatium expeditum. latitudo eius ne minus pedum senûm denûm, nam sic erit ad prelum opus facientibus libera versatio et expedita. sin autem duobus prelis loco opus fuerit, quattuor et viginti pedes latitudini dentur.
chunks.traduccion: The oil press should be placed so that it has light from the south and hot regions. For the oil should not be frozen but rather be weakened by the warmth of the heat. Their sizes should be made according to the quantity of fruit and the number of barrels, which, since they are spoon-shaped, should occupy four feet in the middle. But if the press itself is not turned with screws but is pressed with bars and a press, it should not be less than forty feet long, for in this way there will be an easy space for the transporter. Its width should not be less than ten feet, for in this way those doing the full work will have free and easy movement. But if two presses are needed instead, twenty-four feet should be given to the width.

chunks.texto: Ovilia et caprilia ita sunt magna facienda uti singula pecora areae ne minus pedes quaternos et semipedem, ne plus senos possint habere. granaria sublimata et ad septentrionem aut aquilonem spectantia disponantur, ita enim frumenta non poterint cito concalescere, sed ab flatu refrigerata diu servantur. namque ceterae regiones procreant curculionem et reliquas bestiolas quae frumentis solent nocere. equilibus quae maxime in villa loca calidissima fuerint constituantur, dum ne ad focum spectent. cum enim iumenta proxime ignem stabulantur, horrida fiunt.
chunks.traduccion: Oval and goat pens should be made so large that each herd of cattle cannot have less than four and a half feet, or more than six. Granaries should be elevated and arranged facing north or northeast, for in this way the grain will not be able to heat up quickly, but will be kept cool by the wind for a long time. For other regions breed weevils and other small animals that are accustomed to harm grain. For horses, the warmest places in the village should be placed, so that they do not look at the fire. For when cattle are stabled close to the fire, they become horrified.

chunks.texto: item non sunt inutilia praesepia quae conlocantur extra culinam in aperto contra orientem. cum enim in hieme anni sereno caelo in ea traducuntur matutino boves, ad solem pabulum capientes fiunt nitidiores. horrea fenilia farraria pistrina extra villam facienda videntur, ut ab ignis periculo sint villae tutiores. si quid delicatius in villis faciundum fuerit, ex symmetriis quae in urbanis supra scriptis sunt constitutae ita struantur uti sine inpeditione rusticae utilitatis aedificentur.
chunks.traduccion: Likewise, stables placed outside the kitchen in the open air facing east are not useless. For when in the winter of the year the oxen are brought there in the morning in a clear sky, they become brighter as they feed in the sun. Barns, barns, mills, and bakeries seem to be built outside the village, so that the villages are safer from the danger of fire. If anything more delicate is to be done in the villages, they should be constructed in such a way that they are built without hindering the rural utility, based on the symmetries established in urban buildings above.

chunks.texto: Omniaque aedificia ut luminosa sint, oportet curari; sed quae sunt ad villas, faciliora videntur esse, ideo quod paries nullius vicini potest obstare, in urbe autem aut communium parietum altitudines aut angustiae loci inpediundo faciunt obscuritates. Itaque de ea re sic erit experiundum. Ex qua parte lumen oporteat sumere, linea tendatur ab altitudine parietis, qui videtur obstare, ad eum locum, quo oporteat inmittere, et si ab ea linea, in altitudinem cum prospiciatur, poterit spatium puri caeli amplum videri, in eo loco lumen erit sine inpeditione.
chunks.traduccion: All buildings must be cared for so that they are luminous, but those that are near villages seem to be easier because no neighbor's wall can obstruct them, but in a city either the heights of the common walls or the narrowness of the place obstruct them and cause darkness. Therefore, this is what we should try about this matter. From which side the light should be let in, and if from that line, when looking up into the sky, a large space of pure sky can be seen, in that place there will be light without obstruction.

chunks.texto: sin autem officient trabes ea lumina aut contignationes, de superioribus partibus aperiatur et ita inmittatur. et ad summam ita est gubernandum ut ex quibuscumque partibus caelum prospici poterit, per eas fenestrarum loca relinquantur, sic enim lucida erunt aedificia. cum autem in tricliniis ceterisque conclavibus maximus est usus luminum, tum etiam in itineribus clivis scalis, quod in his saepius alii aliis obviam venientes ferentes sarcinas solent incurrere. Quoad potui distributiones operum nostratium, ut sint aedificatoribus non obscurae, explicui. nunc etiam quemadmodum Graecorum consuetudinibus aedificia distribuantur, uti non sint ignota, summatim exponam.
chunks.traduccion: But if the beams or lintels of the floors obstruct it, it should be opened from the upper parts and let in. And to sum up, it should be so governed that from whatever parts the sky can be seen, places for windows should be left through them, for in this way the buildings will be bright. But since in dining rooms and other rooms the greatest use is made of lights, then also in the paths of stairs, because in these people often encounter each other carrying loads. As far as I could, I have explained the distributions of our works, so that they may not be obscure to the builders. Now I will also briefly explain how buildings are distributed according to the customs of the Greeks, so that they may not be unknown.

chunks.texto: Atriis Graeci quia non utuntur, neque aedificant, sed ab ianua introeuntibus itinera faciunt latitudinibus non spatiosis, et ex una parte equilia, ex altera ostiariis cellas, statimque ianuae interiores finiuntur. hic autem locus inter duas ianuas graece θυρωρεῖον appellatur. deinde est introitus in peristylon. id peristylum in tribus partibus habet porticus inque parte quae spectat ad meridiem duas antas inter se spatio amplo distantes in quibus trabes invehuntur, et quantum inter antas distat, ex eo tertia dempta spatium datur introrsus. hic locus apud non nullos prostas, apud alios pastas nominatur.
chunks.traduccion: The Greeks do not use or build courts, but they make paths that are not very wide for those entering from the door, and on one side they have stalls, on the other the cells for the porters, and immediately the inner doors end. This place between the two doors is called in Greek θυρωρεῖον. Then there is the entrance into the peristyle. This peristyle has a portico on three sides, and on the side that faces south there are two antae, widely spaced apart from each other, upon which beams are carried, and the distance between the arches is taken from that, one third of the space is given inside. This place is called prostas by some, pastas by others.

chunks.texto: in his locis introrsus constituuntur oeci magni, in quibus matres familiarum cum lanificis habent sessionem. in prostadis autem dextra ac sinistra cubicula sunt conlocata, quorum unum thalamos, alterum amphithalamos dicitur. circum autem in porticibus triclinia cotidiana, cubicula, etiam cellae familiaricae constituuntur. haec pars aedificii gynaeconitis appellatur.
chunks.traduccion: Within these are set the great halls (oeci) where the mistresses of the household sit with the wool-workers. To right and left of the prostas are bedchambers, the one called the thalamos, the other the amphithalamos. Around the porticoes are the everyday dining-rooms, bedchambers, and servants’ rooms. This part of the house is called the gynaeconitis, the women’s quarters.

chunks.texto: Coniunguntur autem his domus ampliores habentes lautiora peristylia, in quibus pares sunt quattuor porticus altitudinibus, aut una quae ad meridiem spectat excelsioribus columnis constituitur. id autem peristylum quod unam altiorem habet porticum, rhodiacum dicitur. habent autem eae domus vestibula egregia et ianuas proprias cum dignitate porticusque peristyliorum albariis et tectoriis et ex intestino opere lacunariis ornatas, et in porticibus quae ad septentrionem spectant triclinia cyzicena et pinacothecas, ad orientem autem bybliothecas, exhedras ad occidentem, ad meridiem vero spectantes oecos quadratos ita ampla magnitudine uti faciliter in eo quattuor tricliniis stratis ministrationum ludorumque operis locus possit esse spatiosus.
chunks.traduccion: These houses are joined by larger ones, having more elaborate peristyles, in which there are four porticos of equal height, or one that faces south is built with higher columns. But that peristyle which has one higher portico is called Rhodian. These houses have excellent vestibules and doors of their own, and the porticos of the peristyles are adorned with dignity, with white walls and ceilings and with ceilings of internal work, and in the porticos that face north there are dining rooms and picture galleries, while to the east there are libraries, and to the west there are rooms facing south, and square courtyards of ample size, so that in those four dining rooms there can be easily a spacious place for serving meals and playing.

chunks.texto: in his oecis fiunt virilia convivia. non enim fuerat institutum matres familiarum eorum moribus accumbere. haec autem peristylia domus andronitides dicuntur, quod in his viri sine interpellationibus mulierum versantur. praeterea dextra ac sinistra domunculae constituuntur habentes proprias ianuas triclinia et cubicula commoda, uti hospites advenientes non in peristylia sed in ea hospitalia recipiantur. nam cum fuerunt Graeci delicatiores et fortuna opulentiores, hospitibus advenientibus instruebant triclinia cubicula cum penu cellas primoque die ad cenam invitabant, postero mittebant pullos ova holera poma reliquasque res agrestes. ideo pictores ea quae mittebantur hospitibus picturis imitantes xenia appellaverunt. ita patres familiarum in hospitio non videbantur esse peregre, habentes secretam in his hospitalibus libertatem.
chunks.traduccion: In these rooms, men's banquets are held. For it was not customary for mothers of families to sit down in their manners. But this peristyle of the house is called the Andronitides, because in it the men are occupied without the interruptions of women. Moreover, on the right and left are small houses built, having their own doors, dining rooms and comfortable bedrooms, so that guests arriving may not be received in the peristyle but in that hospital. For when the Greeks were more refined and more wealthy in fortune, they furnished dining rooms, bedrooms with pantry rooms for guests arriving, and on the first day they invited them to dinner, and on the second day they sent them chickens, eggs, vegetables, apples, and other country things. Therefore, painters, imitating the things that were sent to the guests in their paintings, called them xenia. Thus the fathers of families did not seem to be abroad in their hospitality, having a secret liberality in these hospitals.

chunks.texto: inter duo autem peristylia et hospitalia itinera sunt quae mesauloe dicuntur, quod inter duas aulas media sunt interposita, nostri autem eas andronas appellant. Sed hoc valde est mirandum, nec enim graece nec latine potest id convenire. Graeci enim ἀνδρῶνας appellant oecus, ubi convivia virilia solent esse, quod eo mulieres non accedunt. item aliae res sunt similes, uti xystus prothyrum telamones et nonnulla alia eius modi.ξυστός enim est graeca appellatione porticus ampla latitudine, in qua athletae per hiberna tempora exercentur. nostri autem hypaethrus ambulationes xysta appellant, quas Graeci παραδρομίδας dicunt. item πρόθυρα graece dicuntur quae sunt ante ianuas vestibula, nos autem appellamus prothyra quae graece dicuntur διάθυρα.
chunks.traduccion: Between the two peristyles and the guest apartments are passages called mesaulae, because they lie between two courts; our own people, however, call them andrones. Yet this is very strange, for the term agrees with neither Greek nor Latin usage: the Greeks call ἀνδρῶνας the halls where the men’s banquets are held, since women do not enter there. There are other terms of the same kind — xystus, prothyrum, telamones, and a few besides. The ξύστος, in Greek usage, is a portico of ample breadth in which athletes train during the winter season; our people, however, call open-air walks xysta, which the Greeks name παραδρομίδας. Likewise, what in Greek are called πρόθυρα are the vestibules before the doors; but we call prothyra what the Greeks call διάθυρα.

chunks.texto: item si qua virili figura signa mutulos aut coronas sustinent, nostri telamones appellant, cuius rationes quid ita aut quare dicantur ex historiis non inveniuntur, Graeci vero eos ἄτλαντας vocitant. Atlas enim formatur historia sustinens mundum, ideo quod is primum cursum solis et lunae siderumque omnium versationum rationes vigore animi sollertiaque curavit hominibus tradenda, eaque re a pictoribus et statuariis deformatur pro eo beneficio sustinens mundum, filiaeque eius Atlantides, quas nos vergilias, Graeci autem πλειάδας nominant, cum sideribus in mundo sunt dedicatae.
chunks.traduccion: Likewise, if there are those who support the symbols of a man's figure with a mute or crown, ours call them Telamones, the reasons for which are not found in the histories, but the Greeks call them Atlases. For Atlas is formed by history as supporting the world, because he was the first to take care of the course of the sun and moon and the reasons for all the movements of the stars, by the vigor of his mind and skill, to be handed down to men, and for that reason he is deformed by painters and sculptors as supporting the world for his benefit, and his daughters, the Atlanteans, whom we call Vergilias, and the Greeks call Pleiades, are dedicated to the stars in the world.

chunks.texto: nec tamen ego ut mutetur consuetudo nominationum aut sermonis, ideo haec proposui, sed uti non sint ignota philologis exponenda iudicavi. Quibus consuetudinibus aedificia italico more et Graecorum institutis conformantur exposui, et de symmetriis singulorum generum proportiones perscripsi. ergo quoniam de venustate decoreque ante est conscriptum, nunc exponemus de firmitate quemadmodum ea sine vitiis permanentia ad vetustatem conlocentur.
chunks.traduccion: I have not set out these matters to alter established names or ordinary usage, but to make them known to those concerned with language. I have explained the customs according to which buildings are formed in the Italian manner and in the Greek tradition, and have described the proportions of each type. Having discussed beauty and propriety, I shall now turn to strength and explain how buildings can be constructed without defects for lasting service.

chunks.texto: Aedificia quae plano pede instituuntur, si fundamenta eorum facta fuerint ita ut in prioribus libris de muro et theatris a nobis est expositum, ad vetustatem ea erunt sine dubitatione firma. sin autem hypogea concamarationesque instituentur, fundationes eorum fieri debent crassiores quam quae in superioribus aedificiis structurae sunt futurae, eorumque parietes pilae columnae ad perpendiculum inferiorum medio conlocentur, uti solido respondeant. nam si in pendentibus onera fuerint parietum aut columnarum, non poterint habere perpetuam firmitatem.
chunks.traduccion: Buildings that are built on a flat base, if their foundations are made in such a way as we have explained in previous books on walls and theaters, will undoubtedly be strong for a long time. But if basements and chambers are built, their foundations should be made thicker than those that will be used in the structures of the upper buildings, and their walls, pillars, and columns should be placed perpendicular to the middle of the lower ones, so that they correspond to the solid. For if the loads of the walls or columns are on the overhangs, they will not be able to have permanent strength.

chunks.texto: praeterea inter lumina secundum pilas et antas postes si supponentur, erunt non vitiosae. limina enim et trabes structuris cum sint oneratae, medio spatio pandantes frangunt sub lysi structuras. cum autem subiecti fuerint et subcuneati postes, non patiuntur insidere trabes neque eas laedere.
chunks.traduccion: Furthermore, if placed between the openings, by piers and antae, they will not be defective. For thresholds and beams, when loaded with structures, break the suspended structures while they hang in half; but when the posts have been secured and wedged together, they do not allow the beams to rest on them or damage them.

chunks.texto: item administrandum est uti levent onus parietum fornicationes cuneorum divisionibus et ad centrum respondentes earum conclusurae. cum enim extra trabes aut liminum capita arcus cuneis erunt conclusae, primum non pandabit materies levata onere, deinde si quod vetustate vitium ceperit, sine molitione fulturarum faciliter mutabitur.
chunks.traduccion: It is also necessary to ensure that the load on the walls is relieved by the divisions of the wedges and their closures corresponding to the center. For when the outside beams or the capitals of the thresholds are closed with wedges, first the materials will not expand when the load is lifted, and then if they have developed any defect due to age, they can be easily replaced without the need for supports.

chunks.texto: itemque quae pilatim aguntur aedificia, et cuneorum divisionibus coagmentis ad centrum respondentibus fornices concluduntur, extremae pilae in his latiores spatio sunt faciundae, uti vires eae habentes resistere possint, cum cunei ab oneribus parietum pressi per coagmenta ad centrum se prementes extruderent incumbas. itaque si angulares pilae erunt spatiosis magnitudinibus, continendo cuneos firmitatem operibus praestabunt.
chunks.traduccion: Likewise, buildings carried up in piers, when the arches are closed by the divisions of the wedges corresponding to the joints at the center, the outer piers in these should be made wider in space, so that the forces they possess can resist, when the wedges, pressed by the loads of the walls, press themselves through the joints towards the center and extrude themselves. Therefore, if the corner piles are of spacious sizes, by containing the wedges they will provide stability to the works.

chunks.texto: Cum in his rebus animadversum fuerit uti ea diligentia in his adhibeatur, non minus etiam observandum est uti omnes structurae perpendiculo respondeant neque habeant in ulla parte proclinationes. maxima autem esse debet cura substructionum, quod in his infinita vitia solet facere terrae congestio. ea enim non potest esse semper uno pondere quo solet esse per aestatem, sed hibernis temporibus recipiendo ex imbribus aquae multitudinem crescens et pondere et amplitudine disrumpit et extrudit structurarum saeptiones.
chunks.traduccion: Since in these matters it has been observed that such diligence is applied, it is no less important to observe that all structures correspond to the perpendicular and have no inclinations in any part. The greatest care should be taken with the substructures, because in these the accumulation of earth tends to cause infinite defects. For it cannot always be with the same weight as it usually is during the summer, but in winter times, receiving a multitude of water from the rains, it increases in weight and size and bursts and pushes out the partitions of the structures.

chunks.texto: itaque ut huic vitio medeatur. sic erit faciundum ut primum pro amplitudine congestionis crassitudo structurae constituatur, deinde in frontibus anterides, sive erismae sunt, una struantur, eaeque inter se distent tanto spatio quanta altitudo substructionis est futura, crassitudine eadem qua substructio. procurrat autem ab imo pro quam crassitudo constituta fuerit substructionis, deinde contrahatur gradatim ita uti summam habeat prominentiam quanta operis est crassitudo.
chunks.traduccion: Therefore, to remedy this defect, the thickness of the structure should first be fixed in proportion to the mass of earth to be retained; then, on the face, buttresses (anterides, or in Greek erismae) are built, set apart from one another by as much space as the height of the substructure will be, and of the same thickness as the substructure itself. They are carried out from the bottom by as much as the thickness fixed for the structure, and then drawn in so that the part standing in the face is as thick as a fourth part of the height.

chunks.texto: praeterea introrsus contra terrenum coniuncta muro serratim struantur, uti singuli dentes ab muro tantum distent quanta altitudo futura erit substructionis, crassitudines autem habeant dentium structurae uti muri. item in extremis angulis cum recessum fuerit ab interiore angulo spatio altitudinis substructionis, in utramque partem signetur et ab his signis diagonios structura conlocetur, et ab ea media altera coniuncta cum angulo muri. ita dentes et diagonioe structurae non patientur tota vi premere murum, sed dissipabunt retinendo impetum congestionis.
chunks.traduccion: Furthermore, they are built inwards against the ground, connected to the wall, in a serrated manner, so that each tooth is as far from the wall as the future height of the substructure will be, and the thickness of the teeth should be as thick as the structure of the wall. Likewise, in the extreme corners, when there is a recess from the inner corner by the space of the height of the substructure, let diagonals be marked on both sides and from these marks the structure is placed, and from that the other side connected to the corner of the wall. Thus the teeth and diagonals of the structure will not be allowed to press the wall with all their force, but will dissipate the impact of the congestion by retaining it.

chunks.texto: Quemadmodum sine vitiis opera constitui oporteat et uti caveatur incipientibus exposui. namque de tegulis aut tignis aut asseribus mutandis non est eadem cura quemadmodum de his, quod ea quamvis sunt vitiosa, faciliter mutantur. itaque nec solida quia non putantur esse, quibus rationibus haec poterint esse firma et quemadmodum instituantur exposui.
chunks.traduccion: I have explained to beginners how works should be constructed without defects and how precautions should be taken. For there is not the same care in changing tiles or beams or planks as in these, which, although defective, are easily changed. Therefore, I have explained what are not even supposed to be solid, by what means these could be made firm and how they are constructed.

chunks.texto: quibus autem copiarum generibus oporteat uti, non est architecti potestas, ideo quod non in omnibus locis omnia genera copiarum nascuntur, ut in primo volumine est expositum, praeterea in domini est potestate utrum latericio an caementicio an saxo quadrato velit aedificare. itaque omnium operum probationes tripertito considerantur, id est fabrili subtilitate et magnificentia et dispositione. cum magnificenter opus perfectum aspicietur, a domini potestate inpensae laudabuntur, cum subtiliter, officinatoris probabitur exactio, cum vero venuste proportionibus et symmetriis habuerit auctoritatem, tunc fuerit gloria architecti.
chunks.traduccion: The choice of available materials is not entirely within the architect’s power, since not every kind is found in every place, as Book I explains. The owner also decides whether to build in brick, rubble masonry, or ashlar. A work is judged under three heads: craftsmanship, magnificence, and arrangement. When a finished building impresses by its magnificence, the owner’s expenditure earns praise; when by its precision, the workmanship is commended. When beauty acquires authority through proportion and commensurability, the credit belongs to the architect.

chunks.texto: haec autem recte constituuntur, cum is et a fabris et ab idiotis patiatur accipere se consilia. namque omnes homines, non solum architecti, quod est bonum possunt probare, sed inter idiotas et eos hoc est discrimen quod idiota nisi factum viderit, non potest scire quid sit futurum, architectus autem simul animo constituerit, antequam inceperit et venustate et usu et decore quale sit futurum habet definitum. Quas res privatis aedificiis utiles putavi et quemadmodum sint faciundae quam apertissime potui perscripsi. de expolitionibus autem eorum uti sint elegantes et sine vitiis ad vetustatem <>, insequenti volumine exponam.
chunks.traduccion: But these things are rightly established, since he allows himself to be advised by both craftsmen and laymen. For all men, not only architects, can approve what is good, but the difference between laymen and architects is this: a layman cannot know what will be until he sees it done, while an architect, having already established it in his mind, has defined before he begins what it will be in terms of beauty, use, and decorum. I have described as clearly as I could what things are useful for private buildings and how they should be made. But I will explain their refinements, so that they are elegant and without defects for old age, in the following volume.

chunks.texto: Maiores cum sapienter tum etiam utiliter instituerunt, per commentariorum relationes cogitata tradere posteris, ut ea non interirent sed singulis aetatibus crescentia voluminibus edita gradatim pervenirent vetustatibus ad summam doctrinarum subtilitatem. itaque non mediocres sed infinitae sunt his agendae gratiae, quod non invidiose silentes praetermiserunt, sed omnium generum sensus conscriptionibus memoriae tradendos curaverunt.
chunks.traduccion: The ancients, both wisely and usefully, instituted the transmission of their thoughts to posterity through the reports of their commentaries, so that they would not perish, but, published in increasing volumes in each age, would gradually reach the highest subtlety of their doctrines. Therefore, the merits of this work are not moderate but infinite, because they did not pass over it in envious silence, but took care to transmit to memory all kinds of thoughts in writings.

chunks.texto: namque si non ita fecissent, non potuissemus scire quae res in Troia fuissent gestae, nec quid Thales Democritus Anaxagoras Xenophanes reliquique physici sensissent de rerum natura quasque Socrates Platon Aristoteles Zenon Epicurus aliique philosophi hominibus agendae vitae terminationes finissent seu Croesus Alexander Darius ceterique reges quas res aut quibus rationibus gessissent fuissent notae, nisi maiores praeceptorum comparationibus omnium memoriae ad posteritatem commentariis extulissent.
chunks.traduccion: For if they had not done so, we would not have been able to know what things had been done in Troy, nor what Thales, Democritus, Anaxagoras, Xenophanes, and the other natural philosophers had thought about the nature of things, nor what Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Zeno, Epicurus, and other philosophers had concluded the ends of life for men, nor what things Croesus, Alexander, Darius, and the other kings had done, or for what reasons, would have been known, unless the elders had brought forth the memory of all things in their commentaries by comparisons of precepts for posterity.

chunks.texto: itaque quemadmodum his gratiae sunt agendae, contra qui eorum scripta furantes pro suis praedicant sunt vituperandi, quique non propriis cogitationibus scriptorum nituntur, sed invidis moribus aliena violantes gloriantur, non modo sunt reprehendendi, sed etiam quia impio more vixerunt, poena condemnandi. nec tamen haec res non vindicatae curiosius ab antiquis esse memorantur. quorum exitus iudiciorum qui fuerint, non est alienum quemadmodum sint nobis traditi explicare.
chunks.traduccion: Just as gratitude is owed to those who transmit their thoughts, so those who steal others’ writings and proclaim them their own deserve condemnation. Those who claim glory by violating the work of others, instead of relying on their own ideas, merit not merely reproach but punishment for acting dishonourably. Such offenses, it is reported, did not go unpunished among the ancients. It is therefore appropriate to recount the outcomes of those judgments as they have been handed down to us.

chunks.texto: reges Attalici magnis philologiae dulcedinibus inducti cum egregiam bybliothecam Pergami ad communem delectationem instituissent, tunc item Ptolomaeus infinito zelo cupiditatisque incitatus studio non minoribus industriis ad eundem modum contenderat Alexandriae comparare. cum autem summa diligentia perfecisset, non putavit id satis esse nisi propagationibus inseminando curaret augendam. itaque Musis et Apollini ludos dedicavit et quemadmodum athletarum sic communium scriptorum victoribus praemia et honores constituit.
chunks.traduccion: When the Attalic kings, led by the great delights of philology, had established an excellent library at Pergamum for the common enjoyment, then likewise Ptolemy, inspired by infinite zeal and desire, strove with no less diligence to furnish Alexandria with the same. But when he had accomplished it with the utmost diligence, he did not think that it was sufficient unless he took care to increase it by insemination. Accordingly he dedicated games to the Muses and Apollo, and, as he did to athletes, so he established prizes and honors for the victors of common writings.

chunks.texto: his ita institutis cum ludi adessent, iudices litterati qui ea probarent erant legendi. rex cum iam sex civitatis lectos habuisset nec tam cito septumum idoneum inveniret, retulit ad eos qui supra bybliothecam fuerunt et quaesiit si quem novissent ad id expeditum. tunc ei dixerunt esse quendam Aristophanen, qui summo studio summaque diligentia cotidie omnes libros ex ordine perlegeret. itaque conventu ludorum cum secretae sedes iudicibus essent distributae, cum ceteris Aristophanes citatus quemadmodum fuerat locus ei designatus sedit.
chunks.traduccion: As the games approached, learned judges had to be selected to assess them. The king had already chosen six men from the city but could not readily find a suitable seventh. He consulted those in charge of the library and asked whether they knew anyone qualified. They told him of a certain Aristophanes, who read through all the books in order each day with exceptional diligence and attention. When the games assembled and reserved seats had been assigned to the judges, Aristophanes was summoned with the others and took his appointed place.

chunks.texto: primo poetarum ordine ad certationem inducto cum recitarentur scripta, populus cunctus significando monebat iudices quod probarent. itaque cum ab singulis sententiae sunt rogatae, sex una dixerunt et quem maxime animadverterunt multitudini placuisse, ei primum praemium, insequenti secundum tribuerunt. Aristophanes vero cum ab eo sententia rogaretur, eum primum renuntiari iussit qui minime populo placuisset.
chunks.traduccion: When the first order of poets was brought to the competition, and their writings were recited, the whole people indicated by signs to the judges what they should approve. Accordingly, when each was asked for his opinion, the six gave one, and to him whom they observed had most pleased the multitude, they awarded the first prize, and to the next the second. But Aristophanes, when his opinion was asked of him, ordered that the one who had least pleased the people be dismissed first.

chunks.texto: cum autem rex et universi vehementer indignarentur, surrexit et rogando impetravit ut paterentur se dicere. itaque silentio facto docuit unum ex his eum esse poetam, ceteros aliena recitavisse, oportere autem iudicantes non furta sed scripta probare. admirante populo et rege dubitante, fretus memoriae certis armariis infinita volumina eduxit et ea cum recitatis conferendo coegit ipsos furatos de se confiteri. itaque rex iussit cum his agi furti condemnatosque cum ignominia dimisit, Aristophanen vero amplissimis muneribus ornavit et supra bybliothecam constituit.
chunks.traduccion: But when the king and all were greatly indignant, he rose and begged that they be allowed to speak. So, by making silence, he taught that one of them was a poet, and that the others had recited other people's works, but that they judged it necessary to prove that they were not stolen but written. With the people astonished and the king doubtful, he, relying on his memory, brought out an infinite number of volumes from certain cupboards and, comparing them with the ones recited, forced the thieves themselves to confess that they had stolen them. So the king ordered that these be tried and those convicted of theft were released with disgrace, but Aristophanes was adorned with the most magnificent gifts and placed over the library.

chunks.texto: insequentibus annis a Macedonia Zoilus, qui adoptavit cognomen ut Homeromastix vocitaretur, Alexandriam venit suaque scripta contra Iliadem et Odyssean comparata regi recitavit. Ptolomaeus vero cum animadvertisset poetarum parentem philologiaeque omnis ducem absentem vexari et cuius ab cunctis gentibus scripta suspicerentur ab eo vituperari, indignans nullum ei dedit responsum. Zoilus autem cum diutius in regno fuisset, inopia pressus summisit ad regem postulans ut aliquid sibi tribueretur.
chunks.traduccion: In the following years, Zoilus, who adopted the surname Homeromastix, came from Macedonia to Alexandria and read his writings against the Iliad and the Odyssey to the king, having prepared them. But Ptolemy, when he perceived that the father of poets and the leader of all philology was being harassed in his absence, and that his writings, whose writings were highly regarded by all nations, were being censured by him, became indignant and gave him no answer. But Zoilus, when he had been in the kingdom for a long time, was pressed by poverty and sent to the king, requesting that something be given to him.

chunks.texto: rex vero respondisse dicitur Homerum, qui ante annos mille decessisset, aevo perpetuo multa milia hominum pascere, item debere qui meliore ingenio se profiteretur non modo unum sed etiam plures alere posse. et ad summam mors eius ut parricidii damnati varie memoratur. alii enim scripserunt a Philadelpho esse in crucem fixum, nonnulli Chii lapides esse coniectos, alii Zmyrnae vivum in pyram coniectum. quorum utrum ei acciderit, merenti digna constitit poena. non enim aliter videtur promereri qui citat eos quorum responsum, quid senserint scribentes, non potest coram indicari.
chunks.traduccion: The king is said to have replied that Homer, who died a thousand years ago, would feed many thousands of men in perpetuity, and that he who would claim to be superior in genius should be able to feed not only one but also many. And to sum up, his death as a condemned parricide is variously recorded. For some have written that he was crucified at Philadelphia, some that he was stoned at Chios, others that he was thrown alive on a pyre at Smyrna. Whether any of these things happened to him, the punishment he deserved was decidedly worthy. For it does not seem that he deserves otherwise who quotes those whose response, what they thought when writing, cannot be stated in person.
