chunks.texto: ego vero, Caesar, neque alienis indicibus mutatis interposito nomine meo id profero corpus neque ullius cogitata vituperans institui ex eo me adprobare, sed omnibus scriptoribus infinitas ago gratias quod egregiis ingeniorum sollertiis ex aevo conlatis abundantes alius alio genere copias praeparaverunt, unde nos uti fontibus haurientes aquam et ad propria proposita traducentes facundiores et expeditiores habemus ad scribendum facultates talibusque confidentes auctoribus audemus institutiones novas comparare.
chunks.traduccion: But I, Caesar, neither do I produce this body with my own name interposed, having altered the evidence of others, nor do I set out to approve myself by criticizing the thoughts of anyone, but I give infinite thanks to all writers, who, with the excellent skills of their geniuses, brought together from time immemorial, have prepared abundant resources of one kind or another, from which we, drawing water as from springs and translating it for our own purposes, have more eloquent and expeditious faculties for writing, and, trusting in such authors, we dare to compare new compositions.

chunks.texto: Igitur tales ingressus eorum quia ad propositi mei rationes animadverti praeparatos, inde sumendo progredi coepi. namque primum Agatharchus Athenis Aeschylo docente tragoediam scaenam fecit et de ea commentarium reliquit. ex eo moniti Democritus et Anaxagoras de eadem re scripserunt, quemadmodum oporteat ad aciem oculorum radiorumque extentionem certo loco centro constituto lineas ratione naturali respondere, uti de certa re certae imagines aedificiorum in scaenarum picturis redderent speciem et quae in directis planisque frontibus sint figurata, alia abscedentia, alia prominentia esse videantur.
chunks.traduccion: Therefore, such were their entrances, because I observed that the reasons for my purpose were prepared, and I proceeded from there with strength. For first Agatharchus, under the instruction of Aeschylus, staged a tragedy in Athens and left a commentary on it. From him, Democritus and Anaxagoras, advised, wrote on the same subject, how it is necessary for lines to correspond by natural reason to the line of sight and the extension of rays, with a center established at a certain place, so that from an uncertain thing certain images of buildings in stage paintings might give the appearance, and those which are figured on straight and flat fronts might seem to be otherwise absurdly prominent.

chunks.texto: postea Silenus de symmetriis doricorum edidit volumen, de aede Iunonis quae est Sami dorica Theodorus, ionice Ephesi quae est Dianae Chersiphron et Metagenes, de fano Minervae quod est Priene ionicum Pytheos, item de aede Minervae dorice quae est Athenis in arce Ictinos et Carpion, Theodorus Phocaeus de tholo qui est Delphis, Philo de aedium sacrarum symmetriis et de armamentario quod fuerat Piraei portu, Hermogenes de aede Dianae ionice quae est Magnesia pseudodipteros et Liberi Patris Teo monopteros, item Arcesius de symmetriis corinthiis et ionico Trallibus Aesculapio quod etiam ipse sua manu dicitur fecisse, de Mausoleo Satyrus et Pytheos, quibus vero felicitas maximum summumque contulit munus.
chunks.traduccion: Later Silenus published a volume on the symmetries of the Dorics, Theodorus on the temple of Juno, which is the Doric temple of Samos, and Metagenes on the Ionic temple of Ephesus, which is the temple of Diana, Chersiphron and Metagenes, on the temple of Minerva, which is the Ionic temple of Priene, Pytheos, likewise on the Doric temple of Minerva, which is in Athens in the citadel of Ictions and Carpion, Theodore Phocaeus on the tholos which is at Delphi, Philo on the symmetries of sacred buildings and on the armoury which he had made in the port of Piraeus, Hermogenes on the Ionic temple of Diana, which is the temple of Magnesia, and the Theomonopteros of Liberi Patris, Arcesius on the symmetries of Corinth and the Ionic temple of Aesculapius at Trallis, which he himself is said to have made with his own hand, and Satyrs and Pytheos on the Mausoleum, to which, however, fortune bestowed the greatest and most sublime gift.

chunks.texto: quorum enim artes aevo perpetuo nobilissimas laudes et sempiterno florentes habere iudicantur, ei cogitatis egregias operas praestiterunt. namque singulis frontibus singuli artifices sumpserunt certatim partes ad ornandum et probandum Leochares Bryaxis Scopas Praxiteles, nonnulli etiam putant Timotheum, quorum artis eminens excellentia coegit ad septem spectaculorum eius operis pervenire famam.
chunks.traduccion: For their arts are judged to have the most noble praises throughout the ages and to flourish for ever, and they have produced excellent works of design. For on each front, individual artists competed to adorn and prove Leochares, Bryaxis, Scopas, Praxiteles, and some even think Timotheus, whose eminent excellence of art forced the fame of his work to reach seven spectacles.

chunks.texto: praeterea minus nobiles multi praecepta symmetriarum conscripserunt, uti Nexaris Theocydes Demophilos Pollis Leonidas Silanion Melampus Sarnacus Euphranor. non minus de machinationibus, uti Diades Archytas Archimedes Ctesibios Nymphodorus Philo Byzantius Diphilos Democles Charias Polyidos Pyrros Agesistratos. quorum ex commentariis quae utilia esse his rebus animadverti, collecta in unum coegi corpus, et ideo maxime, quod animadverti in ea re ab Graecis volumina plura edita, ab nostris oppido quam pauca. Fuficius enim nimirum de his rebus primus instituit edere volumen, item Terentius Varro de novem disciplinis unum de architectura, P. Septimius duo.
chunks.traduccion: Moreover, many less noble men wrote precepts on symmetry, such as Theocides of Nexaris, Demophilus, Pollis, Leonidas, Silanion, Melampus, Sarnacus, Euphranor. No less on engineering, such as Diades, Archytas, Archimedes, Ctesibius, Nymphodorus, Philo, Byzantius, Diphilus, Democles, Charias, Polyides, Pyrrhus, Agesistratus. From whose commentaries I have observed to be useful in these matters, I have collected several volumes on this subject published by the Greeks, and more than a few by our own people. Fuficius was the first to undertake to publish a volume on these matters, as was Terentius Varro, one on the nine disciplines, on architecture, and Publius Septimius, two.

chunks.texto: amplius vero in id genus scripturae adhuc nemo incubuisse videtur, cum fuissent et antiqui cives magni architecti, qui potuissent non minus eleganter scripta comparare. namque Athenis Antistates et Callaeschros et Antimachides et Porinos architecti Pisistrato aedem Iovi Olympio facienti fundamenta constituerunt, post mortem autem eius propter interpellationem reipublicae incepta reliquerunt. itaque circiter annis <quadringentis> post Antiochus rex cum in id opus inpensam esset pollicitus, cellae magnitudinem et columnarum circa dipteron conlocationem epistyliorumque et ceterorum ornamentorum ad symmetriam distributionem magna sollertia scientiaque summa civis Romanus Cossutius nobiliter est architectatus. id autem opus non modo vulgo sed etiam in paucis a magnificentia nominatur.
chunks.traduccion: But no one seems to have yet devoted himself more to that kind of writing, since there were also great architects among the ancient citizens who could have produced writings no less elegantly. For at Athens the architects Antistates and Callaeschros and Antimachides and Phormus laid the foundations of the temple of Jupiter Olympias which Pisistratus was building, but after his death they abandoned the projects because of the interruption of the state. Accordingly, about four hundred years later, when King Antiochus had promised to spend on that work, the size of the room and the arrangement of the columns around the dipteron and the distribution of the epistyles and other ornaments in a symmetrical manner were nobly designed by the Roman citizen Cossutius with great skill and supreme knowledge. And that work is not only popularly but also in a few places by its magnificence.

chunks.texto: nam quattuor locis sunt aedium sacrarum marmoreis operibus ornatae dispositiones, e quibus propriae de his nominationes clarissima fama nominantur. quorum excellentiae prudentesque cogitationum apparatus suspectus habent in deorum σημαντικοῖς. primumque aedes Ephesi Dianae ionico genere ab Chersiphrone Gnosio et filio eius Metagene est instituta, quam postea Demetrius ipsius Dianae servus et Paeonius Ephesius dicuntur perfecisse. Mileti Apollini item ionicis symmetriis ⟨aedem⟩ idem Paeonius Daphnisque Milesius instituerunt. Eleusine Cereris et Proserpinae cellam inmani magnitudine Ictinos dorico more sine exterioribus columnis ad laxamentum usus sacrificiorum pertexit.
chunks.traduccion: For in four places there are arrangements of sacred buildings adorned with marble works, from which the most famous names are properly named. The excellences and prudent arrangements of which are suspected in the ceremony of the gods. The first temple of Diana at Ephesus was erected in the Ionic style by Chersiphron of Gnosius and his son Metagenes, which is said to have been completed afterwards by Demetrius, the servant of Diana herself, and Paeonius of Ephesus. The same was erected in the Ionic style by Paeonius and Daphnis of Miles. The cella of Ceres and Proserpina at Eleusis was built in the Doric style without exterior columns for the relaxation of sacrifices.

chunks.texto: eam autem postea cum Demetrius Phalereus Athenis rerum potiretur, Philo ante templum in fronte columnis constitutis prostylon fecit. ita aucto vestibulo laxamentum initiantibus operique summam adiecit auctoritatem. in asty vero Olympium amplo modulorum comparatu corinthiis symmetriis et proportionibus, uti supra scriptum est, architectandum Cossutius suscepisse memoratur, cuius commentarium nullum est inventum. nec tamen a Cossutio solum de his rebus scripta sunt desideranda sed etiam a G. Mucio, qui magna scientia confisus aedis Honoris et Virtutis Marianae cellae columnarumque et epistyliorum symmetrias legitimis artis institutis perfecit. id vero si marmoreum fuisset, ut haberet quemadmodum ab arte subtilitatem sic ab magnificentia et inpensis auctoritatem, in primis et summis operibus nominaretur.
chunks.traduccion: But later, when Demetrius Phalerum took possession of Athens, Philo built a prostylon in front of the temple with columns set in front. Having thus built the vestibule, he added a great deal of authority to the workmen who were beginning it. But in Asty, when the Olympos were compared in ample dimensions with the Corinthian symmetries and proportions, as has been written above, it is recorded that Cossutius undertook to design the architectur, of which no commentary has been found. And yet, not only Cossutius is to be missed in writings on these matters, but also Gaius Mucius, who, relying on great knowledge, completed the symmetry of the columns and epistyles of the temple of Honor and Virtue of Mariana, according to the legitimate rules of art. But if it had been made of marble, so that it would have authority from magnificence and expense, as well as from subtlety of art, it would have been named among the first and greatest works.

chunks.texto: Cum ergo et antiqui nostri inveniantur non minus quam Graeci fuisse magni architecti et nostra memoria satis multi, et ex his pauci praecepta edidissent, non putavi silendum sed disposite singulis voluminibus de singulis exponere. rebus itaque quoniam sexto volumine privatorum aedificiorum rationes perscripsi, in hoc qui septimum tenet numerum de expolitionibus quibus rationibus et venustatem et firmitatem habere possint exponam.
chunks.traduccion: Since, therefore, our ancients are found to have been no less great architects than the Greeks, and there are quite a few of them in our memory, and of these few have published precepts, I did not think it necessary to be silent, but to explain each one in order in each volume. Therefore, since in the sixth volume I have written down the methods of private buildings, in this, which contains the seventh volume, I will explain the refinements by which they can have both beauty and strength.

chunks.texto: Primumque incipiam de ruderatione, quae principia tenet expolitionum, uti curiosius summaque providentia solidationis ratio habeatur. et si plano pede erit eruderandum, quaeratur solum si sit perpetuo solidum, et ita exaequetur, et inducatur cum statumine rudus. sin autem omnis aut ex parte congesticius locus fuerit, fistucationibus•cum magna cura solidetur. in contignationibus vero diligenter est animadvertendum ne qui paries qui non exeat ad summum, sit extructus sub pavimentum, sed potius relaxatus supra se pendentem habeat coaxationem. cum enim solidus exit, contignationibus arescentibus aut pandatione sidentibus, permanens structurae soliditate dextra ac sinistra secundum se facit in pavimentis necessario rimas.
chunks.traduccion: Archaeological note — Bk. 7.1 (pavements). Vitruvius transmits the ancient recipe for the layered Roman floor, which archaeology confirms across the Empire (from Fishbourne in Britain to Lod in Israel, from Zippori to Braga). From the bottom up: the statumen (large stones forming the base and draining ground moisture); the rudus or ruderatio (a mortar of broken brick and lime, more than 20 cm thick, rammed down —three parts lime to one if fresh, five if recycled—); the nucleus (a fine layer of three parts crushed potsherd to one of lime, some 15 cm); and above it the setting bed where the tesserae of the pavimentum were fixed. On upper floors the whole is laid over the joists. A key material here is opus signinum (cocciopesto): lime with crushed terracotta, waterproof, of Punic North African origin, spread through Sicily and Italy and used both for floors and for cisterns. The Vitruvian stratigraphy remains the reference framework for the archaeometry of mosaics.

chunks.texto: item danda est opera ne commisceantur axes aesculini querco, quod quercei simul umorem perceperunt se torquentes rimas faciunt in pavimentis. sin autem aesculus non erit et necessitas coegerit, propter inopiam querceis ⟨uti⟩ sic videtur esse faciundum ut secentur tenuiores. quo minus enim valuerint, eo facilius clavis fixi continebuntur deinde in singulis tignis extremis partibus axis bini clavi figantur, uti nulla ex parte possint se torquendo anguli excitare. namque de cerro aut fago seu farno nullus ad vestutatem potest permanere. coaxationibus factis si erit, filex, si non, palea substernatur, uti materies ab calcis vitiis defendatur.
chunks.traduccion: Also, care must be taken not to mix the axes of the aesculinus with the oak, because the oaks, having perceived the moisture at the same time, twist themselves and make cracks in the floors. But if the aesculinus is not available and necessity compels, due to the scarcity of oaks it seems that it is necessary to cut them thinner. For the weaker they are, the more easily they will be held fixed with nails. Then the axes are fixed with two nails in each of the extreme parts of the beams, so that they cannot raise the corners by twisting from any side. For none of the fir, beech or fir can last for a long time. After the coaxings have been made, if there is one, it is covered with straw, if not, so that the materials are protected from the defects of lime.

chunks.texto: tunc insuper statuminetur ne minore saxo quam qui possit manum implere. statuminationibus inductis rudus si novum erit, ad tres partes una calcis misceatur, si redivivum fuerit, quinque ad duo mixtionis habeant responsum. deinde rudus inducatur et vectibus ligneis, decuriis inductis, crebriter pistatione solidetur, et id non minus pinsum absolutum crassitudine sit dodrantis. insuper ex testa nucleus inducatur mixtionem habens ad tres partes unam calcis, ne minore crassitudine [pavimentum] digitorum senûm. supra nucleum ad regulam et libellam exacta pavimenta struantur sive sectilia seu tesseris.
chunks.traduccion: Then, in addition, let it be determined that it should not be made with a smaller stone than can fill the hand. After the determinations, if the raw material is new, it should be mixed with one part lime to three parts, if it is recycled, five parts to two parts of the mixture should be the answer. Then, the raw material should be introduced and solidified with wooden bars, boards, and frequent pounding, and that the absolute paste should not be less than the thickness of the dodrant. In addition, a core of the shell should be introduced, containing one part lime to three parts, so that the thickness of the pavement is less than the fingers of the old man. On top of the core, floors should be built, using a rule and a level, whether it is made of tiles or tiles.

chunks.texto: cum ea structa fuerint et fastigia sua ex structione habuerint, ita fricentur uti si sectilia sint, nulli gradus in scutulis aut trigonis aut quadratis seu favis extent, sed coagmentorum compositio planam habeat inter se directionem. si tesseris structum erit, ut eae omnes angulos habeant aequales. cum enim anguli non fuerint omnes aequaliter plani, non erit exacta ut oportet fricatura. item testacea spicata tiburtina sunt diligenter exigenda, ut ne habeant lacunas nec extantes tumulos, sed <sint> extenta et ad regulam perfricata. super fricaturam, levigationibus et polituris cum fuerint perfecta, incernatur marmor, et supra loricae ex calce et harena inducantur.
chunks.traduccion: When they have been built, the peaks will have their own structure, and they will be rubbed so that if they are sectile, no steps in the scrolls or triangles or squares or honeycombs will extend, but the composition of the joints will have a flat direction between them. If it is built with tiles, it will be so that all of them have equal angles. For since the angles will not all be equally flat, the rubbing will not be as exact as it should be. Likewise, the spiked shells of Tiburtine must be carefully removed, so that they do not have gaps or protruding mounds, but <are> extended and rubbed to the rule. Marble is laid on top, and on top of them are placed armour plates made of lime and sand.

chunks.texto: Subdiu vero maxime idonea faciunda sunt pavimenta, quod contignationes umore crescentes aut siccitate decrescentes seu pandationibus sidentes movendo se faciunt vitia pavimentis, praeterea gelicidia et pruinae non patiuntur integra permanere. itaque si necessitas coegerit, ut minime vitiosa fiant sic erit faciundum. cum coaxatum fuerit, super altera coaxatio transversa sternatur clavisque fixa duplicem praebeat contignationi loricationem. deinde ruderi novo tertia pars testae tunsae admisceatur calcisque duae partes ad quinque mortarii mixtionibus praestent responsum.
chunks.traduccion: But the most suitable pavements should be made in the long term, because floors that increase with moisture or decrease with dryness or that sit on supports by moving themselves cause defects in the pavements, and furthermore frost and frost do not allow them to remain intact. Therefore, if necessity compels them, so that they become the least defective, this is what should be done. When it has been compacted, another compaction is laid across it and nails are fixed to provide a double location for the pavement. Then a third part of crushed stone is mixed with new rubble and two parts of lime to five parts of mortar are mixed to provide the answer.

chunks.texto: statuminatione facta, rudus inducatur, idque pistum absolutum ne minus pede sit crassum. tunc autem nucleo inducto, uti supra scriptum est, pavimentum e tessera grandi circiter binûm digitûm caesa struatur fastigium habens in pedes denos digitos binos, quod si bene temperabitur et recte fricatum fuerit, ab omnibus vitiis erit tutum. uti autem inter coagmenta materies ab gelicidiis ne laboret, fracibus quotannis ante hiemem saturetur. ita non patietur in se recipere gelicidii pruinam.
chunks.traduccion: Having made the determination, the rough is introduced, and the finished dough is not less than a foot thick. Then, after the core has been introduced, as is written above, a floor is built from a large tile cut about two inches thick, having a ridge of ten inches on each foot, which, if well tempered and properly rubbed, will be safe from all defects. But so that the materials between the joints do not suffer from frost, it is saturated with broken pieces every year before winter. In this way it will not be allowed to receive frost from the frost.

chunks.texto: sin autem curiosius videbitur fieri oportere, tegulae bipedales inter se coagmentatae supra rudus substrata materia conlocentur habentes singulis coagmentorum frontibus excelsos canaliculos digitales. quibus iunctis inplicetur calx ex oleo subacta confricenturque inter se coagmenta compressa. ita calx quae erit haerens in canalibus durescendo contexteque solidescendo non patietur aquam neque aliam rem per coagmenta transire. cum ergo fuerit hoc ita perstratum, supra nucleus inducatur et virgis caedendo subigatur. supra autem sive ex tessera grandi sive ex spica testacea ⟨pavimenta⟩ struantur fastigiis quibus est supra scriptum, et cum sic erunt facta, non cito vitiabuntur.
chunks.traduccion: If a more careful construction is required, lay closely jointed two-foot tiles over the prepared bedding on the rudus. Give the meeting edges finger-wide grooves. Work oil-tempered lime into these grooves and rub the joints together under pressure. As the lime hardens into a continuous bond, it prevents water or other matter from passing through. Spread the nucleus over the tiles and compact it by beating with rods. Above it, lay either large tesserae or a herringbone pavement of fired clay, with the falls prescribed earlier. A floor made in this way will not readily deteriorate.

chunks.texto: Cum a pavimentorum cura discessum fuerit, tunc de albariis operibus est explicandum. id autem erit recte, si glaebae calcis optimae ante multo tempore quam opus fuerit macerabuntur, uti si qua glaeba parum fuerit in fornace cocta, in maceratione diuturna liquore defervere coacta uno tenore concoquatur. namque cum non penitus macerata sed recens sumitur, cum fuerit inducta habens latentes crudos calculos pustulas emittit. qui calculi in opere uno tenore cum permacerantur, dissolvunt et dissipant tectorii politiones.
chunks.traduccion: After the construction of pavements, lime finishing must be explained. Soak the best lumps of lime well before they are needed. Any lump insufficiently burned in the kiln can then be thoroughly slaked by prolonged contact with water. Fresh lime used before it is fully soaked contains hidden unslaked particles that form blisters after application. As those particles finally slake within the work, they disrupt and break up the plaster finish.

chunks.texto: cum autem habita erit ratio macerationis et id curiosius operi praeparatum erit, sumatur ascia et quemadmodum materia dolatur, sic calx in lacu macerata ascietur. si ad eam offenderint calculi, non erit temperata. cumque siccum et purum ferrum educetur, indicabit eam evanidam et siticulosam. cum vero pinguis fuerit et recte macerata, circa id ferramentum uti glutinum haerens omni ratione probabit se esse temperatam. tunc autem machinis comparatis camerarum dispositiones in conclavibus expediantur, nisi lacunariis ea fuerint ornata.
chunks.traduccion: Once the soaking has been carefully completed, take an adze and test the lime in its pit as one would hew timber. If the tool strikes hard particles, the lime is not properly prepared. If the iron emerges dry and clean, the lime is lean and thirsty. If the lime is rich and thoroughly slaked, it clings to the tool like glue, showing that it is ready. Then prepare the supporting apparatus and set out the vaulted ceilings in the rooms, unless they are to have coffered ceilings.

chunks.texto: Cum ergo camerarum postulabitur ratio, sic erit faciundum. asseres directi disponantur inter se ne plus spatium habentes pedes binos, et hi maxime cupressei, quod abiegnei ab carie et ab vetustate celeriter vitiantur, hique asseres cum ad formam circinationis fuerint distributi, catenis dispositis ad contignationes, sive tecta erunt, crebriter clavis ferreis fixi religentur, eaeque catenae ex ea materia comparentur cui nec
chunks.traduccion: Where a vaulted ceiling is required, set straight wooden laths no more than two feet apart. Cypress is preferable, since fir is quickly damaged by decay and age. Arrange the laths to the curve of the vault and attach them to the floor or roof framing with closely fixed iron nails and wooden hangers. Choose wood for those hangers that is resistant to

chunks.texto: asseribus dispositis tum tomice ex sparto hispanico harundines graecae tunsae ad eos uti forma postulat religentur. item supra cameram materies ex calce et harena mixta subinde inducatur, ut si quae stillae ex contignationibus aut tectis ceciderint sustineantur. sin autem harundinis graecae copia non erit, de paludibus tenues colligantur et mataxae tomice ad iustam longitudinem una crassitudine alligationibus temperentur, dum ne plus inter duos nodos [alligationibus] binos pedes distent, et hae ad asseres, uti supra scriptum est, tomice religentur cultellique lignei in eas configantur. cetera omnia uti supra scriptum est expediantur.
chunks.traduccion: Once the laths are in place, bind crushed Greek reeds to them with cords of Spanish esparto, following the required curve. Apply a mixture of lime and sand above the vault to catch any drops falling from the floor or roof above. If Greek reeds are unavailable, gather slender marsh reeds and tie them into bundles of even thickness and suitable length, keeping the ties no more than two feet apart. Bind these bundles to the laths in the same manner and fix wooden slips into them. Complete the remaining work as described above.

chunks.texto: Cameris dispositis et intextis, imum caelum earum trullissetur, deinde harena dirigatur, postea autem creta aut marmore poliatur. Cum camerae politae fuerint, sub eas coronae sunt subiciendae, quas maxime tenues et subtiles oportere fieri videbitur. cum enim grandes sunt, pondere deducuntur nec possunt se sustinere. in hisque minime gypsum debet admisceri, sed ex creto marmore uno tenore perduci, uti ne praecipiendo non patiatur uno tenore opus inarescere. etiamque cavendae sunt in cameris priscorum dispositiones, quod earum planitiae coronarum <> gravi pondere inpendentes sunt periculosae.
chunks.traduccion: Once the vaults have been framed and woven, apply a rough coat to their undersides, level them with sand plaster, and finish with chalk or marble. Beneath the finished vaults, form cornices as thin and light as possible: large cornices are pulled down by their own weight and cannot support themselves. Mix no gypsum into them; use sifted marble throughout, so that premature setting does not prevent the work from drying uniformly. Avoid the old arrangements of vaulted ceilings, whose projecting cornices are dangerous because of their weight.

chunks.texto: Coronarum autem sunt < figurae aliae purae> aliae caelatae. conclavibus autem ubi ignis aut plura lumina sunt ponenda, purae fieri debent, ut eo facilius extergeantur. in aestivis et exhedris, ubi minime fumus est nec fuligo potest nocere, ibi caelatae sunt faciendae, semper enim album opus propter superbiam candoris non modo ex propriis sed etiam alienis aedificiis concipit fumum.
chunks.traduccion: Cornices may be ⟨plain or⟩ carved. In rooms where fires or many lamps will be used, make them plain so that they can be cleaned more easily. In summer rooms and exedras, where smoke and soot cause less harm, carved cornices are appropriate. The brilliance of white plaster makes smoke apparent, whether it comes from the building itself or from neighboring buildings.

chunks.texto: Coronis explicatis parietes quam asperrime trullissentur, postea autem supra, trullissatione subarescente, deformentur directiones harenati, uti longitudines ad regulam et ad lineam, altitudines ad perpendiculum, anguli ad normam respondentes exigantur. namque sic emendata tectoriorum in picturis erit species. subarescente, iterum et tertio inducatur. ita cum fundatior erit ex harenato directura, eo firmior erit ad vetustatem soliditas tectorii.
chunks.traduccion: After completing the cornices, give the walls a rough coat. As it begins to dry, apply and straighten the sand-plaster coat, checking horizontal lines with rule and string, verticals with the plumb line, and corners with the square. This improves the appearance of the painted finish. When the coat has partly dried, apply a second and a third. The more substantial this sand-plaster foundation, the more durable the finished plaster will be.

chunks.texto: cum ab harena praeter trullissationem non minus tribus coriis fuerit deformatum, tunc e marmore graneo directiones sunt subigendae, dum ita materies temperetur uti cum subigatur non haereat ad rutrum, sed purum ferrum e mortario liberetur. grandi inducto et inarescente, alterum corium mediocre dirigatur. id cum subactum fuerit et bene fricatum, subtilius inducatur. ita cum tribus coriis harenae et item marmoris solidati parietes fuerint, neque rimas neque aliud vitium in se recipere poterunt.
chunks.traduccion: After at least three sand-plaster coats have been applied in addition to the rough coat, work on a coat of coarse marble plaster. Mix it so that it does not cling to the trowel, but leaves the iron clean when lifted from the mixing vessel. When this coarse coat has been applied and has begun to dry, level on a medium-grained coat. After that has been worked and rubbed smooth, apply a finer one. Walls built up with three coats of sand plaster and three of marble plaster resist cracking and other defects.

chunks.texto: sed et liaculorum subactionibus fundata soliditate marmorisque candore firmo levigata, coloribus cum politionibus inductis nitidos expriment splendores. colores autem, udo tectorio cum diligenter sunt inducti, ideo non remittunt sed sunt perpetuo permanentes, quod calx in fornacibus excocto liquore facta raritatibus evanida, ieiunitate coacta corripit in se quae res forte contigerunt, mixtionibusque ex aliis potestatibus conlatis seminibus seu principiis una solidescendo, in quibuscumque membris est formata cum fit arida redigitur uti sui generis proprias videatur habere qualitates.
chunks.traduccion: Thorough working with the polishing tools gives the finish solidity, while the whiteness of the marble produces a smooth, bright surface. Colors applied as the finish is polished acquire a brilliant sheen. When carefully laid on wet plaster, they remain fast rather than fading. Vitruvius explains this by the lime’s porous, thirsty condition after its moisture has been driven out in the kiln: it draws in substances that come into contact with it. Their constituent principles combine as the material hardens, so that the dry surface seems to possess the colors as qualities of its own.

chunks.texto: itaque tectoria quae recte sunt facta neque vetustatibus fiunt horrida, neque cum extergentur remittunt colores, nisi si parum diligenter et in arido fuerint inducti. cum ergo ita in parietibus tectoria facta fuerint uti supra scriptum est, et firmitatem et splendorem et ad vetustatem permanentem virtutem poterunt habere. cum vero unum corium harenae et unum minuti marmoris erit inductum, tenuitas eius minus valendo faciliter rumpitur nec splendorem politionibus propter inbecillitatem crassitudinis proprium obtinebit.
chunks.traduccion: Properly made plaster does not roughen with age or lose its colors when wiped, unless the pigments were applied carelessly or to a dry surface. Walls finished by the method described above retain strength, brilliance, and lasting quality. If only one sand-plaster coat and one fine marble coat are used, the thin finish readily cracks and lacks the substance needed to acquire the brilliance of a well-polished surface.

chunks.texto: quemadmodum enim speculum argenteum tenui lamella ductum incertas et sine viribus habet remissiones splendoris, quod autem e solida temperatura fuerit factum, recipiens in se firmis viribus politionem fulgentes in aspectu certasque considerantibus imagines reddet, sic tectoria quae ex tenui sunt ducta materia non modo sunt rimosa, sed etiam celeriter evanescunt, quae autem fundata harenationis et marmoris soliditate sunt crassitudine spissa, cum sunt politionibus crebris subacta, non modo sunt nitentia, sed etiam imagines expressas aspicientibus ex eo opere remittunt.
chunks.traduccion: A silver mirror made from a thin sheet gives faint, uncertain reflections, whereas one of substantial material takes a firm polish and returns clear, brilliant images. Plaster is similar: a thin coating cracks and soon deteriorates. A thick finish founded on solid sand and marble coats, repeatedly worked and polished, not only shines but reflects distinct images to the viewer.

chunks.texto: Graecorum vero tectores non solum his rationibus utendo faciunt opera firma, sed etiam mortario conlocato, calce et harena ibi confusa, decuria hominum inducta, ligneis vectibus pisant materiam, et ita ad certamen subacta tunc utuntur. itaque veteribus parietibus nonnulli crustas excidentes pro abacis•utuntur, ipsaque tectoria abacorum et speculorum divisionibus circa se prominentes habent expressiones.
chunks.traduccion: Greek plasterers strengthen their work not only by these methods. They also mix lime and sand in a mixing vessel and set a gang of ten men to pound it with wooden rammers. After this vigorous working, they use the mixture. Some people cut panels from old walls and reuse them; their plaster surfaces carry raised moldings around divisions into panels and mirror-like fields.

chunks.texto: Sin autem in craticiis tectoria erunt facienda, quibus necesse est in arrectariis et transversariis rimas fieri, ideo quod luto cum linuntur necessario recipiunt umorem, cum autem arescunt extenuati in tectoriis faciunt rimas, id ut non fiat haec erit ratio. cum paries totus luto inquinatus fuerit, tunc in eo opere cannae clavis muscariis perpetuae figantur, deinde iterum luto inducto si priores transversariis harundinibus fixae sunt, secundae erectis figantur et ita, uti supra scriptum est, harenatum et marmor et omne tectorium inducatur. ita cannarum duplex in parietibus harundinibus transversis fixa perpetuitas nec segmina nec rimam ullam fieri patietur.
chunks.traduccion: Plaster applied to wattle partitions is liable to crack along the uprights and crosspieces. These absorb moisture when coated with clay and then shrink as they dry, splitting the finish. To prevent this, coat the whole wall with clay and fasten a continuous layer of reeds with broad-headed nails. Apply another clay coat and fix a second reed layer across the first: if the first reeds run horizontally, set the second vertically. Then apply the sand plaster, marble coats, and complete finish as described above. These two continuous layers of reeds, fixed across one another, prevent breaks and cracks.

chunks.texto: Quibus rationibus siccis locis tectoria oporteat fieri dixi, nunc quemadmodum umidis locis politiones expediantur ut permanere possint sine vitiis, exponam. et primum conclavibus quae plano pede fuerint, in imo pavimento alte circiter pedibus tribus pro harenato testa trullissetur et dirigatur, uti eae partes tectoriorum ab umore ne vitientur. sin autem aliqui paries perpetuos habuerit umores, paululum ab eo recedatur et struatur alter tenuis distans ab eo quantum res patietur, et inter duos parietes canalis ducatur inferior quam libramentum conclavis fuerit, habens nares ad locum patentem. item cum in altitudinem perstructus fuerit, relinquantur spiramenta. si enim non per nares umor et in imo et in summo habuerit exitus, non minus in nova structura se dissipabit. his perfectis paries testa trullissetur et dirigatur et tunc tectorio poliatur.
chunks.traduccion: I have explained how plaster finishes should be made in dry places. I shall now describe their treatment in damp places so that they remain sound. In ground-floor rooms, apply and level a crushed-tile plaster instead of sand plaster on the lower part of the wall, to about three feet above the floor. This protects the finish from moisture. Where a wall remains continuously damp, build a second, thin wall a short distance in front of it, as space permits. Between the walls, run a channel below floor level with vents to the open air, and leave ventilation openings at the top. Without outlets both below and above, moisture will spread through the new work as well. When these provisions are complete, rough-coat and level the wall with crushed-tile plaster, then apply the finish.

chunks.texto: sin autem locus non patietur structuram fieri, canales fiant et nares exeant ad locum patentem. deinde tegulae bipedales ex una parte supra marginem canalis inponantur, ex altera parte besalibus <laterculis> pilae substruantur, in quibus duarum tegularum anguli sedere possint, et ita a pariete eae distent ut ne plus pateant palmum. deinde insuper erectae mammatae tegulae ab imo ad summum ad parietem figantur, quarum interiores partes curiosius picentur ut ab se respuant liquorem. item in imo et in summo supra camaram habeant spiramenta.
chunks.traduccion: If there is not enough space to build another wall, make channels with vents opening to the outside. Lay two-foot tiles with one side resting on the channel’s edge; support the other side on piers of eight-inch bricks, so that the corners of two tiles can rest on each pier. Keep the tiles no more than a palm’s breadth from the wall. Above these, fix studded tiles upright against the wall from bottom to top, carefully coating their inner surfaces with pitch to repel moisture. Provide ventilation openings both at the bottom and at the top, above the vault.

chunks.texto: tum autem calce ex aqua liquida dealbentur, uti trullissationem testaceam non respuant. namque propter ieiunitatem quae est a fornacibus excocta non possunt recipere nec sustinere, nisi calx subiecta utrasque res inter se conglutinet et cogat coire. trullissatione inducta pro harenato testa dirigatur, et cetera omnia uti supra scripta sunt in tectorii rationibus perficiantur.
chunks.traduccion: Then they are whitened with lime from liquid water, so that they do not reject the earthenware trowel. For because of the fastness which is produced by the kilns, they cannot receive or withstand it, unless the lime applied adheres both things to each other and forces them to come together. The trowel is then applied instead of the sanded one, and all the other things are carried out as written above in the rules for roofers.

chunks.texto: Ipsi autem politionibus eorum ornatus proprios debent habere ad decoris rationes, uti et ex locis aptas et generum discriminibus non alienas habeant dignitates. tricliniis hibernis non est utilis compositione nec megalographia nec camerarum coronario opere subtilis ornatus, quod ea et ab ignis fumo et ab luminum crebris fuliginibus corrumpuntur. in his vero supra podia abaci•ex atramento sunt subigendi et poliendi, cuneis silaceis seu miniaceis interpositis. et explicandae camerae pure politae, etiam pavimentorum non erit displicens, si qui animadvertere voluerit, Graecorum hibernaculorum usum minime sumptuosus et utilis apparatus.
chunks.traduccion: But their decorations should have their own reasons for decoration, so that they may have dignities that are appropriate to the place and not alien to the differences of gender. In winter dining rooms, neither large-scale painting nor subtle decoration in the crowning work of the chambers is useful in composition, because they are corrupted by the smoke of the fire and by the frequent soot of the lights. In these, however, the above podiabaci are to be subjected and polished with ink, with wedges of siliceous or miniaceous interposed. The chamber, when explained, is clean and polished, and even the pavements will not be displeasing, if anyone wishes to observe, the least costly and useful equipment of the Greeks for the use of winter quarters.

chunks.texto: foditur enim infra libramentum triclinii altitudo circiter pedum binûm, et solo festucato•inducitur aut rudus aut testaceum pavimentum ita fastigatum ut in canali habeat nares. deinde congestis et spisse calcatis carbonibus inducitur e sabulone et calce et favilla mixta materies crassitudine semipedali. ad regulam et libellam summo libramento cote despumato redditur species nigri pavimenti. ita conviviis eorum et quod poculis et pytismatis effunditur simul cadit siccescitque, quique versantur ibi ministrantes etsi nudis pedibus fuerint, non recipiunt frigus ab eius modi genere pavimenti.
chunks.traduccion: For a pit is dug below the dining room level to a depth of about two feet, and on the ground is laid either a rough or earthen floor, so leveled that it has holes in the channel. Then, with heaped and thickly trodden coals, a mixture of sand, lime and ash is laid to a thickness of half a foot. With a ruler and a level, the appearance of a black floor is rendered by skimming the foam from the top of the level. Thus, at their banquets, whatever is poured into cups and bowls falls down and dries up at the same time, and those who are there serving, even if they are barefoot, do not receive the cold from that kind of floor.

chunks.texto: Ceteris conclavibus id est vernis autumnalibus aestivis, etiam atriis et peristylis constitutae sunt ab antiquis ex certis rebus certae rationes picturarum. namque pictura imago fit eius quod est seu potest esse, uti homines, aedificia, naves reliquarumque rerum, e quibus, finitis certisque corporibus, figurata similitudine sumuntur exempla. ex eo antiqui qui initia expolitionibus instituerunt imitati sunt primum crustarum marmorearum varietates et conlocationes, deinde coronarum siliculorum cuneorum inter sese varias distributiones.
chunks.traduccion: For other rooms, that is, for spring, autumn, and summer, and also for atriums and peristyles, the ancients established certain types of paintings from certain things. For painting is an image of what is or can be, such as a man, a building, a ship, and other things, from which, having finite and certain bodies, examples are gathered in figured likeness. From this the ancients, who began the refinements, imitated first the varieties and arrangements of marble crusts, then the various distributions of crowns and wedges of siliceous stone among themselves.

chunks.texto: postea ingressi sunt ut etiam aedificiorum figuras, columnarum et fastigiorum eminentes proiecturas imitarentur, patentibus autem locis uti exhedris propter amplitudines parietum scaenarum frontes tragico more aut comico seu satyrico designarent, ambulationibus vero propter spatia longitudinis varietatibus topiorum ornarent ab certis locorum proprietatibus imagines exprimentes. pinguntur enim portus promunturia litora flumina fontes euripi fana luci montes pecora pastores, nonnulli loci item signorum megalographiam habent et deorum simulacra seu fabularum dispositas explicationes, non minus troianas pugnas seu Ulixis errationes per topia, ceteraque quae sunt eorum similibus rationibus ab rerum natura procreata.
chunks.traduccion: Later, painters began to imitate the forms of buildings and the projecting members of columns and pediments. On the broad walls of open rooms such as exedras, they represented stage facades in the tragic, comic, or satyric manner. Along walks, whose length offered greater scope, they painted varied landscapes drawn from the distinctive features of particular places: harbors, promontories, shores, rivers, springs, canals, sanctuaries, groves, mountains, flocks, and shepherds. Some settings also contain large-scale figure paintings, images of gods, or ordered scenes from myths, including the battles at Troy and the wanderings of Ulysses through landscapes, together with other subjects drawn on similar principles from the natural world.

chunks.texto: sed haec quae ex veris rebus exempla sumebantur, nunc iniquis moribus inprobantur. nam pinguntur tectoriis monstra potius quam ex rebus finitis imagines certae. pro columnis enim struuntur calami, striati cum crispis foliis et volutis, pro fastigiis appagineculi item candelabra aedicularum sustinentia figuras, supra fastigia eorum surgentes ex radicibus cum volutis <> teneri flores habentes in se sine ratione sedentia sigilla, non minus coliculi dimidiata habentes sigilla alia humanis alia bestiarum capitibus.
chunks.traduccion: But these subjects, once drawn from real things, are now condemned by a depraved taste. For upon the plaster are painted monstrosities rather than truthful images of definite things: reeds are set up in place of columns; in place of pediments, fluted scrolls with curling leaves and volutes; candelabra bearing the figures of little shrines; and, above their pediments, springing from roots, a multitude of slender stalks with volutes, bearing for no reason little seated figures, and other stalks half-human and half-animal in their heads.

chunks.texto: haec autem nec sunt nec fieri possunt nec fuerunt.. quemadmodum enim potest calamus vere sustinere tectum aut candelabrûm ornamenta fastigii seu coliculus tam tenuis et mollis sustinere sedens sigillum aut de radicibus et coliculis ex parte flores dimidiataque sigilla procreari? at haec falsa videntes homines non reprehendunt sed delectantur, neque animadvertunt si quid eorum fieri potest necne. ergo ita novi mores coegerunt, uti inertiae mali iudices convincerent artium virtutes. iudiciis autem infirmis obscuratae mentes non valent probare quod potest esse cum auctoritate et ratione decoris. neque enim picturae probari debent quae non sunt similes veritati, nec si factae sunt elegantes ab arte, ideo de his statim debet recte iudicari, nisi argumentationis certas rationes habuerint sine offensionibus explicatas.
chunks.traduccion: Yet such things do not exist, cannot exist and have never existed. How can a reed truly support a roof, a candelabrum the ornaments of a pediment, or a stalk so slender and soft a seated figure? How can flowers and half-figures grow from roots and stalks? Yet people look at these falsehoods without criticism and take pleasure in them, never considering whether any of them could exist. New fashions have thus led bad judges to condemn artistic excellence as ineptitude. Minds obscured by unsound judgment cannot recognize what may properly exist in accordance with the principles of decor. Paintings that bear no resemblance to reality should not be approved; nor, merely because they are elegantly executed, should they immediately be judged sound unless their subjects can be explained by coherent reasoning without inconsistency.

chunks.texto: etenim etiam Trallibus cum Apaturius Alabandeus eleganti manu finxisset scaenam in minusculo theatro, quod ἐκκλησιαστήριον apud eos vocitatur, in eaque fecisset columnas signa Centauros sustinentes epistylia, tholorum rotunda tecta, fastigiorum prominentes versuras, coronasque capitibus leoninis ornatas quae ora stillicidiorum e tectis habent rationem, praeterea supra ea nihilominus episcaenum, in qua tholi pronai semifastigia omnisque tecti varius picturis fuerat ornatus, itaque cum aspectus eius scaenae propter asperitatem eblandiretur omnium visus et iam id opus probare fuissent parati,
chunks.traduccion: For even at Tralles, when Apaturius of Alabanda had painted with elegant hand the stage of the small theater which they call the ἐκκλησιαστήριον, and had set in it columns and statues — Centaurs upholding the architraves, the rounded roofs of domes, the projecting angles of pediments, and cornices ornamented with lions’ heads, all of which belong by rights to the eaves of a roof — men were already prepared to approve the work for its charm, when Licymnius the mathematician came forward.

chunks.texto: tum Licymnius mathematicus prodiit et ait Alabandis satis acutos ad omnes res civiles haberi, sed propter non magnum vitium indecentiae insipientes eos esse iudicatos, quod in gymnasio eorum quae sunt statuae omnes sunt causas agentes, foro discos tenentes aut currentes seu pila ludentes. ita indecens inter locorum proprietates status signorum publice civitati vitium existimationis adiecit. videamus item nunc ne Apaturii scaena efficiat et nos Alabandis aut Abderitas. qui enim vestrum domos supra tegularum tecta potest habere aut columnas seu fastigiorum explicationes? haec enim supra contignationes ponuntur, non supra tegularum tecta. si ergo quae non possunt in veritate rationem habere facti in picturis probaverimus, accedemus et nos his civitatibus quae propter haec vitia insipientes sunt iudicatae.
chunks.traduccion: Then Licymnius the mathematician came forward and said: “The Alabandians are reckoned shrewd enough in all civic affairs; yet for one small fault of impropriety they are held wanting in judgment, for in their gymnasium all the statues are of men pleading causes, while in the forum they hold the discus, or run, or play at ball. Thus the unfitness of the statues to the character of their settings fastened upon the city a public reputation for poor sense. Let us beware, then, lest this scene-painting make us too into Alabandians: for which of you can have, upon the tiled roof of his house, columns or the carved cornices of pediments? Such things rest upon floors, not upon roof-tiles. If, then, we approve in painting what can have no warrant in reality, we join those cities judged wanting in sense.

chunks.texto: itaque Apaturius contra respondere non est ausus, sed sustulit scaenam et ad rationem veritatis commutatam postea correctam adprobavit. utinam dii inmortales fecissent uti Licymnius revivisceret et corrigeret hanc amentiam tectoriorumque errantia instituta. sed quare vincat veritatem ratio falsa, non erit alienum exponere. quod enim antiqui insumentes laborem et industriam probare contendebant artibus, id nunc coloribus et eorum eleganti specie consecuntur, et quam subtilitas artificis adiciebat operibus auctoritatem, nunc dominicus sumptus efficit ne desideretur.
chunks.traduccion: Apaturius therefore dared not reply. He removed the stage painting, revised it in accordance with truth and subsequently secured approval for the corrected work. Would that the immortal gods might bring Licymnius back to life to correct this madness and these misguided practices of wall decoration. It is worth explaining why a false approach prevails over truth. What the ancients sought to commend through art, labor and diligence is now achieved through colors and their elegant appearance. The authority that the craftsman’s subtlety once gave to a work is now supplied by the owner’s expenditure, so that its absence goes unnoticed.

chunks.texto: quis enim antiquorum non uti medicamento minio parce videtur usus esse? at nunc passim plerumque toti parietes inducuntur. accedit huc chrysocolla, ostrum, armenium. haec vero cum inducuntur etsi non ab arte sunt posita, fulgentes colorum reddunt visus, et ideo quod pretiosa sunt, legibus excipiuntur, ut ab domino non a redemptore repraesententur.
chunks.traduccion: Which of the ancients does not seem to have used minium sparingly, as one would a medicine? Now, by contrast, whole walls are commonly coated with it. Chrysocolla, purple and Armenian blue are added as well. Even when applied without artistry, these colors give the eye a brilliant impression. Because they are expensive, contracts make a special provision that the owner, rather than the contractor, should supply them.

chunks.texto: Quae commonefacere potui ut ab errore discedatur in opere tectorio satis exposui, nunc de apparitionibus ut succurrere potuerit dicam, et primum quoniam de calce initio est dictum, nunc de marmore ponam. Marmor non eodem genere omnibus regionibus procreatur, sed quibusdam locis glaebae ut salis micas perlucidas habentes nascuntur, quae contusae et molitae praestant operibus utilitatem. quibus autem locis eae copiae non sunt, caementa marmorea, sive assulae dicuntur, quae marmorarii ex operibus deiciunt, contunduntur et moluntur, <et cum> est subcretum in operibus utuntur. aliis locis, ut inter Magnesiae et Ephesi fines, sunt loca unde foditur ⟨farina⟩ parata quam nec molere nec cernere opus est, sed sic est subtilis quemadmodum si qua est manu contusa et subcreta.
chunks.traduccion: I have said enough to warn against mistakes in plasterwork. I shall now discuss the materials, beginning with marble, since lime has already been treated. Marble does not occur in the same form in every region. In some places lumps containing translucent particles like grains of salt are found; crushed and ground, they are useful in building. Where such supplies are unavailable, the fragments or chips discarded by marble-workers are crushed, ground and, once sifted, used in the work. Elsewhere, as in the territory between Magnesia and Ephesus, a ready-made powder is quarried. It needs neither grinding nor sifting, being as fine as material crushed and sifted by hand.

chunks.texto: Colores vero alii sunt qui per se certis locis procreantur et inde fodiuntur, nonnulli ex aliis rebus tractationibus aut mixtionum temperaturis compositi perficiuntur, uti praestent eandem in operibus utilitatem. primum autem exponemus quae per se nascentia fodiuntur, uti sil, quod graece ὤχρα dicitur. haec vero multis locis ut etiam in Italia invenitur, sed quae fuerat optima, attica ideo nunc non habetur quod Athenis argentifodinae cum habuerunt familias, tunc specus sub terra fodiebantur ad argentum inveniendum. cum ibi vena forte inveniretur, nihilominus uti argentum persequebantur, itaque antiqui egregia copia silis ad politionem operum sunt usi. item rubricae copiosae multis locis eximuntur, sed optimae paucis, uti Ponto Sinope, et Aegypto, in Hispania Balearibus, non minus etiam Lemno, cuius insulae vectigalia Atheniensibus senatus populusque Romanus concessit fruenda. paraetonium vero ex ipsis locis unde foditur habet nomen. eadem ratione melinum, quod eius metallum in sola cycladi Melo dicitur esse.
chunks.traduccion: Some colors occur naturally in particular places and are mined there; others are produced by processing materials or adjusting mixtures to serve the same purpose in building. First I shall describe those extracted in their natural state, such as sil, called ὤχρα in Greek. It is found in many places, including Italy, but the Attic variety, once the best, is no longer available. When the Athenian silver mines employed slave gangs, underground galleries were driven in search of silver. If a vein of ochre was encountered, it was pursued as eagerly as silver, and the ancients consequently had an excellent supply for finishing their buildings. Red ochres are also extracted abundantly in many places, but the finest come from only a few: Sinope in Pontus, Egypt, the Balearic Islands in Hispania and Lemnos, whose revenues the Roman Senate and people granted to the Athenians. Paraetonium takes its name from the place where it is quarried; similarly, melinum is so called because its deposit is said to occur only on Melos in the Cyclades.

chunks.texto: creta viridis item pluribus locis nascitur, sed optima Zmyrnae. hanc autem Graeci θεοδοτεῖον vocant, quod Theodotus nomine fuerat cuius in fundo id genus cretae primum est inventum. auripigmentum, quod ἀρσενικόν graece dicitur, foditur Ponto. sandaraca item pluribus locis, sed optima Ponto proxime flumen Hypanim habet metallum.
chunks.traduccion: Green earth also occurs in several places, but the best is found at Smyrna. The Greeks call it theodoteion after Theodotus, on whose estate that kind of earth was first discovered. Orpiment, called ἀρσενικόν in Greek, is mined in Pontus. Sandaraca occurs in several places too, but its finest deposit is in Pontus near the river Hypanis.

chunks.texto: Ingrediar nunc minii rationes explicare. id autem agris Ephesiorum Cilbianis primum esse memoratur inventum, cuius et res et ratio satis magnas habet admirationes. foditur enim glaeba quae dicitur, antequam tractationibus ad minium perveniant, vena uti ferrum, magis subrufo colore, habens circa se rubrum pulverem. cum id foditur, ex plagis ferramentorum crebras emittit lacrimas argenti vivi, quae a fossoribus statim colliguntur.
chunks.traduccion: I shall now explain minium. It is said to have been discovered first in the Cilbian fields belonging to the Ephesians. Both the substance and its treatment are remarkable. Before processing yields minium, the material is extracted as a lump from a vein resembling iron ore, but more reddish in color and surrounded by red dust. When it is mined, the blows of the tools release frequent drops of quicksilver, which the miners immediately collect.

chunks.texto: hae glaebae cum collectae sunt, in officina propter umoris plenitatem coiciuntur in fornacem ut interarescant, et is qui ex his ab ignis vapore fumus suscitatur cum resedit in solum furni, invenitur esse argentum vivum. exemptis glaebis guttae eae quae residebunt propter brevitates non possunt colligi, sed in vas aquae converruntur et ibi inter se congruunt et una confunduntur. id autem cum sint quattuor sextariorum, mensurae cum expenduntur, invenientur esse pondo centum.
chunks.traduccion: Because these lumps contain much moisture, they are taken to the workshop and put into a furnace to dry. The fumes raised by the heat of the fire, when deposited on the furnace floor, prove to be quicksilver. After the lumps have been removed, the remaining droplets are too small to gather individually. They are swept into a vessel of water, where they unite into a single mass. When the quantity reaches four sextarii, it will be found on weighing to amount to one hundred pounds.

chunks.texto: cum in aliquo vase est confusum, si supra id lapideum centenarium pondus inponatur, natat in summo neque eum liquorem potest onere suo premere nec elidere nec dissipare. centenario sublato si ibi auri scripulum inponatur, non natabit sed ad imum per se deprimetur. ita non amplitudine ponderis sed genere singularum rerum gravitatem esse non est negandum.
chunks.traduccion: When a liquid is mixed in a vessel, if a hundred-year-old stone weight is placed on top of it, it floats on top and cannot press down on the liquid with its own weight, nor can it remove or dissipate it. If a gold coin is placed there after the hundred-year-old stone weight is removed, it will not float but will sink to the bottom by itself. Thus it cannot be denied that gravity is not due to the magnitude of the weight but to the nature of individual things.

chunks.texto: id autem multis rebus est ad usum expeditum. neque enim argentum neque aes sine eo potest recte inaurari. cumque in veste intextum est aurum eaque vestis contrita propter vetustatem usum non habeat honestum, panni in fictilibus vasis inpositi supra ignem comburuntur. is cinis coicitur in aquam, et additur eo argentum vivum. id autem omnes micas auri corripit in se et cogit secum coire. aqua defusa cum id in pannum infunditur et ibi manibus premitur, argentum per panni raritates propter liquorem extra labitur, compressione coactum aurum intra purum invenitur.
chunks.traduccion: But this is for many things for ready use. For neither silver nor brass can be properly gilded without it. When gold is woven into a garment, and that garment, worn out because of its age, is no longer fit for honest use, the cloths are placed in earthenware vessels and burned over a fire. The ashes are thrown into water, and quicksilver is added to it. This, however, seizes all the gold flakes in itself and forces them to coalesce. When the water is poured into the cloth and pressed there with the hands, the silver slides out through the rarefied nature of the cloth because of the liquid, while the gold, forced inside by compression, is found pure.

chunks.texto: Revertar nunc ad minii temperaturam. ipsae enim glaebae cum sunt aridae, contunduntur pilis ferreis, et lotionibus et cocturis crebris relictis stercoribus efficiuntur ut adveniant colores. cum ergo emissae sint ex minio per argenti vivi relictionem quas in se naturales habuerat virtutes, efficitur tenera natura et viribus inbecillis.
chunks.traduccion: I return now to the preparation of minium. Once dry, the lumps are crushed with iron pestles. Repeated washing and heating remove the impurities and bring out the color. When the separation of the quicksilver has deprived the minium of its inherent properties, however, it becomes delicate and weak.

chunks.texto: itaque cum est in expolitionibus conclavium tectis inductum, permanet sine vitiis suo colore. apertis vero id est peristyliis aut exhedris aut ceteris eiusdem modi locis, quo sol et luna possit splendores et radios inmittere, cum ab his locus tangitur, vitiatur et amissa virtute coloris denigratur. itaque cum et alii multi tum etiam Faberius scriba cum in Aventino voluisset habere domum eleganter expolitam, peristyliis parietes omnes induxit minio, qui post dies XXX facti sunt invenusto varioque colore. itaque primo locavit inducendos alios colores.
chunks.traduccion: Applied to the finished plaster of covered rooms, it therefore retains its color without deterioration. In open places, such as peristyles, exedrae and similar spaces, where sunlight and moonlight can reach it, exposure causes it to deteriorate and blacken as its color loses its strength. Among many others, Faberius the scribe, wishing to finish his house on the Aventine elegantly, coated all the walls of its peristyles with minium. Within thirty days they had become discoloured and uneven, and he promptly contracted for other colors to be applied over them.

chunks.texto: at si qui subtilior fuerit et voluerit expolitionem miniaceam suum colorem retinere, cum paries expolitus et aridus fuerit, ceram ponticam igni liquefactam paulo oleo temperatam saeta inducat, deinde postea carbonibus in ferreo vase compositis eam ceram una cum pariete calfaciundo sudare cogat, atque ut peraequetur deinde tunc candela centunculisque puris subigat, uti signa marmorea nuda curantur. haec autem γάνωσις graece dicitur.
chunks.traduccion: A more discerning owner who wishes a minium finish to retain its color should, once the wall is polished and dry, brush it with Pontic wax melted over a fire and mixed with a little oil. Then place coals in an iron vessel and heat the wax together with the wall, causing it to sweat and spread evenly. Finally work it with a wax taper and clean linen, as bare marble statues are treated. This process is called γάνωσις in Greek.

chunks.texto: ita obstans cerae ponticae lorica non patitur nec lunae splendorem nec solis radios lambendo eripere ex his politionibus colorem. quae autem in Ephesiorum metallis fuerunt officinae, nunc traiectae sunt ideo Romam quod id genus venae postea est inventum Hispaniae regionibus, e quibus metallis glaebae portantur et per publicanos Romae curantur. eae autem officinae sunt inter aedem Florae et Quirini.
chunks.traduccion: Thus the breastplate of Pontic wax, standing firm, does not suffer either the brilliance of the moon or the rays of the sun to lick away the color from these polishes. But the workshops which were in the metals of the Ephesians have now been transferred to Rome, because that kind of vein was later discovered in the regions of Spain, from which metals the slabs are brought and treated by the publicans in Rome. Now those workshops are between the temple of Flora and Quirinus.

chunks.texto: Vitiatur minium admixta calce. itaque si qui velit experiri id sine vitio esse, sic erit faciendum. ferrea lamna sumatur, eo minium inponatur, ad ignem conlocetur donec lamna candescat. cum e candore color mutatus fuerit eritque ater, tollatur lamna ab igni et sic refrigeratum si restituatur in pristinum colorem, sine vitio esse probabitur, sin autem permanserit nigro colore, significabit se esse vitiatum.
chunks.traduccion: Let the minium be tainted with lime. Therefore, if anyone wishes to test whether it is without taint, this is what must be done. Take an iron plate, put the minium on it, and place it over the fire until the plate becomes red-hot. When the color has changed from whiteness and become black, remove the plate from the fire and, having cooled it, if it is restored to its original color, it will be proven to be without taint, but if it remains black, it will indicate that it is tainted.

chunks.texto: Quae succurrere potuerunt mihi de minio dixi. chrysocolla adportatur a Macedonia, foditur autem ex îs locis qui sunt proximi aerariis metallis. armenium et indicum nominibus ipsis indicatur quibus in locis procreatur.
chunks.traduccion: I have spoken of those things which could have helped me concerning minium. Chrysocolla is brought from Macedonia, and is mined from those places which are nearest to the precious metals. Armenian and indigo are indicated by the very names in which they are produced.

chunks.texto: Ingrediar nunc ad ea quae ex aliis generibus tractationum temperaturis commutata recipiunt colorum proprietates, et primum exponam de atramento, cuius usus in operibus magnas habet necessitates, ut sint notae quemadmodum praeparentur certis rationibus artificiorum ad id temperaturae.
chunks.traduccion: I will now proceed to those things which receive the properties of colors when changed by other types of treatment temperatures, and I will first explain about ink, the use of which in works has great needs, so that it may be known how it is prepared by certain methods of artificers at that temperature.

chunks.texto: namque aedificatur locus uti laconicum et expolitur marmore subtiliter et levigatur. ante id fit fornacula habens in laconicum nares, et eius praefurnium magna diligentia comprimitur ne flamma extra dissipetur. in fornace resina conlocatur. hanc autem ignis potestas urendo cogit emittere per nares intra laconicum fuliginem, quae circa parietem et camerae curvaturam adhaerescit. inde collecta partim componitur ex gummi subacta ad usum atramenti librarii, reliquum tectores glutinum admiscentes in parietibus utuntur.
chunks.traduccion: Build a room like a Laconian hot room, finish its interior with fine marble plaster, and polish it smooth. In front of it, construct a small furnace with vents opening into the room, and seal the firing chamber carefully so that the flame cannot escape outside. Place resin in the furnace. As it burns, the fire drives soot through the vents into the room, where it adheres to the walls and the curved vault. Collect this soot: work part of it with gum to make writing ink; plasterers mix the remainder with glue for use on walls.

chunks.texto: Si autem hae copiae non fuerint paratae, ita necessitatibus erit administrandum, ne expectatione morae res retineatur. sarmenta aut taedae schidiae comburantur, cum erunt carbones extinguantur, deinde in mortario cum glutino terantur.
chunks.traduccion: But if these supplies are not ready, then the necessities must be managed in this way, so that the matter is not held up by the expectation of delay. The twigs or splinters of firewood are burned, when the coals are extinguished, they are then ground in a mortar with glue.

chunks.texto: ita erit atramentum tectoribus non invenustum. non minus si faex vini arefacta et cocta in fornace fuerit et ea contrita cum glutino in opere inducetur, atramenti suavitatis superque efficiet colorem, et quo magis ex meliore vino parabitur, non modo atramenti sed etiam indici colorem dabit imitari.
chunks.traduccion: Thus the ink will be not unattractive to the painters. No less so if the dregs of wine have been dried and cooked in a furnace and this crushed together with the glue are introduced into the work, on which it will produce a color of the sweetness of the ink, and the more it is prepared from the best wine, it will imitate not only the color of the ink but also of the indicator.

chunks.texto: Caeruli temperationes Alexandriae primum sunt inventae, postea item Vestorius Puteolis instituit faciundum. ratio autem eius e quibus est inventa satis habet admirationis. harena enim cum nitri flore conteritur adeo subtiliter ut efficiatur quemadmodum farina, ea aes cyprum limis crassis uti scobis facta mixta conspargitur ut conglomeretur. deinde pilae manibus versando efficiuntur et ita conligantur ut inarescant. aridae componuntur in urceo fictili, urcei in fornace. ita aes et ea harena ab ignis vehementia confervescendo cum coaluerint, inter se dando et accipiendo sudores a proprietatibus discedunt suisque viribus per ignis vehementiam confectis caeruleo rediguntur colore.
chunks.traduccion: Blue (caeruleum) was first compounded at Alexandria, and afterwards Vestorius set up its manufacture at Puteoli. The method of its discovery is well worth admiration. Sand is ground together with flowers of natron so finely that it becomes as it were flour; copper is filed with coarse files into shavings and sprinkled over it; the mixture is moistened, rolled by hand into balls, dried, and packed in an earthen jar, and the jars are placed in a furnace. So, when the copper and the sand grow incandescent together by the fierceness of the fire, by giving and receiving their properties from one another they take on a blue color.

chunks.texto: usta vero, quae satis habet utilitatis in operibus tectoriis, sic temperatur. glaeba silis boni coquitur ut sit in igni candens. ea autem aceto extinguitur et efficitur purpureo colore.
chunks.traduccion: But the burnt clay, which is quite useful in roofing works, is tempered in this way. A lump of good clay is cooked until it is glowing in the fire. Then it is extinguished with vinegar and becomes purple in color.

chunks.texto: De cerussa aerugineque quam nostri aerucam vocitant non est alienum quemadmodum comparetur dicere. Rhodo enim doliis sarmenta conlocantes aceto suffuso supra sarmenta conlocant plumbeas massas, deinde ea operculis obturant ne spiramento obturatum emittatur. post certum tempus aperientes inveniunt e massis plumbeis cerussam. eadem ratione lamellas aereas conlocantes efficiunt aeruginem quae aeruca appellatur.
chunks.traduccion: Of the lead rust which our people call aeruca, it is not strange to say how it is compared. For in Rhodes, placing vine shoots in barrels, they place lead masses on top of the vine shoots, suffused with vinegar, then close them with lids so that the air cannot escape. After a certain time, opening them, they find lead from the lead masses. In the same way, placing bronze plates, they produce a rust which is called aeruca.

chunks.texto: cerussa vero cum in fornace coquitur, mutato colore ad ignem [incendi] efficitur sandaraca. id autem incendio facto ex casu didicerunt homines, et ea multo meliorem usum praestat quam quae de metallis per se nata foditur.
chunks.traduccion: White lead (cerussa), when baked in a kiln, changes color in the fire and turns into sandarach (red lead). Men learned this by chance, from a fire, and this pigment renders far better service than the one extracted by digging, born of its own accord in the veins.

chunks.texto: Incipiam nunc de ostro dicere, quod et carissimam et excellentissimam habet praeter hos colores aspectus suavitatem. id autem excipitur e conchylio marino, e quo purpura efficitur, cuius non minores sunt quam ceterarum <rerum> naturae considerantibus admirationes, quod habet non in omnibus locis quibus nascitur unius generis colorem, sed solis cursu naturaliter temperatur.
chunks.traduccion: I shall now speak of sea-purple (ostrum), which, beyond all the other colors, has the costliest and most exquisite loveliness of aspect. It is obtained from a marine shellfish, from which the purple dye is made, and to the observer its nature holds wonders not less than those of any other thing; for it does not yield a color of one kind in all the places where it is gathered, but is tempered by the course of the sun.

chunks.texto: itaque quod legitur Ponto et Gallia, quod hae regiones sunt proximae ad septentrionem, est atrum. progredientibus inter septentrionem et occidentem invenitur lividum. quod autem legitur ad aequinoctialem orientem et occidentem, invenitur violaceo colore. quod vero meridianis regionibus excipitur, rubra procreatur potestate, et ideo hoc Rhodo etiam insula creatur ceterisque eiusmodi regionibus quae proximae sunt solis cursui.
chunks.traduccion: Therefore, what is read as Pontus and Gaul, because these regions are closest to the north, is black. As we proceed between the north and the west, it is found to be livid. But what is read as east and west of the equinoctial line is found to be of a violet color. But what is taken up in the southern regions is produced by red power, and therefore this island of Rhodes is also created and other such regions which are closest to the course of the sun.

chunks.texto: ea conchylia cum sunt lecta, ferramentis circa scinduntur, e quibus plagis purpurea sanies uti lacrima profluens excussa in mortariis terendo comparatur, et quod ex concharum marinarum testis eximitur, ideo ostrum est vocitatum. id autem propter salsuginem cito fit siticulosum, nisi mel habeat circa fusum.
chunks.traduccion: When these shells are picked, they are split open with tools, from which wounds a purple sap, like a tear, is obtained by grinding them in mortars, and the testicle taken from the seashells is therefore called oyster. But because of its saltiness it quickly becomes dry, unless it has honey mixed in it.

chunks.texto: Fiunt etiam purpurei colores infecta creta rubiae radice et hysgino, non minus et ex floribus alii colores. itaque tectores cum volunt sil atticum imitari, violam aridam coicientes in vas cum aqua, confervefaciunt ad ignem, deinde cum est temperatum coiciunt in linteum, et inde manibus exprimentes recipiunt in mortarium aquam ex violis coloratam, et eo cretam infundentes et eam terentes efficiunt silis attici colorem.
chunks.traduccion: Purple colors are made by infusing chalk with ruby root and hyssop, and no less other colors are made from flowers. Therefore, when painters wish to imitate Attic sil, they put dry violets in a vessel with water, heat them over the fire, then when it is lukewarm they pour them onto a cloth, and from there, squeezing them with their hands, they take the water colored from the violets into a mortar, and pouring chalk into it and grinding it, they produce the color of Attic sil.

chunks.texto: eadem ratione vaccinium temperantes et lacte miscentes purpuram faciunt elegantem. item qui non possunt chrysocolla propter caritatem uti, herba quae luteum appellatur caeruleum inficiunt, et <> utuntur viridissimum colorem. haec autem infectiva appellatur. item propter inopiam coloris indici cretam selinusiam aut anulariam vitro, quod Graeci ἰσάτιν appellant, inficientes, imitationem faciunt indici coloris.
chunks.traduccion: In the same way, those who temper cranberries and mix them with milk make an elegant purple. Likewise, those who cannot use chrysocolla because of charity, infuse the herb called yellow with blue, and <thus> use a very green color. This is called infective. Likewise, because of the lack of the color of the indicator, infusing selinous or annular chalk with glass, which the Greeks call ἴσατιν, they make an imitation of the color of the indicator.

chunks.texto: Quibus rationibus et rebus ad dispositionem firmitates <> quibusque decoras oporteat fieri picturas, item quas habeant omnes colores in se potestates, ut mihi succurrere potuit in hoc libro perscripsi. itaque omnes aedificationum perfectiones quam habere debeant opportunitatem ratiocinationis, septem voluminibus sunt finitae, insequenti autem de aqua, si quibus locis non fuerit, quemadmodum inveniatur et qua ratione ducatur quibusque rebus si erit salubris et idonea probetur explicabo.
chunks.traduccion: By what means and things the firmness of refinements is reached, and by what means beautiful pictures should be made, and likewise what powers all colors have in themselves, as could be of assistance to me, I have written down in this book. Therefore all the perfections of buildings, which they should have the opportunity of reasoning, are finished in seven volumes, but in the following I will explain about water, if in what places it is not, how it is found and by what means it is drawn, and for what purposes it will be proved wholesome and suitable.

chunks.texto: De septem sapientibus Thales Milesius omnium rerum principium aquam est professus, Heraclitus ignem, Magorum sacerdotes aquam et ignem, Euripides, auditor Anaxagorae, quem philosophum Athenienses scaenicum appellaverunt, aera et terram, eamque e caelestium imbrium conceptionibus inseminatam fetus gentium et omnium animalium in mundo procreavisse, et quae ex ea essent prognata, cum dissolverentur temporum necessitate coacta in eandem redire, quaeque de aere nascerentur, item in caeli regiones reverti neque interitiones recipere et dissolutione mutata in eam recidere, in qua ante fuerant, proprietatem. Pythagoras vero, Empedocles, Epicharmos aliique physici et philosophi haec principia esse quattuor proposuerunt: aerem, ignem, terram, aquam, eorumque inter se cohaerentiam naturali figuratione e generum discriminibus efficere qualitates.
chunks.traduccion: Among the Seven Sages, Thales of Miletus held that water was the first principle of all things; Heraclitus favored fire, and the priests of the Magi both water and fire. Euripides, a pupil of Anaxagoras whom the Athenians called “the philosopher of the stage”, proposed air and earth: the latter, fertilised by rain from the heavens, brought forth human beings and other living creatures. What arose from earth would return to it when dissolved by time, while what arose from air would return to the regions of the sky, not perishing but reverting through dissolution to its former nature. Pythagoras, Empedocles, Epicharmus and other natural philosophers proposed four principles — air, fire, earth and water — whose natural combination produces different qualities.

chunks.texto: Animadvertimus vero non solum nascentia ex his esse procreata, sed etiam res omnes non ali sine eorum potestate neque crescere nec tueri. Namque corpora sine spiritus redundantia non possunt habere vitam, nisi aer influens cum incremento fecerit auctus et remissiones continenter. Caloris vero si non fuerit in corpore iusta comparatio, non erit spiritus animalis neque erectio firma, cibique vires non poterunt habere coctionis temperaturam. Item si non terrestri cibo membra corporis alantur, deficient et ita a terreni principii mixtione erunt deserta.
chunks.traduccion: We observe that the elements not only produce living things: without their power nothing can be nourished, grow or be sustained. Bodies cannot live without a sufficient supply of breath, as incoming air maintains the continual expansion and contraction of breathing. Unless the body has the proper measure of heat, it lacks vitality and strength, and food cannot be digested at the necessary temperature. Unless its members are nourished by food from the earth, they fail, deprived of the contribution of the earthly element.

chunks.texto: Animalia vero si fuerint sine umoris potestate, exsanguinata et exsucata [a principiorum liquore] interarescent. Igitur divina mens, quae proprie necessaria essent gentibus, non constituit difficilia et cara, uti sunt margaritae, aurum, argentum ceteraque, quae neque corpus nec natura desiderat, sed sine quibus mortalium vita non potest esse tuta, effudit ad manum parata per omnem mundum. Itaque ex his, si quid forte defit in corpore spiritus, ad restituendum aer adsignatus id praestat. Apparatus autem ad auxilia caloris solis impetus et ignis inventus tutiorem efficit vitam.
