Pythagorae vero praecepta, Democriti, Platonis, Aristotelis ceterorumque sapientium cotidiana perpetuis industriis culta non solum suis civibus, sed etiam omnibus gentibus recentes et floridos edunt fructus. E quibus qui a teneris aetatibus doctrinarum abundantia satiantur, optimos habent sapientiae sensus, instituunt civitatibus humanitatis mores, aequa iura, leges, quibus absentibus nulla potest esse civitas incolumis.
chunks.traduccion: For what does Milo of Croton, who was undefeated, do to men or to others who were victors of that kind, except that, while they lived, they enjoyed nobility among their citizens? But the precepts of Pythagoras, the daily cultivation of Democritus, Plato, Aristotle, and other wise men by the constant industry, bear fresh and flourishing fruits not only to their own citizens, but also to all nations. From which those who are satisfied from an early age with the abundance of learning, have the best of wise sense, and establish in their cities the morals of humanity, just rights, and laws, without which no city can be safe.

chunks.texto: Cum ergo tanta munera ab scriptorum prudentia privatim publiceque fuerint hominibus praeparata, non solum arbitror palmas et coronas his tribui oportere, sed etiam decerni triumphos et inter deorum sedes eos dedicandos iudicari.
chunks.traduccion: Therefore, since such great gifts have been prepared for men by the prudence of writers, both privately and publicly, I think that not only should palms and crowns be awarded to them, but also that triumphs should be decreed and that they should be judged by being dedicated among the seats of the gods.

chunks.texto: Et primum Platonis e multis ratiocinationibus utilissimis unam, quemadmodum ab eo explicata sit, ponam. Locus aut ager paribus lateribus si erit quadratus eumque oportuerit duplicare, quod opus fuerit genere numeri, quod multiplicationibus non invenitur, eo descriptionibus linearum emendatius reperitur. Est autem eius rei haec demonstratio. Quadratus locus, qui erit longus et latus pedes denos, efficit areae pedes C. Si ergo opus fuerit eum duplicare, id est pedum CC, item e paribus lateribus facere, quaerendum erit, quam magnum latus eius quadrati fiat, ut ex eo CC pedes duplicationibus areae respondeant. Id autem numero nemo potest invenire. Namque si XIIII constituentur, erunt multiplicati pedes CXCVI, si XV, pedes CCXXV.
chunks.traduccion: First I shall set out one of Plato’s many valuable demonstrations, as he himself expounded it. If a place or field is square, with equal sides, and it must be doubled, this cannot be achieved by any number through multiplication, but is obtained instead by the correct drawing of lines. And this is a demonstration of this. A square place, which is ten feet long and ten feet wide, makes an area of 100 feet. Therefore, if it is necessary to double it, to make it 200 feet, and also with equal sides, it will be necessary to find how large the side of its square is made, so that from it 200 feet correspond to the doublings of the area. But no one can find this numerically. For if 14 are formed, the multiplied feet will be 196, if 15, 225 feet.

chunks.texto: Ergo quoniam id non explicatur numero, in eo quadrato, longo et lato pedes X quod fuerit, linea ab angulo ad angulum diagonios perducatur, uti dividantur duo trigona aequa magnitudine, singula areae pedum quinquagenûm, ad eiusque lineae diagonalis longitudinem locus quadratus paribus lateribus describatur. Ita quam magna duo trigona in minore quadrato quinquagenûm pedum linea diagonio fuerint designata, eadem magnitudine et eodem pedum numero quattuor in maiore erunt effecta. Hac ratione duplicatio grammicis rationibus ab Platone, uti schema subscriptum est in ima pagina, explicata est.
chunks.traduccion: Since the result cannot be expressed as a whole-number measure, draw a diagonal from corner to corner of the square ten feet long and ten feet wide. This divides it into two equal triangles, each of fifty square feet. Construct a square with equal sides on the length of that diagonal. The smaller square contains two triangles of fifty square feet; the larger contains four of the same size and area. Plato thus explained the doubling by geometrical construction, as shown in the diagram drawn at the foot of the page.

chunks.texto: Item Pythagoras normam sine artificis fabricationibus inventam ostendit, et quod magno labore fabri normam facientes vix ad verum perducere possunt, id rationibus et methodis emendatum ex eius praeceptis explicatur. Namque si sumantur regulae tres, e quibus una sit pedes III, altera pedes IIII, tertia pedes V, eaeque regulae inter se compositae tangant alia aliam suis cacuminibus extremis schema habentes trigoni, deformabunt normam emendatam. Ad eas autem regularum singularum longitudines si singula quadrata paribus lateribus describantur, quod erit trium latus, areae habebit pedes VIIII, quod IIII, XVI quod V erit, XXV.
chunks.traduccion: Pythagoras also showed how to construct a right angle without relying on a craftsman’s square. His principles provide by reason and method the accuracy that craftsmen can scarcely achieve even with great labor. Take three rules, three, four and five feet long, and join their ends to form a triangle: they will define an accurate right angle. If a square is drawn on each rule, the square on the three-foot side has an area of nine square feet, that on the four-foot side sixteen, and that on the five-foot side twenty-five.

chunks.texto: Ita quantum areae pedum numerum duo quadrata ex tribus pedibus longitudinis laterum et quattuor efficiunt, aeque tantum numerum reddit id unum ex quinque descriptum. Id Pythagoras cum invenisset, non dubitans a Musis se in ea inventione monitum, maximas gratias agens hostias dicitur his immolavisse. Ea autem ratio, quemadmodum in multis rebus et mensuris est utilis, etiam in aedificiis scalarum aedificationibus, uti temperatas habeant graduum librationes, est expedita.
chunks.traduccion: The combined area of the squares on the three-foot and four-foot sides therefore equals the area of the square on the five-foot side. When Pythagoras discovered this, he believed that the Muses had guided him and is said to have offered sacrifices to them in gratitude. The same principle is useful in many calculations and measurements, and also in setting out staircases so that their steps have a convenient inclination.

chunks.texto: Si enim altitudo contignationis ab summa coaxatione ad imum libramentum divisa fuerit in partes tres, erit earum quinque in scalis scaporum iusta longitudine inclinatio. ⟨quare⟩ Quam magnae fuerint inter contignationem et imum libramentum altitudinis partes tres, quattuor a perpendiculo recedant et ibi conlocentur inferiores calces scaporum. Ita si erunt temperatae; ⟨libratae⟩ et graduum ipsarum scalarum erunt conlocationes. Item eius rei erit subscripta forma.
chunks.traduccion: For if the height of the floor from the highest point to the lowest platform is divided into three parts, five of them will be the right length of inclination in the ladders of the rungs. However great the three parts of the height between the floor and the lowest platform, four will recede from the perpendicular and there the lower steps of the rungs will be placed. Thus they will be moderate; and the placements of the steps themselves will be. Likewise the form of this matter will be as follows.

chunks.texto: Archimedis vero cum multa miranda inventa et varia fuerint, ex omnibus etiam infinita sollertia id, quod exponam, videtur esse expressum. nimirum Hiero enim Syracusis auctus regia potestate, rebus bene gestis cum auream coronam votivam diis inmortalibus in quodam fano constituisset ponendam, manupretio locavit faciendam et aurum ad sacomam adpendit redemptori. Is ad tempus opus manu factum subtiliter regi adprobavit et ad sacomam pondus coronae visus est praestitisse.
chunks.traduccion: Among Archimedes’s many remarkable inventions, the one I shall now describe seems to show extraordinary ingenuity. When Hiero had acquired royal power at Syracuse and his affairs had prospered, he decided to dedicate a golden crown to the immortal gods in a temple. He contracted for its manufacture and weighed out the gold to the craftsman on a balance. The completed work was presented to the king at the appointed time, delicately finished, and the crown appeared to match the weight of gold supplied.

chunks.texto: Posteaquam indicium est factum dempto auro tantundem argenti in id coronarium opus admixtum esse, indignatus Hiero se contemptum esse neque inveniens, qua ratione id furtum reprehenderet, rogavit Archimeden, uti in se sumeret sibi de eo cogitationem. Tunc is, cum haberet eius rei curam, casu venit in balineum, ibique cum in solium descenderet, animadvertit, quantum corporis sui in eo insideret, tantum aquae extra solium effluere. idque cum eius rei rationem explicationis ostendisset, non est moratus, sed exsiluit gaudio motus de solio et nudus vadens domum ⟨uni⟩versis significabat clara voce invenisse, quod quaereret; nam currens identidem graece clamabat: εὕρηκα, εὕρηκα.
chunks.traduccion: Later it was reported that some gold had been removed and an equal weight of silver mixed into the crown. Indignant at the deception, but unable to find a way of exposing the theft, Hiero asked Archimedes to investigate. While considering the problem, Archimedes happened to enter a bath. As he lowered himself into the tub, he noticed that the water flowing over its edge corresponded to the volume of his body submerged in it. Realizing that this suggested a way to solve the problem, he immediately leapt from the tub in delight and went home naked, proclaiming aloud that he had found what he sought. As he ran he repeatedly cried in Greek, εὕρηκα, εὕρηκα, “I have found it, I have found it”.

chunks.texto: Tum vero ex eo inventionis ingressu duas fecisse dicitur massas aequo pondere, quo etiam fuerat corona, unam ex auro et alteram ex argento. Cum ita fecisset, vas amplum ad summa labra implevit aquae, in quo demisit argenteam massam. Cuius quanta magnitudo in vasum depressa est, tantum aquae effluxit. Ita exempta massa quanto minus factum fuerat, refudit sextario mensus, ut eodem modo, quo prius fuerat, ad labra aequaretur. Ita ex eo invenit, quantum pondus argenti ad certam aquae mensuram responderet.
chunks.traduccion: Following this discovery, he is said to have made two masses equal in weight to the crown, one of gold and the other of silver. He filled a large vessel to its brim with water and lowered the silver mass into it. The water that overflowed corresponded to the volume of the immersed mass. After removing it, he measured in sextarii the water needed to restore the former level at the brim. In this way he established how a given weight of silver corresponded to a particular volume of water.

chunks.texto: Cum id expertus esset, tum auream massam similiter pleno vaso demisit et ea exempta, eadem ratione mensura addita invenit ex aquae numero sextantum: minore quanto minus magno corpore eodem pondere auri massa esset quam argenti. Postea vero repleto vaso in eadem aqua ipsa corona demissa invenit plus aquae defluxisse in corona quam in aurea eodem pondere massa, et ita ex eo, quod fuerat plus aquae in corona quam in massa, ratiocinatus reprehendit argenti in auro mixtionem et manifestum furtum redemptoris.
chunks.traduccion: He then lowered the gold mass into the full vessel and, after removing it, measured in the same way how much water was needed to refill it. The quantity was smaller: at equal weight, gold occupied less volume than silver. Finally he refilled the vessel and immersed the crown itself. More water overflowed than when the equal weight of gold had been immersed. From this greater displacement he demonstrated the mixture of silver with the gold and exposed the craftsman’s theft.

chunks.texto: Transferatur mens ad Archytae Tarentini et Eratosthenis Cyrenaei cogitata; hi enim multa et grata a mathematicis rebus hominibus invenerunt. Itaque cum in ceteris inventionibus fuerint grati, in eius rei cogitationibus maxime sunt suspecti. Alius enim alia ratione explicaverunt, quod Delo imperaverat responsis Apollo, uti arae eius, quantum haberent pedum quadratorum, id duplicarentur, et ita fore uti, qui essent in ea insula, tunc religione liberarentur.
chunks.traduccion: Let us turn to the discoveries of Archytas of Tarentum and Eratosthenes of Cyrene, who made many contributions in mathematics of benefit to humanity. Their other inventions earned them gratitude, but they are held in particular esteem for their treatment of the following problem. Each explained in a different way how to carry out Apollo’s command, given by an oracle at Delos, that his altars should be doubled in size, and how the people of the island might thus be released from their religious obligation.

chunks.texto: Itaque Archytas cylindrorum descriptionibus, Eratosthenes organica mesolabi ratione idem explicaverunt. Cum haec sint tam magnis doctrinarum iucunditatibus animadversa et cogamur naturaliter inventionibus singularum rerum considerantes effectus moveri, multas res attendens admiror etiam Democriti de rerum natura volumina et eius commentarium, quod inscribitur Χειροκμήτων; †in quo etiam utebatur anulo signaretur amolcie est expertus†.
chunks.traduccion: Archytas explained the problem by constructions involving cylinders, and Eratosthenes by the mechanical method of the mesolabe. Such achievements reveal the great pleasures of learning, and reflection on the effects of individual discoveries naturally moves us to admiration. Among many other works, I also admire Democritus’s writings on nature and his treatise entitled Χειροκμήτων. [The following clause, which refers to the use of a ring, is corrupt in the adopted Latin text and cannot be translated securely.]

chunks.texto: Ergo eorum virorum cogitata non solum ad mores corrigendos, sed etiam ad omnium utilitatem perpetuo sunt praeparata, athletarum autem nobilitates brevi spatio cum suis corporibus senescunt; [itaque neque cum maxime sunt] florentes neque posteritati hi, quemadmodum sapientium cogitata hominum vitae, prodesse possunt.
chunks.traduccion: The discoveries of these men are therefore directed not only towards improving conduct but also towards the lasting benefit of everyone. The renown of athletes, by contrast, ages quickly with their bodies. [Thus, even when at the height of their powers,] they cannot benefit posterity as the discoveries of the wise benefit human life.

chunks.texto: Cum vero neque moribus neque institutis scriptorum praestantibus tribuantur honores, ipsae autem per se mentes aeris altiora prospicientes memoriarum gradibus ad caelum elatae aevo inmortali non modo sententias sed etiam figuras eorum posteris cogunt esse notas. Itaque, qui litterarum iucunditatibus instinctas habent mentes, non possunt non in suis pectoribus dedicatum habere, sicuti deorum, sic Ennii poetae simulacrum; Accii autem carminibus qui studiose delectantur, non modo verborum virtutes sed etiam figuram eius videntur secum habere praesentem esse.
chunks.traduccion: But since honors are not bestowed on the excellent character or institution of writers, but their minds themselves, looking higher than the air, and raised to the heavens by the steps of their memories, compel posterity to know not only their opinions but also their figures. Therefore, those whose minds are innately inclined to the delights of literature cannot help but have in their hearts, as in the case of the gods, the image of the poet Ennis; while those who delight in the study of Accius' poems seem to have present with them not only the virtues of words but also his figure.

chunks.texto: Item plures post nostram memoriam nascentes cum Lucretio videbuntur velut coram de rerum natura disputare, de arte vero rhetorica cum Cicerone, multi posterorum cum Varrone conferent sermonem de lingua latina, non minus etiam plures philologi cum Graecorum sapientibus multa deliberantes secretos cum his videbuntur habere sermones, et ad summam sapientium scriptorum sententiae corporibus absentibus vetustate florentes cum insunt inter consilia et disputationes, maiores habent, quam praesentium sunt, auctoritates omnes.
chunks.traduccion: Likewise, many who were born after our memory will be seen to be discussing with Lucretius, as if in person, about the nature of things, and with Cicero, about the art of rhetoric; many of posterity will converse with Varro about the Latin language; no less will many philologists be seen to be deliberating much with the wise Greeks, having secret conversations with them; and, to sum up, the opinions of wise writers, absent from their bodies, flourishing in antiquity, when they are present in the midst of counsels and discussions, have all greater authority than those of the present.

chunks.texto: Itaque, Caesar, his auctoribus fretus sensibus eorum adhibitis et consiliis ea volumina conscripsi, et prioribus septem de aedificiis, octavo de aquis, in hoc de gnomonicis rationibus, quemadmodum de radiis solis in mundo sunt per umbras gnomonis inventae quibusque rationibus dilatentur aut contrahantur, explicabo.
chunks.traduccion: Relying on these authors, Caesar, and drawing on their ideas and counsel, I have written these books. In the first seven I treated buildings, in the eighth water, and in this one I shall explain gnomonics: how the Sun’s rays are traced through the shadows of gnomons, and by what principles those shadows lengthen or shorten.

chunks.texto: Ea autem sunt divina mente comparata habentque admirationem magnam considerantibus, quod umbra gnomonis aequinoctialis alia magnitudine est Athenis, alia Alexandriae, alia Romae, non eadem Placentiae ceterisque orbis terrarum locis. Itaque longe aliter distant descriptiones horologiorum locorum mutationibus. Umbrarum enim aequinoctialium magnitudinibus designantur analemmatorum formae, e quibus perficiuntur ad rationem locorum et umbrae gnomonum horarum descriptiones. ἀνάλημμα est ratio conquisita solis cursu et umbrae crescentis ad brumam observatione inventa, e qua per rationes architectonicas circinique descriptiones est inventus effectus in mundo.
chunks.traduccion: These things are ordained by the divine mind and excite great wonder in those who consider that the shadow of the equinoctial gnomon is of one size in Athens, another in Alexandria, another in Rome, not the same in Placentia and other parts of the world. Therefore, they differ greatly from the descriptions of the clocks of places. For the sizes of the equinoctial shadows are designated by the forms of the analemmas, from which the descriptions of the places and the shadows of the gnomons of the hours are completed according to the ratio. ἀνάλημμα is a ratio acquired by observing the course of the sun and the shadow growing towards winter, from which the effect in the world is found by architectonic ratios and descriptions of the compass.

chunks.texto: Mundus autem est omnium naturae rerum conceptio summa caelumque sideribus et stellarum cursibus conformatum. Id volvitur continenter circum terram atque mare per axis cardines extremos. Namque in his locis naturalis potestas ita architectata est conlocavitque cardines tamquam centra, unum a terra inmani ⟨spatio⟩ in summo mundo ac post ipsas stellas septentrionum, alterum trans contra sub terra in meridianis partibus, ibique circum eos cardines orbiculos circum centra uti in torno perfecit, qui graece πόλοι nominantur, per quos pervolitat sempiterno caelum. Ita media terra cum mari centri loco naturaliter est conlocata.
chunks.traduccion: Now the world is the conception of all things in nature, the highest heaven and the stars formed. It revolves continuously around the earth and the sea by the extreme pivots of the axis. For in these places the natural power has been architected and placed pivots as centers, one from the earth in the highest world and behind the very stars of the north, the other on the other side under the earth in the southern parts, and there around those pivots it has completed small orbs around the centers as in a wheel, which in Greek are called poles, through which the eternal heaven flies. Thus the earth is naturally placed in the middle with the sea as the center.

chunks.texto: His natura dispositis ita, uti septentrionali parte a terra excelsius habeat altitudinem centrum, in meridiana autem parte in inferioribus locis subiectum a terra obscuretur, tunc etiam per medium transversa et inclinata in meridiem [circuli de] lata zona XII signis est conformata. Eorum species stellis dispositis XII partibus peraequatis exprimit depictam ab natura figurationem. Itaque lucentia cum mundo reliquisque sideribus ornatu circum terram mareque pervolantia cursus perficiunt ad caeli rotunditatem.
chunks.traduccion: These are so arranged by nature that on the northern side the center has a height higher than the earth, on the southern side it is obscured by the earth in lower places, then also through the middle a zone transverse and inclined to the south of the circle is brought in twelve signs and shaped. Which appearance of them expresses the figure depicted by nature with the stars arranged in twelve equal parts. Therefore, shining with the world and the other stars, flying around the earth and sea in their adornment, they complete their courses to the roundness of the sky.

chunks.texto: Omnia autem visitata et invisitata temporum necessitate sunt constituta. Ex quis sex signa numero supra terram cum caelo pervagantur, cetera sub terram subeuntia ab eius umbra obscurantur. Sex autem ex his semper supra terram nituntur. Quanta pars enim novissimi signi depressione coacta versatione subiens sub terram occultatur, tantundem eius contraria e conversationis necessitate suppressa rotatione circumacta trans locis patentibus ex obscuris egreditur ad lucem; namque vis una et necessitas utrimque simul orientem et occidentem perficit.
chunks.traduccion: But all things visited and unvisited are established by the necessity of time. Of which six signs in number wander above the earth with the sky, the rest are obscured by its shadow, coming under the earth. But six of these are always founded above the earth. For as much of the last sign is hidden under the earth by depression, forced by its turning, so much of its opposite, by the necessity of its conversation, suppressed by rotation, goes out from the dark places to the light; for one force and necessity perfects both east and west at the same time.

chunks.texto: Ea autem signa cum sint numero XII partesque duodecumas singula possideant mundi versenturque ab oriente ad occidentem continenter, tunc per ea signa contrario cursu luna, stella Mercurii, Veneris, ipse sol itemque Martis et Iovis et Saturni ut per graduum ascensionem percurrentes alius alia circumitionis magnitudine ab occidente ad orientem in mundo pervagantur. Luna die octavo et vicesimo et amplius circiter hora caeli circumitionem percurrens, ex quo signo coeperit ire, ad id signum revertendo perficit lunarem mensem.
chunks.traduccion: Now since the signs are twelve in number and each occupies a twelfth part of the world and moves continuously from east to west, then through those signs the moon, the stars Mercury, Venus, the sun itself, as well as Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, travel in the opposite direction, as if by ascending degrees, each with a different magnitude of circuit from west to east, and they wander through the world. On the twenty-eighth day and more, the moon, having completed a circuit of the heavens for about an hour, from which it began to go, returns to that sign and completes the lunar month.

chunks.texto: Sol autem signi spatium, quod est duodecuma pars mundi, mense vertente vadens transit; ita XII mensibus XII signorum intervalla pervagando cum redit ad id signum, unde coeperit, perficit spatium vertentis anni. Ex eo, quem circulum luna terdecies in XII mensibus percurrit, eum sol eisdem mensibus semel permetitur. Mercurii autem et Veneris stellae circa solis radios uti per centrum eum itineribus coronantes regressus retrorsus et retardationes faciunt, etiam stationibus propter eam circinationem morantur in spatiis signorum.
chunks.traduccion: Now the sun passes through the space of a sign, which is the twelfth part of the world, as it moves through the space of a month; thus, in twelve months, by wandering through the intervals of twelve signs, when it returns to the sign from which it began, it completes the space of a year. Of that which the moon traverses thirteen times in twelve months, the sun is permitted to pass through that circle once in the same months. But the stars of Mercury and Venus, as they circle the rays of the sun through the center, make a backward and retarded return, and even at stations, because of that circumambulation, they remain in the spaces of the signs.

chunks.texto: Id autem ita esse maxime cognoscitur ex Veneris stella, quod ea, cum solem sequatur, post occasum eius apparens in caelo clarissimeque lucens vesperugo vocitatur, aliis autem temporibus eum antecurrens et oriens ante lucem lucifer appellatur. Ex eoque nonnumquam plures dies in ⟨uno⟩ signo commorantur, alias celerius ingrediuntur in alterum signum. Itaque quod non aeque peragunt numerum dierum in singulis signis, quantum sunt moratae prius, transiliendo celerioribus itineribus perficiunt [iustum cursum. Ita efficitur], uti, quod demorentur in nonnullis signis, nihilominus, cum eripiant se ab necessitate morae, celeriter consequantur iustam circumitionem.
chunks.traduccion: This is especially evident from the star Venus, which, when it follows the sun, appears in the sky after its setting and shines most brightly, and is called the evening star, but at other times, when it precedes it and rises before dawn, it is called the morning star. From this it sometimes remains in a sign for several days, at other times it enters another sign more quickly. Therefore, since they do not complete the same number of days in each sign as they have previously spent, they complete [the correct course] by skipping over it in more rapid courses. This is done so that, although they remain in some signs, nevertheless, when they escape the necessity of delay, they quickly complete their correct circuit.

chunks.texto: Iter autem in mundo Mercurii stella ita pervolitat, uti trecentesimo et sexagensimo die per signorum spatia currens perveniat ad id signum, ex quo priore circumlatione coepit facere cursum, et ita peraequatur eius iter ut circiter tricenos dies in singulis signis habeat numeri rationem.
chunks.traduccion: The journey of the star Mercury in the world is such that on the three hundred and sixty-sixth day, running through the spaces of the signs, it reaches the sign from which it began its course in the previous circulation, and its journey is so equalized that it has about thirty days in each sign.

chunks.texto: Veneris autem, cum est liberata ab inpeditione radiorum solis, XXX diebus percurrit signi spatium. quod minus quadragenos dies in singulis signis patitur, cum stationem fecerit, restituit eam summam numeri in uno signo morata. Ergo totam circinationem in caelo quadringentesimo et octogensimo et quinto die permensa iterum init signum, ex quo signo prius iter facere coepit.
chunks.traduccion: When Venus is free from the obstruction of the Sun’s rays, she passes through a sign in thirty days. Whatever falls short of forty days in each sign is made up when she remains stationary in one of them. Having thus completed the whole circuit of the heavens on the four hundred and eighty-fifth day, she returns to the sign from which her previous course began.

chunks.texto: Martis vero circiter sexcentesimo octogensimo tertio siderum spatia pervagando pervenit eo, ex quo initium faciendo cursum fecerat ante, et in quibus signis celerius percurrit, cum stationem fecit, explet dierum numeri rationem. Iovis autem placidioribus gradibus scandens contra mundi versationem, circiter CCCLX diebus singula signa permetitur, et consistit post annum XI et dies CCCXIII et redit in id signum, in quo ante XII annos fuerat. Saturni vero, mensibus undetriginta et amplius paucis diebus pervadens per signi spatium, anno nono et vicensimo et circiter diebus CLX, in quo ante tricensimo fuerat anno, in id restituitur, ex eoque, quo minus ab extremo distat mundo, tanto maiorem circinationem rotae percurrendo tardior videtur esse.
chunks.traduccion: Mars travels through the zodiac and returns to the point from which its previous course began in about 683 days; where it passes through a sign more rapidly, its stationary period makes up the required number of days. Jupiter advances more slowly against the rotation of the heavens, taking about 360 days to pass through each sign. After eleven years and 313 days it returns to the sign it occupied nearly twelve years earlier. Saturn takes twenty-nine months and a few additional days to cross a sign, returning in twenty-nine years and about 160 days to the sign it occupied nearly thirty years before. Being nearer the outermost part of the universe, it travels a larger circuit and therefore appears slower.

chunks.texto: Ei autem, qui supra solis iter circinationes peragunt, maxime cum in trigono fuerint, quod is inierit, tum non progrediuntur, sed regressus facientes morantur doneque cum idem sol de eo trigono in aliud signum transitionem fecerit. Id autem nonnullis sic fieri placet, quod aiunt solem, cum longius absit abstantia quadam, non lucidis itineribus errantia per ea sidera obscuritatis morationibus inpedire. Nobis vero id non videtur. Solis enim splendor perspicibilis et patens sine ullis obscurationibus est per omnem mundum, ut etiam nobis appareant, cum faciant eae stellae regressus et morationes. Ergo si tantis intervallis nostra species potest id animadvertere, quid ita divinitatibus splendoribusque astrorum iudicamus obscuritates obici posse?
chunks.traduccion: But those who make their rounds above the sun's path, especially when they are in a trine that it has entered, then they do not advance, but make returns and remain, and finally when the same sun has made a transition from that trine to another sign. But some people like to do this in this way, which they say that the sun, when it is farther away by a certain absence, does not hinder the stars wandering through it on their bright paths with delays of darkness. But to us this does not seem to be the case. For the brightness of the sun is perceptible and open without any obscurations throughout the whole world, so that it also appears to us when those stars make returns and stays. Therefore, if our species can observe this at such intervals, why do we judge that the divinations and splendors of the stars can be so much objected to as obscurity?

chunks.texto: Ergo potius ea ratio nobis constabit, quod, fervor quemadmodum omnes res evocat et ad se ducit, ut etiam fructus e terra surgentes in altitudinem per calorem videmus, non minus aquae vapores a fontibus ad nubes per arcus excitari, eadem ratione solis impetus vehemens radiis trigoni forma porrectis insequentes stellas ad se perducit et ante currentes veluti refrenando retinendoque non patitur progredi, sed ad se regredi, in alterius trigoni signum esse.
chunks.traduccion: Therefore, we will rather understand this reason, that just as heat evokes and draws all things to itself, as we also see fruits rising from the earth to a height through heat, and no less water vapors are raised from springs to the clouds by arcs, so by the same reason the vehement force of the sun, with its rays extended in the form of a triangle, draws the following stars to itself, and as if restraining and holding them back, it does not allow them to advance, but to return to itself, being in the sign of another triangle.

chunks.texto: Fortasse desiderabitur, quid ita sol quinto a se signo potius quam secundo aut tertio, quae sunt propiora, facit in his fervoribus retentiones. Ergo, quemadmodum id fieri videatur, exponam. Eius radii in mundo uti trigoni paribus lateribus formae lineationibus extenduntur. Id autem nec plus nec minus est ad quintum ab eo signo. Igitur si radii per omnem mundum fusi circinationibus vagarentur neque extentionibus porrecti ad trigoni formam linearentur, propiora flagrarent. Id autem etiam Euripides, Graecorum poeta, animadvertisse videtur. Ait enim, quae longius a sole essent, haec vehementius ardere, propiora vero eum temperata habere. Itaque scribit in fabula Phaethonte sic: καίει τὰ πόρρω, τἄγγυθεν δ’ εὔκρατ’ ἔχει.
chunks.traduccion: Perhaps it will be wondered why the sun, in the fifth sign from itself rather than the second or third, which are nearer, causes retentions in these fervors. Therefore, I will explain how this seems to be done. Its rays in the world are extended in the form of a triangle with equal sides, by lines. But this is neither more nor less than the fifth sign from that sign. Therefore, if the rays were to wander through the whole world in circles, nor were they to be extended in the form of a triangle, by lines, the nearer things would burn. And Euripides, the Greek poet, seems to have noticed this also. For he says that those things which were farther from the sun burn more vehemently, but those which were nearer he keeps in moderation. Therefore he writes in the fable of Phaethon thus: καῖε τὰ πόρρω, τἀγγύθεν δ' εὔκρατ' ἔχει.

chunks.texto: Si ergo res et ratio et testimonium poetae veteris id ostendit, non puto aliter oportere iudicari, nisi quemadmodum de ea re supra scriptum habemus.
chunks.traduccion: Therefore, if the fact and reason and the testimony of the ancient poet show this, I do not think it should be judged otherwise than in the way we have written about that matter above.

chunks.texto: Quemadmodum, si in rota, qua figuli utuntur, inpositae fuerint septem formicae canalesque totidem in rota facti sint circum centrum imo adcrescentes ad extremum, in quibus hae cogantur circinationem facere, verseturque rota in alteram partem, necesse erit eas contra rotae versationem nihilominus adversus itinera perficere, et quae proximum centrum habuerit, celerius pervagari, quaeque extremum orbem rotae peragat, etiamsi aeque celeriter ambulet, propter magnitudinem circinationis multo tardius perficere cursum: similiter astra nitentia contra mundi cursum suis itineribus perficiunt circumitum, sed caeli versatione redundationibus referuntur cotidiana temporis circumlatione.
chunks.traduccion: Just as if seven ants were placed on a wheel used by potters, and as many channels were made in the wheel around the center at the bottom, increasing towards the end, in which these are forced to make a circuit, and the wheel is turned in the other direction, it will be necessary for them to complete their journeys no less in opposition to the rotation of the wheel, and the one that has the nearest center will travel more quickly, and the one that completes the outer circle of the wheel, even if it walks equally quickly, will complete its course much more slowly because of the magnitude of the circuit: in the same way the shining stars complete their circuit in their journeys against the course of the world, but the rotation of the heavens is referred to by the daily circulation of time.

chunks.texto: Esse autem alias stellas temperatas, alias ferventes, etiamque frigidas haec esse causa videtur, quod omnis ignis in superiora loca habet scandentem flammam. Ergo sol aethera, qui est supra se, radiis exurens efficit candentem, in quibus locis habet cursum Martis stella; itaque fervens ab ardore solis efficitur. Saturni autem, quod est proxima extremo mundo tangit ⟨que⟩ congelatas caeli regiones; vehementer est frigida. Ex eo Iovis, cum inter utriusque circumitiones habeat cursum, a refrigeratione caloreque earum medio convenientes temperatissimosque habere videtur effectus.
chunks.traduccion: But the reason why there are other stars that are temperate, others that are boiling, and also that are cold seems to be that all fire has a flame that rises to higher places. Therefore the sun, burning the aether, which is above it, with its rays, has made it red-hot, in which places the star Mars has its course; therefore it is made hot by the heat of the sun. But Saturn, which is nearest to the outermost world, touches the frozen regions of the sky; it is extremely cold. Hence Jupiter, since it has its course between the orbits of both, seems to have effects that are appropriate and most temperate from the cooling and heat of them.

chunks.texto: Berosus, qui ab Chaldaeorum civitate sive natione progressus in Asia etiam disciplinam Chaldaicam patefecit, ita est professus:
chunks.traduccion: Pilam esse ex dimidia parte candentem, reliqua habere caeruleo colore. Cum autem cursum itineris sui peragens subierit sub orbem solis, tunc eam radiis et impetu caloris corripi convertique candentem propter eius proprietatem luminis ad lumen. Cum autem ea vocata ab solis orbi superiora spectent, tunc inferiorem partem eius, quod candens non sit, propter aeris similitudinem obscuram videri. Cum ad perpendiculum ea sit ad eius radios, totum lumen ad superiorem speciem retineri, et tunc eam vocari primam.

chunks.texto: Cum praeteriens vadat ad orientis caeli partes, relaxari ab impetu solis extremamque eius partem candentiae oppido quam tenui linea ad terram mittere splendorem, et ita ex eo eam secundam vocari. cotidiana autem versationis remissione tertiam, quartam in dies numerari. Septimo die, ⟨cum⟩ sol sit ad occidentem, [luna autem inter orientem et occidentem] medias caeli teneat regiones, quod dimidia parte caeli spatio distet a sole, item dimidiam candentiae conversam habere ad terram. Inter solem vero et lunam cum distet totum mundi spatium et lunae orienti sol trans contra sit ad occidentem, eam, quo longius absit, a radiis remissam XIIII die plena rota totius orbis mittere splendorem, reliquosque dies decrescentia cotidiana ad perfectionem lunaris mensis versationibus et cursu a sole revocationibus subire sub rotam radiosque eius et ita menstruas dierum efficere rationes.
chunks.traduccion: When passing by it goes to the eastern parts of the sky, it is relaxed from the force of the sun and the outer part of its brightness is as thin as a line to the earth, and so from that it is called the second. The daily rotation is reduced to the third, the fourth to the days. On the seventh day, the sun is to the west, [the moon between east and west] it occupies the middle regions of the sky, because it is distant from the sun by half the space of the sky, and also has half of its brightness turned towards the earth. But between the sun and the moon, since the whole space of the world is distant and the sun is on the other side of the moon to the west, it, the farther it burns, is relaxed from the rays and on the fourteenth day it sends out a full wheel of the whole world, and on the remaining days it decreases daily and the perfection of the lunar month by rotations and reversions from the sun, it undergoes under the wheel and its rays and now makes the monthly days.

chunks.texto: Uti autem Aristarchus Samius mathematicus vigore magno rationes varietatis disciplinis de eadem ⟨re⟩ reliquit, exponam. Non enim latet lunam ⟨non⟩ suum propriumque habere lumen, sed esse uti speculum et ab solis impetu recipere splendorem. Namque luna de septem astris circulum proximum terrae in cursibus minimum pervagatur. Ita quot mensibus sub rotam solis radiosque uno die, antequam praeterit, latens obscuratur. Cum est cum sole, nova vocatur. Postero autem die, quo numeratur secunda, praeteriens ab sole visitationem facit tenuem extremae rotundationis. Cum triduum recessit ab sole, crescit et plus inluminatur. Cotidie vero discedens cum pervenit ad diem septimum, distans a sole occidente circiter medias caeli regiones, dimidia lucet, et eius quae ad solem pars spectat, ea est inluminata.
chunks.traduccion: But as Aristarchus the Samian mathematician has vigorously left reasons for the variety of disciplines concerning the same, I will explain. For it is not hidden that the moon does not have its own light, but is like a mirror and receives its brightness from the sun's impact. For the moon travels the nearest circle of the earth in the shortest of the seven stars. Thus, as many months pass under the wheel and rays of the sun, on one day, before it passes, it is hidden and darkened. When it is with the sun, it is called a new day. But on the next day, which is counted as the second, passing by the sun, it makes a thin visitation of extreme roundness. When it has been away from the sun for three days, it grows and becomes more illuminated. But descending daily, when it reaches the seventh day, distant from the sun in the west about half the regions of the sky, half the light, and that part of it which looks towards the sun is illuminated.

chunks.texto: Quarto autem decumo die, cum in diametro spatio totius mundi absit ab sole, perficitur plena et oritur, cum sol sit ad occidentem, ideo quod totum spatium mundi distans consistit contra et impetu solis totius orbis in se recipit splendorem. Septumo decumo die cum sol oriatur, ea pressa est ad occidentem. Vicensimo et altero die cum sol est exortus, luna tenet circiter caeli medias regiones, et id quod spectat ad solem, id habet lucidum reliquis obscura. Item cotidie cursum faciendo circiter octavo et vicensimo die subit sub radios solis, et ita menstruas perficit rationes.
chunks.traduccion: But on the fourteenth day, when it is far from the sun in the diameter of the whole world, it is completed full and rises, since the sun is to the west, for this reason that the whole distant space of the world stands against it and receives the brightness of the whole world by the force of the sun. On the seventeenth day, when the sun rises, it is pressed to the west. On the twenty-second day, when the sun has risen, the moon occupies approximately the middle regions of the sky, and that which looks towards the sun has light, the rest is dark. Likewise, making its daily course, on about the twenty-eighth day it comes under the rays of the sun, and thus completes the monthly calculations.

chunks.texto: Namque cum arietis signum iniit et partem octavam pervagatur, perficit aequinoctium vernum. Cum progreditur ad caudam tauri sidusque vergiliarum, e quibus eminet dimidia pars prior tauri, in maius spatium mundi quam dimidium procurrit procedens ad septentrionalem partem. E tauro cum ingreditur in geminos exorientibus vergiliis, magis crescit supra terram et auget spatia dierum. Deinde <e> geminis cum iniit ad cancrum, qui brevissimum tenet caeli spatium, cum pervenit in partem octavam, perficit solstitiale tempus, et peragens pervenit ad caput et pectus leonis, quod eae partes cancro sunt attributae.
chunks.traduccion: For when it enters the sign of Aries and travels through an eighth part, it completes the vernal equinox. When it advances to the tail of Taurus and the constellation of Vergil, from which the first half of Taurus stands out, it extends over a greater space of the world than half, proceeding towards the northern part. When it enters from Taurus into the rising Gemini, Vergil, it grows more above the earth and increases the lengths of the days. Then, when it enters from Gemini to Cancer, which occupies the shortest space of the sky, when it reaches an eighth part, it completes the solstitial time, and in doing so it reaches the head and breast of the lion, because those parts are attributed to Cancer.

chunks.texto: E pectore autem leonis et finibus cancri solis exitus percurrens reliquas partes leonis inminuit diei magnitudinem et circinationis reditque in geminorum aequalem cursum. Tunc vero a leone transiens in virginem progrediensque ad sinum vestis eius contrahit circinationem et aequat ad eam, quam taurus habet, cursus rationem. E virgine autem progrediens per sinum, qui sinus librae partes habet primas, in librae parte VIII perficit aequinoctium autumnale; qui cursus aequat eam circinationem, quae fuerat in arietis signo.
chunks.traduccion: But the sun's exit from the lion's chest and the ends of Cancer, passing through the remaining parts of the lion, diminishes the magnitude of the day and the circumference and returns to the equal course of the twins. Then, passing from the lion into the virgin and advancing to the bosom, its garment contracts the circumference and equalizes the ratio of the course to that which the bull has. But proceeding from the virgin through the bosom, which bosom has the first parts of Libra, in the eighth part of Libra it completes the autumnal equinox; which course equalizes the circumference which had been in the sign of Aries.

chunks.texto: Scorpionem autem cum sol ingressus fuerit occidentibus vergiliis, minuit progrediens meridianas partes longitudines dierum. E scorpione cum percurrendo init in sagittarium ad <femina> eius, contractiorem diurnum pervolat cursum. Cum autem incipit a <feminibus> sagittarii, quae pars est attributa capricorno, ad partem octavam, brevissimum caeli percurrit spatium. Ex eo a brevitate diurna bruma ac dies brumales appellantur. E capricorno autem transiens in aquarium adauget et aequat sagittarii longitudine diei spatium. Ab aquario cum ingressus est in pisces favonio flante, scorpionis comparat aequalem cursum. Ita sol ea signa circum pervagando certis temporibus auget aut minuit dierum et horarum spatia.
chunks.traduccion: But when the sun enters Scorpio with the setting of the Vergils, it shortens the length of the days as it progresses towards the meridian parts. When it travels from Scorpio to Sagittarius, it flies through a shorter daily course. But when it begins at the thighs of Sagittarius, which is the part assigned to Capricorn, it travels through an eighth part of the sky, covering the shortest distance. From this, from the shortness of the day, the winter days are called Brumac. But when it passes from Capricorn into Aquarius, it increases and equals the length of the day in Sagittarius. When it enters Pisces from Aquarius with the blowing of the Favonius, it equals the course of Scorpio. Thus, as the sun travels around those signs, it increases or decreases the distances of days and hours at certain times.

chunks.texto: Namque septentrio, quem Graeci nominant ἄρκτον sive ἑλίκην, habet post se conlocatum custodem. ab eo Non longe conformata est virgo, cuius supra umerum dextrum lucidissima stella nititur, quam nostri provindemiatorem, Graeci προτρυγητήν vocant; candens autem magis spica eius est colorata. Item alia contra est stella media genuorum custodis arcti: qui arcturus dicitur est ibi dedicatus.
chunks.traduccion: For the north, which the Greeks call ἄρκτον or ἑλίκην, has a guardian placed behind it. Not far away is a virgin, over whose right shoulder shines a very bright star, which ours call the providential, the Greeks call προτρυγητήν; but its spike is colored more brightly. Likewise, on the other side is another star between the knees of the guardian of the arc: he who is called Arcturus is there delicate.

chunks.texto: E regione capitis septentrionis transversus ad pedes geminorum auriga stat in summo cornu tauri -- ita quae in summo cornu laevo est, aurigae pedis una tenet partem stella -- et adplicantur aurigae manui haedi, capra laevo umero. Tauri quidem et arietis insuper Perseus -- dexterioribus subter currentis basem vergiliis, at sinisterioribus caput arietis -- et manu dextra innitens Cassiepiae simulacro, laeva supra tauri tenet gorgoneum ad summum caput, subiciens Andromedae pedibus.
chunks.traduccion: Opposite the head of the Bear, and extending across toward the feet of the Twins, stands the Charioteer at the tip of the Bull’s horn: a single star marks both the tip of the Bull’s left horn and part of the Charioteer’s foot. The Kids lie by his hand, and the Goat is on his left shoulder. Above the Bull and the Ram is Perseus, with the Pleiades beneath his right side and the Ram’s head beneath his left. His right hand rests against the figure of Cassiopeia; with his left he holds the Gorgon’s head above the top of the Bull’s head, placing it beneath Andromeda’s feet.

chunks.texto: Item pisces supra Andromedam, ex aequis ventris ex aequisque sunt supra spinam equi, cuius ventris lucidissima stella finit ventrem equi et caput Andromedae. Manus Andromedae dextra supra Cassiepiae simulacrum est constituta, laeva ⟨supra⟩ aquilonalem piscem. Item aquarii supra equi caput est. Equi ungulae attingunt aquarii ⟨e regione volucrem. inter Cepheum et Andromedae⟩ genua; Cassiepia media est dedicata. Capricorni supra in altitudinem aquila et delphinus. Secundum eos est sagitta. Ab ea autem ⟨non longe⟩ volucris, cuius pinna dextra Cephei manum attingit et sceptrum, laeva supra Cassiepiae innititur. Sub avis cauda pedes equi sunt subiecti.
chunks.traduccion: Likewise, the fish are above Andromeda, and her belly and horse are above the spine of the equine, whose belly the brightest star ends the belly of the horse and the head of Andromeda. The right hand of Andromeda is placed above the image of Cassiopeia, the left a northern fish. Likewise, the aquarius is above the horse's head. The horse's hooves touch the knees of the aquarius; Cassiopeia is dedicated in the middle. Above Capricorn in height is an eagle and a dolphin. Next to them is an arrow. From the eautem birds, whose right wing touches the hand of Cepheus and rests on the scepter, the left one rests above Cassiopeia. Under the bird's tail the horse's feet are covered.

chunks.texto: Inde sagittarii, scorpionis, librae insuper serpens summo rostro coronam tangit. eum medium ophiuchos in manibus tenet serpentem, laevo pede calcans mediam frontem scorpionis. A parte ophiuchi capitis non longe positum est caput eius, qui dicitur nisus in genibus. eorum Autem faciliores sunt capitum vertices ad cognoscendum, quod non obscuris stellis sunt conformati.
chunks.traduccion: Then the serpent touches the crown of Sagittarius, Scorpio, and Libra with the top of its beak. In the middle of it, Ophiuchus holds a serpent in his hands, stepping on the middle forehead of the Scorpion with his left foot. Not far from the head of Ophiuchus is his head, which is said to be bent on its knees. But the tops of their heads are easier to recognize, because they are not shaped like dark stars.

chunks.texto: Pes ingeniculati adit fulcitve capitis tempus serpentis, cuius per vipereos flexus minor arctorum, qui septentriones dicuntur, inplicatur. delphinum; contra volucris rostro est proposita lyra. Inter umeros custodis et geniculati corona est ordinata. In septentrionali vero circulo duae positae sunt arctoe scapularum ⟨e regione⟩ dorsis inter se compositae et pectoribus aversae. E quibus minor κυνόσουρα, maior ἑλίκη a Graecis appellatur. Earumque capita inter se dispicientia sunt constituta, caudae capitibus earum adversae contra dispositae figurantur; utrarumque enim superando eminent.
chunks.traduccion: The kneeling man's foot is supported by the head of a serpent, whose arcs, which are called the north, are entwined. A dolphin is bent slightly by them; a lyre is placed with its beak against the birds. A crown is arranged between the shoulders of the guard and the kneeling man. In the northern circle, however, two arcs are placed, the backs of the shoulder blades being placed together and the breasts facing away. Of these, the smaller is called κυνόσουρα, the larger ἑλίκη by the Greeks. Their heads are placed opposite each other, and their tails are depicted as arranged opposite their heads; for they both stand out by overcoming each other.

chunks.texto: In summo per caudas earum esse dicitur. Item serpens est porrecta, e qua stella quae dicitur polus elucet contra caput maioris septentrionis; namque qua est proxume draconem, circum ⟨polum⟩ caput eius involvitur. ima vero circum cynosurae caput iniecta est flexu porrectaque proxime eius pedes. Haec autem intorta replicataque se attollens reflectitur a capite minoris ad maiorem, circa rostrum et capitis tempus dextrum. Item supra caudam minoris pedes sunt Cephei, ibique ad summum cacumen facientes stellae sunt trigonum paribus lateribus, insuper arietis signum. Septentrionis autem minoris et Cassiepiae simulacri complures sunt stellae confusae.
chunks.traduccion: At the top it is said to be by their tails. Likewise, a serpent is stretched out, from which a star called the pole shines around the head of the greater North; for that which is nearest the dragon is wrapped around its head. But one is thrown around the head of the Cynosura by a stream and stretched out near its feet. But this, twisted and folded with the head of the lesser to the greater, around the beak and the right side of the head. Likewise, above the tail of the lesser are the feet of Cepheus, and there at the highest peak are stars forming a triangle with equal sides, and above it the sign of Aries. But the images of the lesser North and Cassiopeia are several confused stars.

chunks.texto: Primum sub capricorno subiectus piscis austrinus caudam prospiciens ceti. Ab eo ad sagittarium locus est inanis. Turibulum sub scorpionis aculeo. Centauri priores partes proximae sunt librae et scorpioni. Tenet in manibus simulacrum, id quod bestiam astrorum periti nominaverunt. virginem et leonem et cancrum anguis porrigens agmen stellarum intortus succingit, regione cancri erigens rostrum, ad leonem medioque corpore sustinens craterem ad manumque virginis caudam subiciens in qua inest corvus; quae sunt autem supra scapulas, peraeque sunt lucentia.
chunks.traduccion: First, under Capricorn, a southern fish is placed, looking towards the tail of a whale. From there to Sagittarius, there is an empty space. A censer is placed under the sting of a scorpion. The front parts of the centaur are close to Libra and Scorpio. He holds in his hands an image of what the experts in the stars have called the beast. To the Virgin, the Lion, and the Crab, a serpent stretches out a coiled array of stars, raising its beak in the region of the Crab, to the Lion, and in the middle of the body, he holds a bowl, and to the hand of the Virgin, he places the tail in which are ravens; but those which are above the shoulders are equally luminous.

chunks.texto: Ad anguis inferius ventris, sub caudam subiectus est centaurus. Iuxta cratera et leonem navis est, quae nominatur Argo, cuius prora obscuratur, sed malus et quae sunt circa gubernacula eminentia videntur, ipsaque navicula et puppis per summam caudam cani iungitur. Geminos autem minusculus canis sequitur contra anguis caput. Maior item sequitur minorem. Orion vero transversus est subiectus, pressus ungula tauri, manu laeva ⟨pellem⟩ tenens, clavam altera ad geminos tollens.
chunks.traduccion: At the lower corners of the belly, under the tail, is a centaur. Next to the bowl and the lion is a ship, which is called Argo, the prow of which is obscured, but the mast and what is around the rudders are seen to be prominent, and the ship itself and the stern are joined by the top of the dog's tail. But the smaller dog follows the twins with its head turned. The larger one follows the smaller one. Orion, however, is placed across, pressed by the bull's hoof, holding with his left hand, and lifting the twins with his other hand.

chunks.texto: Apud eius vero basim canis parvo intervallo insequens leporem. Arieti et piscibus cetus est subiectus, a cuius crista ordinate utrisque piscibus disposita est tenuis fusio stellarum, quae graece vocitantur ἁρπεδόναι. Magnoque intervallo introrsus pressus nodus serentium, attingit summam ceti cristam. Esse fuit per speciem stellarum flumen. Profluit initium fontis capiens a laevo pede Orionis. Quae vero ab aquario fundi memoratur aqua, profluit inter piscis austrini caput et caudam ceti.
chunks.traduccion: At its base, however, a dog pursues a hare at a great distance. Aries and Pisces are followed by a whale, from whose crest is arranged in orderly order around both fish a fine fusion of stars, which in Greek are called ἁρπεδόναι. And at a great distance, pressed inward by the serpents, it reaches the top of the whale's crest. It was to be a river in the form of stars. It flows out, taking its beginning from the left foot of Orion. But the water that is mentioned from the lower part of Aquarius flows out between the head of the southern fish and the tail of the whale.

chunks.texto: Quae figurata conformataque sunt siderum in mundo simulacra, natura divinaque mente designata, ut Democrito physico placuit, exposui, sed tantum ea, quorum ortus et occasus possumus animadvertere et oculis contueri. Namque uti septentriones circum axis cardinem versantes non occidunt neque sub terram subeunt, sic circa meridianum cardinem, qui est propter inclinationem mundi subiectus terrae, sidera versabunda latentiaque non habent egressus orientis supra terram. Itaque eorum figurationes propter obstantiam terrae non sunt notae. Huius autem rei index est stella Canopi, quae his regionibus est ignota, renuntiant autem negotiatores, qui ad extremas Aegypti regiones proximasque ultimis finibus terrae terminationes fuerunt.
chunks.traduccion: I have explained the figured and shaped images of the stars in the world, designed by nature and divine mind, as Democritus the physicist pleased, but only those whose rising and setting we can observe and see with our eyes. For just as they revolve around the pivot of the north axis, they do not set or go under the earth, so around the pivot of the south, which is subject to the earth because of the inclination of the world, the stars revolve and lie hidden and have no exits of the east above the earth. Therefore their shapes are not known because of the obstruction of the earth. Now an indicator of this is the star Canopus, which is unknown in these regions, but traders who have been to the extreme regions of Egypt and to the farthest ends of the earth report it.

chunks.texto: De mundi circa terram pervolitantia duodecimque signorum ex septentrionali meridianaque parte siderum dispositione, ut sit perspecta docui. Namque ex ea mundi versatione et contrario solis per signa cursu gnomonumque aequinoctialibus umbris analemmatorum inveniuntur descriptiones.
chunks.traduccion: I have taught about the world's rotation around the earth and the arrangement of the twelve signs from the northern and southern sides of the stars, so that it may be seen. For from that rotation of the world and the opposite course of the sun through the signs, descriptions are found of the gnomons and the equinoctial shadows of analemmats.

chunks.texto: Cetera ex astrologia, quos effectus habeant signa XII, stellae V, sol, luna ad humanae vitae rationem, Chaldaeorum ratiocinationibus est concedendum, quod propria est eorum genethlialogiae ratio, uti possint ante facta et futura ex ratiocinationibus astrorum explicare. Eorum autem inventiones reliquerunt, inque ⟨ea re⟩ sollertia acuminibusque fuerunt magnis, qui ab ipsa natione Chaldaeorum profluxerunt. Primusque Berosus in insula et civitate Coo consedit ibique aperuit disciplinam, post ei studens Antipater iterumque Athenodorus, qui etiam non e nascentia sed ex conceptione genethlialogiae rationes explicatas reliquit.
chunks.traduccion: The remaining questions of astrology — the effects of the twelve signs, the five planets, the Sun and the Moon on human life — must be left to the reasoning of the Chaldaeans. Their particular expertise is genethlialogy, the interpretation of birth horoscopes, by which they explain past and future events from the configurations of the stars. Those who transmitted these discoveries and displayed exceptional ingenuity came from the Chaldaean people themselves. Berosus first settled on the island of Cos and taught the subject there; Antipater subsequently studied it, and Athenodorus in turn left accounts of horoscopes calculated from conception rather than birth.

chunks.texto: De naturalibus autem rebus Thales Milesius, Anaxagoras Clazomenius, Pythagoras Samius, Xenophanes Colophonius, Democritus Abderites rationes, quibus e rebus natura rerum gubernaretur quemadmodum quaeque effectus habeat, excogitatas reliquerunt. Quorum inventa secuti siderum ⟨ad ortus⟩ et occasus tempestatum significatus Eudoxus, Euctemon, Callippus, Meto, Philippus, Hipparchus, Aratus ceterique ex astrologia parapegmatorum disciplinis invenerunt et eas posteris explicatas reliquerunt. Quorum scientiae sunt hominibus suspiciendae, quod tanta cura fuerunt, ut etiam videantur divina mente tempestatium significatus post futuros ante pronuntiare. Quas ob res haec eorum curis studiisque sunt concedenda.
chunks.traduccion: But concerning natural things, Thales of Miles, Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, Pythagoras of Samos, Zenophanes of Colophon, Democritus of Abderite have left behind them the methods by which the nature of things should be governed from things, how and what effects it has. Following their discoveries, Eudoxus, Eudemus, Callippus, Meto, Philip, Hipparchus, Aratus and the rest discovered the signs of the stars and their setting and storms from the disciplines of the Parapegmata, and have left them explained to posterity. Their knowledge is to be admired by men, because they were so careful that they even seem to have pronounced the signs of storms in advance by the divine mind. For which reason these things are to be conceded to their care and studies.

chunks.texto: Nobis autem ab his separandae sunt rationes et explicandae menstruae dierum brevitates itemque dilatationes. Namque sol aequinoctiali tempore ariete libraque versando, quas e gnomone partes habet novem, eas umbrae facit VIII in declinatione caeli, quae est Romae. Itemque Athenis quam magnae sunt gnomonis partes quattuor, umbrae sunt tres, ad VII Rhodo V, ad XI Tarenti IX, ad quinque ⟨Alexandriae⟩ tres, ceterisque omnibus locis aliae alio modo umbrae gnomonum aequinoctiales a natura rerum inveniuntur disparatae.
chunks.traduccion: We must set these matters aside and explain how the days shorten and lengthen from month to month. At the equinox, when the Sun moves through Aries or Libra, a gnomon nine units high casts a shadow eight units long at the latitude of Rome. At Athens the corresponding ratio is four to three; at Rhodes, seven to five; at Tarentum, eleven to nine; and at ⟨Alexandria⟩, five to three. In other places the equinoctial shadows of gnomons likewise differ according to their situation.

chunks.texto: Itaque in quibuscumque locis horologia erunt describenda, eo loci sumenda est aequinoctialis umbra, et si erunt quemadmodum Romae gnomonis partes novem, umbrae octo, linea describatur in planitia et e media πρὸς ὀρθᾶς erigatur [ut sit ad normam] quae dicitur gnomon. Et a linea, quae erit planities, in linea gnomonis circino novem spatia dimetiantur; et quo loco nonae partis signum fuerit, centrum constituatur, ubi erit littera A; et diducto circino ab eo centro ad lineam planitiae, ubi erit littera B, circinatio circuli describatur, quae dicitur meridiana.
chunks.traduccion: Wherever a sundial is to be drawn, therefore, establish the local equinoctial shadow. If, as at Rome, the gnomon measures nine units and the shadow eight, draw a line on a plane surface and erect from its midpoint a perpendicular, called the gnomon. From the line representing the plane, measure nine equal intervals with the compasses along the gnomon. At the ninth mark establish the center, A. With that center and a radius extending to B on the line of the plane, describe the circle called the meridian.

chunks.texto: Deinde ex novem partibus, quae sunt a planitia ad gnomonis centrum, VIII sumantur et signentur in linea, quae est in planitia, ubi erit littera C. Haec autem erit gnomonis aequinoctialis umbra. Et ab eo signo et littera C per centrum, ubi est littera A, linea perducatur, ubi erit solis aequinoctialis radius. Tunc a centro diducto circino ad lineam planitiae aequilatatio signetur, ubi erit littera E sinisteriore parte et D ulteriore in extremis lineae circinationis. Et per centrum perducendum, ut aequa duo hemicyclia sint divisa. Haec autem linea a mathematicis dicitur horizon.
chunks.traduccion: Of the nine units between the plane and the center of the gnomon, take eight and mark them on the line of the plane at C. This represents the gnomon’s equinoctial shadow. Draw a line from C through the center A: this represents the equinoctial ray of the Sun. With the compasses opened from the center to the line of the plane, mark an equal distance on the circumference, with E on the left and D at the opposite end. Draw the line through the center to divide the circle into two equal semicircles. Mathematicians call this line the horizon.

chunks.texto: Deinde circinationis totius sumenda pars est XV; et circini centrum conlocandum in linea circinationis, quo loci secat eam lineam aequinoctialis radius, ubi erit littera F; et signandum dextra sinistra, ubi sunt litterae G H. Deinde ab his ⟨et per centrum⟩ lineae usque ad lineam planitiae perducendae sunt, ubi erunt litterae I K. Ita erit solis radius unus hibernus, alter aestivus. Contra autem ⟨E⟩ littera D erit, qua secat circinationem linea, quae est traiecta per centrum, ubi ⟨est littera A; et contra G⟩ erunt litterae I et M; et contra H litterae erunt K et L; et contra C et F et A erit littera N.
chunks.traduccion: Take one-fifteenth of the whole circumference. Set the compass-point at F, where the equinoctial ray intersects the circumference, and mark G and H to either side. From these points draw lines ⟨through the center⟩ to the line of the plane at I and K. One represents the winter ray of the Sun, the other the summer ray. Opposite ⟨E⟩ lies D, where the line through the center A intersects the circumference. Opposite G are I and M; opposite H are K and L; and opposite C, F and A is N.

chunks.texto: Tunc perducendae sunt διαμέτρω ab G ad L et ab H ⟨ad M⟩. Quae erit superior, partis erit aestivae, inferior hibernae. Eaeque διαμέτρω sunt aeque mediae dividendae, ubi erunt litterae O et P, ibique centra signanda. Et per ea signa et centrum A lineae ad extrema lineae circinationis sunt perducendae, ubi erunt litterae Q et R. Haec erit linea πρὸς ὀρθᾶς radio aequinoctiali. Vocabitur autem haec linea mathematicis rationibus axon. Et ab eisdem centris diducto circino ad extremas diametros describantur hemicyclia, quorum unum erit aestivum, alterum hibernum.
chunks.traduccion: Draw diameters from G to L and from H ⟨to M⟩. The upper one belongs to summer and the lower to winter. Bisect these diameters at O and P, marking those points as centers. Through these points and the center A draw lines to Q and R on the circumference. This line is perpendicular to the equinoctial ray and is called the axon in mathematics. From the same centers, with the compasses opened to the ends of the diameters, describe two semicircles, one for summer and the other for winter.

chunks.texto: Deinde in quibus locis secant lineae paralleloe lineam eam quae dicitur horizon, in dexteriore parte erit littera S, in sinisteriore T. Et ab littera S ducatur linea parallelos axoni ad extremum ⟨dextrum⟩ hemicyclium, ubi erit littera V; et ab T ad sinistrum hemicyclium item parallelos linea ducatur ad litteram X. Haec autem paralleloe lineae vocitantur †locothomus. Et tum circini centrum conlocandum est eo loci, quo secat circinationem aequinoctialis radius, ubi erit littera F; et diducendum ad eum locum, quo secat circinationem aestivus radius, ubi est littera H. E centro aequinoctiali intervallo aestivo circinatio circuli menstrui agatur, qui menaeus dicitur. Ita habebitur analemmatos deformatio.
chunks.traduccion: Where the parallel lines intersect the horizon, mark S on the right and T on the left. From S draw a line parallel to the axon to the outer ⟨right-hand⟩ semicircle at V; from T draw another parallel to the left-hand semicircle at X. These parallel lines are called †locothomus. Place the compass-point at F, where the equinoctial ray intersects the circumference, and open it to H, where the summer ray intersects it. From the equinoctial center, with this summer interval as radius, describe the monthly circle, called the menaeus. The layout of the analemma is then established.

chunks.texto: Cum hoc ita sit descriptum et explicatum, sive per hibernas lineas sive per aestivas sive per aequinoctiales aut etiam per menstruas in subiectionibus rationes horarum erunt ex analemmatos describendae, subiciunturque in eo multae varietates et genera horologiorum et describuntur rationibus his artificiosis. Omnium autem figurarum descriptionumque earum effectus unus, uti dies aequinoctialis brumalisque itemque solstitialis in duodecim partes aequaliter sit divisus. Quas ob res non pigritia deterritus praetermisi, sed ne multa scribendo offendam, a quibusque inventa sunt genera descriptionesque horologiorum, exponam. Neque enim nunc nova genera invenire possum nec aliena pro meis praedicanda videntur. Itaque quae nobis tradita sunt et a quibus sint inventa, dicam.
chunks.traduccion: Once this construction has been drawn and explained, the hour-lines on the dial surfaces can be derived from the analemma by means of the winter, summer, equinoctial or monthly lines. These methods yield many kinds and arrangements of sundials. All their constructions have one purpose: to divide the day at the equinox, the winter solstice or the summer solstice into twelve equal parts. I have omitted further details to avoid burdening the reader with excessive writing, rather than through reluctance to undertake the work. I shall instead identify the inventors of the different kinds and constructions of sundials. I cannot now devise new kinds, and it would be improper to claim the inventions of others as my own. I shall therefore describe what has been handed down to us and name its inventors.

chunks.texto: Hemicyclium excavatum ex quadrato ad enclimaque succisum Berosus Chaldaeus dicitur invenisse; scaphen sive hemisphaerium Aristarchus Samius, idem etiam discum in planitia; arachnen Eudoxus astrologus, nonnulli dicunt Apollonium; plinthium sive lacunar, quod etiam in circo Flaminio est positum, Scopinas Syracusius; πρὸς τὰ ἱστορούμενα, Parmenion, πρὸς πᾶν κλῖμα, Theodosius et Andrias, Patrocles pelecinum, Dionysodorus conum, Apollonius pharetram, aliaque genera et qui supra scripti sunt et alii plures inventa reliquerunt, uti conarachnen, conicum plinthium, antiboreum. Item ex his generibus viatoria pensilia uti fierent, plures scripta reliquerunt. Ex quorum libris, si qui velit, subiectiones invenire poterit, dummodo sciat analemmatos descriptiones.
chunks.traduccion: Berosus the Chaldaean is said to have invented the hemicyclium, hollowed out of a square block and cut to the local inclination; Aristarchus of Samos, the scaphe or hemisphaerium, and also the disc on a plane surface; Eudoxus the astronomer — or, according to some, Apollonius — the arachne; Scopinas of Syracuse, the plinthium or lacunar, of the kind also placed in the Circus Flaminius; Parmenion, the type called πρὸς τὰ ἱστορούμενα; Theodosius and Andrias, the πρὸς πᾶν κλῖμα; Patrocles, the pelecinum; Dionysodorus, the cone; and Apollonius, the pharetra. These and other inventors left further types, including the conarachne, the conical plinthium and the antiboreum. Several also wrote about making portable hanging sundials from these forms. Their books can supply further constructions to anyone who understands the layout of the analemma.

chunks.texto: Item sunt ex aqua conquisitae ab eisdem scriptoribus horologiorum rationes, primumque a Ctesibio Alexandrino, qui et vim spiritus naturalis pneumaticasque res invenit. Sed uti fuerint ea exquisita, dignum studiosis agnoscere. Ctesibius enim fuerat Alexandriae natus patre tonsore. Is ingenio et industria magna praeter reliquos excellens dictus est artificiosis rebus se delectare. Namque cum voluisset in taberna sui patris speculum ita pendere, ut, cum duceretur susumque reduceretur, linea latens pondus deduceret, ita conlocavit machinationem.
chunks.traduccion: Also, the principles of clocks were discovered from water by the same writers, and first by Ctesibius of Alexandria, who also discovered natural spirits and pneumatic things. But how exquisite they were, it is worthy of the learned to acknowledge. For Ctesibius was born in Alexandria, the son of a barber. He excelled others in great talent and industry, and was said to have delighted in artistic things. For when he wished to hang a mirror in his father's shop in such a way that, when it was raised and lowered, a hidden line would deduce the weight, he thus arranged the mechanism.

chunks.texto: Canalem ligneum sub tigno fixit ibique trocleas conlocavit; per canalem lineam in angulum deduxit ibique tubulos struxit; in eos pilam plumbeam per lineam demittendam curavit. Ita pondus cum decurrendo in angustias tubulorum premeret caeli crebritatem vehementi decursu per fauces frequentiam caeli compressione solidatam extrudens in aerem patentem effusione acuti sonitus expresserat claritatem.
chunks.traduccion: He fixed a wooden channel under a beam and placed pulleys there; he led a line through the channel into a corner and built tubes there; he arranged for a lead ball to be dropped into them through the line. Thus, when the weight, running down into the narrow spaces of the tubes, pressed the frequency of the air, by its violent course through the throats, extruding the frequency of the air, solidified by compression, into the open air, the impact of the touch had expressed the clarity of the sound.

chunks.texto: Ergo Ctesibius cum animadvertisset ex tractu caeli et expressionibus spiritus ⟨sonitus⟩ vocesque nasci, his principiis usus hydraulicas machinas primus instituit. Item aquarum expressiones automatopoetasque machinas multaque deliciarum genera, in his etiam horologiorum ex aqua comparationes explicuit. Primumque constituit cavum ex auro perfectum aut ex gemma terebrata; ea enim nec teruntur percussu aquae nec sordes recipiunt, ut obturentur.
chunks.traduccion: Therefore, Ctesibius, having observed that from the movement of the sky and the expressions of the spirit and voices arise, using these principles, was the first to invent hydraulic machines. Likewise, he explained the expressions of water and automata and many kinds of delightful machines, including the comparisons of clocks made of water. And he first made a hollow of perfect gold or of a drilled gem; for these are neither worn away by the impact of water nor do they receive dirt to become clogged.

chunks.texto: Namque aequaliter per id cavum influens aqua sublevat scaphium inversum, quod ab artificibus phellos sive tympanum dicitur. In quo conlocata est regula ⟨iuxta⟩ versatile tympanum. Denticulis aequalibus sunt perfecta, qui denticuli alius alium inpellentes versationes modicas faciunt et motiones. Item aliae regulae aliaque tympana ad eundem modum dentata una motione coacta versando faciunt effectus varietatesque motionum, quibus moventur sigilla, vertuntur metae, calculi aut ova proiciuntur, bucinae canunt, reliquaque parerga.
chunks.traduccion: Water entering evenly through the opening raises an inverted vessel, called a phellos or tympanum by craftsmen. A toothed rack is attached to it beside a revolving drum. The equally spaced teeth engage and produce controlled rotations and movements. Other racks and drums, toothed in the same way and driven by the same motion, produce a variety of effects: small figures move, cones turn, pebbles or eggs are released, trumpets sound and other ornamental devices operate.

chunks.texto: In his etiam aut in columna aut parastatica horae describuntur, quas sigillum egrediens ab imo virgula significat in diem totum. Quarum brevitates aut crescentias cuneorum adiectus aut exemptus in singulis diebus et mensibus perficere cogit. Praeclusiones aquarum ad temperandum ita sunt constitutae. Metae fiunt duae, una solida, una cava, ex torno ita perfectae, ut alia in aliam inire convenireque possit et eadem regula laxatio earum aut coartatio efficiat aut vehementem aut lenem in ea vasa aquae influentem cursum. Ita his rationibus et machinatione ex aqua componuntur horologiorum ad hibernum usum conlocationes.
chunks.traduccion: The hours are marked on the apparatus or on a column or pilaster. A small figure rising from below points to them with a rod throughout the day. Adding or removing wedges adjusts the shortening and lengthening of the hours for each day and month. The water regulators consist of two turned cones, one solid and the other hollow, made so accurately that one fits inside the other. Loosening or tightening them regulates whether the water enters the vessels quickly or slowly. By these arrangements water clocks are constructed for use in winter.

chunks.texto: Sin autem cuneorum adiectionibus et detractionibus correptiones dierum aut crescentiae ex cuneis non probabuntur fieri, quod cunei saepissime vitia faciunt, sic erit explicandum. In columella horae ex analemmatos transverse describantur, menstruaeque lineae columella signentur. Eaque columna versatilis perficiatur, uti ad sigillum virgulamque, qua virgula egrediens sigillum ostendit horas, columna versando continenter suis cuiusque mensibus brevitates et crescentias faciat horarum.
chunks.traduccion: If adding and removing wedges does not satisfactorily adjust the shortening and lengthening of the days — wedges often cause faults — use the following arrangement. Mark the hours transversely on a small column according to the analemma, and indicate the monthly lines on it. Make the column capable of turning, so that, as the figure rises and points to the hours with its rod, rotation of the column adjusts their shortening and lengthening for the appropriate month.

chunks.texto: Fiunt etiam alio genere horologia hiberna, quae anaphorica dicuntur perficiunturque rationibus his. Horae disponuntur ex virgulis aeneis ex analemmatos descriptione ab centro dispositae in fronte; in ea circuli sunt circumdati menstrua spatia finientes. Post has virgulas tympanum, in quo descriptus et depictus est mundus signiferque circulus descriptioque ex XII caelestium signorum fit figurata, cuius ex centro deformatio, unum maius, alterum minus. Posteriori autem parte tympano medio axis versatilis est inclusus inque eo axi aenea mollis catena est involuta, ex qua pendet ex una parte phellos (sive tympanum), qui ab aqua sublevatur, altera aequo pondere phelli sacoma saburrale.
chunks.traduccion: Winter clocks are also made in another way, which are called anaphoric and are completed by these methods. The hours are arranged from bronze rods with an analemma description arranged from the center on the front; in it are circles encircling the monthly periods. Behind these rods is a tympanum, in which the world and the standard circle are described and depicted, and a description is made of twelve celestial signs, the deformation of which from the center, one greater, the other less. But in the rear part of the tympanum, a versatile axis is enclosed in the middle, and on that axis a soft bronze chain is wound, from which hangs on one side a phellos (or tympanum), which is lifted by the water, and on the other a sack of equal weight of the phellos.

chunks.texto: Ita quantum ab aqua phellos sublevatur, tantum saburrae pondus infra deducens versat axem, axis autem tympanum. Cuius tympani versatio alias efficit, uti maior pars circuli signiferi, alias minor in versationibus suis temporibus designet horarum proprietates. Namque in singulis signis sui cuiusque mensis dierum numeri cava sunt perfecta, cuius bulla, quae solis imaginem horologiis tenere videtur, significat horarum spatia.
