Parastaticae dextra ac sinistra praeter cardines altae foraminum IIII, crassae foraminum† quinum; cardines foraminis dimidia. ⟨A⟩ parastatica ad foramen spatium foraminis, a foramine ad medianam parastaticam item foraminis. Latitudo parastados mediae unius foraminis et eius ⟨T⟩K, crassitudo foraminis unius.
chunks.traduccion: The size of these openings determines the height and width of the whole head. The upper and lower boards, called peritretoe, should be one opening thick, one and three-quarter openings wide, and one and a half wide at the ends. The side uprights, excluding their tenons, should be four openings high and […] thick; the tenons should measure half an opening. Leave one opening between the side upright and the torsion opening, and another between the opening and the central upright. The central upright should be one opening and […] wide, and one opening thick.

chunks.texto: Intervallum, ubi sagitta conlocatur in media parastade, foraminis partis quartae. Anguli quattuor, qui sunt circa, in lateribus et frontibus lamnis ferreis aut stylis aereis et clavis configantur. Canaliculi, qui graece σῦριγξ dicitur, longitudo foraminum XVIIII. Regularum, quas nonnulli bucculas appellant, quae dextra ac sinistra canalem figuntur, ⟨longitudo⟩ foraminum XVIIII, altitudo foraminis unius et crassitudo. Et adfiguntur regulae duae, in quas inditur sucula, habentes longitudinem foraminum trium, latitudinem dimidium foraminis. Crassitudo bucculae, quae adfigitur (vocitatur scamillum seu, quemadmodum nonnulli, loculamentum) securiclatis cardinibus fixa, foraminis I, altitudo foraminis S¯. Suculae longitudo foraminum::, crassitudo suculae foraminis VIIII.
chunks.traduccion: The space for the arrow in the central upright should be one-quarter of an opening. Secure the four surrounding corners, on the sides and faces, with iron plates or bronze bolts and nails. The channel, called σῦριγξ in Greek, should be nineteen openings long. The rails, sometimes called bucculae, fixed on either side of it should likewise be nineteen openings long, and one opening high and thick. Two further rails, into which the windlass is fitted, should be three openings long and half an opening wide. The attached buccula, also called a scamillum or loculamentum and secured by dovetail tenons, should be one opening thick and […] high. The windlass should be […] openings long; its thickness is given as nine […] of an opening.

chunks.texto: Epitoxidos longitudo foraminis S¯, crassitudo:¯. Item chelonii. Cheles, sive manucla dicitur, longitudo foraminum trium, latitudo et crassitudo S÷. Canalis fundi longitudo foraminum XVI, crassitudo foraminis, altitudo S÷. Columellae basis in solo foraminum VIII, latitudo in plinthide, in qua statuitur columella, foraminis, crassitudo FZ, columellae longitudo ad cardinem foraminum XII, latitudo foraminis S÷, crassitudo. Eius capreoli tres, quorum longitudo foraminum VIIII, latitudo dimidium foraminis, crassitudo Z. Cardines longitudinis foraminis; columellae capitis longitudo ISK; antefixi latitudo foraminis, crassitudo I.
chunks.traduccion: The epitoxis should be […] of an opening long and […] thick; the same applies to the chelonium. The chele, or manucla, should be three openings long, with a width and thickness of […]. The channel floor should be sixteen openings long, one opening thick and […] high. The upright’s ground base should be eight openings long, one opening wide at the plinthis on which the upright rests, and […] thick. The upright should measure twelve openings up to its tenon, with a width and thickness of […]. Its three braces should be nine openings long, half an opening wide and […] thick. The tenons should be one opening long; the upright’s head […] long; the antefixum one opening wide and […] thick.

chunks.texto: Posterior minor columna, quae graece dicitur ἀντίβασις, foraminum VIII, latitudo foraminis SI, crassitudinis FZ. Subiectio foraminum XII, latitudinis et crassitudinis eiusdem, cuius minor columna illa. Supra minorem columnam chelonium, sive pulvinus dicitur, foraminum IIS, altitudinis IIS, latitudinis SI¯ cherolabae sucularum foraminum II S¯, crassitudo foraminis, latitudo IS. Transversariis cum cardinibus longitudo foraminum, latitudo IS et crassitudo. Bracchii longitudo [IS] foraminum VII, crassitudo ab radice foraminis FZ, in summo foraminis ⟨CC⟩Z; curvaturae foraminis VIII.
chunks.traduccion: The smaller rear upright, called ἀντίβασις in Greek, should be eight openings long, […] wide and […] thick. The support should be twelve openings long, with the same width and thickness as that upright. Above it, the chelonium or pulvinus should measure two and a half openings in length and height, and […] in width. The windlass handles should be two openings and […] long, one opening thick and one and a half wide. The crosspieces, including their tenons, should be […] openings long, one and a half wide and equally thick. Each arm should be seven openings long, […] thick at the root and […] at the tip, with a curvature of eight openings.

chunks.texto: Haec his proportionibus aut adiectionibus aut detractionibus comparantur. Nam si capitula altiora, quam erit latitudo, facta fuerint, quae anatona dicuntur, de bracchiis demetur, ut, quo mollior est tonus propter altitudinem capituli, bracchii brevitas faciat plagam vehementiorem. ⟨Si⟩ minus altum capitulum fuerit, quod catatonum dicitur, propter vehementiam bracchia paulo longiora constituentur, uti facile ducantur. Namque quemadmodum vectis, cum est longitudine pedum quinque, quod onus IIII hominibus extollit, id, qui est X, duobus elevat, eodem modo bracchia, quo longiora sunt, mollius, quo breviora, durius ducuntur.
chunks.traduccion: These dimensions are used with the appropriate additions or reductions. When the heads are higher than they are wide, a form called anatonon, the arms should be shortened: the greater height makes the tension gentler, and shorter arms produce a more forceful discharge. When the head is lower, a form called catatonon, make the arms somewhat longer to ease the stronger tension. A five-foot lever requires four men to lift a load that a ten-foot lever raises with two. In the same way, longer arms are easier to draw back, and shorter ones harder.

chunks.texto: Catapultarum rationes, e quibus membris ex portionibus componantur, dixi. Ballistarum autem rationes variae sunt et differentes unius effectus causa comparatae. Aliae enim vectibus suculis, nonnullae polyspastis, aliae ergatis, quaedam etiam tympanorum torquentur rationibus. Sed tamen nulla ballista perficitur nisi ad propositam magnitudinem ponderis saxi, quod id organum mittere debet. Igitur de ratione earum non est omnibus expeditum, nisi qui geometricis rationibus numeros et multiplicationes habent notas.
chunks.traduccion: I have explained the construction of catapults and the dimensions of their members. Ballistae employ several different systems, although all serve one purpose. Some are drawn back with levers and windlasses, others with pulley systems or capstans, and others with drums. Yet every ballista is designed according to the intended weight of the stone it must discharge. Its calculation is therefore readily understood only by those acquainted with numbers and geometrical multiplication.

chunks.texto: Nam quae fiunt in capitibus foramina, per quorum spatia contenduntur capillo maxime muliebri vel nervo funes, magnitudine ponderis lapidis, quem debet ea ballista mittere, ex ratione gravitatis proportiones sumuntur, quemadmodum catapultis de longitudinibus sagittarum. Itaque ut etiam qui geometricen non noverunt, habeant expeditum, ne in periculo bellico cogitationibus detineantur, quae ipse faciundo certa cognovi quaeque ex parte accepi a praeceptoribus, finita exponam, et quibus ⟨ponde⟩ribus Graecorum pensiones ad modulos habeant rationem, ad eam ut etiam nostris ponderibus respondeant, tradam explicata.
chunks.traduccion: The openings in the heads, through which bundles of hair—especially women’s hair—or sinew are stretched, are proportioned to the weight of the stone the ballista is to discharge, just as catapult dimensions are derived from arrow length. To make the rules accessible to those unfamiliar with geometry, and spare them calculations amid the dangers of war, I shall set out what I have established through practice and what I have received from my teachers. I shall also explain how the Greek weight standards correspond to our own.

chunks.texto: Nam quae ballista duo pondo saxum mittere debet, foramen erit in eius capitulo digitorum V; si pondo IIII, digitorum sex et * * * digitorum VII; decem pondo digitorum VIII; viginti pondo digitorum X; XL pondo digitorum XII SK; LX pondo digitorum XIII et digiti octava parte; LXXX pondo digitorum XV; CXX pondo I pedis et sesquidigiti; C et LX pedis I9; C et LXXX pedis et digitorum V; CC pondo pedis et digitorum VI; CC et X ⟨L pondo⟩ pedis I et digitorum VII; CCCLX * * * pedis I S.
chunks.traduccion: A ballista intended to throw a two-pound stone should have a five-finger opening in its head; for four pounds, six fingers; * * *, seven fingers; for ten pounds, eight fingers; for twenty, ten; for forty, twelve and […]; for sixty, thirteen fingers and one-eighth; for eighty, fifteen fingers; for one hundred and twenty, one foot and one and a half fingers; for one hundred and sixty, one foot and […]; for one hundred and eighty, one foot and five fingers; for two hundred, one foot and six fingers; for two hundred and forty, one foot and seven fingers; and for three hundred and sixty * * *, one and a half feet.

chunks.texto: Cum ergo foraminis magnitudo fuerit instituta, describatur scutula, quae graece περίτρητος appellatur, cuius longitudo foraminum †vel, latitudo duo et sextae partis. Dividatur medium lineae descriptae et, cum divisum erit, contrahantur extremae partes eius formae, ut obliquam deformationem habeat longitudinis sexta parte, latitudinis, ubi est versura, quarta parte. In qua parte autem est curvatura, in quibus procurrunt cacumina angulorum, eo foramina convertantur, et contractura latitudinis redeat introrsus sexta parte, foramen autem oblongius sit tanto, quantam epizygis habet crassitudinem. Cum deformatum fuerit, circum levigatur, extremam ut habeat curvaturam molliter circumactam.
chunks.traduccion: Once the opening’s size has been established, draw the scutula, called περίτρητος in Greek. Its length is †…† openings and its width two and one-sixth. Bisect the drawn line, then contract the extremities of the figure so that it assumes an oblique form, by one-sixth of its length and one-quarter of its width at the angle. Where the curve lies, towards which the points of the angles project, turn the openings accordingly. Let the contraction of the width recede inward by one-sixth, and make the opening longer by the thickness of the epizygis. Smooth the outline so that its end has a gently rounded curve.

chunks.texto: Crassitudo eius foraminis constituatur. Modioli foraminum duo, latitudo IS9, crassitudo praeterquam quod in foramine inditur foraminis, ad extremum autem latitudo foraminis. Parastatarum longitudo foraminis VSF; curvatura foraminis pars dimidia; crassitudo foraminis et partis LX. Adicitur autem ad mediam latitudinem, quantum est prope foramen factum in descriptione, latitudine et crassitudine foraminis V, altitudo parte IIII.
chunks.traduccion: Set its thickness at […] of an opening. The cylinders should be two openings long and […] wide; excluding the portion inserted into the opening, their thickness should be […] of an opening, and their width at the end […]. The uprights should be […] long; their curvature half an opening; their thickness […] and one-sixtieth of an opening. Add to the central width the amount established beside the opening in the drawing: in width and thickness, five […] of an opening, and in height one-quarter.

chunks.texto: Regulae, quae est in mensa, longitudo foraminum VIII; latitudo et crassitudo dimidium foraminis. Cardines, crassitudo foraminis. Curvatura regulae. Exterioris regulae latitudo et crassitudo tantundem; longitudo, quam dederit ipsa versura deformationis et parastaticae latitudo ad suam curvaturam K. Superiores autem regulae aequales erunt inferioribus K. Mensae transversarii foraminisk.
chunks.traduccion: The rail on the table should be eight openings long and half an opening wide and thick. The tenons should be […] of an opening thick. The rail’s curvature is […]. The outer rail has the same width and thickness; its length depends on the turn of the drawing and the upright’s width up to its curvature, […]. The upper rails should equal the lower ones, […]. The table’s crosspieces should measure […] of an opening.

chunks.texto: Climacidos scapi longitudo foraminum XIII, crassitudo IK, intervallûm mediûm latitudo foraminis et parte quarta, crassitudo pars VIII K. Climacidos superioris pars quae est proxima bracchiis, quae coniuncta est mensae, tota longitudine dividatur in partes V. Ex his dentur duae partes ei membro, quod Graeci χῆλην vocant, crassitudo 9, longitudo foraminum III et semis K; extantia cheles foraminis S; †plentigomatos foraminis et sicilicus. Quod autem est ad axona, quod appellatur frons transversarius, foraminum trium.
chunks.traduccion: The ladder-frame’s longitudinal member should be thirteen openings long and […] thick; the central interval should be one and a quarter openings wide, and the thickness one-eighth and […]. Divide the whole length of the upper ladder-frame adjoining the arms and the table into five parts. Assign two of these to the member the Greeks call χηλή. Its thickness is […]; its length three and a half openings and […]; the projection of the chele half an opening; and †the plentigoma† […] of an opening and one sicilicus. The transverse front beside the axle should measure three openings.

chunks.texto: Interiorum regularum latitudo foraminis, crassitudo chelonii replum, quod est operimentum, securiculae includitur K. Scaporum climacidos latitudo, crassitudo foraminis XII K. Crassitudo quadrati, quod est ad climacida, foraminis FC, in extremis K, rotundi autem axis diametros aequaliter erit cheles, ad claviculas autem minus parte sexta decuma K.
chunks.traduccion: The inner rails should be one opening wide and […] thick. The replum, or cover, of the chelonium is fitted by a dovetail joint, […]. The ladder-frame’s longitudinal members have a width and thickness of […] of an opening, […]. The square member beside the ladder-frame should be […] thick, and […] at its ends. The diameter of the round axle should equal that of the chele, but be one-sixteenth smaller beside the pins, […].

chunks.texto: Anteridon longitudo foraminum †eius, latitudo in imo foraminis, in summo crassitudo. Basis, quae appellatur ἐσχάρα, longitudo foraminum::::, antibasis foraminum IIII, utriusque crassitudo et latitudo foraminis. Compingitur autem dimidia altitudinis K. Columna, latitudo et crassitudo IS. Altitudo autem non habet foraminis proportionem, sed erit quod opus erit ad usum. Bracchii longitudo foraminum VI, crassitudo in radice foraminis, in extremis F.
chunks.traduccion: The anterides should be †…† openings long, one opening wide at the bottom and […] thick at the top. The base, called ἐσχάρα, should be […] openings long; the antibasis four openings. Each should be one opening wide and thick. The assembly is joined halfway up, […]. The upright should be one and a half openings wide and thick. Its height is determined by practical need rather than by a fixed proportion to the opening. The arm should be six openings long, one opening thick at its root and […] at its ends.

chunks.texto: Sumuntur tigna amplissima longitudine; supra figuntur chelonia, in quibus includuntur suculae. Per media autem spatia tignorum insecantur ⟨et⟩ exciduntur formae, in quibus excisionibus includuntur capitula catapultarum, cuneisque distinentur, ne in contentionibus moveantur. Tum vero modioli aerei in ea capitula includuntur et in eos cuneoli ferrei, quas ἐπιζυγίδας Graeci vocant, conlocantur.
chunks.traduccion: Take timbers of the greatest possible length and fix chelonia above them to receive the windlasses. Cut and hollow out recesses in the middle of the timbers, fit the catapult heads into them and secure them with wedges so that tension cannot shift them. Insert bronze cylinders into the heads and place in them the iron wedges that the Greeks call ἐπιζυγίδες.

chunks.texto: Deinde ansae rudentum induntur per foramina capitulorum, in alteram partem traiciuntur, deinde in suculas coiciuntur ⟨et⟩ involvuntur, uti vectibus per eas ext<enti> rudentes, cum manibus sunt tacti, aequalem utrique sonitus habeant responsum. Tunc autem cuneis ad foramina concluduntur, ut non possint se remittere. Ita traiecti in alteram partem eadem ratione vectibus per suculas extenduntur, donec aequaliter sonent. Ita cuneorum conclusionibus ad sonitum musicis auditionibus catapultae temperantur.
chunks.traduccion: Pass the loops of the bundles through the openings in the heads to the opposite side, lead them to the windlasses and wind them round. Tighten them with levers until, when struck by hand, they produce corresponding sounds on the two sides. Secure them in the openings with wedges so that they cannot loosen. Draw them through to the other side and tighten them in the same way with the windlasses and levers until they sound alike. Thus, with their wedges locked, catapults are adjusted by sound and musical hearing.

chunks.texto: Primum ad oppugnationes aries sic inventus memoratur esse. Carthaginienses ad Gadis oppugnandas castra posuerunt. Cum autem castellum ante cepissent, id demoliri sunt conati. Posteaquam non habuerunt ad demolitionem ferramenta, sumpserunt tignum idque manibus sustinentes capiteque eius summum murum continenter pulsantes summos lapidum ordines deiciebant, et ita gradatim ex ordine totam communitionem dissipaverunt.
chunks.traduccion: The first battering ram is said to have been devised as follows. The Carthaginians encamped to besiege Gades. After taking a fort, they attempted to demolish it. Lacking demolition tools, they took a timber, held it in their hands and repeatedly struck the top of the wall with its end. They brought down the upper courses and gradually dismantled the entire fortification.

chunks.texto: Postea quidam faber Tyrius nomine Pephrasmenos hac ratione et inventione inductus malo statuto ex eo alterum transversum uti trutinam suspendit et reducendo et inpellendo vementibus plagis deiecit Gaditanorum murum. Geras autem Chalcedonius de materia primum basim subiectis rotis fecit supraque compegit arrectariis et iugis varas et in his suspendit arietem coriisque bubulis texit, uti tutiores essent, qui in ea machinatione ad pulsandum murum essent conlocati. is autem, quod tardos conatus habuerat, testudinem arietariam appellare coepit.
chunks.traduccion: A Tyrian craftsman named Pephrasmenos subsequently developed this discovery. He erected a mast and suspended a transverse timber from it like a balance beam. By drawing it back and driving it forward with powerful blows, he demolished the wall of Gades. Geras of Chalcedon was the first to construct a timber base on wheels, assemble a frame of uprights and crosspieces above it, suspend the ram within and cover it with oxhides to protect the men operating it against the wall. Because the engine moved slowly, he began to call it a ram-bearing tortoise.

chunks.texto: His tunc primis gradibus positis ad id genus machinationis, postea cum Philippus, Amyntae filius, Byzantios oppugnaret, Polyidos Thettalos pluribus generibus et facilioribus explicavit, a quo receperunt doctrinam Diades et Charias, qui cum Alexandro militaverunt.
chunks.traduccion: These first steps having been taken at that time for that kind of scheme, later, when Philip, the son of Amyntas, was attacking the Byzantines, Polydius Thettalus explained it in more and easier ways, from whom Diades and Charias, who fought with Alexander, received their instruction.

chunks.texto: Non minus utebatur ariete subrotato, cuius rationes scriptas reliquit. Turrem autem minimam ait oportere fieri ne minus altam cubitorum LX, latitudinem XVII, contracturam autem summam imae partis quintam, arrectaria turris in imo dodrantalia in summo semipedalia. Fieri autem ait oportere eam turrem tabulatorum decem, singulis partibus in ea fenestratis.
chunks.traduccion: He also used a ram that was rotated, the reasons for which he left written. He said that the smallest tower should be made no less than 60 cubits high, 17 cubits wide, and the height of the lowest part should be one-fifth, with the arrectaria in the tower at the bottom and half-foot arches at the top. He said that the tower should be made of ten stories, with windows in each part of it.

chunks.texto: Maiorem vero turrem altam cubitorum CXX, latam cubitorum XXIII <⟨S⟩>, contracturam item quinta parte, arrectaria pedalia in imo, in summo sedigitalia. Hanc magnitudinem turris faciebat tabulatorum XX, cum haberent singula tabulata circumitionem cubitorum ternûm. Tegebat autem coriis crudis, ut ab omni plaga essent tutae.
chunks.traduccion: But the larger tower was 120 cubits high, 23 and a half cubits wide, and was also contracted by a fifth, with straight steps at the bottom and sedigitated at the top. This size of the tower made it 20 stories, since each story had a circumference of 30 cubits. He covered it with rawhides, so that it would be protected from all harm.

chunks.texto: Testudinis arietariae comparatio eadem ratione perficiebatur. Habuerat autem intervallum cubitorum XXX, altitudinem praeter fastigium XIII S, fastigii autem altitudo ab strato ad summum cubita XVI. Exibat autem in altum et supra medium tectum fastigium non minus cubita duo, et supra extollebatur turricula III tabulatorum inque tabulato summo statuebantur scorpiones et catapultae, inferioribus congerebatur aquae magna multitudo ad extinguendum, si qua vis ignis inmitteretur. constituebatur autem in ea arietaria machina, quae graece dicitur κριοδόκις, in qua conlocabatur torus perfectus in torno, in quo insuper constitutus aries rudentium ductionibus et reductionibus efficiebat magnos operis effectus. Tegebatur autem is coriis crudis quemadmodum turris.
chunks.traduccion: The ram-bearing tortoise was constructed on the same principle. It was thirty cubits wide and thirteen and a half high, excluding the roof; the roof rose sixteen cubits from its platform to the top. Above the middle of the covering it projected upward by at least two cubits, and above that stood a small tower of three stories. Scorpions and catapults occupied the highest story, while the lower ones held ample water to extinguish any fire thrown against it. Within stood the apparatus of the ram, called κριοδόκη in Greek. A turned roller supported the ram, which was driven forward and backward by ropes to strike the masonry with great force. Like the tower, the engine was covered with raw hides.

chunks.texto: De terebra has explicuit scriptis rationes. Ipsam machinam uti testudinem in medio habentem conlocatum in orthostatis canalem, quemadmodum in catapultis aut ballistis fieri solet, longitudine cubitorum L, altitudine cubiti, in quo constituebatur transversa sucula. In capite autem dextra ac sinistra trocleae duae, per quas movebatur quod inerat in eo canali capite ferrato tignum. Sub eo autem in ipso canali inclusi tori crebriter celeriores et vehementiores efficiebant eius motus. supra autem tignum, quod inibi erat, arcus tegebantur ad canalem crebriter, uti sustinerent corium crudum, quo ea machina erat involuta.
chunks.traduccion: He explained these reasons for the drill in writing. The machine itself was to be a shell having a shell in the middle placed in an orthostatic channel, as is usually done in catapults or ballistae, fifty cubits long and one cubit high, in which was placed a transverse spindle. On the right and left of the head were two pulleys, by which the iron-headed beam contained in that channel was moved. Underneath that, a bed enclosed in the channel itself made its movements more rapid and violent. Above the beam, which was in it, arches were frequently placed on the channel, so as to support the raw hide that was wrapped around that machine.

chunks.texto: De corace nihil putavi scribendum, quod animadverterest eam machinam nullam habere virtutem. de accessu, quae ἐπιβάθρα graece dicitur, et de marinis machinationibus, †quae per navium aditus habere posse scripsit, tantum pollicitum esse vehementer animadverti neque rationes eorum eum explicavisse. Quae sunt ab Diade de machinis scripta, quibus sint comparationibus, exposui. nunc quemadmodum a praeceptoribus accepi et utilia mihi videntur, exponam.
chunks.traduccion: I decided not to give an account of the corax, having found the engine ineffective. As for the boarding device, called ἐπιβάθρα in Greek, and the naval machines, †which he claimed could provide access aboard ships, I found that he had promised much without explaining their operating principles. I have described the construction of the machines recorded by Diades. I shall now set out what I have learned from my teachers and consider useful.

chunks.texto: Testudo, quae ad congestionem fossarum paratur (eaque etiam accessus ad murum potest habere), sic erit facienda. Basis compingatur, quae graece ἐσχάρα dicitur, quadrata habens quoqueversus latera singula pedum XXI et transversaria IIII. Haec autem contineantur ab alteris duobus crassis FS, latis S; distent autem transversaria inter se circiter pedes III S. Supponanturque in singulis intervallis eorum arbusculae, quae graece ἁμαξόποδες dicuntur, in quibus versantur rotarum axes conclusi lamnis ferreis. Eaeque arbusculae ita sint temperatae, ut habeant cardines et foramina, quo vectes traiecti versationes earum expediant, uti ante et post et ad dextrum seu sinistrum latus, sive oblique ad angulos opus fuerit, ad id per arbusculas versatis progredi possint.
chunks.traduccion: A tortoise intended for filling ditches, and capable also of reaching the wall, should be built as follows. Assemble a square base, called ἐσχάρα in Greek, twenty-one feet on each side, with four crosspieces. Secure these with two further timbers […] thick and half a foot wide, leaving about three and a half feet between the crosspieces. Beneath each interval fit supports, called ἁμαξόποδες, in which the iron-plated wheel axles turn. Give the supports pivots and openings for levers, so that they can be turned to move the engine forward, backward, right, left or obliquely as required.

chunks.texto: Conlocentur autem insuper basim tigna duo in utramque partem proiecta pedes senos, quorum circa proiecturas figantur altera proiecta duo tigna ante frontes pedes XII, crassa et lata uti in basi sunt scripta. Insuper hanc compactionem erigantur postes compactiles praeter cardines pedum VIIII, crassitudine quoquoversus palmopedales, intervalla habentes inter se sesquipedis. Ea concludantur superne intercardinatis trabibus. Supra trabes conlocentur capreoli cardinibus alius in alium conclusi, in altitudine excitati pedes XII. Supra capreolos conlocetur quadratum tignum, quo capreoli coniungantur.
chunks.traduccion: Above the base place two timbers projecting six feet on either side. Around their projecting ends secure two more, extending twelve feet beyond the fronts, with the thickness and width specified for the base. On this assembly erect jointed uprights nine feet high excluding their tenons, one foot and a palm thick on each side, spaced one and a half feet apart. Close them above with tenoned beams. On these set rafters, joined by tenons, rising twelve feet; a square timber above should tie the rafters together.

chunks.texto: Ipsi autem laterariis circa fixis contineantur teganturque tabulis maxime palmeis, si non, ex cetera materia, quae maxime habere potest virtutem, praeter pinum aut alnum; haec enim sunt fragilia et faciliter recipiunt ignem. Circum tabulata conlocentur crates ex tenuibus virgis creberrime textae maximeque recentibus. Percrudis coriis duplicibus consutis, fartis alga aut paleis in aceto maceratis, circa tegatur machina tota. ita ab his reicientur plagae ballistarum et impetus incendiorum.
chunks.traduccion: Secure them with longitudinal members fixed around the frame, and cover them with planks, preferably of palm, or otherwise of the strongest available timber, excluding pine and alder, which are brittle and readily catch fire. Around the boarding place closely woven hurdles of thin rods, as fresh as possible. Cover the entire engine with very raw hides sewn in two layers and packed with seaweed or straw soaked in vinegar. These will resist the blows of ballistae and attacks by fire.

chunks.texto: Est autem et aliud genus testudinis, quod reliqua omnia habet, quemadmodum quae supra scripta sunt, praeter capreolos, sed habet circa pluteum et pinnas ex tabulis et superne subgrundas proclinatas, supraque tabulis et coriis firmiter fixis continentur. Insuper vero argilla cum capillo subacta ad eam crassitudinem inducatur, ut ignis omnino non possit ei machinae nocere. Possunt autem, si opus fuerit, eae machinae ex VIII rotis esse, si ad loci naturam ita opus fuerit temperare. Quae autem testudines ad fodiendum comparantur ( ὀρυκτίδες graece dicuntur), cetera omnia habent, uti supra scriptum est, frontes vero earum fiunt quemadmodum anguli trigoniorum, uti a muro tela cum in eas mittantur, non planis frontibus excipiant plagas sed ab lateribus labentes, sine periculoque fodientes, qui intus sunt, tueantur.
chunks.traduccion: Another kind of tortoise follows the same arrangement except for the rafters. It has a surrounding parapet and timber battlements, with sloping eaves above, secured with firmly fixed boards and hides. Spread over them clay kneaded with hair, thick enough to prevent fire from harming the engine. If the ground requires it, these engines may have eight wheels. Tortoises used for digging, called ὀρυκτίδες in Greek, otherwise follow the same construction, but have triangular fronts. Projectiles thrown from the wall then glance off their sloping sides instead of striking a flat face, protecting the men digging within.

chunks.texto: Non mihi etiam videtur esse alienum de testudine, quam Hegetor Byzantius fecit, quibus rationibus sit facta, exponere. Fuerat enim eius baseos longitudo pedum LXIII, latitudo XLII. Arrectaria, quae supra compactionem erant quattuor conlocata, ex binis tignis fuerant compacta, in altitudinibus singula pedum XXXVI, crassitudine palmopedali, latitudine sesquipedali. Basis eius habuerat rotas VIII, quibus agebatur. Fuerat autem earum altitudo pedum VI, S÷ crassitudo pedum III, ita fabricata triplici materia: alternis se contra subscudibus inter se coagmentatae lamnisque ferreis ex frigido ductis alligatae.
chunks.traduccion: It is also appropriate to explain the construction of the tortoise built by Hegetor of Byzantium. Its base was sixty-three feet long and forty-two wide. Four uprights above the frame were each assembled from two timbers thirty-six feet high, one foot and a palm thick and one and a half feet wide. Eight wheels carried the base. They were six feet and […] high and three feet thick, built from three layers of timber joined with alternating opposed tenons and bound with cold-worked iron plates.

chunks.texto: Eae in arbusculis, sive amaxopodes dicuntur, habuerant versationes. Ita supra transtrorum planitiem, quae supra basim fuerat, postes erant erecti pedes XVIII, latitudine, S÷ crassitudine, FZ distantes inter se IS÷. Supra eos trabes circumclusae continebant totam compactionem latae pede I, crassae. S÷ Supra eam capreoli extollebantur altitudine pedum XII; supra capreolos tignum conlocatum coniungebat capreolorum compactiones. Item fixa habuerant lateraria in transverso, quibus insuper contabulatio circumdata contegebat inferiora.
chunks.traduccion: The wheels turned in supports called amaxopodes. Above the surface of the crosspieces over the base rose posts eighteen feet high, […] wide and […] thick, spaced […] apart. Surrounding beams one foot wide and […] thick held the assembly together. Rafters rose twelve feet above them, tied at the top by a timber connecting their joints. Transverse longitudinal members were also fixed in place, carrying boarding that enclosed the lower parts.

chunks.texto: Habuerat autem mediam contabulationem supra trabiculas, ubi scorpiones et catapultae conlocabantur. erigebantur Et arrectaria duo compacta pedum XXXXV, crassitudine sesquipedali, latitudine, ΡΙΙ coniuncta capitibus transversario cardinato tigno et altero mediano inter duos scapos cardinato et lamnis ferreis religato. Quo insuper conlocata erat alternis materies inter scapos et transversarium traiecta e cheloniis et anconibus firmiter inclusa. In ea materia fuerunt ex torno facti axiculi duo, e quibus funes alligati retinebant arietem.
chunks.traduccion: An intermediate deck rested on smaller beams and carried scorpions and catapults. Two jointed uprights rose forty-five feet, one and a half feet thick and […] wide. A transverse timber joined their upper ends by tenons, while another joined the two longitudinal members midway and was bound with iron plates. Above it lay a further timber across the longitudinal members and crosspiece, firmly secured with chelonia and angle pieces. Two small turned axles in this timber carried the ropes from which the ram hung.

chunks.texto: Supra caput eorum, qui continebant arietem, conlocatum erat pluteum turriculae similitudine ornatum, uti sine periculo duo milites tuto stantes prospicere possent et renuntiare, quas res adversarii conarentur. Aries autem eius habuerat longitudinem pedum CLXXX, latitudine in imo palmopedali, crassitudine ⟨bi⟩pedali, contracto capite in latitudine †pes, crassitudine S.
chunks.traduccion: Above the heads of the men supporting the ram stood a parapet resembling a small tower, allowing two soldiers to stand safely, observe the enemy and report their intentions. The ram was one hundred and eighty feet long, one foot and a palm wide at the bottom and two feet thick. Its head tapered to a width of †one foot† and a thickness of half a foot.

chunks.texto: Is autem aries habuerat de ferro duro rostrum, ita uti naves longae solent habere, et ex ipso rostro lamminae ferreae IIII circiter pedum XV fixae fuerant in materia.
chunks.traduccion: The ram had a beak of hard iron, such as is fitted to long warships. Four iron plates, each about fifteen feet long, were fastened to its timber from the beak itself.

chunks.texto: Item habuerat proiectura eius ex tabulis arcam compactam et confixam, in qua * * * rudentibus maioribus extentis, per quarum asperitates non labentibus pedibus faciliter ad murum perveniebatur. Atque ea machina sex modis movebatur: progressu, ⟨regressu,⟩ item latere dextra et sinistra, porrectiones non minus in altitudinem extollebantur et in imum inclinatione demittebantur. Erigebatur autem machina in altitudinem ad disiciendum murum circiter pedes C, item a latere dextra ac sinistra procurrendo praestringebat non minus pedes C. Gubernabant eam homines C habentem pondus talentûm quattuor milium, quod fit C̅C̅C̅C̅L̅X̅X̅X̅ pondo.
chunks.traduccion: The projecting structure also carried a box assembled and fixed from planks, in which * * * larger ropes were stretched. Their rough surface gave the feet a secure hold and allowed easy access to the wall. The engine moved in six ways: forwards and ⟨backwards⟩, to the right and left, and by raising or lowering its projecting parts. It could be raised to attack a wall about one hundred feet high and could sweep across a comparable distance to either side. One hundred men operated the machine, which weighed four thousand talents, equivalent in the text to 480,000 Roman pounds.

chunks.texto: De scorpionibus et catapultis et ballistis etiamque testudinibus et turribus, quae maxime mihi videbantur idonea et a quibus essent inventa et quemadmodum fieri deberent, explicui. Scalarum autem et carchesiorum et eorum, quorum rationes sunt inbecilliores, non necesse habui scribere. Haec etiam milites per se solent facere. Neque ea ipsa omnibus locis neque eisdem rationibus possunt utilia esse, quod differentes sunt munitiones munitionibus nationumque fortitudines. Namque alia ratione ad audaces et temerarios, alia ad diligentes, aliter ad timidos machinationes debent comparari.
chunks.traduccion: I have explained the construction of scorpions, catapults, ballistae, tortoises and towers, identifying their inventors and the arrangements I considered most suitable. I have not thought it necessary to describe ladders, carchesia and other simpler devices, since soldiers commonly make these for themselves. The same engines cannot serve every site or follow identical rules: fortifications differ, as does the resolve of their defenders. One kind of engine is needed against the bold and reckless, another against the vigilant, and another against the fearful.

chunks.texto: Itaque his praescriptionibus si qui attendere voluerit ⟨et⟩ ex varietate eorum eligendo in unam comparationem conferre, non indigebit auxiliis, sed quascumque res ex rationibus aut locis opus fuerit, sine dubitatione poterit explicare. De repugnatoriis vero non est scriptis explicandum. Non enim ad nostra scripta hostes comparant res oppugnatorias, sed machinationes eorum ex tempore sollerti consiliorum celeritate sine machinis saepius evertuntur. Quod etiam Rhodiensibus memoratur usu venisse.
chunks.traduccion: Anyone who attends to these prescriptions and combines appropriate elements from their variety into a single construction will need no further assistance, but will be able to solve the requirements of the design and the site without hesitation. Defensive devices, however, cannot be prescribed in writing in the same way. The enemy does not prepare its siege engines according to our books; its machinery is often defeated without machinery, through quick and shrewd decisions taken as circumstances arise. Such an event is recorded at Rhodes.

chunks.texto: Diognetus enim fuerat Rhodius architectus, et ei de publico quotannis certa merces pro artis dignitate tribuebatur ad honorem. Eo tempore quidam architectus ab Arado nomine Callias Rhodum cum venisset, acroasin fecit exemplarque protulit muri et supra id machinam in carchesio versatili constituit, quae helepolim ad moenia accedentem corripuit et transtulit intra murum. Hoc exemplar Rhodii cum vidissent, admirati ademerunt Diogneto, quod fuerat quotannis constitutum, et eum honorem ad Calliam transtulerunt.
chunks.traduccion: Diognetus was the Rhodians’ architect and received a fixed annual payment from public funds in recognition of his professional standing. An architect from Aradus named Callias arrived at Rhodes, gave a lecture and presented a model wall. Above it he installed a machine on a rotating carchesium, which seized a helepolis approaching the fortifications and transferred it inside. Astonished by the demonstration, the Rhodians withdrew Diognetus’s annual allowance and conferred it on Callias.

chunks.texto: Interea rex Demetrius, qui propter animi pertinaciam Poliorcetes est appellatus, contra Rhodum bellum comparando Epimachum Atheniensem nobilem architectum secum adduxit. Is autem comparavit helepolim sumptibus inmanibus industria laboreque summo, cuius altitudo fuerat pedum CXXXV, latitudo pedum LX. Ita eam ciliciis et coriis crudis confirmavit, ut posset pati plagam lapidis ballista inmissi pondo CCCLX; ipsa autem machina fuerat milia pondo CCCLX. Cum autem Callias rogaretur ab Rhodiis, contra eam helepolim machinam pararet, ut illam, uti pollicitus erat, transferret intra murum, negavit posse.
chunks.traduccion: Meanwhile King Demetrius, called Poliorcetes for his persistence, prepared for war against Rhodes and brought with him the distinguished Athenian architect Epimachus. At immense expense and with exceptional skill and labor, Epimachus built a helepolis one hundred and thirty-five feet high and sixty wide. He strengthened it with goat-hair cloth and raw hides so that it could withstand a ballista stone weighing three hundred and sixty pounds. The engine itself weighed three hundred and sixty thousand pounds. When the Rhodians asked Callias to construct the device he had promised to carry this helepolis inside the wall, he admitted that he could not.

chunks.texto: Non enim omnia eisdem rationibus agi possunt, sed sunt alia, quae exemplaribus non magnis similiter magna facta habent effectus; alia autem exemplaria non possunt habere, sed per se constituuntur; nonnulla vero sunt, quae in exemplaribus videntur veri similia, cum autem crescere coeperunt, dilabantur. Ut etiam possumus sic animum advertere. Terebratur terebra foramen semidigitale, digitale, sesquidigitale. Si eadem ratione voluerimus palmare facere, non habet explicationem, semipedale autem ⟨aut⟩ maius ne cogitandum quidem videtur omnino.
chunks.traduccion: Not everything can be achieved by the same methods. Some devices retain their effect when enlarged from small models; others can only be established at full size; and others seem plausible in a model but fail as their scale increases. A drill illustrates the point. It can bore a hole half a finger, one finger or one and a half fingers wide. The same method cannot simply be extended to a hole a palm wide, and one half a foot wide or larger scarcely seems worth considering.

chunks.texto: Sic item in nonnullis exemplaribus videntur, quae admodum in minimis fieri videntur, absque eodem modo in maioribus. ideo eodem modo Rhodii ea de ratione decepti iniuriam cum contumelia Diogneto fecerunt. Itaque posteaquam viderunt hostem pertinaciter infestum,, machinationem ad capiendam urbem comparatam, periculum servitutis, vastitatem civitatis expectandam, procubuerunt Diogneto rogantes, ut auxiliaretur patriae.
chunks.traduccion: In the same way, what appears practicable in a very small model may fail at a larger scale. Misled by such reasoning, the Rhodians had dishonored Diognetus. When they saw the enemy’s determination, the machinery prepared to take their city and the prospect of enslavement and devastation, they prostrated themselves before him and begged him to save his country.

chunks.texto: Is primo negavit se facturum. Posteaquam ingenuae virgines et ephebi cum sacerdotibus venerunt ad deprecandum, tunc est pollicitus his legibus, uti, si eam machinam cepisset, sua esset. his ita constitutis, qua machina accessura erat, ea regione murum pertudit et iussit omnes publice et privatim quod quisque habuisset aquae, stercoris, luti per eam fenestram per canales progredientes effundere ante murum. Cum ibi magna vis aquae, luti, stercoris nocte profusa fuisset, postero die helepolis accedens, antequam adpropinquaret ad murum, in umido voragine facta consedit nec progredi nec egredi postea potuit. Itaque Demetrius, cum vidisset sapientia Diogneti se deceptum esse, cum classe sua discessit.
chunks.traduccion: At first Diognetus refused. When the freeborn maidens and youths came with the priests to plead with him, he agreed on condition that, if he captured the machine, it would belong to him. Once this was settled, he pierced the wall where the engine was expected to approach. He ordered everyone, acting publicly and privately, to pour whatever water, manure and mud they had through the opening and along projecting channels in front of the wall. A great quantity was discharged there during the night. The next day, as the helepolis advanced, it sank into the sodden ground before reaching the wall and could neither move forward nor withdraw. Demetrius, realizing that Diognetus’s ingenuity had defeated him, departed with his fleet.

chunks.texto: Tunc Rhodii Diogneti sollertia liberati bello publice gratias egerunt honoribusque omnibus eum et ornamentis exornaverunt. Diognetus eam helepolim reduxit in urbem et in publico conlocavit et inscripsit 'Diognetus e manubiis id populo dedit munus'. Ita in repugnatoriis rebus non tantum machinae, sed etiam maxime consilia sunt comparanda.
chunks.traduccion: Then the Rhodians, freed from the war by the skill of Diognetus, gave him public thanks and honored him with every distinction and adornment. Diognetus brought that helepolis back into the city, set it up in the public square, and inscribed upon it: “Diognetus gave this gift to the people from the spoils of war.” Thus in matters of defense it is not engines so much as the ingenuity to outwit engines that must be made ready.

chunks.texto: Non minus Chio cum supra naves sambucarum machinas hostes comparavissent, noctu Chii terram, harenam, lapides progesserunt in mare ante murum. Ita illi postero die cum accedere voluissent, naves supra aggerationem, quae fuerat sub aqua, sederunt nec ad murum accedere nec retrorsus se recipere potuerunt, sed ibi malleolis confixae incendio sunt conflagratae. Apollonia quoque cum circumsederetur et specus hostes fodiendo cogitarent sine suspicione intra moenia penetrare, id autem a speculatoribus esset Apolloniatibus renuntiatum, perturbati nuntio propter timorem consiliis indigentes animis deficiebant, quod neque tempus neque certum locum scire poterant, quo emersum facturi fuissent hostes.
chunks.traduccion: At Chios, when the enemy fitted ships with sambucae, the inhabitants cast earth, sand and stones into the sea before the wall during the night. The next day the approaching ships grounded on the submerged bank. Unable either to reach the wall or to withdraw, they were struck by incendiary missiles and destroyed by fire. At Apollonia, the besiegers intended to enter the city secretly through tunnels. When spies reported this to the inhabitants, fear left them at a loss: they could establish neither the time nor the precise place where the enemy would emerge.

chunks.texto: Tum vero Trypho Alexandrinus ibi fuerat architectus; ⟨is⟩ intra murum plures specus designavit et fodiendo terram progrediebatur extra murum dumtaxat extra sagittae missionem et in omnibus vasa aenea suspendit. Ex his in una fossura, quae contra hostium specus fuerat, vasa pendentia ad plagas ferramentorum sonare coeperunt. Ita ex eo intellectum est, qua regione adversarii specus agentes intra penetrare cogitabant, Sic lineatione cognita temperavit aenea aquae ferventis et picis de superne contra capita hostium et stercoris humani et harenae coctae candentis. Dein noctu pertudit crebra foramina et per ea repente perfundendo qui in eo opere fuerunt hostes omnes necavit.
chunks.traduccion: Trypho of Alexandria was then the architect there. He marked out several galleries inside the wall and drove them outward only as far as an arrow could reach, hanging bronze vessels in all of them. In the gallery opposite the enemy’s tunnel, the suspended vessels began to ring with the blows of the digging tools, revealing where the attackers intended to break through. Once he had determined their direction, he prepared cauldrons of boiling water and pitch above them, together with human dung and red-hot sand. During the night he pierced numerous openings and suddenly poured these materials through, killing the men working below.

chunks.texto: Item Massilia cum oppugnaretur et numero supra XXX specus tum agerent, Massilitani suspicati totam quae fuerat ante murum fossam altiore fossura depresserunt. Ita specus omnes exitus in fossam habuerunt. Quibus autem locis fossa non potuerat fieri, intra murum barathrum amplissima longitudine et amplitudine uti piscinam fecerunt contra eum locum, qua specus agebantur, eamque e puteis et e portu impleverunt. Itaque cum specus esset repente naribus apertis, vehemens aquae vis inmissa supplantavit fulturas, quique intra fuerunt, et ab aquae multitudine et ab ruina specus omnes sunt oppressi.
chunks.traduccion: Likewise, when Massilia was besieged and the enemy drove more than thirty tunnels towards it, the inhabitants suspected the attempt and deepened the whole ditch before the wall, so that every tunnel opened into it. Where a ditch could not be dug, they excavated a very long and broad basin inside the wall, opposite the approaching tunnels, and filled it from the wells and harbour. When the tunnel mouths suddenly broke through, the rush of water undermined their supports. Those inside were overwhelmed by the water and the collapsing galleries.

chunks.texto: Etiam cum agger ad murum contra eos compararetur et arboribus excisis eoque conlocatis locus operibus exaggeraretur, ballistis vectes ferreos candentes in id mittendo totam munitionem coegerunt conflagrare. Testudo autem arietaria cum ad murum pulsandum accessisset, permiserunt laqueum et eo ariete constricto, per tympanum ergata circumagentes suspenso capite eius non sunt passi tangi murum. Denique totam machinam malleolis candentibus et ballistarum plagis dissipaverunt. Ita eae victoriae civitatum ⟨civitates⟩ non machinis, sed contra machinarum rationem architectorum sollertia sunt liberatae.
chunks.traduccion: When a siege mound was built against their wall and raised with felled trees and other works, they fired red-hot iron bars into it with ballistae and set the whole structure ablaze. When a ram-bearing tortoise approached the wall, they lowered a noose, caught the ram and used a capstan and drum to suspend its head, preventing it from striking the masonry. Finally they destroyed the entire engine with burning missiles and ballista shots. These cities were thus saved through the ingenuity of architects who defeated the principles of the enemy’s machinery, rather than through machinery alone.
